which are the 0-1 loss, the cross-entropy (CE) loss, the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, the hinge loss, and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss, where OneHot : *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1) → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si72.png) returns a binary vector with a ‘1’ in the class of maximum probability from *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si73.png), and ‘0’ for all other classes, *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si74.png) denotes the indicator function, and *f*[*θ*]^((**y**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si75.png) returns the output from the model *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si73.png) for the class indexed by the one-hot vector (**y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si76.png). The training of the classifier to estimate the optimal parameter *θ* ∈ *Θ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si28.png) using the joint probability of sample *X* and noisy label *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si31.png) is achieved by minimizing the loss function:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si77.png)(2.14) 

which is unfeasible since *p*(*X*, *Ỹ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si4.png) is unknown. This is mitigated by using the training set containing noisy labels $\\mathcal{D} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si33.png), where $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si34.png), to minimize the empirical risk with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si35.png)(2.15) 

We show the results of two multi-class classification experiments, with one relying on the 2-step sampling process described in [(2.10)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq10), and the other based on the 3-step sampling process from [(2.12)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq12) (see [Fig. 2.5](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0030)). In both experiments, the 2-D data is generated by a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) using four components, with each component representing a separate class, where the class means are ( − 2,  − 2)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si79.png), ( − 2, 2)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si80.png), (2,  − 2)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si81.png), (2, 2)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si82.png), covariances are denoted by an identity matrix of size 2 × 2![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si83.png), and mixture weights are equal to 0.25. The two experiments use a model *f*[*θ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si36.png) that consists of a multi-layer perceptron (1 hidden layer with 5 nodes and Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) activation functions, and an output layer with a softmax output), which is trained with ERM in [(2.15)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq15) that minimizes the BCE loss in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq13).

![Figure 2.5 Classification using a 2-stage and a 3-stage sampling processes from (2.10) and (2.12), respectively.The top-left figure shows the underlying GMM distribution of the four classes (each Gaussian model represents by a different class) with means (−2,−2), (−2,2), (2,−2), (2,2), identity covariances, and mixture weights of 0.25. The top-right figure shows the label distribution given data, where higher color saturation denotes larger probability. Using the 2-stage sampling process from (2.10), we draw (from the GMM) the data samples X = \\mu + \\Sigma \\times \\epsilon\_{\\mathcal{X}}Image, which are then labeled with noisy labels sampled from \\widetilde{Y} = T\_{\\mathcal{X}}^{- 1}(u;\\mathbf{x})Image using label distribution given data from the top-right figure. After training the model fθ(x) to minimize the ERM in (2.15) with the BCE loss in (2.13) using the samples in the middle-left figure, the classification predictions are shown in the middle-right figure. Relying on the 3-stage process from (2.12), we again draw data samples labeled with noisy labels, first sampled from Y = T\_{\\mathcal{X}}^{- 1}(u;\\mathbf{x})Image and then sampled from \\widetilde{Y} = T\_{\\mathcal{YX}}^{- 1}(u;\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})Image, both using label distribution given data from the top-right figure. The bottom-right figure shows the outputs of the model trained with the data from the bottom-left figure.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr005.jpg)

Figure 2.5 Classification using a 2-stage and a 3-stage sampling processes from [(2.10)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq10) and [(2.12)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq12), respectively.The top-left figure shows the underlying GMM distribution of the four classes (each Gaussian model represents by a different class) with means (−2,−2), (−2,2), (2,−2), (2,2), identity covariances, and mixture weights of 0.25. The top-right figure shows the label distribution given data, where higher color saturation denotes larger probability. Using the 2-stage sampling process from [(2.10)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq10), we draw (from the GMM) the data samples *X* = *μ* + *Σ* × *ϵ*[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si37.png), which are then labeled with noisy labels sampled from *Ỹ* = *T*[𝒳]^( − 1)(*u*; **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si84.png) using label distribution given data from the top-right figure. After training the model *f*[*θ*](**x**) to minimize the ERM in [(2.15)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq15) with the BCE loss in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq13) using the samples in the middle-left figure, the classification predictions are shown in the middle-right figure. Relying on the 3-stage process from [(2.12)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq12), we again draw data samples labeled with noisy labels, first sampled from *Y* = *T*[𝒳]^( − 1)(*u*; **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si85.png) and then sampled from *Ỹ* = *T*[𝒴𝒳]^( − 1)(*u*; **y**, **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si86.png), both using label distribution given data from the top-right figure. The bottom-right figure shows the outputs of the model trained with the data from the bottom-left figure.

For **multi-label classification problems** (see [Fig. 2.4](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0025)(b)), the training samples **x** are annotated with $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y} \\subset {\\{ 0,1\\}}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si87.png), with $0 \\leq \\sum\_{c = 1}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c) \\leq |\\mathcal{Y}|$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si88.png), so each sample can be labeled with no classes or multiple classes. This modification from the multi-class classification scenario requires some changes in the definitions presented above.

First, the model needs to be redefined as *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → \[0, 1\]^(|𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si89.png), which means that each label can have a separate probability of being present in the data. The noisy-label distribution also needs a redefinition with $p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|t\_{\\mathcal{X}}^{\\mathcal{P}}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si90.png), where *t*[𝒳]^𝒫 : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(2^(|𝒴|) − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si91.png) outputs a categorical distribution at each **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si1.png), with *Δ*^(2^(|𝒴|) − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si92.png) denoting the probability simplex for the label power set 𝒫![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si93.png). In this power set, each of the 2^(|𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si94.png) labels in 𝒫![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si93.png) denotes a different label combination from the classes in 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si14.png) ([Spolaôr et al., 2013](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1650)). Following the idea above, we extend $p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}};t\_{\\mathcal{X}}^{\\mathcal{P}}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\prod\_{c \\in \\mathcal{P}}\\mathbf{t}^{\\mathcal{P}}{(c)}^{\\delta(\\mathcal{P}(c) = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si95.png), with **t**^𝒫 = *t*[𝒳]^𝒫(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si96.png), *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si74.png) being the indicator function, and 𝒫(*c*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si97.png) representing the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si98.png) element of the power set 𝒫![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si93.png).

For training the classification model, we could consider the same loss functions from [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq13) if we regard the problem as a multi-class problem, where the classes are the label combinations in the power set 𝒫![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si93.png). However, the size of this power set quickly becomes intractable, so in practice, multi-label problems use the BCE loss from [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq13) and the class-wise 0-1 loss defined by $\\ell\_{01 - ML}(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\prod\_{c = 1}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}\\delta\\left( \\mathbf{y}(c) \\neq \\mathsf{Squash}\\left( f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c})}(\\mathbf{x}),\\tau \\right) \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si99.png), where **y**(*c*) ∈ {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si100.png) represents the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si98.png) element of the label vector **y**, Squash : \[0, 1\] × \[0, 1\] → {0, 1}^(|𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si101.png) is a function that thresholds the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si98.png) output of the model to be either 0 or 1 per label (using a threshold *τ* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si102.png)), with this *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si98.png) model output denoted by *f*[*θ*]^((**y**[*c*]))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si103.png). Training is similarly done by minimizing the empirical risk in [(2.15)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq15).

### 2.2.3 Semantic segmentation

The semantic segmentation problem mainly applies to images, as shown in [Fig. 2.4](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0025)(c), where the input image is denoted by **x** ∈ 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ^(*H* × *W* × *R*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si104.png) (with *H*\= height, *W*\= width, *R*\= number of color channels), which is labeled by $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y} \\subset {\\{ 0,1\\}}^{H \\times W \\times C}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si105.png) (with *C*\= being number of segmentation classes, and $\\sum\_{c = 1}^{C}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c) = 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si106.png) for *ω* ∈ *Ω*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si107.png) indexing the image lattice of size *H* × *W*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si108.png)). The segmentation model, parameterized by *θ* ∈ *Θ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si28.png), is defined by *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → {*Δ*[*ω*]^(|𝒴| − 1)}[*ω* ∈ *Ω*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si109.png), which outputs a pixel-wise categorical distribution for the image **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si1.png). The segmentation problem is an extension of the whole image classification problem from Section [2.2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0025) to a pixel-wise classification. Hence all definitions in Section [2.2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0025) can be extended to the segmentation problem, but with the modifications explained below.

The joint probability from [(2.9)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq9) needs to redefine the categorical distribution function from *t*[𝒳] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si51.png) to *t*[*Ω*𝒳] : 𝒳 → {*Δ*[*ω*]^(|𝒴| − 1)}[*ω* ∈ *Ω*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si110.png), which represents a function that outputs a pixel-wise categorical distribution. Furthermore, we also redefine $p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}};t\_{\\Omega\\mathcal{X}}) = \\prod\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\prod\_{c = 1}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}\\mathbf{t}{(\\omega,c)}^{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c)}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si111.png), where **t**(*ω*, *c*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si112.png) denotes the probability of the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si98.png) class at the pixel *ω* computed from **t** = *t*[*Ω*𝒳](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si113.png), $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si114.png) represents the label of the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si98.png) class at *ω*, and it is assumed that the pixel-wise categorical distribution is independent within the image lattice Ω. The sampling process for the segmentation problem is similar to the one for classification in [(2.10)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq10) with the same step 1, and step 2 performed in a pixel-wise manner with *Ỹ*(*ω*) = *T*[*Ω*𝒳]^( − 1)(*u*; **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si115.png) for *ω* ∈ *Ω*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si107.png) and *u* ∼ 𝒰(0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si56.png), which is the inverse cumulative distribution function computed from *t*[*Ω*𝒳](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si116.png). When introducing the latent clean label variable *Y*, the joint distribution *p*(*X*, *Ỹ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si4.png) from [(2.11)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq11) needs to use *t*[*Ω*𝒳𝒴] : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → {*Δ*[*ω*]^(|𝒴| − 1)}[*ω* ∈ *Ω*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si117.png), where sampling in [(2.12)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq12) is done with *Ỹ*(*ω*) = *T*[*Ω*𝒳𝒴]^( − 1)(*u*; **y**, **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si118.png), which is the inverse cumulative distribution function computed from *t*[*Ω*𝒳𝒴](**y**, **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si119.png).

Another difference is in the definition of the loss functions, where the losses in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq13) are now defined in a pixel-wise manner, but a global loss can also be considered, such as the Dice loss ([Milletari et al., 2016](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1280)):

$\\ell\_{Dice}(\\mathbf{y},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\frac{2\\sum\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\mathbf{y}{(\\omega)}^{\\top}\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega)}{\\sum\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\mathbf{y}{(\\omega)}^{\\top}\\mathbf{y}(\\omega) + \\sum\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}{(\\omega)}^{\\top}\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega)},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si120.png)(2.16) 

where $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si121.png). Segmentation problems are constrained to a single label per pixel, so we do not consider the multi-label classification for segmentation problems. Training with a noisy label dataset $\\mathcal{D} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si33.png) is usually done by minimizing a combination of a pixel-wise loss and a global loss, as with the ERM in:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\left( \\frac{1}{|\\Omega|}\\sum\\limits\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega),\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega)) \\right) + \\lambda \\times \\ell\_{Dice}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si122.png)(2.17) 

where $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si121.png), and *λ* weights the contribution of the Dice loss.

### 2.2.4 Detection

To deal with the detection of visual objects from images (see [Fig. 2.4](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0025)(d)), we define the input image as **x** ∈ 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ^(*H* × *W* × *R*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si104.png) (with *H*\= height, *W*\= width, *R*\= number of color channels), which is associated with *B* bounding boxes, each represented by the top-left and bottom-right two-dimensional coordinates denoted by **b** ∈ ℬ ⊂ ℝ⁴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si123.png) and labeled with the object class $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y} \\subset {\\{ 0,1\\}}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si87.png). The detection model, parameterized by *θ* ∈ *Θ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si28.png), is defined by *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → {*Δ*[*a*]^(|𝒴| − 1)×ℬ[*a*]}[*a* = 1]^(*A*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si124.png), where *A* is the fixed number of detections produced by the model. The detection problem can be seen as an extension of the image classification and regression problems, where we aim to regress a set of *A* bounding boxes of visual objects, together with their classification.

The joint distribution includes image, noisy bounding boxes, and labels, as follows:

$p(X = \\mathbf{x},{\\widetilde{Y}}\_{1} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1},{\\widetilde{B}}\_{1} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{1},...,{\\widetilde{Y}}\_{A} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{A},{\\widetilde{B}}\_{A} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{A}) = p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{1} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1},{\\widetilde{B}}\_{1} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{1},...,{\\widetilde{Y}}\_{A} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{A},{\\widetilde{B}}\_{A} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{A}|\\mathbf{x}) \\times p(X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\prod\\limits\_{a = 1}^{A}p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{a} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{a},{\\widetilde{B}}\_{a} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a}|X = \\mathbf{x}) \\times p(X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\prod\\limits\_{a = 1}^{A}p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{a} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{a}|{\\widetilde{B}}\_{a} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a},X = \\mathbf{x}) \\times p({\\widetilde{B}}\_{a} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a}|X = \\mathbf{x}) \\times p(X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\prod\\limits\_{a = 1}^{A}p({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{a};t\_{\\mathcal{X}}(\\mathbf{x}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a}))) \\times \\mathcal{N}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a};\\mu\_{\\mathcal{B}}(\\mathbf{x}),\\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{B}}(\\mathbf{x})) \\times \\mathcal{N}(\\mathbf{x};\\mu,\\Sigma),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si125.png)(2.18) 

where the *A* bounding boxes are assumed to be independent from each other, $t\_{\\mathcal{X}}(\\mathbf{x}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si126.png) is the categorical distribution, defined in [(2.9)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq9), at the image region inside the bounding box ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si127.png) (denoted by $\\mathbf{x}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si128.png)), $p({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{a};t\_{\\mathcal{X}}(\\mathbf{x}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{a})))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si129.png) is defined in [(2.9)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq9), *μ*[ℬ] : 𝒳 → ℬ![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si130.png) returns the bounding box mean in image **x** and *Σ*[ℬ] : 𝒳 → ℬ × ℬ![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si131.png) returns the bounding box covariance for the multivariate normal distribution 𝒩(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si132.png), and 𝒩(**x**; *μ*, *Σ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si63.png) is defined in [(2.1)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq1).

The sampling process for each bounding box happens in three stages:

$\\text{1.~}X = \\mu + \\Sigma \\times \\epsilon\_{\\mathcal{X}}\\text{2.~}\\widetilde{B} = \\mu\_{\\mathcal{B}}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{B}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\times \\epsilon\_{\\mathcal{B}}\\text{3.~}\\widetilde{Y} = T\_{\\mathcal{X}}^{- 1}(u;\\mathbf{x}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si133.png)(2.19) 

where *ϵ*[𝒳] ∼ *n*(0[𝒳], **I**[𝒳])![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si18.png) is defined as in [(2.3)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq3), *ϵ*[ℬ] ∼ *n*(0[ℬ], **I**[ℬ])![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si134.png) follow the definitions from [(2.3)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq3), *u* ∼ 𝒰(0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si56.png) denotes a uniform random number in \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si57.png), and *T*[𝒳]^( − 1)(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si66.png) is the inverse cumulative distribution from *t*[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si135.png), as defined in [(2.10)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq10).

Similarly to the regression problem in Section [2.2.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0020) and the classification problem in Section [2.2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0025), we can introduce the clean label variable *Y* and clean bounding box variable *B*. We then define the transition probability function that estimates the noisy bounding box given *X* with *p*(*B̃*|*X*) = ∫*p*(*B*, *B̃*|*X*)*d**B* = ∫*p*(*B̃*|*B*, *X*)*p*(*B*|*X*)*d**B*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si136.png). We also need to define the transition probability function that estimates the noisy categorical distribution of *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si31.png) given *Y*, *B̃*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si137.png), and *X* with *p*(*Ỹ*|*B̃*, *X*) = ∑[*Y*]*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *B̃*, *X*)*p*(*Y*|*B̃*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si138.png). Hence, we have

$p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widetilde{B} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{B} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}},X = \\mathbf{x}) \\times p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{B} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}},X = \\mathbf{x}) \\times \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\int p(\\widetilde{B} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}|B,X = \\mathbf{x}) \\times p(B|X = \\mathbf{x})dB = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}};t\_{\\mathcal{Y}\\mathcal{X}}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}))) \\times p(\\mathbf{y};t\_{\\mathcal{X}}(\\mathbf{x}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}))) \\times \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\int\\mathcal{N}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}};\\mu\_{\\mathcal{BX}}(B,\\mathbf{x}),\\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{BX}}(B,\\mathbf{x})) \\times \\mathcal{N}(B;\\mu\_{\\mathcal{B}}(\\mathbf{x}),\\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{B}}(\\mathbf{x}))dB,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si139.png)(2.20) 

where we follow the same definitions as in [(2.4)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq4) and [(2.11)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq11).

The sampling process for each bounding box is based on five stages:

$\\text{1.~}X = \\mu + \\Sigma \\times \\epsilon\_{\\mathcal{X}}\\text{2.~}B = \\mu\_{\\mathcal{B}}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{B}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\times \\epsilon\_{\\mathcal{B}}\\text{3.~}\\widetilde{B} = \\mu\_{\\mathcal{B}\\mathcal{X}}(\\mathbf{b},\\mathbf{x}) + \\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{B}\\mathcal{X}}(\\mathbf{b},\\mathbf{x}) \\times \\epsilon\_{\\mathcal{B}\\mathcal{X}}\\text{4.~}Y = T\_{\\mathcal{X}}^{- 1}(u;\\mathbf{x}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}))\\text{5.~}\\widetilde{Y} = T\_{\\mathcal{Y}\\mathcal{X}}^{- 1}(u;\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si140.png)(2.21) 

where we follow the definitions from [(2.5)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq5), [(2.12)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq12), and [(2.19)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq19).

The detector is trained to minimize a combination of regression and classification loss functions using a noisy label dataset $\\mathcal{D} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}}) \\right\\}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si141.png), with the ERM defined as follows:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{A|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ \\sum\\limits\_{a = 1}^{A}\\left( \\ell\_{C}(\\mathbf{y}\_{i,a}^{\\ast},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}) + \\delta(\\mathbf{y}\_{i,a}^{\\ast} \\neq 0\_{\\mathcal{Y}}) \\times \\ell\_{R}(\\mathbf{b}\_{i,a}^{\\ast},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si142.png)(2.22) 

where ${\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}\\}}\_{a = 1}^{A} = f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si143.png), $\\mathbf{b}\_{i,a}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\_{\\mathbf{b} \\in {\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}}}\\mathsf{IoU}(\\mathbf{b},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si144.png), with $\\mathsf{IoU}(A,B) = \\frac{|A\\bigcap B|}{|A\\bigcup B|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si145.png) denoting the intersection over union operator and ${\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si146.png) representing the noisy bounding box annotation. Also in [(2.22)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq22), we have

$\\mathbf{y}\_{i,a}^{\\ast} = \\begin{cases} {{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j},} & {\\text{if~}\\mathsf{IoU}(\\mathbf{b}\_{i,a}^{\\ast},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}) > \\tau} \\\\ {0\_{\\mathcal{Y}},} & \\text{otherwise} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si147.png)(2.23) 

where each bounding box in ${\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si148.png) can be associated with only one detection in ${\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{A}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si149.png), and 0[𝒴]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si150.png) is a vector with zeros of size |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si48.png). In [(2.22)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq22), the loss ℓ[*C*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si151.png) is represented by one of the classification losses in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq13), and the loss ℓ[*R*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si152.png) is one of the regression losses in [(2.6)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq6).

## 2.3 Label noise problems

Recall that the label noise discussed in Section [2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0015) is represented by the joint probability distribution *p*(*X*, *Ỹ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si4.png), which can be decomposed in two ways, one depending on the intrinsic label distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si153.png), and the other relying on the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) and clean distribution *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si155.png). The intrinsic label noise for classification and regression problems is shown in Figs. [2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0035) and [2.7](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0040). Also recall that label noise can be decomposed into two types, namely: an irreducible term that is associated with the difficulty of the annotation and therefore impossible to eliminate, and a labeling error introduced by human or semi-automated labelers. The algorithms presented in this book target to mitigate the second type of noise since the first type is in principle impossible to eliminate.

![Figure 2.6 Intrinsic classification label noise.Example of the training data (rightmost graph) sampled from the GMM (leftmost graph shows the probability of data given label, and middle figure shows the probability of label given data) from Fig. 2.5, where the label is affected only by the intrinsic label noise.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr006.jpg)

Figure 2.6 Intrinsic classification label noise.Example of the training data (rightmost graph) sampled from the GMM (leftmost graph shows the probability of data given label, and middle figure shows the probability of label given data) from [Fig. 2.5](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0030), where the label is affected only by the intrinsic label noise.

![Figure 2.7 Intrinsic regression label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the ground truth regression model from Fig. 2.2, containing only intrinsic label noise.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 2.7](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cs0010_2) Intrinsic regression label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the ground truth regression model from [Fig. 2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0015), containing only intrinsic label noise.

To define the label noise process made by labelers, we introduce the **noise rate** *η* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si156.png), and the **noise type** *ν*, which can be **symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent**. To account for this noise, we need to re-define the joint probabilities from Section [2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0015). First, let us re-define the decomposed joint probability by conditioning it on *η* and *ν*, as follows:

*p*(*X*, *Ỹ*|*η*, *ν*) = *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *η*, *ν*) × *p*(*X*) = ((1−*η*)×*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)+*η*×*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*,*ν*)) × *p*(*X*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si157.png)(2.24) 

where *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si153.png) denotes latent conditional label distribution defined in [(2.1)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq1) for regression problems and [(2.9)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq9) for classification problems, and *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si158.png) represents the latent conditional noisy label distribution of type *ν*. By taking the transition distribution into account, the joint probability is re-defined as

$p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|\\eta,\\nu) = \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\\nu,\\eta) \\times p(Y|X) \\times p(X) = \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\left( (1 - \\eta) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) + \\eta \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\\nu) \\right) \\times p(Y|X) \\times p(X),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si159.png)(2.25) 

where the latent transition probability *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) is as defined in [(2.4)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq4) for regression and in [(2.11)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq11) for classification, while *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si160.png) represents the latent noisy transition distribution of type *ν*, and the sum is replaced by an integral for the regression problem of [(2.4)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq4). This joint distribution can then be used to build the noisy training set with samples $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|\\eta,\\nu)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si161.png).

The definitions in [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24) and [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25) are related to the definition of the label noise process explained in the first challenge presented in Section [1.3](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml), which is related to definition of the label noise generation process that can be based on a label distribution ([Thiel, 2008](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1715); [Domingos, 2000](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0450)) as in [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24), or a label transition process ([Pérez et al., 2007](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1415); [Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1025)) as in [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25).

## 2.4 Closed set label noise problems

The defining property of closed-set label noise problems is that the hidden clean label of the data is always in the set (for classification) or range (for regression) of training labels 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si14.png). Below we present closed-set label noise problems for classification and regression problems since both subsume the other applications (i.e., segmentation and detection).

### 2.4.1 Symmetric

In closed-set symmetric *classification* label noise, the noise is uniform and independent of the input data *X* and label *Y*, so this type of noise can be explained by encoding or communication errors, as mentioned in Section [1.2](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml). Essentially, given a data sample *X*, with label distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si153.png), a symmetric label noise will mix a uniform distribution with the label distribution, so that the labeling process produces a noisy label that can produce an arbitrary random label. [Fig. 2.8](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0045) shows an example of a training set with symmetric label noise in a classification problem, where it is clear that labels are corrupted in an uniform manner. Also, in [Fig. 2.9](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0050), we see how a uniform label noise affects a regression problem, with an *η* rate of samples showing a uniform distribution of labels. This type of noise is defined by the latent conditional noisy label distribution of type *ν* = *s**y**m*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si162.png) from [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24), with

*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *s**y**m*) = 𝒰(𝒴),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si163.png)(2.26) 

where 𝒰(𝒴)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si164.png) represents a uniform distribution, where the probability for each label is $\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si165.png). Similarly, if we are working with the latent transition distribution $p(Y|\\overline{Y},X)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si166.png) as in [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25), we define the latent noisy transition as

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *s**y**m*) = 𝒰(𝒴).

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si167.png)(2.27) 

![Figure 2.8 Closed-set symmetric classification label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the GMM from Fig. 2.6, where the label is affected by symmetric label noise with η = 50%. Note that the label noise is uniformly distributed among the training samples.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr008.jpg)

[Figure 2.8](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cf0535) Closed-set symmetric classification label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the GMM from [Fig. 2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0035), where the label is affected by symmetric label noise with *η* = 50%. Note that the label noise is uniformly distributed among the training samples.

![Figure 2.9 Closed-set symmetric regression label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the ground truth regression model from Fig. 2.2, containing symmetric label noise with η = 50%. Notice how the y-values are uniformly distributed within the IQR as defined in (2.28) and (2.29).](images/B9780443154416000113/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 2.9](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cf0540) Closed-set symmetric regression label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the ground truth regression model from [Fig. 2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0015), containing symmetric label noise with *η* = 50%. Notice how the y-values are uniformly distributed within the *IQR* as defined in [(2.28)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq28) and [(2.29)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq29).

The closed-set symmetric *regression* label noise is similarly defined, but we need to establish a closed-set domain for the labels, which is in principle unbounded for regression problems. Therefore, we use a common definition of inlier from statistics ([Wilcox, 2011](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1915)) which defines that the closed set for the labels is 1.5× the interquartile range (*IQR*), where

*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*)) = *Q*3(*p*(*Ỹ*)) − *Q*1(*p*(*Ỹ*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si168.png)(2.28) 

with *Q*3(*p*(*Ỹ*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si169.png) being the upper quartile defined as the median of the second half of *p*(*Ỹ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si170.png), and *Q*1(*p*(*Ỹ*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si171.png) denoting the lower quartile defined as the median of the first half of *p*(*Ỹ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si170.png), and *p*(*Ỹ*) = ∫*p*(*X*, *Ỹ*)*d**X*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si172.png). For the purpose of defining regression label noise, we consider a low outlier value *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si31.png) for *p*(*Ỹ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si170.png) to be less than *Q*1(*p*(*Ỹ*)) − 1.5 × *I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si173.png), and a high outlier to be more than *Q*3(*p*(*Ỹ*)) + 1.5 × *I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si174.png). Hence, for closed-set symmetric *regression* label noise, the latent conditional noisy label distribution of [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24) is defined by

*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *s**y**m*) = 𝒰(*Q*1(*p*(*Ỹ*))−1.5×*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*)),*Q*3(*p*(*Ỹ*))+1.5×*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*))),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si175.png)(2.29) 

where $\\mathcal{U}(a,b) = \\frac{1}{b - a}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si176.png) if *Ỹ* ∈ \[*a*, *b*\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si177.png) and 0 otherwise. Similarly, if we are working with the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) as in [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25), we define the latent noisy transition as

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *s**y**m*) = 𝒰(*Q*1(*p*(*Ỹ*))−1.5×*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*)),*Q*3(*p*(*Ỹ*))+1.5×*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*))).

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si178.png)(2.30) 

### 2.4.2 Asymmetric

In closed-set asymmetric *classification* label noise, the label noise depends only on the true label denoted by *Y*, but not on the data *X*. In image classification, typical examples are the inherent ambiguity in classifying visual classes that are naturally similar, such as ‘wolf’ and ‘coyote’, or ‘crow’ and ‘raven’, as explained in Section [2.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0010). This noise type can happen due to unreliable labeling or the intrinsic variability among labelers. In this type of error, given the data *X* with label distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si153.png) and noisy label transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png), an asymmetric label noise will increase the probability of pre-defined pairwise label flippings. This type of noise can only be defined with the transition distribution and the latent conditional noisy label distribution of type *ν* = *a**s**y**m*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si179.png) from [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25), as follows

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *a**s**y**m*) = **T**,

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si180.png)(2.31) 

where **T** ∈ \[0, 1\]^(|𝒴| × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si181.png) is a stochastic matrix with the label flipping probabilities

**T**[*i*, *j*] = *p*(*Ỹ* = **y**[*i*]|*Y* = **y**[*j*]),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si182.png)(2.32) 

for **y**[*i*], **y**[*j*] ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si183.png) denoting the one-hot label with the *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si184.png) and *j*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si185.png) labels active, respectively. [Fig. 2.10](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0055) shows an example of asymmetric label noise using the transition distribution depicted on the right-hand side of the image.

![Figure 2.10 Closed-set asymmetric classification label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the GMM from Fig. 2.6, where the label is affected by asymmetric label noise using the label transition matrix depicted on the right hand side of the image. Note from the transition matrix that the labels of classes 0 (red) and 1 (blue) can be flipped with 50% probability, while the labels from classes 2 (purple) and 3 (gray) do not flip.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr010.jpg)

[Figure 2.10](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cf0580) Closed-set asymmetric classification label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the GMM from [Fig. 2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0035), where the label is affected by asymmetric label noise using the label transition matrix depicted on the right hand side of the image. Note from the transition matrix that the labels of classes 0 (red) and 1 (blue) can be flipped with 50% probability, while the labels from classes 2 (purple) and 3 (gray) do not flip.

The closed-set asymmetric *regression* label noise can be similarly defined with the latent transition distribution in [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25) as in:

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *a**s**y**m*) = *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si188.png)(2.33) 

where *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si189.png) is similarly defined as in [(2.4)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq4), i.e.,

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*) = 𝒩(*Ỹ*; *μ*[𝒴](*Y*), *Σ*[𝒴](*Y*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si190.png)(2.34) 

where *μ*[𝒴] : 𝒴 → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si191.png) and *Σ*[𝒴] : 𝒴 → 𝒴 × 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si192.png). [Fig. 2.11](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0060) displays an asymmetric label noise regression problem with a simple *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si189.png) defined as a Gaussian with mean 2 × *Y*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si193.png).

![Figure 2.11 Closed-set asymmetric regression label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the ground truth regression model from Fig. 2.2, containing asymmetric label noise, where \\mu\_{\\mathcal{Y}}(\\mathbf{y}) = 2 \\times \\mathbf{y}Image and \\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{Y}}(\\mathbf{y}) = 1Image in (2.34).](images/B9780443154416000113/gr011.jpg)

[Figure 2.11](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cf0595) Closed-set asymmetric regression label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the ground truth regression model from [Fig. 2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0015), containing asymmetric label noise, where *μ*[𝒴](**y**) = 2 × **y**![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si186.png) and *Σ*[𝒴](**y**) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si187.png) in [(2.34)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq34).

### 2.4.3 Instance-dependent

Instance dependent *classification* label noise consists of a noisy labeling process that depends on the data *X* and possibly on *Y*. Compared with the symmetric and asymmetric noise types above, instance-dependent noise is more realistic since the label noise distribution depends on the input data, taking into account that some instances are harder to label than other instances. This noise type can happen due to insufficient information in the data for a reliable labeling, unreliable labeling or the intrinsic variability among labelers. From [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24), given an instance *X*, with label distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si153.png), instance-dependent noise (IDN) adds a noisy label distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si194.png), defined as:

*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*) = *p*(*Ỹ*; *t*[𝒳]^(*i**d**n*)(*X*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si195.png)(2.35) 

where *t*[𝒳]^(*i**d**n*) : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si196.png) is a function that returns a categorical noisy-label distribution for instance *X*. For the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) in [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25), we define the latent noisy transition as

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*) = *p*(*Ỹ*; *t*[𝒴𝒳](*Y*, *X*)) = **T**(*X*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si197.png)(2.36) 

where *t*[𝒴𝒳] : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si198.png) is a function that returns a categorical noisy-label transition for instance *X*, and **T** ∈ \[0, 1\]^(|𝒴| × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si181.png) is a stochastic matrix with instance-dependent label flipping probabilities defined as

**T**[*i*, *j*](*X*) = *p*(*Ỹ* = **y**[*i*]|*Y* = **y**[*j*], *X*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si199.png)(2.37) 

for **y**[*i*], **y**[*j*] ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si183.png) denoting the one-hot vector with the *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si184.png) and *j*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si185.png) labels active, respectively. [Fig. 2.12](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0065) shows an example of instance dependent label noise, where the IDN increases the chances of a sample to be corrupted by a symmetric label noise if it is closer to the origin.

![Figure 2.12 Closed-set instance-dependent classification label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the GMM from Fig. 2.6, where the label is affected by instance-dependent label noise with samples closer to the origin being more likely to be affected by a symmetric label noise.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr012.jpg)

[Figure 2.12](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cf0610) Closed-set instance-dependent classification label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the GMM from [Fig. 2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0035), where the label is affected by instance-dependent label noise with samples closer to the origin being more likely to be affected by a symmetric label noise.

The closed-set instance-dependent *regression* label noise is similarly defined using the label distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si153.png) from [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24), given an instance *X*, as follows:

*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*) = 𝒩(*Ỹ*; *μ*[𝒳](*X*), *Σ*[𝒳](*X*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si202.png)(2.38) 

where *μ*[𝒳] : 𝒳 → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si13.png) and *Σ*[𝒳] : 𝒳 → 𝒴 × 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si15.png). For the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) in [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25), we define the latent noisy transition as

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*) = *p*(*Ỹ*; *μ*[𝒴𝒳](*Y*, *X*), *Σ*[𝒴𝒳](*Y*, *X*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si203.png)(2.39) 

where *μ*[𝒴𝒳] : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si24.png) and *Σ*[𝒴𝒳] : 𝒴 × 𝒳 → 𝒴 × 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si25.png). [Fig. 2.13](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0070) shows an instance-dependent label noise regression problem with *μ*[𝒴𝒳](**y**, **x**) = 2 × **y** × **x**![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si204.png) and *Σ*[𝒴𝒳](**y**, **x**) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si201.png) in [(2.39)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq39).

![Figure 2.13 Closed-set instance-dependent regression label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the ground truth regression model from Fig. 2.2, containing instance-dependent label noise, where \\mu\_{\\mathcal{YX}}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}) = 2 \\times \\mathbf{y} \\times |\\mathbf{x}|Image and \\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{YX}}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}) = 1Image in (2.39).](images/B9780443154416000113/gr013.jpg)

[Figure 2.13](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cf0625) Closed-set instance-dependent regression label noise.Example of the training data sampled from the ground truth regression model from [Fig. 2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0015), containing instance-dependent label noise, where *μ*[𝒴𝒳](**y**, **x**) = 2 × **y** × |**x**|![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si200.png) and *Σ*[𝒴𝒳](**y**, **x**) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si201.png) in [(2.39)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq39).

## 2.5 Open-set label noise problems

Open-set label noise problems are defined by having data instances whose clean labels are not in the set (for classification) or range (for regression) of training labels 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si14.png). For classification problems containing open-set label noise, the training set contains samples from both the closed and open sets, where closed-set samples are defined by

$\\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta}^{c} = \\left\\{ \\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{X} \\middle| \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = 1\\text{~and~}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\notin \\mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = 0 \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si205.png)(2.40) 

where *P*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si206.png) is the latent distribution of clean labels, and open-set samples are defined by

$\\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta}^{o} = \\left\\{ \\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{X} \\middle| \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = 0\\text{~and~}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\notin \\mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = 1 \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si207.png)(2.41) 

with 𝒳 = 𝒳[*η*]^(*c*)⋃𝒳[*η*]^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si208.png) and $\\eta = \\frac{|\\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta}^{o}|}{|\\mathcal{X}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si209.png).

For regression problems, the training set also contains samples from both the closed and open sets, where closed-set samples are defined by

𝒳[*η*]^(*c*) = {**x**∈𝒳|∫[*Y* ∈ 𝒴]*p*(*Y*|*X*\=**x**)*d**Y*\=1 and ∫[*Y* ∉ 𝒴]*p*(*Y*|*X*\=**x**)*d**Y*\=0},

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si210.png)(2.42) 

where 𝒴 = 𝒰(*Q*1(*p*(*Y*)) − 1.5 × *I**Q**R*(*p*(*Y*)), *Q*3(*p*(*Y*)) + 1.5 × *I**Q**R*(*p*(*Y*)))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si211.png), with *p*(*Y*) = ∫*p*(*X*, *Y*)*d**X*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si212.png) and *Q*1(*p*(*Y*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si213.png), *I**Q**R*(*p*(*Y*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si214.png) and *Q*3(*p*(*Y*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si215.png) being defined in [(2.29)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq29), and open-set samples are defined by

𝒳[*η*]^(*o*) = {**x**∈𝒳|∫[*Y* ∈ 𝒴]*p*(*Y*|*X*\=**x**)*d**Y*\=0 and ∫[*Y* ∉ 𝒴]*p*(*Y*|*X*\=**x**)*d**Y*\=1},

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si216.png)(2.43) 

with 𝒳 = 𝒳[*η*]^(*c*)⋃𝒳[*η*]^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si208.png) and $\\eta = \\frac{|\\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta}^{o}|}{|\\mathcal{X}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si209.png).

In open-set classification and regression noise, the noise rate *η* defines the proportion of samples belonging to the open set 𝒳[*η*]^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si217.png), so the latent conditional noisy label distribution from [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24) is re-defined as

*p*(*X*, *Ỹ*|*η*, *ν*) = (*δ*(*X*∈𝒳[*η*]^(*c*))×*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)+*δ*(*X*∈𝒳[*η*]^(*o*))×*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*,*ν*)) × *p*(*X*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si218.png)(2.44) 

where *η* is as defined in [(2.41)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq41), and *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si74.png) denotes an indicator function. Similarly, if we are working with the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) as in [(2.25)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq25), we define the latent noisy transition as

$p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|\\eta,\\nu) = p(X) \\times \\left( \\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta}^{c}) \\times \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) \\times p(Y|X) + \\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta}^{o}) \\times \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\notin \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\\nu) \\times p(Y|X) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si219.png)(2.45) 

where *η* is defined in [(2.41)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq41), and *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si74.png) denotes the indicator function. For regression problem, the sums in [(2.44)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq44) and [(2.45)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq45) are replaced by integrals.

### 2.5.1 Open-set symmetric

The open-set symmetric *classification* label noise is uniform and independent of the input data *X* and clean label *Y*, where an open-set data sample in 𝒳[*η*]^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si217.png) is labeled with any of the closed-set labels by sampling a uniform distribution (see [Fig. 2.14](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0075), on the left). Considering the latent conditional noisy label distribution for the open set samples of type *ν* = *s**y**m*^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si220.png) from [(2.44)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq44), we have

*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *s**y**m*^(*o*)) = 𝒰(𝒴),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si221.png)(2.46) 

where 𝒰(𝒴)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si164.png) is a uniform distribution with label probability equal to $\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{U}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si222.png). When working with the latent transition distribution from [(2.45)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq45), we have

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *s**y**m*^(*o*)) = 𝒰(𝒴).

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si223.png)(2.47) 

![Figure 2.14 Open-set symmetric label noise.For the classification problem on the left, we take the training data sampled from the GMM of Fig. 2.6 and introduce data sampled from an open-set distribution with a unimodal multi-dimensional Gaussian with mean (−6,0) and identity covariance, where each sample is randomly labeled with one of the 4 training labels. For the regression problem on the right, we take the training data sampled from the regression model of Fig. 2.2 and add data sampled from an open-set distribution with a Gaussian of mean −6 and unit variance, with each sample randomly labeled with any value in the range of inliers, as described in (2.48) and (2.49).](images/B9780443154416000113/gr014.jpg)

Figure 2.14 Open-set symmetric label noise.For the classification problem on the left, we take the training data sampled from the GMM of [Fig. 2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0035) and introduce data sampled from an open-set distribution with a unimodal multi-dimensional Gaussian with mean (−6,0) and identity covariance, where each sample is randomly labeled with one of the 4 training labels. For the regression problem on the right, we take the training data sampled from the regression model of [Fig. 2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0015) and add data sampled from an open-set distribution with a Gaussian of mean −6 and unit variance, with each sample randomly labeled with any value in the range of inliers, as described in [(2.48)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq48) and [(2.49)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq49).

For the open-set symmetric *regression* (see [Fig. 2.14](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0075), on the right), the latent conditional noisy label distribution of [(2.44)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq44) is defined by

*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *s**y**m*^(*o*)) = 𝒰(*Q*1(*p*(*Ỹ*))−1.5×*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*)),*Q*3(*p*(*Ỹ*))+1.5×*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*))),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si224.png)(2.48) 

where *p*(*Ỹ*) = ∫[*X* ∈ 𝒳[*η*]^(*c*)]*p*(*X*, *Ỹ*|*η*, *ν*)*d**X*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si225.png), *I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*)) = *Q*3(*p*(*Ỹ*)) − *Q*1(*p*(*Ỹ*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si226.png), and $\\mathcal{U}(a,b) = \\frac{1}{b - a}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si176.png) if *Ỹ* ∈ \[*a*, *b*\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si177.png) and 0 otherwise. With the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) from [(2.45)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq45), we define the latent noisy label transition as

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *s**y**m*^(*o*)) = 𝒰(*Q*1(*p*(*Ỹ*))−1.5×*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*)),*Q*3(*p*(*Ỹ*))+1.5×*I**Q**R*(*p*(*Ỹ*))),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si227.png)(2.49) 

where *X* ∈ 𝒳^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si228.png).

### 2.5.2 Open-set asymmetric

Similarly to the closed-set asymmetric classification noise, the open-set asymmetric label noise depends only on the true label denoted by *Y*, as shown in [Fig. 2.15](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0080), on the left. Asymmetric label noise will affect the latent conditional noisy label distribution of type *ν* = *a**s**y**m*^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si229.png) from [(2.44)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq44)

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *a**s**y**m*^(*o*)) = **T**,

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si230.png)(2.50) 

where **T** ∈ \[0, 1\]^(|𝒴| × |𝒴^(*o*)|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si231.png) is a stochastic matrix with the label flipping probabilities between the labels inside and outside the set 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si14.png), with the outside labels denoted by 𝒴^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si232.png) and

**T**[*i*, *j*] = *p*(*Ỹ* = **y**[*i*]|*Y* = **y**[*j*]),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si182.png)(2.51) 

for **y**[*i*] ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si233.png) and **y**[*j*] ∈ 𝒴^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si234.png) denoting the one-hot vectors with the *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si184.png) and *j*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si185.png) labels active, respectively.

![Figure 2.15 Open-set asymmetric label noise.For the classification problem on the left, we take the training data sampled from the GMM of Fig. 2.6 and introduce data sampled from an open-set distribution with a unimodal multi-dimensional Gaussian with mean (−6,0) and identity covariance, where each sample is randomly labeled with training labels of classes 0 or 1, each with 50% probability. For the regression problem on the right, we take the training data sampled from the regression model of Fig. 2.2 and add data sampled from an open-set distribution with a Gaussian of mean −6 and unit variance, with each sample affected by an asymmetric label noise with \\mu\_{\\mathcal{Y}}(\\mathbf{y}) = 2 \\times \\mathbf{y}Image and \\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{Y}}(\\mathbf{y}) = 1Image.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr015.jpg)

Figure 2.15 Open-set asymmetric label noise.For the classification problem on the left, we take the training data sampled from the GMM of [Fig. 2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0035) and introduce data sampled from an open-set distribution with a unimodal multi-dimensional Gaussian with mean (−6,0) and identity covariance, where each sample is randomly labeled with training labels of classes 0 or 1, each with 50% probability. For the regression problem on the right, we take the training data sampled from the regression model of [Fig. 2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0015) and add data sampled from an open-set distribution with a Gaussian of mean −6 and unit variance, with each sample affected by an asymmetric label noise with *μ*[𝒴](**y**) = 2 × **y**![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si186.png) and *Σ*[𝒴](**y**) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si187.png).

The open-set asymmetric *regression* label noise can also be defined with the latent transition distribution in [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24), as displayed on the right graph of [Fig. 2.15](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0080), as in:

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *a**s**y**m*^(*o*)) = *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si235.png)(2.52) 

where *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si189.png) can be defined as in [(2.4)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq4), i.e.,

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*) = 𝒩(*Ỹ*; *μ*[𝒴](*Y*), *Σ*[𝒴](*Y*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si190.png)(2.53) 

where *μ*[𝒴] : 𝒴^(*o*) → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si237.png) and *Σ*[𝒴] : 𝒴^(*o*) → 𝒴 × 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si238.png).

### 2.5.3 Open-set instance-dependent

Open-set instance dependent *classification* label noise consists of a noisy labeling process that depends on the data *X* and possibly on *Y*, as displayed on the left of [Fig. 2.16](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0085). From [(2.44)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq44), given an instance *X*, with label distribution *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si155.png), instance-dependent noise (IDN) adds a noisy label distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*^(*o*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si239.png), defined as:

*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*^(*o*)) = *p*(*Ỹ*; *t*[𝒳]^(*i**d**n*^(*o*))(*X*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si240.png)(2.54) 

where *t*[𝒳]^(*i**d**n*^(*o*)) : 𝒳[*η*]^(*o*) → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si241.png) is a function that returns a categorical open-set noisy-label distribution for instance *X*. For the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) in [(2.45)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq45), we define the latent noisy transition as

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*^(*o*)) = *p*(*Ỹ*; *t*[𝒴𝒳]^(*i**d**n*^(*o*))(*Y*, *X*)) = **T**(*X*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si242.png)(2.55) 

where *t*[𝒴𝒳]^(*i**d**n*^(*o*)) : 𝒴^(*o*) × 𝒳[*η*]^(*o*) → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si243.png) is a function that returns a categorical noisy-label distribution for instance *X*, and **T**(*X*) ∈ \[0, 1\]^(|𝒴| × |𝒴^(*o*)|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si244.png) is a stochastic matrix with instance-dependent label flipping probabilities defined as

**T**[*i*, *j*](*X*) = *p*(*Ỹ* = **y**[*i*]|*Y* = **y**[*j*], *X*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si199.png)(2.56) 

for **y**[*i*] ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si233.png) and **y**[*j*] ∈ 𝒴^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si234.png) denoting the one-hot vectors with the *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si184.png) and *j*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si185.png) labels active, respectively, and *X* ∈ 𝒳^(*o*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si228.png).

![Figure 2.16 Open-set IDN label noise.For the classification problem on the left, we take the training data sampled from the GMM of Fig. 2.6 and introduce data sampled from an open-set distribution with a unimodal multi-dimensional Gaussian with mean (−6,0) and identity covariance, where each sample is labeled by sampling the probability of label given the data from the original 4-class of Fig. 2.6. For the regression problem on the right, we take the training data sampled from the regression model of Fig. 2.2 and add data sampled from an open-set distribution with a Gaussian of mean −6 and unit variance, with each sample affected by an asymmetric label noise with \\mu\_{\\mathcal{YX}}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}) = 2 \\times \\mathbf{y} \\times |\\mathbf{x}|Image and \\Sigma\_{\\mathcal{YX}}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}) = 1Image.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr016.jpg)

Figure 2.16 Open-set IDN label noise.For the classification problem on the left, we take the training data sampled from the GMM of [Fig. 2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0035) and introduce data sampled from an open-set distribution with a unimodal multi-dimensional Gaussian with mean (−6,0) and identity covariance, where each sample is labeled by sampling the probability of label given the data from the original 4-class of [Fig. 2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0035). For the regression problem on the right, we take the training data sampled from the regression model of [Fig. 2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0015) and add data sampled from an open-set distribution with a Gaussian of mean −6 and unit variance, with each sample affected by an asymmetric label noise with *μ*[𝒴𝒳](**y**, **x**) = 2 × **y** × |**x**|![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si200.png) and *Σ*[𝒴𝒳](**y**, **x**) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si201.png).

The open-set instance-dependent *regression* label noise (see right of [Fig. 2.16](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0085)) is similarly defined using the label distribution *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si155.png) from [(2.44)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq44), given an instance *X*, as follows:

*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*^(*o*)) = 𝒩(*Ỹ*; *μ*[𝒳](*X*), *Σ*[𝒳](*X*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si246.png)(2.57) 

where *μ*[𝒳] : 𝒳[*η*]^(*o*) → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si247.png) and *Σ*[𝒳] : 𝒳[*η*]^(*o*) → 𝒴 × 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si248.png). For the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) in [(2.45)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq45), we define the latent noisy transition as

*p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*, *ν* = *i**d**n*^(*o*)) = *p*(*Ỹ*; *μ*[𝒴𝒳](*Y*, *X*), *Σ*[𝒴𝒳](*Y*, *X*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si249.png)(2.58) 

where *μ*[𝒴𝒳] : 𝒴^(*o*) × 𝒳[*η*]^(*o*) → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si250.png) and *Σ*[𝒴𝒳] : 𝒴^(*o*) × 𝒳[*η*]^(*o*) → 𝒴 × 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si251.png).

## 2.6 Label noise problem setup

The label noise problems discussed in Sections [2.4](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0045) and [2.5](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0065) generally have a setup involving three datasets:

*   •  a **training set** $\\mathcal{D} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si33.png), where ${(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i} \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|\\eta,\\nu)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si252.png), with unknown *η* > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si253.png) and *ν* ∈ {*s**y**m*, *a**s**y**m*, *i**d**n*, *s**y**m*^(*o*), *a**s**y**m*^(*o*), *i**d**n*^(*o*)}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si254.png);
*   •  a **testing set** that is formed with a noise rate *η* = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si255.png) and represented by $\\mathcal{T} = {\\{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i})\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{T}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si256.png), where $(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si257.png); and 
*   •  a **validation set**, with a noise rate *η* = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si255.png), denoted by $\\mathcal{V} = {\\{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i})\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{V}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si258.png), where $(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si257.png).

Hence, the main challenge is on how to train a model using a noisy-label training set 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si259.png) with unknown noise rate *η* and type *ν*, and to test the trained model with the testing set 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si260.png) with *η* = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si255.png). Some problems also rely on the validation set 𝒱![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si261.png), where |𝒱| <  < |𝒟|![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si262.png), that is formed with a noise rate *η* = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si255.png) to facilitate the adaptation of the trained model to the testing set.

Another important point is that some problems may have a combination of *E* different noise types at different noise rates, so effectively, the joint distribution for these problems is denoted by *p*(*X*, *Ỹ*|{*η*[*e*], *ν*[*e*]}[*e* = 1]^(*E*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si263.png). When all noise types in {*η*[*e*], *ν*[*e*]}[*e* = 1]^(*E*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si264.png) are closed-set label problems, the decomposed joint probability from [(2.24)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq24) is re-defined as

$p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|{\\{\\eta\_{e},\\nu\_{e}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E}) = p(\\widetilde{Y}|X,{\\{\\eta\_{e},\\nu\_{e}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E}) \\times p(X) = \\left( \\left( 1 - \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\right) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|X) + \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|X,\\nu\_{e}) \\right) \\times p(X),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si265.png)(2.59) 

and by taking the transition distribution into account, the joint probability is re-defined as

$p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|{\\{\\eta\_{e},\\nu\_{e}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E}) = \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,{\\{\\eta\_{e},\\nu\_{e}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E}) \\times p(Y|X) \\times p(X) = \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\left( \\left( 1 - \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\right) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) + \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\\nu\_{e}) \\right) \\times p(Y|X) \\times p(X).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si266.png)(2.60) 

When all noise types in {*η*[*e*], *ν*[*e*]}[*e* = 1]^(*E*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si264.png) are open-set label noise problems, the latent conditional noisy label distribution from [(2.44)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq44) is re-defined as

$p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|{\\{\\eta\_{e},\\nu\_{e}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E}) = \\left( \\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\sum\\eta\_{e}}^{c}) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|X) + \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta\_{e}}^{o}) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|X,\\nu\_{e}) \\right) \\times p(X),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si267.png)(2.61) 

where $\\sum\\eta\_{e} = \\frac{\\sum\_{e = 1}^{E}|\\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta\_{e}}^{o}|}{|\\mathcal{X}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si268.png) represents the sum of all *E* noise rates, so this means that the proportion of closed-set samples 𝒳[∑*η*[*e*]]^(*c*) ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si269.png) is $\\left( 1 - \\sum\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si270.png). When working with the latent transition distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si154.png) as in [(2.45)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq45), we define the latent noisy transition as

$p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|{\\{\\eta\_{e},\\nu\_{e}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E}) = p(X) \\times \\left( \\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\sum\\eta\_{e}}^{c}) \\times \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) \\times p(Y|X) + \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta\_{e}}^{o}) \\times \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\notin \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\\nu\_{e}) \\times p(Y|X) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si271.png)(2.62) 

We can also have a combination of closed-set and open-set label noise. Let us represent the closed-set noise set with {*η*[*e*], *ν*[*e*]}[*e* = 1]^(*E*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si264.png) and the open-set noise with {*η*[*e*]^(*o*), *ν*[*e*]^(*o*)}[*e* = 1]^(*E*^(*o*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si272.png), then the latent conditional noisy label distribution is defined as

$p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|{\\{\\eta\_{e},\\nu\_{e}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E},{\\{\\eta\_{e}^{o},\\nu\_{e}^{o}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E^{o}}) = \\left( \\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\sum\\eta\_{e}^{o}}^{c}) \\times \\left( \\left( 1 - \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\right) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|X) + \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|X,\\nu\_{e}) \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E^{o}}\\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta\_{e}^{o}}^{o}) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|X,\\nu\_{e}^{o}) \\right) \\times p(X),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si273.png)(2.63) 

and the latent noisy transition as

$p(X,\\widetilde{Y}|{\\{\\eta\_{e},\\nu\_{e}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E},{\\{\\eta\_{e}^{o},\\nu\_{e}^{o}\\}}\_{e = 1}^{E^{o}}) = p(X) \\times \\left( \\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\sum\\eta\_{e}^{o}}^{c}) \\times \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\left( \\left( 1 - \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\right) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X) + \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E}\\eta\_{e} \\times p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\\nu\_{e}) \\right) \\times p(Y|X) + \\sum\\limits\_{e = 1}^{E^{o}}\\delta(X \\in \\mathcal{X}\_{\\eta\_{e}^{o}}^{o}) \\times \\sum\\limits\_{Y \\notin \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\\nu\_{e}^{o}) \\times p(Y|X) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si274.png)(2.64) 

The second and fifth challenges from Section [1.3](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml) are related to the setup of the problem. In particular, the second challenge is about the experimental setup of the problem, where the datasets, noise rate, and noise type can lead to a combinatorial explosion in the number of benchmarks, which can hinder progress given the impossibility of assessing all proposed models on all benchmarks. Another point highlighted in the second challenge is the possible presence of label noise in the testing and validation sets. This issue can happen in real-world datasets since it may not be possible to acquire clean-label testing and validation sets. For instance, the diagnosis of certain conditions from medical images can be challenging, leading to high-level of label noise due the uncertainty of the diagnosis, making it impossible to have a clean label, unless we use a different source of information for the labels, such as pathology or surgery. The fifth challenge is about the estimation of the label noise rate and type present in a dataset, which is hard to obtain, but can be useful during the training process ([Xiao et al., 2015](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1960); [Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1130)). [Frénay and Verleysen (2014)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0525) introduced a generic way to use such noise estimation information with a graphical model to explain closed-set symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise, where a binary random variable represents the presence of error in the labeling process.

## 2.7 Datasets and benchmarks

In this section, we introduce the main datasets and benchmarks used to assess noisy label learning methods. We present the amount of training, validation, and testing images present in each dataset and benchmark, the estimated proportion and type of noise present, and the task (e.g., classification, segmentation, detection, etc.) used in the assessment. We divided the datasets into Computer Vision Datasets, Medical Image Analysis Datasets, and Non-image Datasets.

### 2.7.1 Computer vision datasets and benchmarks

Let us first introduce the datasets that contain approximately 0% of intrinsic label noise in the training, validation, and testing sets. **MNIST** ([LeCun, 1998](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1030))^([⁴](#fn4))

**Tiny-ImageNet** ([Karpathy et al., 2016](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0855))^([⁵](#fn5))

While the datasets above have negligible amount of noise, the next datasets were collected in such a way that they naturally contain label noise introduced by the labeling process in the training set, but the validation and testing sets still contains approximately 0% of intrinsic label noise. **Animal-10N** ([Song et al., 2019](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1640))^([⁶](#fn6))

The **CIFAR-10N, CIFAR-100N** ([Wei et al., 2021a](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1885))^([⁷](#fn7))

**Food-101N** ([Lee et al., 2018](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1045))^([⁸](#fn8))

The dataset **Clothing1M** ([Xiao et al., 2015](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1960))^([⁹](#fn9))

**WebVision** ([Li et al., 2017](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1070))^([^(10)](#fn10))

For the assessment of noisy-label methods for segmentation and detection problems, the main datasets used are Cityscapes ([Cordts et al., 2016](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0330)), COCO ([Lin et al., 2014](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1100)), PASCAL VOC ([Everingham et al., 2010](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0485)), and Potsdam+Vaihingen ([Potsdam, 2018](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1435); [Vaihingen, 2018](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1770)). The **Cityscapes** ([Cordts et al., 2016](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0330))^([^(11)](#fn11))

#### 2.7.1.1 Classification benchmarks

The real-world classification benchmarks are represented by the datasets Animal-10N ([Song et al., 2019](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1640)), CIFAR-10N, CIFAR-100N ([Wei et al., 2021a](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1885)), Food-101N ([Lee et al., 2018](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1045)), Clothing1M ([Xiao et al., 2015](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1960)), and WebVision ([Li et al., 2017](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1070)). These datasets contain specific types and rates of label noise, and methods are compared by verifying their classification accuracy on their clean testing sets. Even though useful, the real-world noisy label datasets above have fixed label noise rates and types, which do not allow for a systematic evaluation of the methods. To address this issue, many benchmarks have been proposed, where different types and rates of label noise are artificially introduced to the clean label datasets from [Table 2.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#t0010) (i.e., all datasets that have noise rate *η* ≈ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si282.png)). Such artificially built benchmarks enable a systematic assessment of the methods with respect to label noise.

Table 2.1

Datasets used for assessing noisy-label learning computer vision algorithms and models.
