| --- |

The most common artificial benchmark explored in the field is the one proposed by [Tanaka et al. (2018)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1695); [Patrini et al. (2017)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1400), comprising **symmetric and asymmetric label noise applied to CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100** (first four rows in [Table 2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#t0015)), which are applied as explained in Sections [2.4.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0050) and [2.4.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0055), respectively. For the asymmetric label noise in CIFAR-10, [Tanaka et al. (2018)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1695); [Patrini et al. (2017)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1400) proposed the following four pairs of label transitions to be used in the transition matrix described in Section [2.4.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0055): TRUCK → AUTOMOBILE, BIRD → AIRPLANE, DEER → HORSE, CAT ↔ DOG. These transitions are parameterized by *η* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si156.png), where the probability of the ground truth (in the diagonal of the transition matrix) and noisy-label transition are *η* − 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si283.png) and *η*, respectively. The asymmetric label noise for CIFAR-100 ([Karim et al., 2022](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0835)) relies on a transition matrix that contains label flippings for each class to the next one within the super-classes (note that the 100 classes in the CIFAR-100 are grouped into 20 super-classes).

All benchmarks above assume an unrealistic balanced distribution of samples per class, which facilitates the learning process of various techniques explored for noisy-label learning. The **FSR/RoLT/INOLML** benchmark ([Zhang and Pfister, 2021](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br2170); [Hoang et al., 2022](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0715); [Wei et al., 2021b](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1890)) proposes to combine symmetric noise on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, with rates in {10%, 20%, 30%, 40%, 50%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si298.png) with an imbalanced learning problem, with imbalance ratio *ρ* ∈ {10, 50, 100, 200}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si299.png). The imbalance ratio is the ratio between the sample sizes of the largest majority class and the smallest minority class.

(2022)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1215) proposed three noisy-label segmentation benchmarks. The first is the **symmetric pixel-wise** label noise, where randomly selected pixels have their labels switched to another random labels, with *η* ∈ {5%, 10%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si303.png). The second is the **symmetric region-wise** label noise, where randomly selected contiguous regions have their labels switched to another random labels, with *η* ∈ {5%, 10%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si303.png). The third is the **relative shift of object boundaries**, where labels are spatially shifted in random direction by 5 or 10 pixels.

Synthetic benchmarks based on symmetric noise on ISIC 2017 and PatchCamelyon have been introduced by [Xue et al. (2022)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1990). For instance, the benchmark **Random Noise ISIC** uses extra 1582 training images from the ISIC archive, and the **Random Noise PCam** relies on the original training set. On these two datasets, the symmetric noise has rate *η* ∈ {5%, 10%, 20%, 40%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si311.png). The segmentation benchmark **IDN SegTHOR** ([Liu et al., 2022b](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1115))^([^(34)](#fn34))

The noisy-label benchmarks proposed in ([Zhang et al., 2020a](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br2120))^([^(35)](#fn35))

The benchmark in ([Zhang et al., 2020b](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br2125)) uses the **JSRT** dataset ([Shiraishi et al., 2000](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1590)) that contains 247 chest X-rays of size 2048 × 2048![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si308.png) pixels, which are annotated with three anatomical structures, namely: clavicle, heart, and lung. Images are resized to 256 × 256![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si305.png) pixels, and the original set is split into 197 training and 50 validation images. Similarly to the methods above, the label noises are simulated with various morphological operators (e.g., dilating, eroding, and edge-distorting) applied to the original manual annotations. By varying the proportion and extent of the synthesized label noise, the benchmark aims to systematically assess methods using the variables *η* and *β*. The variable *η* defines the proportion of corruption, where each mask is dilated, eroded, or edge-distorted by *β* ± 3![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si321.png). The training sets have *η* ∈ {30%, 50%, 70%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si322.png). The benchmark also proposes two sets of values for *β*, with the first set defined by *β*[*c**l**a**v**i**c**l**e*] = 5![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si323.png), *β*[*h**e**a**r**t*] = 10![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si324.png), *β*[*l**u**n**g*] = 15![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si325.png); and the second set defined by *β*[*c**l**a**v**i**c**l**e*] = 10![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si326.png), *β*[*h**e**a**r**t*] = 15![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si327.png), β=lung20![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si328.png).

### 2.7.4 Non-image datasets and benchmarks

Even though we focus on image datasets for noisy-label learning, we can also find non-image datasets available for the same task, as displayed in [Table 2.7](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#t0040). For instance, the dataset **NEWS** ([Lang, 1995](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1015))^([^(36)](#fn36))

## 2.8 Evaluation

Noisy-label learning methods are assessed using many of the measures already used in the field to test regular classification, segmentation, and detection methods, but using the noise rate *η* as an independent variable, when it is available. When *η* is not available or fixed at a specific value, e.g., for real-world datasets, then comparisons are done with pre-defined training and testing sets. For the evaluations described below, the training is performed with a training set containing noisy labels $\\mathcal{D} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si33.png), with noise rate *η* > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si253.png), while the evaluation measure is computed using the clean testing set denoted by $\\mathcal{T} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{T}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si333.png), which as explained in Section [2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0085), is formed with a noise rate *η* = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si255.png). Below, we list the most common measures to assess multi-class and multi-label classification, segmentation, and detection approaches.

### 2.8.1 Classification evaluation

For multi-class classification problems (see [Fig. 2.17](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0090)), the most common measure is the accuracy in the testing set, computed from:

$\\mathsf{Accuracy} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{T}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si334.png)(2.65) 

where the test image label produced by the model is represented by $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si335.png), with *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si69.png) being the trained model and OneHot : *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1) → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si72.png) denoting a function to produce a one-hot prediction from the model [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq13). Accuracy represents a sample-wise measure that works well when the number of samples per class in the testing set 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si260.png) is balanced. However, when the number of samples per class is imbalanced, accuracy can provide a result that is biased toward the classes that contain the majority of samples. For instance, assume that we have a binary classification problem with 90 samples for class 1 and 10 samples for class 2, and the model predicts the correct class for all 90 samples of class 1, but predicts the correct class for only 5 samples of class 2, so even though the accuracy from [(2.65)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq65) is 95%, the accuracy for class 2 is only 50%. Hence, in problems where we have highly imbalanced distributions of samples per class, the label-wise measures that we explain below are preferred.

![Figure 2.17 Classification evaluation.Using a simple binary classification problem (images of square versus images of circle), we show example of the following classification evaluations: accuracy from (2.65), \\mathsf{AUROC}Image and \\mathsf{AUPRC}Image computed from \\mathsf{TPR}Image (or \\mathsf{Recall}Image) and \\mathsf{FPR}Image in (2.66), and \\mathsf{Precision}Image from (2.68).](images/B9780443154416000113/gr017.jpg)

Figure 2.17 Classification evaluation.Using a simple binary classification problem (images of square versus images of circle), we show example of the following classification evaluations: accuracy from [(2.65)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq65), AUROC![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si336.png) and AUPRC![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si337.png) computed from TPR![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si338.png) (or Recall![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si339.png)) and FPR![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si340.png) in [(2.66)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq66), and Precision![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si341.png) from [(2.68)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq68).

A common label-wise measure is the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC), which is displayed in [Fig. 2.17](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0090). To compute this curve, we need to compute the following the true positive rate (TPR, also known as recall or sensitivity) and the false positive rate (FPR or 1-specificity) per class *c* ∈ {1, ..., |𝒴|}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si342.png) at several classification thresholds *τ* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si102.png),

$\\mathsf{TPR}(c,\\tau) = \\frac{\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau)}{\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau) + \\mathsf{FN}(c,\\tau)}\\mathsf{FPR}(c,\\tau) = \\frac{\\mathsf{FP}(c,\\tau)}{\\mathsf{TN}(c,\\tau) + \\mathsf{FP}(c,\\tau)},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si343.png)(2.66) 

with

$\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau) = \\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c) \\times \\delta(f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\geq \\tau),\\mathsf{FN}(c,\\tau) = \\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c) \\times \\delta(f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c})}(\\mathbf{x}) < \\tau),\\mathsf{FP}(c,\\tau) = \\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}(1 - \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c)) \\times \\delta(f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\geq \\tau),\\mathsf{TN}(c,\\tau) = \\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}(1 - \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c)) \\times \\delta(f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c})}(\\mathbf{x}) < \\tau),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si344.png)(2.67) 

where *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si74.png) is an indicator function, and *f*[*θ*]^((**y**[*c*]))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si103.png) represents the probability of classification for the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si98.png) class. The ROC curve per class *c* is computed by interpolating the values of TPR(*c*, *τ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si345.png) as a function of FPR(*c*, *τ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si346.png) by varying the threshold *τ* from 1 to 0. The AUROC for *c* is then computed as the area under the ROC curve for the class *c*, and the result for all classes is computed from the mean of the AUROC for all classes.

Another common label-wise measure used in classification problems is the area under the precision and recall curve (AUPRC), shown in [Fig. 2.17](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0090), and the mean average precision (mAP). Both measures need the plotting of the precision-recall curve, where Recall(*c*, *τ*) = TPR(*c*, *τ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si347.png) in [(2.66)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq66), and

$\\mathsf{Precision}(c,\\tau) = \\frac{\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau)}{\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau) + \\mathsf{FP}(c,\\tau)},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si348.png)(2.68) 

where TP(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si349.png), FP(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si350.png) are defined in [(2.67)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq67). The PR curve is then computed by interpolating the values of Precision(*c*, *τ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si351.png) as a function of Recall(*c*, *τ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si352.png) by varying the threshold *τ* from 1 to 0. Even though PR and ROC curves are equivalent, PR curves are preferred for datasets that show highly imbalanced label distributions ([Davis and Goadrich, 2006](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0365)). From the PR curves, there are two label-wise measures that are usually computed to summarize the performance of methods. The AUPRC is the area under the PR curve, while the mAP is calculated from the average precision (AP), estimated as the weighted sum of precision values, where recall increases, as follows:

$\\mathsf{AP}(c) = \\sum\\limits\_{t = 1}^{|\\mathcal{R}| - 1}\\left( \\mathsf{Recall}(c,\\tau(t)) - \\mathsf{Recall}(c,\\tau(t + 1)) \\right) \\times \\mathsf{Precision}(c,\\tau(t)),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si353.png)(2.69) 

where ℛ![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si354.png) denotes the set of threshold values where recall increases, *τ*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si355.png) is the threshold at position *t* in ℛ![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si354.png), Recall(*c*, *τ*(|ℛ|)) = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si356.png), and Precision(*c*, *τ*(|ℛ|)) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si357.png). The mAP is then computed as the mean of the AP(*c*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si358.png) over the classes *c* ∈ {1, ..., |𝒴|}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si342.png).

Multi-label classification problems are generally evaluated with AUROC, mAP, and AUPRC since these measures can be computed in a class-wise manner and then summarized over the classes. Nevertheless, other measures have also been used by noisy-label multi-label learning approaches ([Xie and Huang, 2021](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1965)), such as the following ([Zhang and Zhou, 2013](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br2130)):

$\\mathsf{HammingLoss}(\\tau) = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{T}| \\times |\\mathcal{Y}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{c \\in \\{ 1,...,|\\mathcal{Y}|\\}}\\delta\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c) \\neq {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\tau}(c) \\right),\\mathsf{OneError} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{T}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\arg\\max\\limits\_{c \\in \\{ 1,...,|\\mathcal{Y}|\\}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c})}(\\mathbf{x})) = 0,\\mathsf{Coverage} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{T}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\max\\limits\_{c:{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}(c) = 1}\\mathsf{rank}(f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{\\mathbf{c}})}(\\mathbf{x})) - 1,\\mathsf{RankLoss} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{T}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\frac{1}{\\#(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = 1) \\times \\#(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = 0)}|\\mathcal{K}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si359.png)(2.70) 

where ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}^{\\tau} = \\mathsf{Squash}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}),\\tau)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si360.png) with the Squash(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si361.png) defined in Section [2.2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0025) as a function that thresholds the output using *δ*(*f*[*θ*](**x**) > *τ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si362.png), rank(*f*[*θ*]^((**y**[*c*]))(**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si363.png) returns the rank of the label *c* according to the classification confidence *f*[*θ*]^((**y**[*c*]))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si103.png), $\\#(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = 1)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si365.png) is a function that returns the number of labels in $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si6.png) annotated with “1”, $\\#(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = 0)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si366.png) returns the number of labels annotated with “0”, and $\\mathcal{K}(f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c})}(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\{(c^{\\prime},c^{''})|f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c^{\\prime}})}(\\mathbf{x}) < f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c^{''}})}(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c^{\\prime}) = 1,\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c^{''}) = 0\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si367.png) is the set of mis-ranked labels.

### 2.8.2 Segmentation evaluation

The evaluation of noisy-label segmentation methods can in principle be done with pixel-wise accuracy, using the formula in [(2.65)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq65). However, segmentation problems tend to present extremely imbalanced distributions of classes, so accuracy is not well suited. A particularly interesting measure that is robust to such imbalanced distributions is the intersection over union (IoU), or also known as the Jaccard index. Recall that the pixel-wise segmentation label is denoted by $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c) \\in \\{ 0,1\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si369.png) where *ω* ∈ *Ω*![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si107.png) and *c* ∈ {1, ..., |𝒴|}![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si342.png), and the segmentation model produces a pixel-wise classification $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si335.png), where $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c) \\in \\{ 0,1\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si370.png). The IoU is computed for each image and class *c* as follows (see [Fig. 2.18](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0095)):

$\\mathsf{IoU}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) = \\frac{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}\\bigcap{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}}{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}\\bigcup{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}} = \\frac{\\mathsf{TP}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c})}{\\mathsf{TP}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) + \\mathsf{FP}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) + \\mathsf{FN}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si371.png)(2.71) 

where ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si372.png) denotes the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si98.png) channel of the segmentation map $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si373.png) (similarly for ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si374.png)), and

$\\mathsf{TP}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c) \\times \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c),\\mathsf{FP}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c) \\times (1 - \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c)),\\mathsf{FN}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\omega \\in \\Omega}(1 - \\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c)) \\times \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\omega,c).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si375.png)(2.72) 

In [(2.71)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq71), elements that have division by zero are generally ignored. Then, the mean IoU (mIoU) is computed with

$\\mathsf{mIoU} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{T}| \\times |\\mathcal{Y}|}\\sum\\limits\_{c \\in \\{ 1,...,|\\mathcal{Y}|\\}}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\mathsf{IoU}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si376.png)(2.73) 

![Figure 2.18 Segmentation evaluation.Computation of the segmentation evaluation measure \\mathsf{IoU}Image to assess the performance of the segmentation of the visual object ‘Swan’. Given the ground truth annotation (top-middle) and detection (bottom-middle), the \\mathsf{IoU}Image is computed by dividing the intersection (top-right) and the union (bottom-right) of the ground truth annotation and detection segmentation maps.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr018.jpg)

[Figure 2.18](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cf2090) Segmentation evaluation.Computation of the segmentation evaluation measure IoU![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si368.png) to assess the performance of the segmentation of the visual object ‘Swan’. Given the ground truth annotation (top-middle) and detection (bottom-middle), the IoU![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si368.png) is computed by dividing the intersection (top-right) and the union (bottom-right) of the ground truth annotation and detection segmentation maps.

Another measure commonly used to assess semantic segmentation methods is the Dice measure, computed for each image and class *c* as

$\\mathsf{Dice}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},c) = \\frac{2 \\times \\mathsf{IoU}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c})}{1 + \\mathsf{IoU}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{c})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si377.png)(2.74) 

and the mean Dice over testing images and classes provides the final measure for the method. Dice and IoU allow similar interpretation of methods, but notice that Dice is larger than IoU, particularly when IoU is small, when Dice is two times larger.

In segmentation problems, it is possible that we have a set of labels per image ([Zhang et al., 2020a](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br2120)) and that the method also produces a set of predictions per image, allowing us to estimate a distribution of labels instead of a single binary mask per class. The measure used for such cases is the class-wise generalized energy distance (GED) ([Székely and Rizzo, 2013](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1685); [Salimans et al., 2018](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br1515); [Bellemare et al., 2017](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br0120); [Zhang et al., 2020a](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#br2120)), computed as

$D\_{GED}^{2}\\left( p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x}),p(\\widehat{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x}),c \\right) = 2 \\times \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack d(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},c) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack d(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\prime},c) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack d(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\prime},c) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si378.png)(2.75) 

where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\prime} \\sim p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si379.png) denote samples from the ground truth annotation distribution, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\prime} \\sim p(\\widehat{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si380.png) represent samples from the distribution learned by the trained model, and $d(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},c) = 1 - \\mathsf{IoU}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},c)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si381.png) is a distance measure. Then, by averaging *D*[*G**E**D*]²(*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*\=**x**[*i*]),*p*(*Ŷ*|*X*\=**x**[*i*]),*c*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si382.png) over the classes, we obtain the GED measure for the method.

### 2.8.3 Detection evaluation

The evaluation of detectors depends not only on the correct localization of the visual object, but also on the classification of the detected region. Recall from Section [2.2.4](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#s0035) that the detection testing set is denoted by $\\mathcal{T} = \\left\\{ \\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}} \\right\\}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{T}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si383.png), and the model outputs ${\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}\\}}\_{a = 1}^{A} = f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si384.png), where ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{4}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si385.png), ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j} \\in {\\{ 0,1\\}}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si386.png), and ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a} \\in \\Delta^{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si387.png). Detection methods are usually evaluated with mAP, but with the following re-definitions of precision and recall:

$\\mathsf{Precision}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}) = \\frac{\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU})}{\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}) + \\mathsf{FP}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU})},\\mathsf{Recall}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}) = \\frac{\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU})}{\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}) + \\mathsf{FN}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si388.png)(2.76) 

where

$\\mathsf{TP}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{T}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}}{\\mathsf{TP}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c}\\}}\_{a = 1}^{A},\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}),\\mathsf{FP}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{T}|}\\sum\\limits\_{a = 1}^{A}{\\mathsf{FP}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}},\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}),\\mathsf{FN}(c,\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{T}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}}{\\mathsf{FN}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c}\\}}\_{a = 1}^{A},\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si392.png)(2.77) 

In [(2.77)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq77), we have

*   •  ${\\mathsf{TP}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c}\\}}\_{a = 1}^{A},\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si393.png) first checks if ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c} = 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si394.png), then if at least one of the detections in ${\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c}\\}}\_{a = 1}^{A}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si395.png) has $\\mathsf{IoU}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c}) > \\tau\_{IoU}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si396.png) and ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c} \\geq \\tau$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si397.png), then returns “1”; otherwise returns “0”;
*   •  ${\\mathsf{FP}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}},\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si398.png) first checks if ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c} \\geq \\tau$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si397.png), then if all annotations in ${\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{B\_{i}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si399.png) have ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c} = 0$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si400.png) or ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c} = 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si394.png) and $\\mathsf{IoU}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c}) < \\tau\_{IoU}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si401.png), then returns “1”; otherwise returns “0”;
*   •  ${\\mathsf{FN}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c}\\}}\_{a = 1}^{A},\\tau,\\tau\_{IoU})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si402.png) first check if ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}^{c} = 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si394.png), then if all detections in ${\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c}\\}}\_{a = 1}^{A}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si395.png) have ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c} < \\tau$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si403.png) or ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,a}^{c} \\geq \\tau$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si397.png) and $\\mathsf{IoU}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,j}^{c},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{b}}}\_{i,a}^{c}) < \\tau\_{IoU}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si401.png), then returns “1”; otherwise returns “0”.

Given the precision and recall computed from [(2.76)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq76), we can compute AP(*c*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si358.png) per class as from [(2.69)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#deq69), and then the mAP as the mean of AP(*c*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si358.png) over all classes at a particular IoU![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si368.png) threshold *τ*[*I**o**U*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si404.png). [Fig. 2.19](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#f0100) shows examples of TP\_Detection![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si389.png), FP\_Detection![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si390.png), and FN\_Detection![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si391.png) for the detection of people from images.

![Figure 2.19 Detection evaluation.Examples of \\mathsf{TP}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}Image, \\mathsf{FP}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}Image, and \\mathsf{FN}\\\_\\mathsf{Detection}Image for the detection of people from images, using the ground truth in top-middle and detection in bottom-middle.](images/B9780443154416000113/gr019.jpg)

[Figure 2.19](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml#cf2145) Detection evaluation.Examples of TP\_Detection![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si389.png), FP\_Detection![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si390.png), and FN\_Detection![Image](images/B9780443154416000113/si391.png) for the detection of people from images, using the ground truth in top-middle and detection in bottom-middle.

## 2.9 Conclusion

In this chapter, we presented the formal definition of the different types of label noise for classification, regression, segmentation, and detection problems. We then presented the datasets and benchmarks relevant for the study of label noise, followed by an explanation of the main methods used to assess the performance of methods designed to address label noise problems. Next, we focus on theoretical aspects of noisy-label learning, then on noisy-label learning techniques and proposed methods.

# Chapter 3: Theoretical aspects of noisy-label learning

Bias-variance decomposition, label transition distribution, and PAC learning

## Abstract

This chapter introduces three approaches developed to improve our basic understanding of the noisy-label learning problem. We first explain the bias-variance decomposition that divides the training error into three components (i.e., bias, variance, and irreducible noise), which behave differently when symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise affect the training set. Then, we explain the necessary and sufficient conditions for the identifiability of the transition matrix for noisy-label learning problems. We conclude the chapter with a brief overview of the use of Valiant's probably approximately correct (PAC) model of learning to explain noisy-label learning.

### Keywords

Bias-variance decomposition; Identifiability of transition matrix; Probably approximately correct learning

## 3.1 Introduction

This chapter introduces useful tools to improve the theoretical understanding of the learning with noisy-label problem. We start with an analysis of the problem from the bias-variance decomposition viewpoint, which divides the error estimated by machine learning methods into components that can explain the different types of error affecting the learning of a model. Even though the bias-variance decomposition formulation has been valuable to explain machine learning methods, it has been under-utilized for clarifying noisy-label learning problems. In this chapter, we first define the bias-variance decomposition for regression and classification problems ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450); [Zhu et al., 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2235)), and then use this decomposition to explain how label noise affects the minimization of the expected loss and the learning difficulty of data.

Another tool that has been used to theoretically explain label noise learning is the study of the identifiability of the label transition matrix needed for dealing with the asymmetric and instance-dependent noisy-label learning problems ([Natarajan et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1315); [Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1400); [Han et al., 2020a](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0630); [Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545)). Such study investigates the necessary and sufficient conditions to enable the identification of the exact parameters of the transition matrix from the training data ([Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545); [Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140); [Blanchard et al., 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0170)). These conditions are based on the number of labels that are needed to be sampled from the label distribution of each training data, which results on the development of a different style of learning algorithms that can use training sets containing label noise.

We conclude the chapter with an overview of the use of probably approximately correct (PAC) model of learning ([Valiant, 1984](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1775)) to explain noisy-label learning. PAC learning studies the learnability of certain types of classifiers on different categories of noisy-label binary classification learning problems. Even though the results from this PAC-learning analysis are limited to binary classification problems, they contain important bounds that can improve our understanding of the noisy-label learning problem.

## 3.2 Bias variance decomposition

The training of classifiers and regressors relies on the minimization of loss functions, as explained in Chapter [2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml). Recall that the training set is represented by $\\mathcal{D} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si1.png) and that the goal of the training process is to estimate the parameter *θ* ∈ *Θ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si2.png) for the model *f*[*θ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si3.png) that minimizes the loss:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si4.png)(3.1) 

where the loss is a function that is minimized when the output from *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si5.png) approximates the label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si6.png) (some examples for regression and classification losses are represented in [(2.6)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) and [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml)). Therefore, the goal of the training process is to estimate the model parameter that minimizes the mean loss of the training samples. As described in Chapter [2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), the label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si6.png) is in fact the result of a non-deterministic process that depends on the data **x** by sampling the function *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png). The optimal prediction for the data sample **x**, denoted by **y**, is the following ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)):

$\\mathbf{y} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si8.png)(3.2) 

where the domain for $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si9.png) can be a continuous space 𝒴 ⊂ ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si10.png) for regression problems or the probability simplex 𝒴 ⊂ *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si11.png) for classification problems. Following this definition, the optimal model is the one that outputs the optimal prediction **y** with *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si5.png). Note that different training sets will enable the learning of different models, but this dependency of the model on the training set can be removed by averaging the training process over all possible training sets of a particular size |𝒟|![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si12.png). Let us represent this set of all training sets of size |𝒟|![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si12.png) by 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si13.png), so we can now compute the expected loss for a data sample **x** as the expectation with respect to *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png) and training sets 𝒟 ∈ 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si14.png), denoted by

$\\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x}),\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si15.png)(3.3) 

where *θ*^𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si16.png) is the model parameter estimated for training set 𝒟 ∈ 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si14.png).

The general bias-variance decomposition breaks the expected loss in [(3.3)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq3) into three components: bias, variance, and irreducible noise. Both bias and variance require the definition of the main prediction, as follows ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)):

$\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si17.png)(3.4) 

which represents the prediction that has a minimum mean loss relative to all predictions obtained from models trained with each training set 𝒟 ∈ 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si14.png) using the regression and classification domains described in [(3.2)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq2). The bias of the training process for a data sample **x** is defined as the loss between the main prediction $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si18.png) and the optimal prediction **y**, defined as ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)):

$\\mathsf{Bias}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\ell(\\mathbf{y},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si19.png)(3.5) 

where **y** is the optimal prediction from [(3.2)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq2) and $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si18.png) is the main prediction from [(3.4)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq4). The variance of the training process for a data sample **x** is represented by fluctuations around a mean response for different training sets, computed from the mean loss produced by predictions from *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si5.png) with respect to the main prediction $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si18.png), as in ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)):

$\\mathsf{Var}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack\\ell(\\overline{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si20.png)(3.6) 

The irreducible noise independent of the training process is defined as

$\\mathsf{N}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y})\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si21.png)(3.7) 

where **y** is the optimal prediction from [(3.2)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq2). Note that Bias(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si22.png) does not depend on any specific training set and reduces to zero when the main prediction is equal to the optimal prediction, Var(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si23.png) does not depend on the optimal prediction and reduces to zero when the model outputs the same prediction independently of training set in 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si13.png), and N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png) is independent of the training algorithm and model ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)).

Given an example **x** with label distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png) and a training process that produces a model *f*[*θ*^𝒟](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si25.png) using one of the training sets in 𝒟 ∈ 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si14.png), then for some loss functions, the expected loss for **x** from [(3.3)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq3) is decomposed as follows ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)):

$\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S},p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack = c1 \\times \\mathsf{N}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\mathsf{Bias}(\\mathbf{x}) + c2 \\times \\mathsf{Var}(\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si26.png)(3.8) 

where *c*1 and *c*2 vary for different loss functions. The extension of the sample-wise bias-variance decomposition in [(3.8)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq8) to the whole data space 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si27.png) is obtained with

$\\mathbb{E}\_{p(X),\\mathcal{S},p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\_{p(X)}\\lbrack c1 \\times \\mathsf{N}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\mathsf{Bias}(\\mathbf{x}) + c2 \\times \\mathsf{Var}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si28.png)(3.9) 

In this section, we first describe the bias-variance decomposition for regression and classification problems, and then we explain how label noise affects this decomposition. [Zhu et al. (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2235) show that this decomposition can be used to identify sample learning complexity, which in turn can suggest the presence of label noise.

### 3.2.1 Regression

Let us first consider a regression problem to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) loss, with $\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x})) = {(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} - f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si29.png). Using Theorem 1 from ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)), we have

$\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S},p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} - f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))}^{2}\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} - \\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack)}^{2}\\rbrack + {(\\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack - \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack)}^{2} + \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack{(\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack - f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))}^{2}\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si30.png)(3.10) 

where the first, second, and third terms represent the irreducible noise N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png) from [(3.7)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq7), Bias(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si22.png) from [(3.5)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq5), and Var(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si23.png) from [(3.6)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq6), respectively, the optimal prediction in [(3.2)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq2) is $\\mathbf{y} = \\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si31.png), and the main prediction in [(3.4)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq4) is $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si32.png) ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)). Hence, the formulation in [(3.10)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq10) is equal to the one in [(3.8)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq8) by setting *c*1 = *c*2 = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si33.png).

The decomposition of the expected MSE loss above implies that variance and irreducible noise are always additive, which means that biased (i.e., $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} \\neq \\mathbf{y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si34.png)) and unbiased (i.e., $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si35.png)) training samples will increase the expected loss with an increase of their variance or irreducible noise.

### 3.2.2 Classification

For a binary classification problem trained with a loss function ℓ : *Δ*¹ × *Δ*¹ → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si36.png) where ∀**y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si37.png), ℓ(**y**, **y**) = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si38.png) and $\\forall\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si39.png) such that $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\neq \\mathbf{y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si40.png), $\\ell(\\mathbf{y},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}) \\neq 0$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si41.png), the bias-variance decomposition is defined from [(3.8)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq8) using Theorem 1 in ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)) as:

$c1 = P\_{\\mathcal{S}}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{y}) - \\frac{\\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))}{\\ell(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}),\\mathbf{y})} \\times P\_{\\mathcal{S}}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\neq \\mathbf{y}),c2 = \\begin{cases} {+ 1,} & {\\text{~if~}\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y},} \\\\ {- \\frac{\\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}))}{\\ell(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}),\\mathbf{y})},} & {\\text{~otherwise},} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si42.png)(3.11) 

where *P*[𝒮](*f*[*θ*^𝒟](**x**) = **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si43.png) represents the probability over training sets in 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si13.png) that the model outputs the optimal prediction **y** from [(3.2)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq2), and $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si18.png) denotes the main prediction from [(3.4)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq4). Note in [(3.11)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq11) that when the loss is symmetric, i.e., ℓ(**y**, *f*[*θ*^𝒟](**x**)) = ℓ(*f*[*θ*^𝒟](**x**), **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si44.png), then *c*1 = 2 × *P*[𝒮](*f*[*θ*^𝒟](**x**) = **y**) − 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si45.png) and *c*2 = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si46.png) when $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si35.png), and *c*2 =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si47.png), otherwise. Hence, in such symmetric loss scenario, the decomposition described in [(3.8)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq8) with multiplicative factors from [(3.11)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq11) shows that variance is additive (i.e., it increases the expected loss) in unbiased examples (i.e., $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si35.png)) and subtractive (i.e., it decreases the expected loss) in biased examples (i.e., $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} \\neq \\mathbf{y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si34.png)). This is an interesting result because if the model is biased for **x**, then increasing the variance reduces the expected loss. Furthermore, the irreducible noise term N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png) in [(3.8)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq8) becomes subtractive for training samples **x** where *P*[𝒮](*f*[*θ*^𝒟](**x**) = **y**) < 0.5![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si48.png) since this implies *c*1 < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si49.png) in [(3.11)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq11), so a high irreducible noise N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png) in [(3.7)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq7) for these samples will reduce the expected loss, which means that a high noise level can be beneficial to performance under these circumstances ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)).

The definition in [(3.11)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq11) can be extended to the multi-class classification problem that relies on the 0-1 loss from [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), as follows (Theorem 3 in [Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)):

$c1 = P\_{\\mathcal{S}}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{y}) - P\_{\\mathcal{S}}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\neq \\mathbf{y}) \\times P\_{\\widetilde{Y}}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y} \\neq \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),c2 = \\begin{cases} {+ 1,} & {\\text{~if~}\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y},} \\\\ {- P\_{\\mathcal{S}}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{y}|f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\neq \\overline{\\mathbf{y}}),} & {\\text{~otherwise},} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si50.png)(3.12) 

where $P\_{\\widetilde{Y}}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y} \\neq \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = 1 - \\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\ell\_{01}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}))|\\mathbf{y} \\neq \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si51.png) and $P\_{\\mathcal{S}}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{y}|f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\neq \\overline{\\mathbf{y}}) = 1 - \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack\\ell\_{01}(f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}))|f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) \\neq \\overline{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si52.png).

For the multi-class classification problems that optimize the 0-1 loss, the samples whose variance contribute to reduce the loss are the ones that have *f*[*θ*^𝒟](**x**) = **y**![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si53.png) for all training sets in 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si13.png), where $f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\neq \\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si54.png). This means that for 0-1 loss, the tolerance for variance decreases with an increasing number of classes ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)). The results above for 0-1 loss are useful, but unfortunately, the empirical risk minimization of this loss for training modern deep learning models is known to be intractable ([Feldman et al., 2012](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0505)). Recently, researchers have worked on approximations to the zero-one loss ([Hasan and Pal, 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0660)) that can alleviate this issue, but the bias-variance decomposition for this approximation is still to be developed.

An alternative solution for this issue is to consider the bias-variance decomposition for multi-class classification problems that minimize a tractable loss function, such as the negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss defined in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml). The decomposition is as follows ([Heskes, 1998](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0705)):

$\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S},p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack\\ell\_{NLL}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\_{p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\lbrack - \\log(p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack + KL\\lbrack\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\|\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack + \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack KL\\lbrack\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}\\| f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si55.png)(3.13) 

where $KL\\lbrack\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}||\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si56.png) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si6.png) and $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si18.png), $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\Delta^{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si57.png), *f*[*θ*^𝒟] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si58.png), and the main prediction is defined as

$\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\Delta^{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1}}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\lbrack KL\\lbrack\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}\\| f\_{\\theta^{\\mathcal{D}}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{Z}\\exp(\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{S}}\\log(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si59.png)(3.14) 

with *Z* being a normalization factor independent of *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si5.png).

The bias-variance decomposition above shows that an increase in irreducible noise and variance can decrease the expected loss under the conditions denoted in [(3.11)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq11) and [(3.12)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq12). Such decomposition has also been explored by [Zhu et al. (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2235) to detect hard training samples, which are relevant because such samples have a higher likelihood of containing noisy labels, even though they may just be located close to classification boundaries, but annotated with clean labels.

### 3.2.3 Explaining label noise with bias variance decomposition

[Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010) shows the following examples of the sample-wise bias-variance decomposition: 1) [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010)a presents a regression problem unaffected by labeling noise (i.e., containing only the intrinsic noise from [Fig. 2.7](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml)); 2) [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010)b displays a regression affected by the symmetric noise explained in [Fig. 2.9](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml); 3) [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010)c shows another regression problem affected by the asymmetric noise from [Fig. 2.11](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml); and 4) [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010)d displays a regression problem affected by the instance-dependent noise shown in [Fig. 2.13](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml). Note that the irreducible noise N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png) (denoted by the blue points in the Noise Decomposition graphs in [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010)) can reasonably measure the amount of labeling noise in each label, but that measure requires access to multiple labels sampled from *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png), which is problematic given that it is rarely the case that we have access to *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png), and noisy training samples tend to have a single label drawn from that distribution, limiting our ability to compute the expected value in [(3.10)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq10) to obtain N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png). The bias B(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si60.png) term can also identify samples with labeling noise, but it is less effective since it cannot estimate symmetric noise as reliably as the irreducible noise, as clearly displayed in [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010)b. The variance term V(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si61.png) is effective to identify poor model predictability for samples at the edge of training set support, but it is not reliable to estimate label noise. Hence, to estimate the noise present in the labeling process, one needs to approximate the computation of N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png) with multiple labels per training sample drawn from *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png) that are affected by the intrinsic noise, but not the labeling nose.

![Figure 3.1 Bias-variance decomposition in regression problems.Examples of decomposition for regression problems affected by different types of labeling noise. The graphs on the left show the training samples in blue, with the ground truth in dashed red curve, the graphs in the middle display the model prediction (dashed black curve), and the graphs on the right show the sample-wise bias-variance decomposition (blue = irreducible noise, red = bias, green = variance).](images/B9780443154416000125/gr001.jpg)

Figure 3.1 Bias-variance decomposition in regression problems.Examples of decomposition for regression problems affected by different types of labeling noise. The graphs on the left show the training samples in blue, with the ground truth in dashed red curve, the graphs in the middle display the model prediction (dashed black curve), and the graphs on the right show the sample-wise bias-variance decomposition (blue = irreducible noise, red = bias, green = variance).

[Fig. 3.2](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0015) shows several examples of the sample-wise bias-variance decomposition for a binary classification problem using a model trained with the cross-entropy loss, which satisfies the criterion for Theorem 1 in ([Domingos, 2000](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0450)). The examples considered are the following: 1) [Fig. 3.2](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0015)a presents a classification problem unaffected by labeling noise (i.e., containing only the intrinsic noise, like the one in [Fig. 2.6](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml)); 2) [Fig. 3.2](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0015)b displays a classification affected by the symmetric noise explained from [Fig. 2.8](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml); 3) [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010)c shows another classification problem affected by the asymmetric noise similar to the one from [Fig. 2.11](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), but using the following transition matrix $p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y,X,\\nu = asym) = \\begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\\\ 0.0 & 1.0 \\\\ \\end{bmatrix}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si62.png); and 4) [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0010)d displays a classification problem affected by an instance-dependent noise similar to the one in [Fig. 2.12](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), where samples closer to the classification boundary are more likely to be affected by a symmetric label noise. Similarly to the regression problems, the irreducible noise N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png) (graphs in the third column of [Fig. 3.2](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0015)) produces a reliable map of the training samples affected by the labeling noise. However, this irreducible noise needs to access multiple labels sampled from *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png) that are affected by the intrinsic but not the labeling noise, so it is unlikely to be available. Also, noisy-label training samples tend to have a single label drawn from that distribution, which does not allow a robust computation of the expected value in [(3.10)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq10) to obtain N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png). The bias and variance terms, B(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si60.png) and V(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si61.png) respectively, tend to have overwhelmingly higher values at the classification boundary than at labeling noise regions, making these measures relatively ineffective at identifying samples containing label noise. Similarly to the conclusion for the regression problem above, the estimation of the noise present in the labeling process requires the approximation of the computation of N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png) using multiple labels per training sample drawn from *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png).

![Figure 3.2 Bias-variance decomposition in classification problems.Examples of decomposition for classification problems affected by different types of labeling noise. From left to right, the graphs on the first column show the training samples in red (class 0) and blue (class 1), the second column graphs display the prediction from the model trained with the samples from the first column, and the graphs in the third, fourth, and fifth columns show contour plots representing the components (irreducible noise, bias, and variance, respectively) of the sample-wise bias-variance decomposition.](images/B9780443154416000125/gr002.jpg)

Figure 3.2 Bias-variance decomposition in classification problems.Examples of decomposition for classification problems affected by different types of labeling noise. From left to right, the graphs on the first column show the training samples in red (class 0) and blue (class 1), the second column graphs display the prediction from the model trained with the samples from the first column, and the graphs in the third, fourth, and fifth columns show contour plots representing the components (irreducible noise, bias, and variance, respectively) of the sample-wise bias-variance decomposition.

A recent pre-print paper by [Zhu et al. (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2235) explored the bias-variance decomposition to identify samples containing label noise based on a theoretical definition of sample learning difficulty. [Zhu et al. (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2235) assume that bias decreases and variance increases with model complexity, where this complexity can be computed with the mean square values of the network weights. Hence, the expected error in [(3.9)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq9) first decreases and then increases as a function of model complexity, as shown in [Fig. 3.3](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0020). Such decomposition can be plot for the whole training set and for individual training samples, and the optimal model complexity is estimated by minimizing the expected error in [(3.9)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq9). Therefore, we can define easy and hard learning samples by looking at the ratio between the optimal complexity of the training sample and the whole training set, where a value larger than one represents a hard sample to learn, and smaller than one, an easy sample to learn. Hard samples to learn are more likely to contain noisy labels, but as observed from our examples in [Fig. 3.2](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#f0015), there is no guarantee that these samples contain label noise.

![Figure 3.3 Bias-variance decomposition to define sample learning difficulty.From left to right, we show a representation of the bias-variance decomposition as a function of model complexity, where the first graph shows this decomposition for the whole training set, with the optimal complexity denoted by c⁎. The second and third graphs show the decomposition for training samples (\\mathbf{x}\_{1},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1})Image and (\\mathbf{x}\_{2},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{2})Image, with respective optimal complexity \\mathbf{c}\_{1}^{\\ast} > \\mathbf{c}^{\\ast}Image, indicating a hard sample to learn, and \\mathbf{c}\_{2}^{\\ast} < \\mathbf{c}^{\\ast}Image, defining an easy sample to learn. According to Zhu et al. (2022), samples with noisy labels are hard to learn and can be detected using the condition \\mathbf{c}\_{1}^{\\ast} > \\mathbf{c}^{\\ast}Image.](images/B9780443154416000125/gr003.jpg)
