The second and third graphs show the decomposition for training samples $(\\mathbf{x}\_{1},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si63.png) and $(\\mathbf{x}\_{2},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{2})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si64.png), with respective optimal complexity **c**[1]^(\*) > **c**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si65.png), indicating a hard sample to learn, and **c**[2]^(\*) < **c**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si66.png), defining an easy sample to learn. According to [Zhu et al. (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2235), samples with noisy labels are hard to learn and can be detected using the condition **c**[1]^(\*) > **c**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si65.png).

## 3.3 The identifiability of the label transition distribution

As explained in Section [2.2.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) and Section [2.2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), the joint probability *p*(*X*, *Ỹ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si67.png) can be computed from the label transition distribution *T*(*X*) = *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si68.png) that represents the transition probability from *Y* to *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si69.png) given *X* and the clean label distribution *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si70.png). The challenging estimation of this transition distribution has been widely studied to address noisy-label learning problems ([Natarajan et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1315); [Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1400); [Han et al., 2020a](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0630); [Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545)), but its inaccurate estimation can lead to poor performance ([Natarajan et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1315); [Liu and Wang, 2021](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1155); [Xia et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1950); [Zhu et al., 2021c](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2240)). Hence, it is important to understand if *T*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si71.png) can be accurately estimated (such accurate estimation is generally known as the identifiability problem), which leads to a learnable noisy-label problem.

We start by studying the problem of the class-conditional (i.e., instance independent) label transition distribution identifiability ([Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545)), where *T*(*X*) = *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si72.png), ∀**x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si73.png). [Scott et al. (2013)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545) prove that the identifiability of *T*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si71.png) for a binary classification problem depends on: 1) the majority of the observed labels being correct, and 2) the true class-conditional distributions being “mutually irreducible” (such condition is defined to limit the similarity between two distributions). Following the formulation in ([Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545)) and assuming a binary classification problem, we define *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si74.png) and *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si75.png) as the class-conditional distributions for classes 0 and 1, and *η*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si76.png), *η*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si77.png) as the noise rates affecting samples in classes 0 and 1, respectively, as follows:

*P̃*[0] = (1 − *η*[0])*P*[0] + *η*[0]*P*[1], *P̃*[1] = (1 − *η*[1])*P*[1] + *η*[1]*P*[0].

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si78.png)(3.15) 

The necessary and sufficient conditions to uniquely define *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si74.png), *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si75.png), *η*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si76.png), *η*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si77.png) given samples drawn from *P̃*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si79.png), *P̃*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si80.png) are:

*   •  *Total noise level*: *η*[0] + *η*[1] < 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si81.png),
*   •  *Mutual irreducibility*: It is not possible to write *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si74.png) as a nontrivial mixture of *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si75.png) and some other distribution, and vice versa. 

The first condition roughly means that the majority of the labels are correct on average, leading to the following proposition 1 from ([Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545)):

$\\frac{p\_{1}(X)}{p\_{0}(X)} > \\gamma\\Leftrightarrow\\frac{{\\widetilde{p}}\_{1}(X)}{{\\widetilde{p}}\_{0}(X)} > \\lambda,\\text{~where}\\lambda = \\frac{\\eta\_{1} + \\gamma(1 - \\eta\_{1})}{1 - \\eta\_{0} + \\gamma\\eta\_{0}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si82.png)(3.16) 

where *p*[0](*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si83.png) and *p*[1](*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si84.png) represent the densities of *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si74.png) and *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si75.png), *p̃*[0](*X*) = (1 − *η*[0])*p*[0](*X*) + *η*[0]*p*[1](*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si85.png), and *p̃*[1](*X*) = (1 − *η*[1])*p*[1](*X*) + *η*[1]*p*[0](*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si86.png). According to this proposition, the likelihood ratio test (LRT) described in [(3.16)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq16) of the true densities is identical to the LRT of the noisy densities using a different threshold, but note that the LRT using the noisy densities forms a classifier for the noisy samples that is not necessarily optimal for the clean samples. Hence, it is necessary to estimate the clean classifier performance using estimates of the label noise proportions, as shown below.

To enable the estimation of such performance, we first introduce the alternate contamination model using Lemma 2 from ([Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545)), which assumes that *P*[0] ≠ *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si87.png) and that the *Total noise level* condition holds (i.e., *η*[0] + *η*[1] < 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si81.png)), then *P̃*[1] ≠ *P̃*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si88.png) and there is a unique *η̃*[0], *η̃*[1] ∈ \[0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si89.png), such that:

*P̃*[0] = (1 − *η̃*[0])*P*[0] + *η̃*[0]*P̃*[1], *P̃*[1] = (1 − *η̃*[1])*P*[1] + *η̃*[1]*P̃*[0],

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si90.png)(3.17) 

where ${\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{0} = \\frac{\\eta\_{0}}{1 - \\eta\_{1}} < 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si91.png), and ${\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{1} = \\frac{\\eta\_{1}}{1 - \\eta\_{0}} < 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si92.png). Furthermore, Lemma 3 from ([Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545)) assumes that [(3.17)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq17) holds and *P̃*[1] ≠ *P̃*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si88.png), which allows us to conclude that *P*[1] ≠ *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si93.png), $\\eta\_{0} = \\frac{{\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{0}(1 - {\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{1})}{1 - {\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{0}{\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{1}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si94.png), and $\\eta\_{1} = \\frac{{\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{1}(1 - {\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{0})}{1 - {\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{0}{\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{1}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si95.png), and the *Total noise level* condition holds. The Lemmas 2 and 3 defined above imply that for *P*[0] ≠ *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si87.png), we have a one-to-one correspondence between (*η*[0], *η*[1])![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si96.png) and (*η̃*[0], *η̃*[1])![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si97.png), assuming the *Total noise level* condition holds and *η̃*[0], *η̃*[1] ∈ \[0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si89.png). The alternate representations for *P̃*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si79.png) and *P̃*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si80.png) in [(3.17)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq17) motivate the mutual irreducibility between *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si74.png) and *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si75.png) that with the *Total noise level* condition ensures that *η̃*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si98.png) and *η̃*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si99.png) are identifiable. In particular, *η̃*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si98.png) and *η̃*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si99.png) are separately estimated by reducing it to the problem of mixture proportion estimation (MPE).

The MPE problem is defined by taking independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples from probability distributions *F* and *H* defined over a Hilbert space 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si100.png) to estimate *κ* for ([Scott et al., 2013](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1545)):

*F* = (1 − *κ*)*J* + *κ**H*,

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si101.png)(3.18) 

where *J* is an unknown probability distribution in 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si100.png), and *κ* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si102.png). The identifiability problem in this MPE context consists of finding the mixture proportion *κ* in [(3.18)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq18), using the Proposition 1 from ([Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140); [Blanchard et al., 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0170)), which states that *κ* is identifiable if *J* is irreducible with respect to *H* (i.e., *J* cannot be written as *J* = *γ**H* + (1 − *γ*)*F*^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si103.png), where *γ* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si104.png) and *F*^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si105.png) is another distribution). By noting that the two problems in [(3.17)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq17) are MPE problems, and assuming that *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si74.png) is irreducible with respect to *P̃*[1] = (1 − *η*[1])*P*[1] + *η*[1]*P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si106.png) and *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si75.png) is irreducible with respect to *P̃*[0] = (1 − *η*[0])*P*[0] + *η*[0]*P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si107.png), then we can estimate *η̃*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si98.png) and *η̃*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si99.png) from the proposition above. Then, the one-to-one correspondence defined above enables the identification of *η*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si76.png) and *η*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si77.png). Next, *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si74.png) and *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si75.png) are recovered from [(3.17)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq17). A stronger result can follow, which is that for any arbitrary *P̃*[0] ≠ *P̃*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si108.png), there is a unique solution *P*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si74.png), *P*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si75.png), *η*[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si76.png), *η*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si77.png) (referred to as the mutually irreducible solution) that satisfies the (Total noise level) and (Mutual irreducibility) conditions.

The results above provided theoretical guarantees for the identification of label transition distributions for noisy-label classification problems, and many methods have been developed based on such theory ([Yao et al., 2020b](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2035); [Zhu et al., 2021c](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2240); [Li et al., 2021](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1075)). Nevertheless, these theoretical results are limited to binary classification problems, and class-dependent transition distributions.

Recently, a pre-print paper by [Liu (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140) proposed a new theoretical result to address these two issues by elaborating a more general solution that can be applied to noisy-label multi-class classification problems on instance-dependent transition distribution. The result in ([Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140)) explores Kruskal's identifiability ([Kruskal, 1976](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0960), [1977](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0965)) to establish that multiple noisy labels per training sample are needed to show the identifiability of the instance-dependent transition distribution. Kruskal's identifiability defines a hidden variable, which we consider to be the clean label variable *Y* that takes values from a discrete domain 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si109.png) with prior *P*(*Y* = **y**) > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si110.png), for all **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si111.png). Instead of observing *Y*, we observe *L* variables represented by {*Ỹ*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*L*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si112.png) that takes values from 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si109.png). We can represent the matrix **M**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si113.png) of size |𝒴|²![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si114.png) containing rows denoted by vectors \[*P*(*Ỹ*[*i*] = **y**[1]|*Y* = **y**[*j*]), ..., *P*(*Ỹ*[*i*] = **y**[|𝒴|]|*Y* = **y**[*j*])\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si115.png), where **y**[*i*] ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si116.png) denotes a one-hot label vector, with the *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si117.png) class active. Hence, \[**M**[1], ..., **M**[*L*]\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si118.png) and prior *P*(*Y* = **y**[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si119.png) represent the hidden parameters required to generate the observations. The Kruskal's identifiability results depend on the Kruskal rank of a matrix, denoted by Kr(**M**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si120.png), defined as the largest number *I* such that every set of *I* rows from **M** are linearly independent, and a theorem ([Kruskal, 1976](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0960), [1977](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0965); [Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140)) that states that \[**M**[1], ..., **M**[*L*]\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si118.png) are identifiable, up to label permutation, if

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{L}\\mathsf{Kr}(\\mathbf{M}\_{i}) \\geq 2|\\mathcal{Y}| + L - 1.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si121.png)(3.19) 

Below, we describe the main steps of the demonstration to reach a result based on using *L* = 3![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si122.png) labels drawn from *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si7.png) per training sample **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png) to enable the identification of the transition distribution *T*(*X*) = *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*, *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si68.png) and clean distribution *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si70.png).

This demonstration assumes that the noisy label is informative, which is achieved with rank(*T*(*X*)) = |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si124.png) (i.e., *T*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si71.png) is full rank) ([Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140)). Based on this assumption, [Liu (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140) proposes a theorem that states that *L* = 3![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si122.png) informative i.i.d. noisy labels are both sufficient and necessary to identify *T*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si71.png). Recalling that *Ỹ*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si125.png) corresponds to **M**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si113.png), where **M**[*i*]\[*j*, *k*\] = *p*(*Ỹ*[*i*] = **y**[*k*]|*Y* = **y**[*j*], *X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si126.png), we have that **M**[*i*] = *T*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si127.png) for all *i* ∈ {1, 2, 3}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si128.png). If *T*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si71.png) is full rank, then all rows in {**M**[*i*]}[*i* = 1]³![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si129.png) are independent, so the Kruskal ranks satisfy Kr(**M**[1]) = Kr(**M**[2]) = Kr(**M**[3]) = |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si130.png), leading to

$\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{3}\\mathsf{Kr}(\\mathbf{M}\_{i}) = 3|\\mathcal{Y}| \\geq 2|\\mathcal{Y}| + 2,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si131.png)(3.20) 

which proves sufficiency ([Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140)). The necessity is proven only for binary classification by showing that less than 3 informative labels do not guarantee identifiability ([Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140)). Such necessity part of the proof still appears to be incomplete since it shows only the binary classification problem. In addition, the assumption that *L* = 3![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si122.png) informative i.i.d. noisy samples may be hard to meet in practice.

A similar identifiability result has been achieved from extensions of the Dawid-Skene model ([Dawid and Skene, 1979](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0370)) that was designed to learn from crowd-sourced data. This problem assumes to have *M* annotators labeling the training samples, where the goal of the model is to estimate the latent true label of the training samples. Under the Dawid-Skene model, we have:

$p({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,1},...,{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,M}|\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) = \\sum\\limits\_{y}\\prod\\limits\_{m}p({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,m}|\\mathbf{y}\_{i},\\mathbf{x}\_{i})p(\\mathbf{y}\_{i}|\\mathbf{x}\_{i}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si132.png)(3.21) 

which assumes that the crowd-sourced labels ${\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,m}\\}}\_{m = 1}^{M}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si133.png) are independent given the true sample label **y**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si134.png). The estimation of the transition matrices ${\\{ p({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,m}|\\mathbf{y}\_{i},\\mathbf{x}\_{i})\\}}\_{m = 1}^{M}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si135.png) and prior *p*(**y**[*i*]|**x**[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si136.png) has been proposed with the Expectation-Maximization algorithm ([Dempster et al., 1977](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0395)). More reliable methods that do not make the conditional independence assumption from [(3.21)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq21) have been proposed ([Traganitis et al., 2018](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1740); [Ibrahim et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0755)), but they are based on higher-order statistics that are harder to estimate given the usual limited amount of training labels per sample. Using tensor algebra, [Traganitis et al. (2018)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1740) show that the identifiability of the transition matrices requires that at least three transition matrices in ${\\{ p({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,m}|\\mathbf{y}\_{i},\\mathbf{x}\_{i})\\}}\_{m = 1}^{M}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si135.png) have full column ranks, or in other words, that at least three annotators have different responses to different classes, resulting in at least three matrices that do not have two co-linear columns. Note that this identifiability result agrees with the one proposed by [Liu (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140), even though they were proposed to solve slightly different, but related problems, namely: noisy-label learning ([Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140)) and crowd-sourced true label ([Traganitis et al., 2018](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1740)).

Another recently published pre-print paper ([Nguyen et al., 2023](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1330)) has a similar motivation to solve the identifiability problem by stating that a single noisy label per training sample does not allow the learning of a unique solution unless that clean label samples are available or strong assumptions are made. [Nguyen et al. (2023)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1330) define identifiability as the ability to recover the exact distribution parameters given a set of observed variables, where ∀*θ*, *θ*^′ ∈ *Θ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si137.png); if *θ* ≠ *θ*^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si138.png) then *p*(*X*|*θ*) ≠ *p*(*X*|*θ*^′)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si139.png), where *p*(*X*|*θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si140.png) represents a distribution of *X* using a function parameterized by *θ* ∈ *Θ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si2.png). The noisy label learning problem can then be formulated as a multinomial mixture model ([Nguyen et al., 2023](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1330)), as follows:

$p(\\widetilde{Y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x})p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x})\\mathsf{Mult}(\\widetilde{Y};N,\\rho\_{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si141.png)(3.22) 

where *p*(*Y* = **y**|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si142.png) is the mixture coefficient, and Mult(*Ỹ*; *N*, *ρ*[**y**])![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si143.png) is a mixture component formed by a multinomial distribution with number of trials denoted by *N* ∈ ℕ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si144.png) and success probability vector represented by |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si145.png) classes *ρ*[**y**] ∈ *Δ*^(|𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si146.png). Such mixture model formulation of the noisy-label learning problem in [(3.22)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq22) allows us to borrow the identifiability constraints from the study of mixture models. More specifically, using Lemma 2.2 from ([Kim, 1984](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0885)) and Theorem 4.2 from ([Elmore and Wang, 2003](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0470)), we can conclude that the mixture model [(3.22)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq22) is identifiable (up to label permutation) if *N* ≥ 2|𝒴| − 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si147.png). In other words, the noisy label learning formulated as a mixture of multinomial models is identifiable, if we have at least 2|𝒴| − 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si148.png) noisy labels per training sample.

Note that the result by [Nguyen et al. (2023)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1330) is more conservative than the results by [Liu (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140) and [Traganitis et al. (2018)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1740) since ([Nguyen et al., 2023](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1330)) requires a number of labels that is linear in the number of classes, instead of the fixed number of labels per class from [Liu (2022)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140); [Traganitis et al. (2018)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1740). However, note that the identifiability result in ([Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140); [Traganitis et al., 2018](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1740)) requires a minimum number annotators to have different responses to different classes, which can be hard to achieve in practice, while ([Nguyen et al., 2023](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1330)) does not make such strong assumption. Nevertheless, all results ([Liu, 2022](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1140); [Traganitis et al., 2018](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1740); [Nguyen et al., 2023](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1330)) show that in order to accurately estimate the model parameters, we need to obtain multiple noisy labels for each training sample. Interestingly, the need for multiple noisy labels per training sample is a result that was also informally concluded from the bias-variance decomposition from Section [3.2.3](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#s0030) to enable the estimation of the intrinsic noise function N(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si24.png). The results in this section suggest that noisy-label training algorithms should need multiple labels per training sample, which is generally known as a multi-rater problem.

## 3.4 PAC learning and noisy-label learning

This section is based on the literature review provided by [Jabbari (2010)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775) on the use of Valiant's probably approximately correct (PAC) model of learning ([Valiant, 1984](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1775)) to explain noisy-label learning. PAC learning aims to find a learning algorithm that estimates an accurate binary target concept using a finite number of training examples. The learning algorithm estimates the target concept by selecting from a set of binary valued concept functions, where this set is called the concept class. Even though the learning algorithm aims to find highly accurate target concept estimates, the stochasticity of the sampling of training examples means that the learning algorithm can fail with some probability. During this process, the learning algorithm can use a number of examples that is polynomial in the inverse of its estimation error and the inverse of its probability of failure. The original PAC-learning model ([Valiant, 1984](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1775)) assumes that the labels of training examples are clean, so the theory needs adaptation when dealing with label noise.

In this section, a concept is defined by *c* : 𝒳 → {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si149.png), where the concept class 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) is a set of concepts over 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si27.png), or a probabilistic concept defined by *c* : 𝒳 → \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si151.png). The set of all probability distributions in 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si27.png) is denoted by 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si152.png). Assuming that we have a specific 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png) and *c* is a probabilistic concept, then the oracle EX(*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si154.png) is a procedure that produces examples (**x**, **y**) ∈ 𝒳 × {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si155.png), where the instance **x** ∼ 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si156.png), the label **y** ∼ Bernoulli(*c*(**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si157.png), and repeated calls to EX(*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si154.png) produce independent samplings. The support of 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si158.png), denoted by supp(𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si159.png), is the smallest closed set $\\widehat{\\mathcal{X}} \\subseteq \\mathcal{X}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si160.png) with $\\mathsf{\\Pr}\\lbrack\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{X} \\smallsetminus \\widehat{\\mathcal{X}}\\rbrack = 0$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si161.png), so all instances of examples produced by EX(*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si154.png) are in supp(𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si159.png). Multi-sets 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si13.png) of elements in 𝒳 × {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si162.png) are called samples over 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si27.png), where the multiplicity that examples occur in a sample contains important information. Furthermore, in a binary classification task where the target concept *c* : 𝒳 → {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si149.png), the training set is represented by a sample of examples produced by EX(*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si154.png), and a procedure (i.e., the learning algorithm) predicts the labels of potentially unseen instances from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si158.png) (forming the test set).

PAC-learning can be defined as follows ([Valiant, 1984](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1775); [Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)): A concept class 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) is PAC-learnable if there is a learning algorithm ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) and *m* : (0, 0.5) × (0, 0.5) → ℕ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si164.png) such that for any *c*^(\*) ∈ 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si165.png), for all *ϵ*, *δ* ∈ (0, 0.5)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si166.png) and for any 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png), if ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) can access EX(*c*^(\*), 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si167.png) and inputs *ϵ* and *δ*, then with probability at least 1 − *δ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si168.png), after seeing a sample 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si13.png) of *m*(*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si169.png) examples, where *m*(*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si169.png) is polynomial in $\\frac{1}{\\epsilon}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si170.png) and $\\frac{1}{\\delta}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si171.png), ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) outputs a concept *c* ∈ 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si172.png) that satisfies Pr [**x** ∼ 𝒟]\[*c*(**x**) ≠ *c*^(\*)(**x**)\] ≤ *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si173.png). Note that the error *ϵ* happens because ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) only sees a finite number of examples. Also, the learning algorithm does not need to succeed all the time. In fact, it can fail with probability at most *δ*, which happens when the examples poorly represent the distribution 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si158.png). Increasing the sample size results in a reduction of *ϵ* and *δ*. Learning complexity depends on the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension (VC-dimension) of the concept class, defined below.

The VC-dimension *d* of a concept class 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) over the input space 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si27.png) is defined as follows ([Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 2015](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1795); [Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)): if arbitrarily large finite sets $\\widehat{\\mathcal{X}} \\subseteq \\mathcal{X}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si160.png) can be shattered by 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png), then the VC-dimension is ∞; otherwise, the VC-dimension is the cardinality of the largest $\\widehat{\\mathcal{X}} \\subseteq \\mathcal{X}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si160.png) that can be shattered by 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png), where shattering is defined as ([Kearns and Vazirani, 1994](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0875); [Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)): let $\\widehat{\\mathcal{X}} = \\{\\mathbf{x}\_{1},...,\\mathbf{x}\_{m}\\} \\subseteq \\mathcal{X}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si174.png) and *Π*[𝒞](𝒳) = {(*c*(**x**[1]), ...*c*(**x**[*M*]))|*c* ∈ 𝒞}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si175.png). If *Π*[𝒞](𝒳) = {0, 1}^(*M*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si176.png), then $\\widehat{\\mathcal{X}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si177.png) is shattered by 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png). Finally, a concept class 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) is PAC-learnable if and only if it has VC-dimension *d* < ∞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si178.png) ([Blumer et al., 1986](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0185); [Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)).

We now extend PAC-learning to problems involving label noise. The label noise model over 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si27.png) is a mapping *Φ* : 2^𝒳 × 𝒟[𝒳] × 𝒳 → 2^(\[0, 1\])![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si179.png), which is deterministic if |*Φ*(*c*, 𝒟, **x**)| = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si180.png) for all *c* ∈ 2^𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si181.png), 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png), **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png), else it is non-deterministic. When we fix the distribution 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si158.png) and concept *c*, we can define the Φ-noisy concept with the function *Φ*[*c*, 𝒟] : 𝒳 → \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si182.png), which allows the definition of the oracle with EX[*Φ*](*c*, 𝒟) = EX(*Φ*[*c*, 𝒟], 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si183.png) ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)). This noisy concept defines a probabilistic concept from *c* by applying a label noise process according to *Φ*[*c*, 𝒟]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si184.png) and 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si158.png) via EX(*Φ*[*c*, 𝒟], 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si185.png). For example, assume that *c*(**x**) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si186.png), then if *Φ*(*c*, 𝒟, **x**) = 0.4![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si187.png), then EX[*Φ*](*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si188.png) labels **x** with 1 with probability 40%, which results in a probability of 60% of mislabeling **x**. The probability of mislabeling can be defined as the noise rate *n**r*[*c*, 𝒟](**x**) = |*c*(**x**) − *Φ*[*c*, 𝒟](**x**)|![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si189.png) ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)).

The noisy concept *Φ*[*c*, 𝒟] : 𝒳 → \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si182.png) can be deterministic or non-deterministic. For the deterministic case, the oracle EX(*Φ*[*c*, 𝒟], 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si185.png) runs the following steps ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)):

1.  **1.**  Draw example (**x**, *c*(**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si190.png) from oracle EX(*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si154.png)
2.  **2.**  With probability *n**r*[*c*, 𝒟](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si191.png), let **y** = 1 − *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si192.png), else **y** = *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si193.png)
3.  **3.**  Return (**x**, **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si194.png)

For the non-deterministic case, the oracle EX(*Φ*[*c*, 𝒟], 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si185.png) runs the following steps ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)):

1.  **1.**  Draw example (**x**, *c*(**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si190.png) from oracle EX(*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si154.png)
2.  **2.**  Non-deterministically, pick a value *p*^′ ∈ *Φ*(*c*, 𝒟, **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si195.png)
3.  **3.**  With probability *p*^′ = |*c*(**x**) − *p*^′|![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si196.png), let **y** = 1 − *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si192.png), else **y** = *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si193.png)
4.  **4.**  Return (**x**, **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si194.png)

Using the label noise model defined above, we define a variant of Valiant's PAC learning model.

A concept class 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) is PAC[*ϵ*, *δ*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si197.png)\-learnable with respect to label noise model Φ, *ϵ*, *δ* ∈ \[0, 0.5)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si198.png), and a class of distributions $\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}} \\subseteq \\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathcal{X}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si199.png) if there exists a learning algorithm ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) and function *m* : (0, 0.5) × (0, 0.5) → ℕ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si164.png) such that for all $\\epsilon \\in (\\underset{\\\_}{\\epsilon},0.5)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si200.png) (assuming $\\underset{\\\_}{\\epsilon} \\in \\lbrack 0,0.5)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si201.png)), for all $\\delta \\in (\\underset{\\\_}{\\delta},0.5)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si202.png) (assuming $\\underset{\\\_}{\\delta} \\in \\lbrack 0,0.5)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si203.png)), for all $\\mathcal{D} \\in \\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si204.png), and for all target concepts *c*^(\*) ∈ 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si165.png), the following property is fulfilled ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)): ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png), given *ϵ* and *δ*, requests a sample *S* of *m*(*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si169.png) independent draws from EX(*Φ*[*c*, 𝒟], 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si185.png), where *m*(*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si169.png) is polynomial in $\\frac{1}{\\epsilon}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si170.png) and $\\frac{1}{\\delta}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si171.png); then ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png), with probability  ≥ (1 − *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si205.png), returns a concept *c* ∈ 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si172.png), such that Pr [**x** ∼ 𝒟]\[*c*(**x**) − *c*^(\*)(**x**)\] ≤ *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si206.png) ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)).

Based on the formulation above, we present some basic label noise models such as the random classification noise (RCN) model *Φ*[*r**c**n*(*η*)]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si207.png) by [Angluin and Laird (1988)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0045), which is a deterministic label noise model defined as

$\\Phi\_{rcn(\\eta)}(c,\\mathcal{D},\\mathbf{x}) = \\begin{cases} {(1 - \\eta),} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 1,} \\\\ {\\eta,} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 0,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si208.png)(3.23) 

where *c* ∈ 2^𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si181.png), 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png), **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png). With this model, a learning algorithm ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) draws an example (**x**, **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si194.png) from EX[*Φ*[*r**c**n*(*η*)]](*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si209.png) and **y** = *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si193.png) with probability 1 − *η*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si210.png), and **y** = 1 − *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si192.png) with probability *η*. Note that this model defines the symmetric noise model for a binary classification problem, where the noisy concept for **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png) only depends on *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si211.png). With this model, and assuming 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) to be a finite concept class, *η* ∈ \[0, 0.5)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si212.png), [Angluin and Laird (1988)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0045) proved that 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) is PAC[0,0]\-learnable with respect to the *η*\-random classification noise and 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si152.png). [Laird (2012)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0995) extends the PAC[0,0]\-learnable with respect to this *η*\-random classification noise for concept classes of finite VC-dimension.

Such random classification noise model has been generalized to allow different noise rates in different partitions of the space 𝒳 × {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si162.png) ([Decatur, 1997](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0375)). More specifically, assuming *k* ∈ ℕ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si213.png), *η* = (*η*[1], ..., *η*[*k*]) ∈ \[0, 1\]^(*k*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si214.png), *π* = (*π*[1], ..., *π*[*k*]) ⊆ 𝒳 × {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si215.png) denotes a k-tuple of pairwise disjoint sets such that *π*[1]⋃...⋃*π*[*k*] = 𝒳 × {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si216.png), then the (*η*, *π*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si217.png)\-constant-partition classification noise (CPCN) model is defined by

$\\Phi\_{cpcn(\\eta)}(c,\\mathcal{D},\\mathbf{x}) = \\begin{cases} {(1 - \\eta\_{i}),} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 1,} \\\\ {\\eta\_{i},} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 0,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si218.png)(3.24) 

where *c* ∈ 2^𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si181.png), 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png), **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png), and *i* ∈ {1, ..., *k*}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si219.png) with (**x**, *c*(**x**)) ∈ *π*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si220.png). The PAC-learnability of CPNC was proven by [Ralaivola et al. (2006)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1450) by showing the equivalence between CPNC from [(3.24)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq24) and RCN from [(3.23)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq23) ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)).

Another important basic model is the non-deterministic malicious classification noise (MCN) model ([Sloan, 1995](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1615)), defined by

$\\Phi\_{mcn(\\eta)}(c,\\mathcal{D},\\mathbf{x}) = \\begin{cases} {\\lbrack 1 - \\eta,1\\rbrack,} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 1,} \\\\ {\\lbrack 0,\\eta\\rbrack,} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 0,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si221.png)(3.25) 

where *c* ∈ 2^𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si181.png), 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png), and **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png). With this model, a learning algorithm ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) draws an example (**x**, **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si194.png) from EX[*Φ*[*m**c**n*(*η*)]](*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si222.png) and **y** = *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si193.png) with probability at least 1 − *η*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si210.png), and **y** = 1 − *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si192.png) with probability *η*. Assuming that 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) is a finite concept class, and *η* ∈ \[0, 0.5)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si212.png), [Sloan (1995)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1615) proved that 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) is PAC[0,0]\-learnable with respect to *Φ*[*m**c**n*(*η*)]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si223.png) and 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si152.png) ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)).

The label noise models above mostly assume that the noise is independent of the instances, distribution, and target concept, but as we have already seen particularly with instance-dependent label noise, this does not apply to real-world problems ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)). For example, instances are more likely to be mislabeled if the target concept labels part of the instances in their local neighborhood with label 0 and the other part with label 1. An instance-dependent label noise model shown by [Jabbari (2010)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775) is the *ρ*\-distance random classification noise model, defined by

*Φ*[*d**r**b**a**l**l*(*ρ*)](*c*, 𝒟, **x**) = {Pr [**x**^′ ∼ 𝒟]\[*c*(**x**^′) = 1|**x**^′ ∈ DB[*ρ*](**x**)\]},

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si224.png)(3.26) 

where *c* ∈ 2^𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si181.png), 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png), **x** ∈ supp(𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si225.png), and DB[*ρ*](**x**) = {**x**^′ ∈ 𝒳|dist(**x**, **x**^′) ≤ *ρ*}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si226.png), with dist(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si227.png) being a metric on 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si27.png). Note that *Φ*[*d**r**b**a**l**l*(*ρ*)](*c*, 𝒟, **x**) = {0}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si228.png) for **x** ∉ supp(*D*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si229.png). With this model, a learning algorithm ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) draws an example (**x**, **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si194.png) from EX[*Φ*[*d**r**b**a**l**l*(*ρ*)]](*c*, 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si230.png) and **y** = *c*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si193.png) if all points in the *ρ*\-distance ball around **x** have the same label under *c*, otherwise, if points of the two classes lie in the *ρ*\-distance ball around **x**, the **y** will be drawn from {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si231.png) following the distribution of labels within the *ρ*\-distance ball around **x** ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)). This model is proven to be PAC[0,0]\-learnable with respect to *Φ*[*d**r**b**a**l**l*(*ρ*)]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si232.png) and 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si152.png), assuming *ρ* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si233.png) ([Jabbari, 2010](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0775)).

If we do not make any geometric assumptions about the noise, like in [(3.26)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq26) which assumes that noise is potentially large if the nearest neighbors have mixed labels, then we can refer to the Massart ([Diakonikolas et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0420)) and Tsybakov Noise ([Diakonikolas et al., 2021](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0430)) models. The Massart Noise ([Diakonikolas et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0420); [Massart and Nédélec, 2006](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1245)) is defined by

$\\Phi\_{mas(\\alpha)}(c,\\mathcal{D},\\mathbf{x}) = \\begin{cases} {(1 - \\eta(\\mathbf{x},\\alpha)),} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 1,} \\\\ {\\eta(\\mathbf{x},\\alpha),} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 0,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si234.png)(3.27) 

where *c* ∈ 2^𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si181.png), 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png), **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png), *α* ∈ \[0, 0.5)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si235.png), and *η*(**x**, *α*) ∈ \[0, *α*\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si236.png). Hence, the Massart noise in [(3.27)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq27) is a noise model that has an instance-dependent upper-bounded noise rate *η*(**x**, *α*) ≤ *α*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si237.png) that extends the RCN noise in [(3.23)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq23) which has a fixed *η*(**x**) = *η*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si238.png) for all **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png). The Tsybakov noise ([Diakonikolas et al., 2021](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0430); [Mammen and Tsybakov, 1999](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1230)) generalizes the Massart noise by replacing the fixed upper bound *α* by a probability that is arbitrarily close to 0.5 for a fraction of the examples, as follows:

$\\Phi\_{tsy(\\alpha,A)}(c,\\mathcal{D},\\mathbf{x}) = \\begin{cases} {(1 - \\eta(\\mathbf{x};\\alpha,A)),} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 1,} \\\\ {\\eta(\\mathbf{x};\\alpha,A),} & {\\text{if~}c(\\mathbf{x}) = 0,} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si239.png)(3.28) 

where *c* ∈ 2^𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si181.png), 𝒟 ∈ 𝒟[𝒳]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si153.png), **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si123.png), and for any *t* ∈ (0, 0.5\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si240.png) we have $\\mathsf{\\Pr}\_{\\mathbf{x} \\sim \\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathcal{X}}}\\lbrack\\eta(\\mathbf{x};\\alpha,A) \\geq 0.5 - t\\rbrack \\leq At^{\\frac{\\alpha}{1 - \\alpha}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si241.png).

Many papers studied the PAC learnability of the halfspace concept class for the Massart and Tsybakov noise models defined above in [(3.27)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq27) and [(3.28)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq28). The halfspace concept class 𝒞![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si150.png) is defined by *c*(**x**) = sign(**w**^⊤**x** − *θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si242.png), where **w** ∈ ℝ^(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si243.png) is a weight vector, *θ* ∈ ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si244.png) is a threshold, and sign(*u*) =  + 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si245.png) if *u* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si246.png) and sign(*u*) =  − 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si247.png) otherwise. The learnability with the halfspace concept class is a fundamental machine learning problem ([Rosenblatt, 1958](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1500)), which has been proved to be PAC-learnable ([Valiant, 1984](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1775)) if no label noise is present. However, with agnostic noise ([Kearns et al., 1992](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0870); [Haussler, 2018](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0665)), where an arbitrary *η* < 0.5![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si248.png) fraction of the labels are corrupted, the learning of the halfspace concept class becomes computationally intractable ([Diakonikolas et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0420); [Guruswami and Raghavendra, 2009](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0615); [Feldman et al., 2006](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0500); [Daniely, 2016](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0360)). With the simpler RCN noise model presented in [(3.23)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq23), where labels are perturbed in an instance-independent manner with a fixed probability *η* ∈ \[0, 0.5)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si212.png), the learning of the halfspace concept class becomes feasible ([Diakonikolas et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0420); [Blum et al., 1998](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0175)).

The Massart noise model in [(3.27)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq27) ([Massart and Nédélec, 2006](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1245)) is more challenging than RCN, but it is not as complicated as the agnostic learning, and for this reason it has become an important instance-dependent noise model to be studied. [Diakonikolas et al. (2019)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0420) successfully proved the PAC-learnability of the halfspace concept class by presenting a learning algorithm ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) for all *α* ∈ (0, 0.5)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si249.png), on a set of i.i.d. examples from EX[*Φ*[*m**a**s*(*α*)]](*c*^(\*), 𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si250.png), where *c*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si251.png) is an unknown halfspace on ℝ^(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si252.png). ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si163.png) is polynomial in *d*, *b*, $\\frac{1}{\\epsilon}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si170.png), where *b* is an upper bound on the bit complexity of the examples, and outputs a concept *c* that satisfies Pr [**x** ∼ 𝒟]\[*c*(**x**) ≠ *c*^(\*)(**x**)\] ≤ *η* + *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si253.png). It is important to mention that many other papers provided similar results for the Massart noise model ([Awasthi et al., 2015](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0075), [2016](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0080); [Zhang et al., 2017c](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2145); [Yan and Zhang, 2017](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1995); [Zhang, 2018](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2095)), with the results above being one of the latest to be published and making less restrictive assumptions on the distribution.

The Tsybakov noise in [(3.28)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#deq28) is more challenging than the Massart noise, particularly when *α* decreases, where previous papers recognized that a necessary and sufficient condition to learn halfspaces with this noise model is a number of examples that is exponential in 1/*α*![Image](images/B9780443154416000125/si254.png) ([Diakonikolas et al., 2021](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0430)). The proposal of a tractable learning algorithm for the homogeneous halfspaces concept class^([^(39)](#fn39))

The use of Valiant's PAC learning model ([Valiant, 1984](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1775)) is a powerful tool to unequivocally establish the learnability of certain concept classes for some data distributions under particular noise models. While the noise models presented in this section can adequately represent the noise models explained in previous sections, the concept classes tend to be too simple to represent the complex classifiers based on deep learning models. In general, finite concept classes or finite VC dimension concept classes are assumed in the problems above, but it is unclear if deep learning models can in general be considered to be a member of such concept classes. Hence, it is important that theoretical and applied noisy-label learning researchers collaborate more to enable new discoveries that can improve our general understand of noisy-label learning.

## 3.5 Conclusion

The theoretical tools presented in this chapter represent the initial attempts to better understand the noisy-label learning problem. Many results achieved from the bias-variance decomposition and the identifiability of the label transition distribution matrix suggest that there may be a need for multiple labels per training sample. A similar problem has been studied by many computer vision and machine learning researchers for addressing an issue that is related to the noisy-label learning problem, which is the multi-rater learning ([Guan et al., 2018](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0610); [Jensen et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0780); [Jungo et al., 2018](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0825); [Baumgartner et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br0105); [Sudre et al., 2019](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br1660); [Yu et al., 2020a](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml#br2065)). In multi-rater learning, each training instance has many labels provided by multiple annotators (who may disagree on the annotation), and the goal is to train a model that uses such uncertainty information to better understand the reasoning behind the disagreement among annotators. There are clear similarities between the two problems, so it is expected that these two problems will merge in the near future. The use of PAC learning to study the types of classifiers that can be learned under certain types of label noise is interesting, but the classifiers and classification problems being investigated are still not as complex as what applied researchers are studying. Therefore, it is necessary that applied and theoretical researchers actively collaborate to improve our understanding of noisy-label learning problem.

# Chapter 4: Noisy-label learning techniques

Loss function design, training algorithm, training data processing, and model architecture

## Abstract

In this chapter, we introduce the main techniques developed to mitigate the noisy-label learning problem. We present a hierarchical structure of the techniques, enabling us to provide a clearer explanation of the relationships between them. In addition to detailed explanations, we provide practical examples in simulated noisy-label learning problems. The understanding of this chapter is essential to facilitate the introduction of the state-of-the-art approaches that are presented in Chapter [5](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml).

### Keywords

Noisy-label learning techniques; Noisy-label learning loss functions; Noisy-label learning algorithms; Noisy-label learning data processing; Noisy-label learning model

## 4.1 Introduction

In this chapter, we explain the main techniques developed to address the learning with noisy-label problem. Our explanation follows the hierarchy presented in [Fig. 4.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0010), which provides an organization of the main approaches proposed by many researchers to solve the problem of learning with label noise. Such hierarchy in [Fig. 4.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0010) and the explanations present in this chapter also follow some of the material introduced by recently published surveys ([Han et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0640); [Song et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1645); [Karimi et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0840); [Cordeiro and Carneiro, 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0325)), but we propose new materials and insights.

![Figure 4.1 Hierarchical structure of the techniques developed to solve noisy-label learning problems.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr001.jpg)

Figure 4.1 Hierarchical structure of the techniques developed to solve noisy-label learning problems.

As explained in Chapter [1](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml), the motivation to design new techniques to handle noisy-label learning problems stems from the overfitting issue generally experienced by regression and classification models based on conventional model architectures (e.g., a multi-layer perceptron) and optimizers (e.g., Adam optimizer ([Kingma and Ba, 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0905))) trained on datasets containing label noise, as shown in [Fig. 4.2](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0015) for regression and [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020) for classification. Note that to facilitate the visualization of the overfitting issue, we reduced the original number of training samples for the instance-dependent noise for a regression problem presented in [Fig. 2.13](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) from 1000 to 200 and increased the number of hidden nodes from 10 to 100. For the classification problem, we also reduced the number of training samples for the instance-dependent noise presented in [Fig. 2.13](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) from 3000 to 300 and increased the number of hidden nodes from 4 to 50.

![Figure 4.2 Overfitting of a regressor.The training of a regressor overfits a training set containing instance-dependent label noise from Fig. 2.13, where we increased the number of nodes from 10 to 100 and decreased the number of training samples from 1000 to 200. The left-most graph shows the training samples (blue points) and the ground truth (red curve), while the right-most graph shows the model output (dashed black line) and the ground truth (red curve), and the middle graph shows the training and testing MSE losses as a function of the number of training epochs.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr002.jpg)

Figure 4.2 Overfitting of a regressor.The training of a regressor overfits a training set containing instance-dependent label noise from [Fig. 2.13](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), where we increased the number of nodes from 10 to 100 and decreased the number of training samples from 1000 to 200. The left-most graph shows the training samples (blue points) and the ground truth (red curve), while the right-most graph shows the model output (dashed black line) and the ground truth (red curve), and the middle graph shows the training and testing MSE losses as a function of the number of training epochs.

![Figure 4.3 Overfitting of a classifier.The training of classifier overfits a training set containing the instance-dependent label noise from Fig. 2.12, where we increased the number of nodes from 4 to 50 and decreased the number of training samples from 3000 to 300. The left-most top plot shows the training samples (each represented by a different color) and the bottom plot shows the testing samples with clean labels, while the right-most top map shows the model output (region colors represent different classes) and the bottom map displays the ground truth, and the middle graph shows the training and testing binary cross-entropy (BCE) losses as a function of the number of training epochs.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr003.jpg)

Figure 4.3 Overfitting of a classifier.The training of classifier overfits a training set containing the instance-dependent label noise from [Fig. 2.12](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), where we increased the number of nodes from 4 to 50 and decreased the number of training samples from 3000 to 300. The left-most top plot shows the training samples (each represented by a different color) and the bottom plot shows the testing samples with clean labels, while the right-most top map shows the model output (region colors represent different classes) and the bottom map displays the ground truth, and the middle graph shows the training and testing binary cross-entropy (BCE) losses as a function of the number of training epochs.

The training with noisy labels for regression and classification in Figs. [4.2](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0015) and [4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020) show the overfitting issue, where the loss in the noisy-label training set decreases and stabilizes at a low value, while the loss in the clean-label testing set reduces at the beginning of the training, and then starts to increase after a certain point in the training. Such problem has been investigated by [Zhang et al. (2017a)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2100) and [Zhang et al. (2021a)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2105), who concluded that deep artificial neural networks can easily fit a random labeling of the training data, which can be considered to be the symmetric label noise presented in Section [2.4.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml). An interesting phenomenon that can be observed in Figs. [4.2](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0015) and [4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020) is the early-learning phenomenon ([Liu et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1120)), which divides the noisy-label training process into two stages: the early learning stage, where the model learns to predict the clean labels even when trained with noisy labels (note the testing loss going down at the beginning of the training), followed by the memorization stage, where the model memorizes the noisy labels and makes incorrect predictions for the testing samples containing clean labels (this is when the testing loss starts to rise in the later training stages).

To mitigate the overfitting to the noisy-label training samples, many papers in the field have proposed many techniques, summarized in [Fig. 4.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0010), that modify one or more of the following core components of regressors and classifiers:

*   •  Loss Function,
*   •  Training Algorithm,
*   •  Data Processing, and
*   •  Model Architecture.

The loss function strategy aims to change regression and classification losses in order to automatically correct mislabelings ([Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1400)), weight training samples ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)), make the loss robust to noisy labels ([Long and Servedio, 2008](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1160)), or regularize the loss according to the early-learning phenomenon ([Liu et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1120)). The training algorithm strategy focuses on changing several stages of the training process, such as by adding a self-supervised pre-training ([Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2190)), introducing meta-parameters to handle noisy-label samples in a bi-level meta-learning optimization ([Ren et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1475)), detecting noisy-label samples, and estimating clean labels with co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)) and co-training ([Yu et al., 2007](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2060)), or by transforming noisy-label learning into a semi-supervised learning problem, where confidently-labeled training samples form the labeled set and the remaining training samples are assumed to be un-labeled. The data-processing strategy aims to modify the training data, with for example adversarial training ([Goodfellow et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0585)), or data augmentation ([Nishi et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1350)). The model architecture strategy introduces new layers trained to learn the label transition model ([Goldberger and Ben-Reuven, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0575)), or graph-based models ([Iscen et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0770)).

In this chapter, we explain each one of the strategies in [Fig. 4.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0010), highlighting the most representative papers for each strategy.

## 4.2 Loss function

Recalling from Section [2.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), the optimization for the regression and classification problems consists of optimizing the model parameters to minimize the following empirical risk:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si1.png)

defined in [(2.7)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), where the loss function can be, for example, the L1 and L2 losses, respectively defined in [(2.6)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) as

$\\ell\_{L1}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = {\\|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} - f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})\\|}\_{1},\\ell\_{L2}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\left\\| \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} - f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\|\_{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si2.png)

or the 0-1 loss, the cross-entropy (CE) loss, the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, the hinge loss, and the negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss for the classification problem, respectively defined in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) as

$\\ell\_{01}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\delta(\\mathbf{y} \\neq \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))),\\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = - \\mathbf{y}^{\\top}\\log(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),\\ell\_{BCE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = - \\mathbf{y}^{\\top}\\log(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - {(1 - \\mathbf{y})}^{\\top}\\log(1 - f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),\\ell\_{HNG}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = - \\max(0,1 - \\mathbf{y}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),\\ell\_{NLL}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = - \\log(f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x})).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si3.png)(4.1) 

In general the methods described in this section are based on modifying the loss functions above to make them more robust to the noise present in the labels of the training samples. We start by describing label noise robust losses that are designed in such a way that they do not penalize too much samples that cannot be fitted by the model, which tends to mitigate overfitting. Then, we explain different strategies to regularize loss functions to make them less prone to overfitting noisy-label samples. The re-weighting of training samples is then discussed, where the goal is to automatically up-weight clean-label samples and down-weight noisy-label samples, where the challenge is on how to design weighting functions that can reliably identify clean and noisy-label samples. Next, we discuss techniques that change the model prediction so it can fit the noisy-label learning, but at the same time produce a clean-label model. Alternatively, training labels can be automatically modified to represent their most likely latent clean-label. We conclude the chapter with the presentation of loss functions designed to adapt from a noisy-label training domain to a clean-label domain.

### 4.2.1 Label noise robust loss

The design of loss functions that are intrinsically robust to noisy labels aims to avoid the need to estimate noise rate, particularly regarding the transition between ambiguous labels (e.g., estimating the probability of mislabeling an image of a cat with the label dog). We start the discussion on robust loss with a theoretically motivated loss function by [Van Rooyen et al. (2015)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1790), who studied the paper ([Long and Servedio, 2008](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1160)), which claims that convex losses are not robust to the random classification noise (RCN) ([Angluin and Laird, 1988](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0045)) defined in [(3.23)](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml) over the concept class of linear classifiers. This means that training under these conditions can produce a classification performance equivalent to random guessing. However, [Van Rooyen et al. (2015)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1790) show that a convex loss that is negatively unbounded, formed by modifying the hinge loss to not be clamped at zero avoids the robustness issue described in ([Long and Servedio, 2008](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1160)). Such a loss is the unhinged loss defined by

$\\ell\_{UNH}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = 1 - {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si4.png)(4.2) 

[Fig. 4.4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0025) shows the graphs of a few examples of classification losses, including the unhinged loss from [(4.2)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq4). Also, [Fig. 4.5](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0030) shows an example of the training of a classifier with the robust loss function in [(4.2)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq4). Although the result above was limited to binary classification problems and linear classifiers, it inspired many researchers to study other types of robust loss functions that could avoid overfitting noisy-label training samples.

![Figure 4.4 Loss functions.Typical loss functions used for classification problems, and some examples of robust losses, such as MSE, MAE, Unhinged, and MAE + CE.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr004.jpg)

Figure 4.4 Loss functions.Typical loss functions used for classification problems, and some examples of robust losses, such as MSE, MAE, Unhinged, and MAE + CE.

![Figure 4.5 Classifier trained with a loss function robust to label noise.The training of classifier with the unhinged loss from (4.2) using the same problem described in Fig. 4.3. Note that this noisy-label robust loss no longer overfits to the noisy-label training set and produces a model output (region colors represent different classes) that is reasonably similar to the ground truth at the bottom map on the right.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 4.5](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf0580) Classifier trained with a loss function robust to label noise.The training of classifier with the unhinged loss from [(4.2)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq4) using the same problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020). Note that this noisy-label robust loss no longer overfits to the noisy-label training set and produces a model output (region colors represent different classes) that is reasonably similar to the ground truth at the bottom map on the right.

[Manwani and Sastry (2013)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1240) define the noise tolerance as a property of learning methods that can produce a binary classifier with the same classification accuracy, independently if they are trained with or without label noise. They concluded that risk minimization under 0-1 loss function has outstanding noise tolerance and MSE loss is robust only to symmetric noise. Then [Ghosh et al. (2017)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0550) extended the work above by defining the noise tolerance property for learning methods that can produce a multi-class deep-learning classifier. This work concluded that the MAE loss is tolerant to symmetric and asymmetric label noise, cross-entropy (CE) loss is not tolerant to any label noise, and MSE loss is in between MAE and CE losses. [Kumar et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0975) extended the noise tolerance property for learning methods that can produce a multi-label classifier and concluded that Hamming loss is robust to symmetric multi-label noise.

Even though MAE is known to be a robust training loss, it suffers from slow convergence, with poor fitting of hard classification problems ([Song et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1645)). Hence, to combine the convergence of CE loss and robustness of MAE loss, [Zhang and Sabuncu (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2175) proposed the noise-robust loss that combines CE and MAE losses, as follows (see MAE+CE in [Fig. 4.4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0025)):

$\\ell\_{MAE + CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\frac{1 - {({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))}^{q}}{q},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si5.png)(4.3) 

where *q* ∈ (0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si6.png). In ([Zhang and Sabuncu, 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2175)), it is shown that when $\\lim\_{q\\rightarrow 0}\\ell\_{MAE + CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si7.png) and when *q* = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si8.png), [(4.3)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq5) approximates the unhinged loss, so a small value for *q* facilitates training convergence, but risks overfitting, and large *q* leads to slower convergence, but better robustness to label noise. The loss in [(4.3)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq5) has been empirically shown to work well for closed-set and open-set label noise. It is possible to find loss functions that have been proposed to have good convergence and solid robustness to label loss, such as the two-temperature loss based on the Tsallis divergence ([Amid et al., 2019b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0035)), bi-tempered loss based on the Bregman divergence ([Amid et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0030)), and the symmetric cross entropy (SCE) loss ([Wang et al., 2019c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1865)) that is defined by

$\\ell\_{SCE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = - \\alpha({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\log(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))) - \\beta(f\_{\\theta}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\top}\\log(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si9.png)(4.4) 

where log (0) = *A*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si10.png), with *A* < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si11.png) being a constant. In the loss in [(4.4)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq6), the first term is the CE loss, while the second term is the reverse CE loss, which is proved in ([Wang et al., 2019c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1865)) to be robust to label noise.

As already discussed above by [Manwani and Sastry (2013)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1240), the 0-1 loss has outstanding label noise tolerance. Such tolerance is achieved by noting that the 0-1 loss minimizes the (worst-case) adversarial risk ([Lyu and Tsang, 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1185); [Hu et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0740)), assuming that the model is trained from the noisy-label training distribution, and the model should perform well on the worst case estimate of the clean-label testing distribution that is unknown during training. Unfortunately, the 0-1 loss is non-differentiable and has zero gradients almost everywhere, which makes is hard to minimize. Therefore, [Lyu and Tsang (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1185) proposed a surrogate for the 0-1 loss based in curriculum learning. [Ma et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1195) introduced the active passive loss that combines an active (a.k.a. positive) loss that maximizes the confidence of belonging to the labeled class and a passive (a.k.a. negative) loss that minimizes the confidence of belonging to the non-labeled classes. A similar loss function that explores negative and positive learning was explored by [Kim et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0900).

Gradient clipping is a widely known technique to provide generic robustness to training, but [Menon et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1255) showed that this technique is not helpful for training with noisy-label samples. Instead, a more helpful method is based on loss clipping, which provides a better robustness to label noise than CE loss ([Menon et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1255)).

Symmetric losses (i.e., losses where ℓ(*z*) + ℓ( − *z*)=![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si12.png) constant) have been studied by [Charoenphakdee et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0255), who theoretically demonstrated that such losses are robust to label noise. Their paper corroborates the label noise robustness of the unhinged loss ([Van Rooyen et al., 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1790)), which is a symmetric loss. However, in practice, the use of unhinged loss to train complex deep learning models is observed to perform poorly, most likely because of the negative unboundedness of the unhinged loss. They then proposed a new convex barrier hinge loss that is robust to label noise, but not negatively unbounded, even though it is not symmetric everywhere.
