Abstention learning has been explored to prevent the model from training from confusing samples, while training from the non-abstained examples ([Thulasidasan et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1730); [Sachdeva et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1505)). This type of learning relies on the deep abstaining classifier (DAC) that adds an abstention class |𝒴| + 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si13.png), with a loss

$\\ell\_{DAC}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\left( 1 - f\_{\\theta}^{(|\\mathcal{Y}| + 1)}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)\\left( - {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\log\\frac{f\_{\\theta}^{(1..|\\mathcal{Y}|)}(\\mathbf{x})}{1 - f\_{\\theta}^{(|\\mathcal{Y}| + 1)}(\\mathbf{x})} \\right) + \\alpha\\log\\frac{1}{1 - f\_{\\theta}^{(|\\mathcal{Y}| + 1)}(\\mathbf{x})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si14.png)(4.5) 

where *f*[*θ*]^((|𝒴| + 1))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si15.png) denotes the abstention class prediction, and *f*[*θ*]^((1..|𝒴|))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si16.png) the training classes' predictions. In [(4.5)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq7), a large *α* leads the model to not abstain, and on the contrary, when *α* is small, then the model abstains from training all training samples. In general, [Thulasidasan et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1730) showed that DAC works well for many types of noisy-label learning, and [Sachdeva et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1505) demonstrated that abstention learning enables the detection of open-set label noise.

A new family of label noise robust loss functions, referred to as peer loss functions, has been introduced by [Liu and Guo (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1145). These peer loss functions are based on peer prediction mechanisms, where we assume to have multiple classification tasks. The peer loss function is defined by

$\\ell\_{peer}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si17.png)(4.6) 

where $(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si18.png) and $(\\mathbf{x}\_{j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si19.png) are two training samples randomly sampled from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) with replacement. In general, the first term of the peer loss [(4.6)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq8) aims to maximize the stochastic correlation between the noisy labels $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) and model predictions *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si22.png), while minimizing the risk of overfitting by penalizing incorrect correlations between samples and labels from different tasks in the second term of the peer loss. This peer loss is shown to lead to optimal or a near-optimal classifier as if training with the clean-label training set.

[Xu et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1975) proposed the ℒ[DMI]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si23.png), which is a determinant-based mutual-information loss function that is robust to asymmetric label noise. This paper shows that by training with the loss:

ℒ[DMI](𝒟, *θ*) =  − log (DMI(*Ỹ*, *f*[*θ*](*X*))) =  − log (|det (**Q**)|),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si24.png)(4.7) 

where **Q** is a |𝒴| × |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si25.png) matrix representing the joint distribution between *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si26.png) and *f*[*θ*](*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si27.png) computed with

$\\mathbf{Q}\_{\\widetilde{c},c} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}\_{c})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\times \\delta(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\widetilde{c}) = 1),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si28.png)(4.8) 

with *f*[*θ*]^((**y**[*c*]))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si29.png) denoting the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si30.png) output from the model and $\\delta(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\widetilde{c}) = 1)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si31.png) representing the indicator function that is equal to one when $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\widetilde{c}) = 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si32.png), and zero otherwise. [Xu et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1975) show that by training with ℒ[DMI](𝒟, *θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si33.png) from [(4.7)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq9), it is possible to prove that

ℒ[DMI](noisy data, *θ*) = ℒ[DMI](clean data, *θ*) + noise rate.

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si34.png)(4.9) 

Robust losses have been intensively studied, with many papers showing solid theoretical foundations with certain performance guarantees. The main idea explored by the proposed methods is focused on reducing the influence of the loss from misclassified samples and, at the same time, allow well-classified samples to influence the training even after they have already been successfully fit. The main advantage of these robust loss functions, with respect to other techniques that will be presented in the next sections, is that they do not require the estimation of noise rate. However, a major challenge of this strategy is the difficulty to determine if a misclassified sample is mislabeled or is just a hard sample to fit. Consequently, these approaches are limited to problems that are not naturally hard, where the noise rate is not too high and the number of classes is relatively small ([Song et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1645)). Nevertheless, robust loss function can be explored as part of complex noisy-label learning methods that include other techniques to handle label noise.

### 4.2.2 Loss regularization

Loss regularization represents a straightforward way to make the empirical risk minimization (ERM) of [(2.8)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) more robust by avoiding overfitting in general. The optimization using loss regularization is defined as follows

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\Omega(\\theta),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si35.png)(4.10) 

where *Ω*(*θ*) = ∥*θ*∥[2]²![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si36.png) for the Tikhonov regularization (ℓ[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si37.png)\-norm) or *Ω*(*θ*) = ∥*θ*∥[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si38.png) for the ℓ[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si39.png)\-norm regularization for the model parameters ([Tibshirani, 1996](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1735)). [Fig. 4.6](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0035) shows a few examples of loss regularization functions. One of the first papers to propose a deep learning method robust to noisy labels was ([Azadi et al., 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0085)) that introduced a new auxiliary image regularizer (AIR), which is a group sparse norm. This regularizer automatically selects relevant training samples for training and gives them higher learning weights, while irrelevant or noisy samples are forced to have near zero learning weight. This means that only the selected samples will contribute to model learning. The penalization of low entropy predictions is also a common way to regularize the loss function ([Pereyra et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1410)), with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\beta H(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si40.png)(4.11) 

where *H*(*f*[*θ*](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si41.png) measures the negative entropy of the prediction from *f*[*θ*](**x**[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si42.png). Such entropy regularization prevents the model to become over-confident in the prediction of the training samples, mitigating the overfitting of the training set.

![Figure 4.6 Loss regularization.Different types of loss regularization to make training robust to noisy labels. Model regularization constrains model parameters to specific values, as in (4.10). Entropy regularization constrains model predictions to have high entropy, as in (4.11). Early stopping halts training before model convergence using the training loss. Prediction regularization constrains model predictions to be similar to outputs from the model trained at the early training epochs, as in (4.14).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 4.6](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf0770) Loss regularization.Different types of loss regularization to make training robust to noisy labels. Model regularization constrains model parameters to specific values, as in [(4.10)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq12). Entropy regularization constrains model predictions to have high entropy, as in [(4.11)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq13). Early stopping halts training before model convergence using the training loss. Prediction regularization constrains model predictions to be similar to outputs from the model trained at the early training epochs, as in [(4.14)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq16).

A simple, but powerful regularization technique for noisy-label learning is early-stopping ([Rolnick et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1490); [Li et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1065)), which we already discussed informally in Figs. [4.2](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0015) and [4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020). [Li et al. (2020b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1065) show that by running empirical risk minimization with CE or MSE loss functions using a small number of epochs (i.e., early stopping) allows the learning of a model that fits well the clean labels and ignores the noisy label. Naturally, because of the small number of epochs, the learned model will be close to its initialization, and the farther it moves from this initialization, the more likely it fits the noisy label. Estimating the number of epochs is not straightforward, but [Li et al. (2020b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1065) showed that this number is a linear function of the number of data clusters *K* > |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si43.png) in the training set. [Hu et al. (2019b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0735) extended this idea with the regularization function:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\lambda{\\|\\theta - \\theta(0)\\|}\_{2}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si44.png)(4.12) 

where *θ*(0)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si45.png) denotes the model initialization, which explicitly forces the learning to keep the estimated *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si46.png) close to its initialization *θ*(0)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si45.png). Alternatively, [Hu et al. (2019b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0735) proposed the introduction of a sample-wise training variable **b**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si47.png) to be used when fitting the *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si48.png) training label, as follows:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta,{\\{\\mathbf{b}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) + \\lambda\\mathbf{b}\_{i}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si49.png)(4.13) 

where **b**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si47.png) is initialized as a |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si50.png)\-vector of zeros. The regularization in [(4.13)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq15) worked better than the one in [(4.12)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq14) and the early stopping of ([Li et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1065)). Early-stopping was also explored in the early-learning regularization (ELR) by [Liu et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1120), who introduced a regularization to boost the gradient of training samples with clean labels and to dampen the gradient of training samples with noisy labels, once the training passes the early-learning phase. This is reached with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) + \\lambda\\log\\left( 1 - f\_{\\theta}{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})}^{\\top}\\mathbf{t}\_{i} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si51.png)(4.14) 

where ⟨., .⟩![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si52.png) represents the inner product operator, and **t**[*i*] ∈ *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si53.png) denotes a target probability for sample *i*, which is estimated with a moving average at iteration *k* with **t**[*i*]^((*k*)) = *β***t**[*i*]^((*k* − 1)) + (1 − *β*)*f*[*θ*]^((*k*))(**x**[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si54.png), with *β* ∈ \[0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si55.png). When fitting a clean label, the loss term of [(4.14)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq16) goes to zero, but the regularizer becomes negative because *f*[*θ*](**x**[*i*]) ≈ **t**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si56.png), boosting the gradient of clean-label samples, forcing the continuing learning from the clean-label samples. On the other hand, for a noisy label, the loss term of [(4.14)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq16) increases, which is compensated by the regularizer that becomes negative since the target **t**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si57.png) tends to keep the early learning fitted label, which is likely to be the clean label that coincides with the model output *f*[*θ*](**x**[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si42.png) (see [Fig. 4.7](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0040)).

![Figure 4.7 Classifier trained with a regularized loss function.The training of classifier with the ELR loss from (4.14) using the same problem described in Fig. 4.3. Note that the ELR loss is robust to the noisy-label samples and produces a model output (region colors represent different classes) that is relatively similar to the ground truth at the bottom map on the right. Also note how the loss reduces boundlessly.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 4.7](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf0845) Classifier trained with a regularized loss function.The training of classifier with the ELR loss from [(4.14)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq16) using the same problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020). Note that the ELR loss is robust to the noisy-label samples and produces a model output (region colors represent different classes) that is relatively similar to the ground truth at the bottom map on the right. Also note how the loss reduces boundlessly.

An alternative form of regularization can be achieved via the general-purpose dropout ([Jindal et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0810)) or nested dropout ([Chen et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0280)) regularizers. Dropout ([Jindal et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0810)) randomly selects nodes to be switched off during a training iteration, which means that these nodes do not contribute to the forward pass and their weights are not updated during the backward pass. On the other hand, nested dropout ([Chen et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0280)) drops feature activations instead of nodes. Both types of regularization have been proposed in the context of regularizing the training of a model to avoid overfitting the training data. As a result, their application to noisy-label learning is quite natural and has produced interesting results, especially when combined with sophisticated noisy-label learning techniques ([Chen et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0280)).

### 4.2.3 Loss re-weighting

In the loss re-weighting approach, each training sample is weighted differently during training, where samples with noisy labels are assigned smaller weights, while samples with clean labels are assigned larger weights ([Wang et al., 2017a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1840); [Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)). As shown in Figs. [4.8](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0045) and [4.9](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0050), the optimization problem is defined as

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si58.png)(4.15) 

where $w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si59.png) is the function that returns the weight assigned to the training sample $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si60.png). Therefore, the noisy-label training samples with smaller values of $w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si59.png) in [(4.15)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq17) will have smaller influence to the training of the model *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si22.png).

![Figure 4.8 Loss re-weighting.The basic architecture of loss re-weighting techniques consists of leveraging information from the model prediction fθ(x) and training noisy label \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}Image to produce a weight for the training sample. In general, samples that are likely to contain noisy labels are weighted down to prevent overfitting to those samples, while clean-label samples are weighted up.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr008.jpg)

Figure 4.8 Loss re-weighting.The basic architecture of loss re-weighting techniques consists of leveraging information from the model prediction *f*[*θ*](**x**) and training noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) to produce a weight for the training sample. In general, samples that are likely to contain noisy labels are weighted down to prevent overfitting to those samples, while clean-label samples are weighted up.

![Figure 4.9 Classifier trained with loss re-weighting.The training of classifier with the loss re-weighting in (4.15) using the same problem described in Fig. 4.3. We train for 100 iterations, where the first 50 iterations are with unweighted samples, and the remaining are with weighted samples, using a Gaussian mixture model to classify samples into clean or noise based on their loss values. At the bottom, in the middle, we also show a histogram of confidence for the clean and noisy-label samples and a scatter plot of the weight versus loss (note that samples with large loss value have zero weight).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 4.9](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cs0025_2) Classifier trained with loss re-weighting.The training of classifier with the loss re-weighting in [(4.15)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq17) using the same problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020). We train for 100 iterations, where the first 50 iterations are with unweighted samples, and the remaining are with weighted samples, using a Gaussian mixture model to classify samples into clean or noise based on their loss values. At the bottom, in the middle, we also show a histogram of confidence for the clean and noisy-label samples and a scatter plot of the weight versus loss (note that samples with large loss value have zero weight).

Assuming a binary classification problem, [Liu and Tao (2015)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130) formulate noisy-label learning as a domain adaptation problem, where the source domain is represented by the noisy-label training set, and the target domain, by the clean-label testing set. Then, ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)) propose the use of importance re-weighting ([Gretton et al., 2009](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0595)), which re-weights the loss expectation with respect to the joint probability distribution of the sample and true label, as follows:

$\\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) \\sim p(X,Y)}\\lbrack\\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{p(X = \\mathbf{x},Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{p(X = \\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})}\\left\\lbrack w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si61.png)(4.16) 

where

$w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\frac{p(X = \\mathbf{x},Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{p(X = \\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} = \\frac{p(Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})p(X = \\mathbf{x})}{p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})p(X = \\mathbf{x})} = \\frac{p(Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})}{p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si62.png)(4.17) 

Then, ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)) proves that

$p(Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x}) - \\rho\_{- \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}}{(1 - \\rho\_{+ 1} - \\rho\_{- 1})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si63.png)(4.18) 

where

$\\rho\_{- 1} = p(\\widetilde{Y} = + 1|Y = - 1),\\rho\_{+ 1} = p(\\widetilde{Y} = - 1|Y = + 1),\\rho\_{- \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{X}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si64.png)(4.19) 

with $\\rho\_{- \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si65.png) representing a consistent estimator of noise rate. The paper ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)) shows how to estimate $p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si66.png) and the label transition probabilities in [(4.19)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq21) to allow the computation of the weight $w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si59.png) in [(4.17)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq19).

Selecting easy samples ([Bengio et al., 2009](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0130); [Kumar et al., 2010](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0980)) or hard samples ([Shrivastava et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1600)) for the early learning part of the training of a general classifier has been shown to improve the learning of neural networks in different scenarios. In noisy-label learning, these strategies have pros and cons. For instance, learning from easy samples first provides more guarantees that the training will be done with clean-label samples, but these easy samples will have small losses and gradients, which can compromise convergence. On the other hand, learning from hard samples first may force the model to learn from not only the hard samples, but also from the noisy-label samples, which can result in overfitting.

Active bias ([Chang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0250)) aims to place high weights to samples containing high variance in their prediction probability over the last *H* training iterations, which implies that these samples are neither easy, nor hard because we should observe small variance for easy and hard training samples. Such strategy is similar to how active learning selects informative samples to be labeled ([Settles, 2012](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1565)). One of the strategies presented in ([Chang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0250)) defines the weight in [(4.15)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq17) as

$w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\frac{1}{Z}(s(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) + \\epsilon),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si67.png)(4.20) 

with *Z* denoting a normalization factor, *ϵ* representing a smoothness constant, and

$s(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\sqrt{\\mathsf{var}\\left( \\left\\{ f\_{\\theta^{t}}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\}\_{t = T - H + 1,...,T} \\right) + \\frac{\\mathsf{var}\\left( \\left\\{ f\_{\\theta^{t}}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\}\_{t = T - H + 1,...,T} \\right)^{2}}{H - 1}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si68.png)(4.21) 

where $\\mathsf{var}\\left( \\left\\{ f\_{\\theta^{t}}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\}\_{t = T - H + 1,...,T} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si69.png) denotes the prediction variance for class $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) for the last *H* training iterations.

The open-set noisy label problem was introduced by [Wang et al. (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1860), who proposed a loss re-weighting mechanism to enable the learning from clean-label samples and avoid the learning from noisy-label samples. Their method has a noisy-label detection method called probabilistic and cumulative Local Outlier Factor algorithm (pcLOF) based on the features of the network, which we will describe in more detail in [(4.69)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq71) of Section [4.3.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0060). This algorithm estimates the probability that a training sample is an outlier, denoted by pcLOF(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si70.png) that outputs a score in \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si71.png). This is followed by the estimation that a training sample belongs to the set of clean-label samples, defined by 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) that contains samples with pcLOF(**x**) ≈ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si73.png), or the set of noisy-label samples, defined by 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si74.png) that contains samples with pcLOF(**x**) ≈ 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si75.png). The model parameters are learned with a loss function that weighs the samples in 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si74.png) with $w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = 1 - \\mathsf{pcLOF}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si76.png) as follows ([Wang et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1860)):

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}| + |\\mathcal{D}\_{n}|}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}}w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si77.png)(4.22) 

[Li et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1060) propose a loss re-weighting mechanism specifically designed for the WebVision dataset ([Li et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1070)). The weighting function is defined based on five challenges present in large-scale noisy datasets, namely: 1) high class imbalances, 2) ambiguity between certain pairs of classes, 3) label noise, 4) training samples that poorly represent classes, and 5) training samples that can belong to multiple classes. The challenges above motivate the design of particular weighting functions that are multiplied together to form the final $w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si59.png) in [(4.15)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq17). Unfortunately, this loss was only tested in the WebVision dataset, and still needs to be verified in other datasets.

The use of Bayesian learning for up-weighting clean-label samples and down-weighting noisy-label samples is explored by [Wang et al. (2017c)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1855). The Reweighted Probabilistic Model (RPM) optimizes the following model [Wang et al. (2017c)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1855):

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta,\\mathbf{w} \\in \\mathcal{W}} - \\log p\_{\\theta}(\\theta) - \\log p\_{w}(\\mathbf{w}) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\mathbf{w}\_{i}\\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si78.png)(4.23) 

where *p*[*θ*](*θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si79.png) is a prior on model parameters, *p*[*w*](**w**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si80.png) is a prior on the weights for the |𝒟|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si81.png) samples denoted by **w** ∈ 𝒲 ⊂ ℝ[+]^(|𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si82.png). The paper ([Wang et al., 2017c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1855)) proposes three types of priors on the weights, namely a bank of Beta distributions, a scaled Dirichlet distribution, and a bank of Gamma distributions, where this prior encourages weights to be close to one, unless the sample appears to be noisy which pushes the weight to be close to zero.

[Arazo et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0050) proposed an influential method to weight samples using a 2-component Beta mixture model (BMM) to automatically cluster clean-label and noisy-label samples. With this method, it is possible to weight each training sample based on its probability of belonging to the clean-label set. More specifically, given the loss values for sample *i* and its respective loss function value $\\ell\_{i} = \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si83.png), the BMM is computed as

$p(\\ell\_{i}) = \\sum\\limits\_{k \\in \\{\\text{noisy,clean}\\}}\\lambda\_{k} \\times p(\\ell\_{i}|k),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si84.png)(4.24) 

where *λ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si85.png) denoted the mixing weights for the *k* ∈ {*n**o**i**s**y*, *c**l**e**a**n*}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si86.png), and *p*(ℓ[*i*]|*k*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si87.png) is modeled by the Beta distribution:

$p(\\ell\_{i}|k) = \\frac{\\Gamma(\\alpha\_{k} + \\beta\_{k})}{\\Gamma(\\alpha\_{k}) + \\Gamma(\\beta\_{k})}\\ell\_{i}^{\\alpha\_{k} - 1}{(1 - \\ell\_{i})}^{\\beta\_{k} - 1},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si88.png)(4.25) 

with *α*[*k*], *β*[*k*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si89.png) and *Γ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si90.png) representing the Gamma function. The sample weight is computed from the posterior probability that the sample *i* was generated by mixture component *k* = clean![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si91.png), as follows:

$\\mathbf{w}\_{i} = \\frac{\\lambda\_{k = \\text{clean}} \\times p(\\ell\_{i}|k = \\text{clean})}{\\sum\_{j \\in \\{\\text{noisy,clean}\\}}\\lambda\_{j} \\times p(\\ell\_{i}|j)}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si92.png)(4.26) 

In ([Arazo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0050)), this sample weight is not used as in [(4.15)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq17), but as way to smooth the training label ([Reed et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1470)), as in:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\mathbf{w}\_{i} \\times {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} + (1 - \\mathbf{w}\_{i}) \\times \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}))),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si93.png)(4.27) 

where **w**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si94.png) is the sample weight from [(4.26)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq28).

A modified gradient-based optimization algorithm is proposed in ([Han et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0630), [2018a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0625)), which relies on stochastic gradient descent for reliable data and learning-rate-reduced gradient ascent on unreliable data. This paper explores the idea that training is divided into two stages. An initial stage where the model learns reliable data patterns ([Arpit et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0065)), followed by a second stage where the model learns unreliable data such as outliers and noisy-label data. To learn from reliable data, while avoiding the learning from unreliable data, Han et al. ([2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0630), [2018a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0625)) propose the stochastic integrated gradient under-weighted ascent (SIGUA) and the Pumpout losses that can be summarized as follows:

$\\mathcal{L}\_{\\text{SIGUA}} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\mathcal{R}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\gamma \\times \\mathcal{U}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si95.png)(4.28) 

where $\\mathcal{R}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si96.png) returns 1 if the training data $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si97.png) belongs to the set of reliable samples (otherwise it returns 0), $\\mathcal{U}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si98.png) returns 1 if the training data $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si97.png) belongs to the set of unreliable samples (otherwise it returns 0), and *γ* weights negatively the loss for the unreliable samples. The sets of reliable and unreliable samples are formed using sample selection techniques that will be introduced in Section [4.3.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0060).

Another method to weight training samples is the improved MAE (IMAE) ([Wang et al., 2019b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1845)), which down-weights samples that are either too easy or too hard to learn, and simultaneously up-weights challenging training samples with

$w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\exp\\left( T \\times \\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\times \\left( 1 - {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si99.png)(4.29) 

where *T* > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si100.png) is a constant that controls the exponential base. Essentially, when ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\approx 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si101.png) or ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\approx 0$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si102.png), $w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\approx 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si103.png), and when ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\approx 0.5$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si104.png), then $w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) > 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si105.png).

The definitions of the sample weighting functions provided in this section tend to be intuitive, but arbitrary, and to depend on hyper-parameters that are hard to define. The papers by [Wang et al. (2017c)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1855) and [Arazo et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0050) started the discussion about the small-loss hypothesis, which links small loss values with clean labels and high-loss values with noisy labels. Many papers followed the idea of using the small-loss hypothesis to weight or select clean samples ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805); [Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055)), but in most cases, the Beta mixture model was replaced by the Gaussian mixture model.

In [Fig. 4.8](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0045), we show an example of the training process using the loss re-weighting from [(4.15)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq17). In this example, the posterior probability that the sample *i* was generated by mixture component *k* = clean![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si91.png) of a Gaussian mixture model estimated from the training loss values with *p*(ℓ[*i*]|*k*) = 𝒩(ℓ[*i*]; *μ*[*k*], *σ*[*k*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si106.png), where *μ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si107.png) and *σ*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si108.png) denote the mean and standard deviation of the component *k* of the mixture model (the component with smaller mean denotes the clean label component), where the first 50 training iterations rely on the unweighted training samples to stabilize the model. The results shown by loss re-weighting tend to be reasonably good, but it is usually explored in combination with other methods to provide competitive noisy-label learning results.

Another form of loss re-weighting is proposed in meta-learning methods, which are described in more detail below in Section [4.4.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0090). In meta-learning, the weights are defined as a meta-parameter that can be automatically learned using a bi-level optimization and a validation set, which mitigates the two issues mentioned above about the arbitrariness of the weight function and the hyper-parameters. However, the downside of meta-learning approaches is that they tend to take much longer to train than other methods.

### 4.2.4 Loss correction

Loss correction methods enable the learner to re-label a sample when the trained model disagrees with the label from the training set. One of the earliest works in the field that explored this idea was the method called bootstrapping ([Reed et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1470)), shown in [Fig. 4.10](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0055)(a), where the learner bootstraps itself by re-labeling training samples with a convex combination of the model's prediction and the training label. The intuition of bootstrapping is that as training progresses, the model's predictions become more consistent and if these predictions agree with the training label, then the loss becomes a trivial cross-entropy loss with a “one-hot” training label. When predictions disagree with the training label, then the loss becomes a cross entropy with multiple targets, namely the training label and the model prediction. Two types of bootstrapping were proposed: 1) the soft bootstrapping that uses the predicted class probabilities from *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si22.png) for the loss, as in:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\beta \\times \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} + (1 - \\beta) \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si109.png)(4.30) 

where *β* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si110.png) weights the training label and model prediction; and 2) the hard bootstrapping which is trained with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\beta \\times \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} + (1 - \\beta) \\times \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si111.png)(4.31) 

where OneHot : *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1) → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si112.png) was defined in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) to return a one-hot vector with a ‘1’ in the class of maximum probability from *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si22.png), and ‘0’ for all other classes.

![Figure 4.10 Loss correction.In loss correction approaches, the loss is modified either with a modification of the training label (a – bootstrapping (Reed et al., 2014)), or a modification of the model prediction (b – forward prediction (Patrini et al., 2017)).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr010.jpg)

Figure 4.10 Loss correction.In loss correction approaches, the loss is modified either with a modification of the training label (a – bootstrapping ([Reed et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1470))), or a modification of the model prediction (b – forward prediction ([Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1400))).

[Patrini et al. (2017)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1400) proposed the forward and backward loss correction methods to address the problem of asymmetric label noise ([Fig. 4.10](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0055)(b) shows the forward loss correction method). Recall from Section [2.4.2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) that asymmetric label noise is defined by a label transition matrix $\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si113.png) for $\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si114.png) indexing the rows and columns of **T**, respectively. The backward approach corrects the loss with the inverse **T**^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si115.png) by first approximating this transition matrix with a prediction using a model trained without correction, leading to the estimate $\\widehat{\\mathbf{T}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si116.png). Then, the model is re-trained by correcting the label of training sample $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si60.png) with a linear combination of the losses for class labels and the estimated inverse transition matrix ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{T}}}^{- 1}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si117.png), as in

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\overset{\\leftarrow}{\\ell}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si118.png)(4.32) 

where

$\\overset{\\leftarrow}{\\ell}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\left( {\\widehat{\\mathbf{T}}}^{- 1}\\left\\lbrack \\ell(\\mathbf{y}\_{1},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),...,\\ell(\\mathbf{y}\_{|\\mathcal{Y}|},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack^{\\top} \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si119.png)(4.33) 

with **y**[*k*] ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si120.png) denoting the one-hot vector of |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si50.png) dimensions with the *k*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si121.png) dimension equal to one, and ℓ(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si122.png) representing any of the losses in Chapter [2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml). The forward correction works similarly, but instead of relying on the inverse of the transition matrix, it works directly with the estimated $\\widehat{\\mathbf{T}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si116.png). The re-training in this forward approach relies on a linear combination of the model predictions as follows:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\overset{\\rightarrow}{\\ell}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si123.png)(4.34) 

where

$\\overset{\\rightarrow}{\\ell}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},{\\widehat{\\mathbf{T}}}^{\\top}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si124.png)(4.35) 

The forward/backward correction methods in [(4.32)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq34) and [(4.34)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq36) critically depend on an accurate estimation of **T**, which is challenging particularly for problems with large noise rates or a large number of classes. This motivated the gold loss correction (GLC) approach that proposes the use of a clean-label validation set $\\overline{\\mathcal{D}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si125.png), which is also referred to as anchor points, to estimate **T**, with ([Hendrycks et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0690)):

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{T}}}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = \\frac{1}{|{\\overline{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{\\mathbf{y}}|}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x} \\in {\\overline{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{\\mathbf{y}}}p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si126.png)(4.36) 

where ${\\overline{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si127.png) is the set of clean-label data of label **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si128.png), and $p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si129.png) is trained using the original noisy-label training set. Empirically, a more accurate estimate of **T** enables a more robust result by the GLC model trained with the forward correction method from [(4.34)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq36).

A simpler alternative to the estimation of the transition matrix is based on smoothing the training label with a uniform label vector ([Szegedy et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1680)). [Lukasik et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1165) extended this idea to the noisy-label learning problem with a label smearing framework that is related to the backward approach in [(4.32)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq34), with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell\_{\\text{SM}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si130.png)(4.37) 

where

$\\ell\_{\\text{SM}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\left( \\mathbf{M}\\left\\lbrack \\ell(\\mathbf{y}\_{1},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),...,\\ell(\\mathbf{y}\_{|\\mathcal{Y}|},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack^{\\top} \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si131.png)(4.38) 

In [(4.38)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq40), **M** denotes a smearing matrix that is defined in three ways:

*   •  As the identity matrix **I**, i.e., **M** = **I**![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si132.png), forming the standard training;
*   •  As the label smoothing matrix $\\mathbf{M} = (1 - \\alpha)\\mathbf{I} + \\frac{\\alpha\\mathbf{J}}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si133.png), where **J** is the all-ones matrix and *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si134.png) is a tuning parameter;
*   •  As the inverse of a symmetric noise transition matrix, defined by $\\mathbf{M} = \\frac{1}{1 - \\alpha} \\times \\left( \\mathbf{I} - \\frac{\\alpha\\mathbf{J}}{|\\mathcal{Y}|} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si135.png).

[Fig. 4.11](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0060) displays an example of a classifier trained with the loss correction in [(4.37)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq39) for the problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020) using the label smoothing smearing matrix $\\mathbf{M} = (1 - \\alpha)\\mathbf{I} + \\frac{\\alpha\\mathbf{J}}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si133.png), with *α* = 0.5![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si136.png).

![Figure 4.11 Classifier trained with loss correction.The training of classifier with the loss correction in (4.37) using the same problem described in Fig. 4.3. We train for 100 iterations using the label smoothing smearing matrix \\mathbf{M} = (1 - \\alpha)\\mathbf{I} + \\frac{\\alpha\\mathbf{J}}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}Image, with α = 0.5.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr011.jpg)

Figure 4.11 Classifier trained with loss correction.The training of classifier with the loss correction in [(4.37)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq39) using the same problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020). We train for 100 iterations using the label smoothing smearing matrix $\\mathbf{M} = (1 - \\alpha)\\mathbf{I} + \\frac{\\alpha\\mathbf{J}}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si133.png), with *α* = 0.5.

Loss correction techniques are heavily used as an auxiliary method to address the learning with noisy-label problem given their simple implementation and relative efficacy. However, it is not a technique that alone can provide competitive results for noisy-label learning. Among the challenges faced by loss correction methods, we have: 1) difficult estimation of *β* in [(4.30)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq32) and [(4.31)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq33); 2) challenging estimation of the label transition matrix $\\widehat{\\mathbf{T}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si116.png) in [(4.33)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq35) and [(4.35)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq37); and 3) over-smoothing of the decision boundaries with [(4.38)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq40), as shown in [Fig. 4.11](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0060).

### 4.2.5 Domain adaptation/generalization

The noisy-label learning problem can be seen as an instance of the domain adaptation/generalization problem ([Wang and Deng, 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1835); [Zhou et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2215)), where the source domain 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si138.png) is the one that produces the noisy-label training set, while the target domain 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png) is the one that generates the clean-label target set ([Konstantinov and Lampert, 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0930)). In fact, as shown in [Fig. 4.12](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0065), it is possible to have multiple source domains {𝒮[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*N*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si140.png), each generating a separate training set denoted by 𝒟(𝒮[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si141.png), where the *α*\-weighted empirical risk of the model *f*[*θ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si142.png) is:

$\\mathcal{L}\_{\\alpha}\\left( \\theta,{\\{\\mathcal{S}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{N} \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\alpha\_{i}\\mathcal{L}(\\theta,\\mathcal{S}\_{i}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\frac{\\alpha\_{i}}{|\\mathcal{D}(\\mathcal{S}\_{i})|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}(\\mathcal{S}\_{i})}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si143.png)(4.39) 

where $\\sum\_{i = 1}^{N}\\alpha\_{i} = 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si144.png) and *α*[*i*] ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si145.png) for all *i* ∈ {1, ..., *N*}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si146.png). The discrepancy between one of the source distributions 𝒟(𝒮[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si141.png) and the target distribution 𝒟(𝒯)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si148.png) is computed as follows:

$d\_{\\theta}(\\mathcal{S}\_{i},\\mathcal{T}) = \\sup\\limits\_{\\theta \\in \\Theta}(|\\mathcal{L}(\\theta,\\mathcal{S}\_{i}) - \\mathcal{L}(\\theta,\\mathcal{T})|),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si150.png)(4.40) 

where ℒ(*θ*, 𝒮[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si151.png) denotes the empirical loss of the training set from the source domain 𝒮[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si152.png) and ℒ(*θ*, 𝒯)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si153.png) is the empirical loss of the testing set from the target domain 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png). The discrepancy in [(4.40)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq42) between 𝒮[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si152.png) and 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png) is large if there is at least one model that performs well on one and badly on the other, but it is small if all models perform similarly on 𝒮[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si152.png) and 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png). The model is learned from the multiple sources by first estimating the domain weights with

$\\alpha^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{{\\{\\alpha\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{N}}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\alpha\_{i}d\_{\\theta}(\\mathcal{S}\_{i},\\mathcal{T}) + \\lambda\\sqrt{\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\frac{\\alpha\_{i}^{2}}{|\\mathcal{D}(\\mathcal{S}\_{i})|}} s.t.\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{N}\\alpha\_{i} = 1\\text{,\\ and~}\\alpha\_{i} \\geq 0\\text{~for\\ all~}i,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si154.png)(4.41) 

where *λ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si155.png) is a hyper-parameter. Then, the model is learned with *θ*^(\*) = arg min[*θ*]ℒ[*α*^(\*)](*θ*,{𝒮[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*N*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si156.png) from [(4.39)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq41). Note that the optimization in [(4.41)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq43) implies that we need to access a clean testing set (sampled from the target clean-label distribution 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png)) and multiple noisy-label training sets (sampled from source noisy-label distributions {𝒮[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*N*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si140.png)). We show the results of a training using this domain adaptation in [Fig. 4.13](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0070). Similarly, [Han et al. (2020c)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0655) and [Yu et al. (2020b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2085) propose relatively similar domain adaptation approaches, but with the difference of formulating a re-weighted loss in [(4.39)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq41), like the approaches presented in Section [4.2.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0030) to mitigate the negative influence of label noise.

![Figure 4.12 Domain adaptation/generalization.Domain adaptation/generalization methods assume the availability of N noisy-label training domains {\\{\\mathcal{S}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{N}Image, each generating a separate training set denoted by \\mathcal{D}(\\mathcal{S}\_{i})Image, and a clean-label testing domain \\mathcal{T}Image that produces a testing set \\mathcal{D}(\\mathcal{T})Image (Konstantinov and Lampert, 2019). The goal is to learn a model that can generalize well to the testing domain using a combination of training domains weighted by {\\{\\alpha\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{N}Image.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr012.jpg)

[Figure 4.12](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf1215) Domain adaptation/generalization.Domain adaptation/generalization methods assume the availability of *N* noisy-label training domains {𝒮[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*N*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si140.png), each generating a separate training set denoted by 𝒟(𝒮[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si141.png), and a clean-label testing domain 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png) that produces a testing set 𝒟(𝒯)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si148.png) ([Konstantinov and Lampert, 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0930)). The goal is to learn a model that can generalize well to the testing domain using a combination of training domains weighted by {*α*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*N*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si149.png).

![Figure 4.13 Classifier trained with domain adaptation.Using the problem described in Fig. 4.3, we train a domain adaptation model for 500 epochs using the classification loss in (4.39) and domain adaptation loss (4.41) that targets the minimization of loss discrepancy between the single source noisy-label domain and the target clean-label domain. Note that we keep only the training samples from the source domain that have small losses with the condition \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < 10 \\times \\frac{t}{T}Image, where t is the current epoch, while T is the total number of epochs.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr013.jpg)

[Figure 4.13](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf1235) Classifier trained with domain adaptation.Using the problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020), we train a domain adaptation model for 500 epochs using the classification loss in [(4.39)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq41) and domain adaptation loss [(4.41)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq43) that targets the minimization of loss discrepancy between the single source noisy-label domain and the target clean-label domain. Note that we keep only the training samples from the source domain that have small losses with the condition $\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < 10 \\times \\frac{t}{T}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si157.png), where *t* is the current epoch, while *T* is the total number of epochs.

Domain adaptation and generalization techniques ([Wang and Deng, 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1835); [Zhou et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2215)) are promising for addressing noisy-label learning problems since it is quite clear that noisy-label training samples and clean-label testing samples represent data from different domains. Despite that, the field has not widely explored domain adaptation and generalization methods for noisy-label learning. There may be some reasons behind that, such as the operational difficulties to set up domain adaptation/generalization problems. For instance, the need for testing set samples is not widely adopted in noisy-label learning benchmarks, making the comparison with domain adaptation/generalization approaches hard. Nevertheless, we believe that domain adaptation and generalization techniques should still be explored in noisy-label learning problems in the future.

## 4.3 Data processing

In this section, we will discuss strategies that involve the processing of data to facilitate the training with noisy-label samples. We start by discussing adversarial training ([Miyato et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1300); [Goodfellow et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0585); [Fawzi et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0495)), which is a method designed to improve the robustness of models to data noise by applying small perturbations to the input training samples ([Alayrac et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0010); [Fatras et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0490); [Zhu et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2230)). Alternatively, the selection of clean-label and informative samples from the training set by an external method is explored by data cleaning methods ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805); [Shen and Sanghavi, 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1585); [Chen et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0260); [Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)). These selected samples form a new training set to be used in the training of a regular classifier. Sample selection methods ([Ding et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0440); [Huang et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0750); [Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055); [Arazo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0050); [Kim et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0890)) also aim to select clean-label samples, but the training of the classifier relies on both the selected clean-label samples and the samples classified as noisy, with algorithms that follow different strategies for the two sets. Another possible way of modifying the training data is by including multiple labels per training sample, in a problem known as multi-rater learning ([Tanno et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1700)). The exploration of prior knowledge about the data, for example by building super-classes that will have significantly less label noise ([Seo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1560)) or by constraining label transition matrix structures ([Han et al., 2018b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635)), is another way of processing the input data to handle label noise. A widely explored data processing approach consists of relying on data augmentation techniques for training and testing. Such data augmentation methods can also work together with semi-supervised learning techniques. We conclude the section with the presentation of pseudo-labeling techniques ([Zhang et al., 2021c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2160); [Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1625); [Albert et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0015); [Yao et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2045); [Wei et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1890)).

### 4.3.1 Adversarial training

While noisy-label learning addresses the problem of learning a robust model given that an unknown a subset of the training set is contaminated with label noise, adversarial training ([Miyato et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1300); [Goodfellow et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0585); [Fawzi et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0495)) generates small adversarial perturbations to the input training data to deceive the model to make mistakes ([Song et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1645)). Adversarial learning is a strategy usually adopted for safety-critical applications that need to be robust to challenging input data noise.

Let us introduce the virtual adversarial training (VAT) ([Miyato et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1300)) to exemplify adversarial training approaches. VAT proposes a loss to enforce a smooth model output distribution around each training sample without knowing the label information, resulting in robustness to small changes to input data. VAT assumes that the dataset is divided into labeled and unlabeled sets, represented by 𝒟[*l*], 𝒟[*u*] ⊂ 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si160.png), and the model optimization is defined by:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{l}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{l}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\frac{\\lambda}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{l}| + |\\mathcal{D}\_{u}|} \\times \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{l}\\bigcup\\mathcal{D}\_{u}}\\ell\_{LDS}(\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\theta},\\theta),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si161.png)(4.42) 

where *θ̂*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si162.png) denotes a model parameter at a specific step in the training process, and the local distributional smoothness (LDS) is represented by

ℓ[*L**D**S*](**x**, *θ̂*, *θ*) = *D*\[*f*[*θ̂*](**x**)∥*f*[*θ*](**x**+**r**[vadv])\]

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si163.png)(4.43) 

with **r**[vadv] = arg max[**r**, ∥**r**∥[2] ≤ *ϵ*]*D*\[*f*[*θ̂*](**x**)∥*f*[*θ*](**x**+**r**)\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si164.png), and *D*\[.∥.\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si165.png) representing a non-negative distribution divergence function (e.g., Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence).

Surprisingly, the common goal of noisy-label learning and adversarial training, consisting of learning robust representations and models from noisy observations, has not attracted too much interest from the scientific community. Remarkable exceptions are the papers by [Alayrac et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0010); [Fatras et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0490); [Zhu et al. (2021b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2230). In ([Alayrac et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0010)), the authors show that adversarial training, such as the one in [(4.42)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq44), makes the trained model *f*[*θ*^(\*)](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si166.png) robust to label noise. We depict this approach in [Fig. 4.14](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0075), where the optimization from [(4.42)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq44) is updated for noisy-label learning as follows:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\lambda \\times \\ell\_{LDS}(\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\theta},\\theta),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si167.png)(4.44) 

where *θ̂*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si162.png) is the model parameter at a specific training epoch, and the ℓ[*L**D**S*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si168.png) is defined in [(4.43)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq45). The result from the optimization from [(4.44)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq46) is shown in [Fig. 4.15](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0080). The approach introduced in ([Alayrac et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0010)) motivated the Wasserstein adversarial regularization (WAR) on label noise ([Fatras et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0490)) that re-defines *D*\[.\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si169.png) in [(4.43)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq45) as the Wasserstein distance computed in the label space 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si170.png). [Zhu et al. (2021b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2230) analyzed the adversarial training in noisy-label learning problems and suggested that the number of projected gradient descent (PGD) steps to find an adversarial sample in the proximity of a training point is an effective way to decide the cleanliness of its label. This paper follows the adversarial training from ([Madry et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1210)), which optimizes the model using just labeled data, as in

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si171.png)(4.45) 

where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{x}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si172.png) is an adversarial variant of input data inside the *ϵ*\-ball centered at **x**. The generation of adversarial variants, starting from initial sample **x**^((0)) = **x**![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si173.png) follows the PGD steps, defined by

$\\mathbf{x}^{(t + 1)} = \\Pi\_{\\mathcal{B}(\\mathbf{x}^{(0)},\\epsilon)}\\left( \\mathbf{x}^{(t)} + \\alpha\\mathsf{sign}(\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}^{(t)})) \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si174.png)(4.46) 

where **x**^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si175.png) is the adversarial sample at PGD step t, and *Π*[ℬ(**x**^((0)), *ϵ*)](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si176.png) denotes the function to project the adversarial sample into the *ϵ*\-ball centered at **x**^((0))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si177.png). This paper ([Zhu et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2230)) also concluded that the regularization from the adversarial training in [(4.45)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq47) helps to make the training robust to noisy labels.

![Figure 4.14 Adversarial training.In adversarial training, the goal is to regularize the usual model training with an adversarial loss that estimates a noise vector rvadv (of limited length {\\|\\mathbf{r}\_{\\text{vadv}}\\|}\_{2} < \\epsilonImage) to maximize the discrepancy D\[.‖.\] between the prediction of the input data x from a model trained in a previous epoch (i.e., f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x})Image) and the prediction of the noisy input data x + rvadv from the current model fθ(.)](images/B9780443154416000137/gr014.jpg)

[Figure 4.14](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf1435) Adversarial training.In adversarial training, the goal is to regularize the usual model training with an adversarial loss that estimates a noise vector **r**[vadv] (of limited length ∥**r**[vadv]∥[2] < *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si158.png)) to maximize the discrepancy *D*\[.‖.\] between the prediction of the input data **x** from a model trained in a previous epoch (i.e., *f*[*θ̂*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si159.png)) and the prediction of the noisy input data **x** + **r**[vadv] from the current model *f*[*θ*](.)

![Figure 4.15 Classifier trained with adversarial training.The training of classifier with adversarial training from (4.44) using the same problem described in Fig. 4.3. We train for 1000 iterations assuming that λ = 0 for the first 14 iterations, and λ = 5 between iterations 15 and 1000.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr015.jpg)

[Figure 4.15](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf1455) Classifier trained with adversarial training.The training of classifier with adversarial training from [(4.44)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq46) using the same problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020). We train for 1000 iterations assuming that *λ* = 0 for the first 14 iterations, and *λ* = 5 between iterations 15 and 1000.

Adversarial training is a strategy that links label noise and data noise, which can be seen as two complementary aspects of a unified concept. This topic deserves more attention from the scientific community not only because it will allow a better understanding of how data and label noise affect the learning problem, but also because it may lead to more effective noisy-label learning mechanisms. Recently, [Sanyal et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1530) studied how deep learning models become vulnerable to adversarial attacks. One of the reasons for that vulnerability was found to be the presence of label noise in the training set, while the other reason was the tendency of training procedures to learn simple classification boundaries.

### 4.3.2 Data cleaning

Data cleaning methods are designed to build a new training set by minimizing the likelihood that it contains data with noisy labels, as shown in [Fig. 4.16](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0085). Thus the model optimization is achieved with:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))\\text{s.t.~}\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\widetilde{\\mathcal{D}} \\subset \\mathcal{D}}\\mathsf{clean}(\\widetilde{\\mathcal{D}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si180.png)(4.47) 

where $\\mathsf{clean}(\\widetilde{\\mathcal{D}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si181.png) represents a function that returns a measure of label cleanliness of $\\widetilde{\\mathcal{D}} \\subset \\mathcal{D}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si182.png) that is maximized by including as many clean-label samples as possible and as little noisy-label samples as possible. Given that the selection of samples to be included into 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) consists of a combinatorial problem, it usually resorts to greedy optimization strategies, where the label cleanliness of each sample in 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) is studied to determine if that sample will be included or rejected from 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png).

![Figure 4.16 Data cleaning.Data cleaning methods rely on an optimization that trains the model with a training set \\mathcal{D}\_{c} \\subset \\mathcal{D}Image found by selecting training samples that are likely to have clean labels using the function \\mathsf{clean}(.)Image](images/B9780443154416000137/gr016.jpg)

[Figure 4.16](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf1500) Data cleaning.Data cleaning methods rely on an optimization that trains the model with a training set 𝒟[*c*] ⊂ 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si178.png) found by selecting training samples that are likely to have clean labels using the function clean(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si179.png)

![Figure 4.17 Classifier trained with data cleaning.Using the classification problem described in Fig. 4.3, we train a classifier for 200 iterations with data cleaning from (4.47) and \\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\begin{cases}
{\\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\frac{\\tau \\times \\text{iteration}}{200}\\},} & {\\text{~if~}\\text{iteration} > 10} \\\\
{\\mathcal{D},} & \\text{~otherwise~} \\\\
\\end{cases}Image, where τ = 10, and iteration ∈ {1,...,200} denotes the training epoch.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr017.jpg)

[Figure 4.17](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf0115) Classifier trained with data cleaning.Using the classification problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020), we train a classifier for 200 iterations with data cleaning from [(4.47)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq49) and $\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\begin{cases} {\\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\frac{\\tau \\times \\text{iteration}}{200}\\},} & {\\text{~if~}\\text{iteration} > 10} \\\\ {\\mathcal{D},} & \\text{~otherwise~} \\\\ \\end{cases}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si183.png), where *τ* = 10, and iteration ∈ {1,...,200} denotes the training epoch.

Before the advent of deep learning approaches, there have been many methods that aimed at producing such clean-label training sets by studying their weights in bagging or boosting approaches ([Wheway, 2001](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1905); [Sluban et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1620)), their k-nearest neighbor classification ([Delany et al., 2012](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0385)), their compression measure (e.g., minimum description length) ([Gamberger et al., 2000](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0535)), or their outlier measure ([Thongkam et al., 2008](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1725)). Such ideas have been extended to deep learning approaches, as we explain below.

Data cleaning has been explored in deep learning, particularly with MentorNet ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805)), Iterative Trimmed Loss Minimization (ITLM) ([Shen and Sanghavi, 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1585)), Iterative Noisy Cross-Validation (INCV) ([Chen et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0260)), and Co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)). Even though these methods introduce different definitions for the function clean(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si179.png) in [(4.47)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq49), all definitions are based on the assumption that large-loss samples are likely to have noisy labels. This assumption is based on the work by [Arpit et al. (2017)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0065), who showed that deep learning models tend to learn simple patterns first (with clean-label samples showing small losses and noisy-label samples displaying large losses), and then gradually overfit to all training samples (with all samples presenting small losses). Such demonstration enables the formulation of the small-loss trick, which treats small-loss samples as clean-label samples. MentorNet uses a pre-trained a teacher model to select small-loss samples to be inserted into 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png), which is used to train the student model. ITLM alternates between selecting small-loss samples and re-training the model with these samples. INCV breaks the training set into two halves, using one half to train the model and the other half to select clean samples (by checking if the prediction by the trained model matches the training label). Co-teaching uses two models, where each model selects a proportion of its small-loss training samples from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) to train the other model.
