By avoiding noisy-labeled data, these models mitigate the risk of overfitting these mislabeled samples, but they also reduce the amount of informative training samples that are useful for training robustness even though they have a relatively large loss value ([Shrivastava et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1600); [Chang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0250); [Lin et al., 2017b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1095)).

The SELectively reFurbIsh unclEan samples (SELFIE) method ([Song et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1640)) addresses this issue by selecting not only clean, but also informative training samples (referred as refurbishable training samples), as follows:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{r}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{r}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{r}}\\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{r},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))s.t.\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\tau \\right\\}\\mathcal{D}\_{r} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{r})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\frac{\\mathbb{H}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta^{(t - q),...,(t - 1)}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack}{\\delta} < \\epsilon,\\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{r} = \\mathsf{mode}\\left( \\mathsf{OneHot}\\left( f\_{\\theta^{(t - q),...,(t - 1)}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right) \\right\\}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si184.png)(4.48) 

where 𝒟[*c*]⋂𝒟[*r*] = ⌀![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si185.png), ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{r}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si186.png) is the most common label predicted in the last *q* iterations, ℍ\[*f*[*θ*^((*t* − *q*), ..., (*t* − 1))](**x**)\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si187.png) computes the entropy of the aggregated probability classification of the model from the previous *q* training iterations, *τ* and *ϵ* are thresholds used for sample selection, and *δ* is a normalization factor. Even with the improvement above, SELFIE still suffers from the inability to distinguish between samples with noisy labels and informative samples with clean labels because of limited information available from model predictions or loss values.

This issue has recently been addressed by considering prediction uncertainty with the use of interval loss estimation ([Xia et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1940)), where the goal is to distinguish between noisy-label samples and informative clean-label samples. [Xia et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1940) propose the soft truncation and hard truncation robust mean estimators, where the soft truncation provides a robust mean loss estimation of a training sample's observed training losses ℒ[*t*] = {ℓ[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si188.png) by changing the behavior of losses, as follows

${\\widetilde{\\mu}}\_{s} = \\frac{1}{t}\\sum\\limits\_{\\ell\_{i} \\in \\mathcal{L}\_{t}}\\psi(\\ell\_{i}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si189.png)(4.49) 

where *ψ*(ℓ[*i*]) = log (1 + ℓ[*i*] + ℓ[*i*]²/2)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si190.png), with ℓ[*i*] ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si191.png), is a non-decreasing influence function. The criterion to select samples for training is designed based on concentration inequalities ([Xia et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1940)) and the number of times a sample has been selected, with

$\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},s(\\mathcal{L}\_{t}) < \\tau \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si192.png)(4.50) 

where

$s(\\mathcal{L}\_{t}) = {\\widetilde{\\mu}}\_{s} - \\frac{\\sigma^{2}\\left( t + \\frac{\\sigma^{2}\\log(2t)}{t^{2}} \\right)}{n\_{t} - \\sigma^{2}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si193.png)(4.51) 

with *μ̃*[*s*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si194.png) defined in [(4.49)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq51), *σ* denoting the standard deviation of ℒ[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si195.png), and *n*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si196.png) representing the number of times a sample has been selected. The hard truncation first removes *t*[*o*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si197.png) outliers from the losses in ℒ[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si195.png), forming the set ℒ[*t* − *t*[*o*]] ⊂ ℒ[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si198.png), and then estimates the robust mean loss

${\\widetilde{\\mu}}\_{h} = \\frac{1}{t - t\_{o}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\ell\_{i} \\in \\mathcal{L}\_{t - t\_{o}}}\\psi(\\ell\_{i}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si199.png)(4.52) 

The hard truncation selection relies on the same criteria from [(4.50)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq52) by replacing *s*(ℒ[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si200.png) by

$h(\\mathcal{L}\_{t}) = {\\widetilde{\\mu}}\_{h} - \\frac{2\\sqrt{2\\tau\_{min}}L(t + \\sqrt{2}t\_{o})}{(t - t\_{o})\\sqrt{t}}\\sqrt{\\frac{\\log(4t)}{n\_{t}}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si201.png)(4.53) 

where *μ̃*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si202.png) is defined in [(4.52)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq54), *L* is an upper-bound for the loss, and *τ*[*m**i**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si203.png) represents the minimal mixing time. For the selection criteria in [(4.51)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq53) and [(4.53)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq55), the first term prioritizes samples with small robust mean loss, while the second term prioritizes samples with large *σ*²![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si204.png) or *τ*[*m**i**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si203.png) (i.e. uncertain samples) and small *n*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si196.png) (i.e., less selected samples).

The problem mentioned above about the difficulty to differentiate between noisy-label samples from clean-label informative samples has been addressed in ([Zhou et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2220)) with the Robust Curriculum Learning (RoCL). More specifically, RoCL applies data cleaning at the beginning of the training, and gradually start training from noisy data that are pseudo-labeled using a time-ensemble of the model and data augmentation. Similarly to ([Xia et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1940); [Song et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1640)), the data selection in ([Zhou et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2220)) relies on the history of the training process. In particular, [Zhou et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2220) hypothesize that the training sample's label is more likely to be correct given a consistently low dynamic loss computed with

$\\ell\_{i}^{(t + 1)} = \\begin{cases} {\\gamma\\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) + (1 - \\gamma)\\ell\_{i}^{(t)},} & {\\text{if~}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}} \\\\ {\\ell\_{i}^{(t)},} & \\text{otherwise} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si205.png)(4.54) 

where *γ* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si206.png) represents a discounting factor, and *t* denotes the training epoch. RoCL also explores an empirical observation that the model output tends to be an accurate representation of the clean label if the output is consistent over the training history and across data augmentations of the training sample, as in

$c\_{i}^{(t + 1)} = \\begin{cases} {\\gamma\\zeta\_{i}^{(t)} + (1 - \\gamma)c\_{i}^{(t)},} & {\\text{if~}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}} \\\\ {c\_{i}^{(t)},} & \\text{otherwise} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si207.png)(4.55) 

where *γ* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si206.png) is a discounting factor, $\\zeta\_{i}^{(t)} = \\frac{1}{m}\\sum\_{j = 1}^{m}\\ell(f\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}),{\\overline{f}}\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}^{(j)}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si208.png) is the instantaneous consistency loss with ${\\overline{f}}\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) = \\frac{1}{m}\\sum\_{j = 1}^{m}f\_{{\\overline{\\theta}}^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}^{(j)})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si209.png), and ${\\overline{\\theta}}^{(t)} = \\gamma\\theta^{(t - 1)} + (1 - \\gamma){\\overline{\\theta}}^{(t)}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si210.png). The selection of samples to be included into 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) is performed by drawing samples from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) with the following probability distribution that combines the clean label detection and the consistency loss:

𝒫[*i*]^((*t*)) = *γ**p*[*i*]^((*t*)) + (1 − *γ*)*q*[*i*]^((*t*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si211.png)(4.56) 

where

$p\_{i}^{(t)} = \\frac{\\exp(\\tau\_{1}\\ell\_{i}^{(t)})}{\\sum\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\exp(\\tau\_{1}\\ell\_{j}^{(t)})},\\ \\ \\ q\_{i}^{(t)} = \\frac{\\exp(\\tau\_{2}c\_{i}^{(t)})}{\\sum\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\exp(\\tau\_{2}c\_{j}^{(t)})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si212.png)(4.57) 

with *τ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si213.png), *τ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si214.png) being the curriculum parameters to prioritize the clean label detection and the consistency loss. When *τ*[1] < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si215.png), samples with clean labels tend to have high *p*[*i*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si216.png); conversely, when *τ*[1] > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si217.png), samples with noisy labels tend to have high *p*[*i*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si216.png). Also, when *τ*[2] < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si218.png), samples with smaller consistency loss tend to have high *q*[*i*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si219.png), and with *τ*[2] > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si220.png), samples with higher consistency loss tend to have high *q*[*i*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si219.png). Thus, when *τ*[1] < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si215.png), the training is focused on clean data already learned by the model, and when *τ*[2] < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si218.png), the training is focused on data that shows consistent losses. To motivate exploration of the data, *τ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si213.png) and *τ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si214.png) need to move toward zero. Alternatively, *τ*[1] < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si215.png) and *τ*[2] > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si220.png) focus on clean data that show inconsistent model outputs, while *τ*[1] > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si217.png) and *τ*[2] < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si218.png) strengthen noisy samples with consistent outputs. [Zhou et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2220) suggest a curriculum learning starting from *τ*[1] < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si215.png) and *τ*[2] > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si220.png) that gradually move to *τ*[1] > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si217.png) and *τ*[2] < 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si218.png), which suggests a training starting from the learning from clean data and finishing with the learning from consistent samples.

Other recently published methods propose data cleaning approaches based on early stopping ([Bai et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0100)), combined with test time augmentation ([Wang et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1825)) and dropout ([Srivastava et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1655)) to select a balanced set of pseudo clean-label samples ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1625)). Furthermore, [Pleiss et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1425) studied the training with noisy labels dynamics and introduced the area under the margin (AUM) statistic. In essence, they discovered that the average difference between the logits of a training sample's assigned class and its highest non-assigned class can characterize this sample, which is measured as follows:

$\\mathsf{AUM}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\sum\\limits\_{t = 1}^{T}f\_{\\theta^{(t)}}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) - \\max\\limits\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\neq \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}f\_{\\theta^{(t)}}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si221.png)(4.58) 

where $f\_{\\theta^{(t)}}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si222.png) denotes the ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{th}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si223.png) output from the model obtained at the *t*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si224.png) training iteration. Clean-label samples tend to have larger AUM than noisy-label samples, so the method proposed in ([Pleiss et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1425)) removes the samples with AUM less than a threshold that is automatically set based on a clean set or on the use of a non-existing training class.

The detection of clean samples can also be done directly with the training samples' feature representations instead of loss values or model predictions, under mild assumptions (data density has a compact support, true conditional distributions of labels are continuous, and class-wise decision region of the Bayes optimal classifier is connected). For example, [Wu et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1925) explore a high-order topological information of data that assumes that clean data are clustered together while noisy-label data are spread out and isolated. The proposed algorithm starts with an early-stopping trained model *f*[*θ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si142.png) using the whole 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png). The next step builds a K-nearest neighbor graph for the training samples' representations using one of the intermediate layers of *f*[*θ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si142.png) and finds the class-wise largest components, which are likely to contain most of the clean labels for the class. Next, the outermost layer of each largest component is removed to mitigate the noisy-label samples present at the boundary of these clusters. [Wu et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1925) prove the purity (selected data are likely to be clean) and abundancy (majority of clean data is collected by the method) properties of the algorithm.

The geometric structure of feature representations and model predictions have also been explored to reject noisy-label samples ([Wu et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1935)) with the Noisy Graph Cleaning (NGC) approach. NGC builds a k-nearest neighbor graph that rejects open-set and closed-set noisy-label samples based on their low-confidence model predictions. Then, each class will be formed by a sub-graph that corresponds to the largest connected component for that class. During testing, this method can detect open-set data by calculating the distance between their representations and the representations of learned class prototypes. Data cleaning from the K-nearest neighbors of logit representations ([Bahri et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0095)) or data representations from an intermediate model layer ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0515)) have also been explored by removing the samples that disagree with their neighbors.

More recently, the cleanlab studio^([^(40)](#fn40))

$t\_{\\mathbf{c}} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{c}}|}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{c}}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{c})}(\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si229.png)(4.59) 

where $\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{c}} = \\{\\mathbf{x}|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{\\text{out}},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{c}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si230.png) (with 𝒟[out]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si231.png) denoting an out-of-sample set), and *f*[*θ*]^((**c**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si232.png) is the model (probabilistic) output for label **c** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si228.png). Then the set of samples for clean class **k** from noisy class **c** is defined by

$\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{c},\\mathbf{k}} = \\left\\{ \\mathbf{x}|\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{c}},f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{k})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\geq t\_{\\mathbf{k}},\\mathbf{k} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y},f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}) > t\_{\\mathbf{y}}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si233.png)(4.60) 

where **k** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si234.png). This allows us to estimate the joint distribution between noisy and clean labels, with

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{Q}}}\_{= \\mathbf{c},\\mathbf{k}} = \\frac{|\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{c},\\mathbf{k}}|}{\\sum\_{{\\mathbf{i},\\mathbf{j}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}|\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{i},\\mathbf{j}}|}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si235.png)(4.61) 

The last step of CL is then to clean the data by ranking and pruning it, where [Northcutt et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1360) suggest that samples belonging to the set {**x**|**x** ∈ 𝒟[**c**, **k**], **c** ≠ **k**}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si236.png) are classified as noisy-label samples. The samples belonging to this noisy-label set are sorted by the normalized margin, defined with $f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) - f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si237.png), where $\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\_{\\mathbf{y} \\neq \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si238.png) ([Wei et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1875)).

[Kuan and Mueller (2022)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0970) analyzed many different data-centric noisy-label scores that, similarly to cleanlab's CL, are independent of the model. The self-confidence score is the model's probability of the training label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png), defined as $\\mathsf{Score}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta) = f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si239.png). The normalized margin score is computed from the difference between the training label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) and the most likely class that is not the training label, defined as $\\mathsf{Score}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta) = f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) - f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si240.png), where $\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\_{\\mathbf{y} \\neq \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si238.png). The confidence-weighted entropy is defined by the ratio of the self-confidence and the log normalized entropy of the model probabilities, defined by $\\mathsf{Score}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta) = \\frac{f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})}{(1/\\log(|\\mathcal{Y}|))\\mathbb{H}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si241.png). The negative entropy and least-confidence scores do not require the training label and are respectively defined as $\\mathsf{Score}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta) = - \\mathbb{H}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si242.png) and $\\mathsf{Score}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta) = f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si243.png) where **y**^(\*) = arg max[**y** ∈ 𝒴]*f*[*θ*]^((**y**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si244.png). These scores can be adjusted to account for model biases, with $\\mathsf{AdjustedScore}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta) = \\mathsf{Score}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\overline{\\theta})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si245.png), where $f\_{\\overline{\\theta}}^{(\\mathbf{c})}(\\mathbf{x}) = f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) - \\mathbf{t}\_{\\mathbf{c}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si246.png), with **t**[**c**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si247.png) defined in [(4.59)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq61). We can also have an ensemble of *K* models that are aggregated with $\\sum\_{i = 1}^{K}w\_{i} \\times f\_{\\theta\_{i}}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si248.png), with $\\sum\_{i = 1}^{K}w\_{i} = 1$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si249.png). In this case, the ensemble label quality score is produced by $\\mathsf{Score}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},{\\{\\theta\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{K}) = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{K}w\_{i} \\times \\mathsf{Score}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si250.png). Experiments in this paper show that confidence weighted entropy and self-confidence scores are the top-performing scores, while the least-confidence and negative entropy scores perform poorly overall.

In open set noise ([Wang et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1860)), recent methods formulate a data selection process to classify samples belonging to the closed and open sets ([Sachdeva et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1505)) with the following optimization

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{\\text{closed}}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{\\text{closed}}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))s.t.\\ \\ \\mathcal{D}\_{\\text{closed}} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\widetilde{\\mathcal{D}} \\subset \\mathcal{D}}\\mathsf{closed}(\\widetilde{\\mathcal{D}},\\theta\_{open}^{\\ast}),\\theta\_{open}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{open}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell\_{open}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{open}}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si251.png)(4.62) 

where closed(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si252.png) represents a function that detects (clean- or noisy-label) samples belonging to one of the training classes, and *f*[*θ*[*o**p**e**n*]](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si253.png) is a model trained to detect open-set samples. EvidentialMix ([Sachdeva et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1505)) uses the subjective logic (SL) loss function in ℓ[*o**p**e**n*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si254.png) ([Sensoy et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1555)), defined in [(4.5)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq7), to train closed(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si252.png). The SL loss is designed to quantify classification uncertainty, which tends to be small for clean-label samples, large for noisy-label samples, and of an intermediate value for open-set samples. This observation leads to a natural formulation of a 3-component Gaussian mixture model to represent the distribution of loss values of the training set, where the function closed(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si252.png) detects the samples belonging to the component with the smallest mean (i.e., the clean-label closed-set samples) or the largest mean (i.e., the noisy-label closed-set samples), and rejects all remaining samples classified as open-set.

Data cleaning is one of the most studied and utilized techniques in noisy-label learning, as can be seen from the number of methods explained in this section that depend on it. Nevertheless, defining a function that can reliably select clean-label samples from a training set with a minimum number of false positives and false negatives remains challenging. For this reason, data cleaning is rarely used isolated as a method for handling noisy-label samples. Furthermore, training only with the clean-label samples while disregarding the noisy-label samples may not be the best strategy since there is plenty of evidence, which we will show next in Section [4.3.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0060), that these noisy-label samples can improve the generalization of the model. Nevertheless, given the importance of this technique, we anticipate that many innovative methods will still depend on data cleaning methods.

### 4.3.3 Sample selection

Sample selection techniques classify samples into clean or noisy, but differently from the data cleaning methods in Section [4.3.2](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0055), they do not discard any subset of the training samples. In general, the optimization for sample selection approaches, depicted in [Fig. 4.18](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0095) can be defined as:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell\_{c}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{n}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}}\\ell\_{n}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))s.t.\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\mathsf{clean}(\\mathcal{D}),\\mathcal{D}\_{n} = \\mathcal{D} \\smallsetminus \\mathcal{D}\_{c},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si257.png)(4.63) 

where 𝒟[*c*], 𝒟[*n*] ∈ 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si258.png) denote the clean and noisy-label training sets. [Fig. 4.19](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0100) shows the training results of the optimization from [(4.63)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq65), where ℓ[c](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si259.png) is defined as the cross-entropy loss and ℓ[n](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si260.png) as the mean absolute error loss. Some sample selection techniques work together with the data re-weighting methods from Section [4.2.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0030) by classifying clean-label and noisy-label samples and weighting them differently during training.

![Figure 4.18 Sample selection.Sample selection methods rely on the function \\mathsf{clean}(\\mathcal{D})Image that forms the dataset \\mathcal{D}\_{c} \\subset \\mathcal{D}Image with the training samples from \\mathcal{D}Image that are likely to contain clean labels, with the remaining samples forming the set \\mathcal{D}\_{n} = \\mathcal{D} \\smallsetminus \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image. The optimization uses a loss ℓc(.) for the samples in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image and the loss ℓn(.) for the samples in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}Image.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr018.jpg)

[Figure 4.18](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf1770) Sample selection.Sample selection methods rely on the function clean(𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si255.png) that forms the dataset 𝒟[*c*] ⊂ 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si178.png) with the training samples from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) that are likely to contain clean labels, with the remaining samples forming the set 𝒟[*n*] = 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si256.png). The optimization uses a loss *ℓ*[c](.) for the samples in 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) and the loss *ℓ*[n](.) for the samples in 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si74.png).

![Figure 4.19 Classifier trained with sample selection.Similarly to Fig. 4.17, we use the classification problem described in Fig. 4.3 to train a classifier for 200 iterations with sample selection from (4.63) and \\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\begin{cases}
{\\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\frac{\\tau \\times \\text{iteration}}{200}\\},} & {\\text{~if~}\\text{iteration} > 10} \\\\
{\\mathcal{D},} & \\text{~otherwise~} \\\\

[Figure 4.19](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf1775) Classifier trained with sample selection.Similarly to [Fig. 4.17](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0090), we use the classification problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020) to train a classifier for 200 iterations with sample selection from [(4.63)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq65) and $\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\begin{cases} {\\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\frac{\\tau \\times \\text{iteration}}{200}\\},} & {\\text{~if~}\\text{iteration} > 10} \\\\ {\\mathcal{D},} & \\text{~otherwise~} \\\\ \\end{cases}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si183.png), and 𝒟[*n*] = 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si256.png), where *τ* = 10, and iteration ∈ {1,...,200} denotes the training epoch. Also from [(4.63)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq65), *ℓ*[c](.) is defined as the cross-entropy loss and *ℓ*[n](.) as the mean absolute error loss.

The most common sample selection approach applied in the definition of the function clean(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si179.png) in [(4.63)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq65) is based on the small-loss trick ([Arpit et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0065)), which defines the function clean(𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si255.png) to return the following set

$\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\ell\_{c}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\tau \\right\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si263.png)(4.64) 

Given the difficulty in defining a value for the threshold *τ*, many papers have proposed different ways to use this small-loss trick to select clean-label samples. As already described in Section [4.2.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0030) [Arazo et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0050) proposed the use of a Beta mixture model to represent the distribution of the losses from the training samples in [(4.24)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq26), where the component associated with the small loss values denotes the clean-label component. Small-loss sample selection has also been applied in SIGUA ([Han et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0630)) that relies on the loss function defined in [(4.28)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq30). In this loss function, the training samples are ranked based on their loss values, then the p% smaller loss samples are inserted into the reliable set ℛ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si264.png) for gradient descent, the mid-loss samples, composed by the next q% of ranked samples are inserted into the unreliable set 𝒰![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si265.png) for weighted gradient ascent. SIGUA rejects the remaining higher loss samples, which means that it combines sample selection, loss re-weighting, and data cleaning technique. Similarly, PumpOut ([Han et al., 2018a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0625)) also ranks the training samples in terms of their losses and uses the smallest p% samples for regular stochastic gradient descent, while the remaining 100% − p% of the training samples are used for weighted gradient ascent. The ProMix approach ([Wang et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1830)) introduced an extended small loss criterion by selecting not only samples that have small cross-entropy losses, but samples with high-confidence prediction for the training label. SELF ([Huang et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0750)) introduces a sample selection approach to select noisy-label samples using a temporal ensembling of predictions with ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t + 1)} = \\alpha \\times {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t)} + (1 - \\alpha) \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si266.png), where ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(0)} = 0$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si267.png) and ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t)}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si268.png) represents the prediction ensemble at training iteration *t*. Then, training samples where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\neq \\mathsf{OneHot}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t + 1)})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si269.png) have their labels erased (i.e., they become un-labeled).

Sample selection has been effectively combined with semi-supervised learning (SSL), which will be described in more detail in Section [4.4.4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0105), where ℓ[*c*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si270.png) in [(4.63)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq65) is formulated as a supervised loss and ℓ[*u*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si271.png) denotes an unsupervised loss. [Ding et al. (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0440) introduced an SSL approach, where the clean(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si179.png) function in [(4.63)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq65) selects the training samples that: 1) have the model predictions matching the training label, i.e., $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\arg\\max\_{\\mathbf{y}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si272.png); and 2) $f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) > 0.9$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si273.png). If less than 10% of the training images of any of the classes are selected based on these conditions, then images that do not meet the second condition are added until we have 10% of the training images of that class. [Kong et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0925) proposed an SSL method that, in every epoch *t*, selects a proportion *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png) of the training samples with smallest losses for each class. DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055)) introduced a sample selection approach that is based on an unsupervised classification using a 2-component Gaussian mixture model to represent the loss distribution. DivideMix's sample selection works in the same way as the 2-component Beta mixture model (BMM) ([Arazo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0050)) in [(4.24)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq26).

Most methods above need a warm-up stage, where the model is trained for a few epochs on the noisy-label training, so it can fit the clean-label samples without memorizing the noisy-label samples. An important question remains to be answered about this early-learning stage, which is why can a model trained on noisy-label data identify noisy-label samples based on prediction confidence? [Zheng et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2200) provide a theoretical result that proves that such models indeed have low confidence on noisy-label data. They also propose an algorithm that finds noisy-label samples by thresholding the ratio $\\mathsf{LR}(\\theta,\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si275.png) between the model's prediction of the training label $f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si276.png) and the model's maximum prediction *f*[*θ*]^((**m**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si277.png), where **m** = OneHot(*f*[*θ*](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si278.png). If $\\mathsf{LR}(\\theta,\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) < \\delta$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si279.png), the sample label is flipped from $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) to **m**.

The feature space present in intermediate model layers has also been used in sample selection. For instance, [Ortego et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1380) added a projection model *g*[*ϕ*] : 𝒱 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si280.png) on top of the model backbone *f*[*θ̂*] : 𝒳 → 𝒱![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si281.png), which is trained using the following sample-wise contrastive learning loss:

$\\ell(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\delta(i \\neq j)\\delta({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j})\\mathbf{P}\_{i,j},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si282.png)(4.65) 

where

$\\mathbf{P}\_{i,j} = - \\log\\frac{\\exp(\\mathbf{z}\_{i}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z}\_{j}/\\tau)}{\\sum\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{k},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{k}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\delta(k \\neq i)\\exp(\\mathbf{z}\_{i}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z}\_{k}/\\tau)}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si283.png)(4.66) 

$\\mathcal{D}\_{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}} \\subset \\mathcal{D}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si284.png) represents the training subset of the samples from class ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si285.png), **z**[*i*] = *g*[*ϕ*](*f*[*θ̂*](**x**[**i**]))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si286.png), **P**[*i*, *j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si287.png) denotes the j-th component of the *τ* scaled normalized softmax distribution of the dot product of the representations from the samples *i* and *j* represented by **z**[*i*]^⊤**z**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si288.png), and *δ*()![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si289.png) is the indicator function. The proposed Multi-Objective Interpolation Training (MOIT) ([Ortego et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1380)) relies on three stages, namely: 1) regularization to prevent overfitting, 2) semi-supervised learning based on sample selection, and 3) model refinement. The sample selection process consists of the small-loss criterion using a K nearest neighbor classifier from the pseudo-labeled samples. The set of pseudo-clean samples is formed by:

$\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},d(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) < \\gamma\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si290.png)(4.67) 

where

$d(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = - {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\log\\widehat{\\mathbf{p}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si291.png)(4.68) 

with $\\widehat{\\mathbf{p}} \\in \\Delta^{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si292.png) representing the probability of finding samples of each of the |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si50.png) classes withing the K nearest neighbors of **x** in the space 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si293.png) produced by the projector *g*[*ϕ*](*f*[*θ̂*](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si294.png). The Sample Selection and Relabeling (SSR) approach ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0515)) follows a similar sample selection idea, where samples are classified as clean only if their K nearest neighbor classifier prediction matches with the training label.

A similar feature-based selection process, referred to as probabilistic and cumulative Local Outlier Factor algorithm (pcLOF), was proposed to filter out open-set samples in the loss re-weighting method in ([Wang et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1860)). The pcLOF score represents the probability that a sample is an outlier, which is defined as

$\\mathsf{pcLOF}(\\mathbf{x}) = g\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{t = 1}^{T}\\mathsf{LOF}^{(t)}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si295.png)(4.69) 

where *t* denotes the training iteration, *g*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si296.png) represents a local Gaussian statistics transformation to scale the cumulative LOF score into \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si71.png),

$\\mathsf{LOF}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{\\sum\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{j} \\in \\mathcal{N}\_{k}(\\mathbf{x})}\\frac{d(\\mathbf{x}\_{j})}{d(\\mathbf{x})}}{|\\mathcal{N}\_{k}(\\mathbf{x})|},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si297.png)(4.70) 

with 𝒩[*k*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si298.png) being the set of *k* nearest neighbors of **x**, and

$d(\\mathbf{x}) = \\left( \\frac{\\sum\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{j} \\in \\mathcal{N}\_{k}(\\mathbf{x})}\\mathsf{reach}\_{k}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{x}\_{j})}{|\\mathcal{N}\_{k}(\\mathbf{x})|} \\right)^{- 1}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si299.png)(4.71) 

representing the local reachability density of **x**. In [(4.71)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq73), reach[*k*](**x**, **x**[*j*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si300.png) returns the distance between **x** and **x**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si301.png), if they are far away from each other, but if they are close to each other, reach(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si302.png) returns the distance of **x**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si301.png) to its *k*\-th nearest neighbor.

The selection of samples belonging to closed-set and open-set samples, with a further differentiation of closed set samples into clean or noisy-label samples was proposed in ([Albert et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0015)), following a similar idea presented in the data cleaning method of ([Sachdeva et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1505)). [Albert et al. (2022)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0015) proposed the Softening of Out-of-distribution Samples (DSOS) that is based on the collision entropy score, defined by:

$s\_{DSOS}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\sum\\limits\_{c = 1}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|} - \\log\\left( \\mathbf{y}\_{int}(c) \\right)^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si303.png)(4.72) 

where $\\mathbf{y}\_{int}(c) = \\frac{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c) + f\_{\\theta}^{(c)}(\\mathbf{x})}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si304.png) is the intermediate label, $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si305.png) denotes the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si30.png) component of the label vector, and *f*[*θ*]^((*c*))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si306.png) represents the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si30.png) model output. The collision entropy score in [(4.72)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq74) has the property that when the model is certain about an output that is different from the training label, then **y**[*i**n**t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si307.png) will be 0 in all dimensions, except for the training label and model prediction dimensions, which will be 0.5, leading to $s\_{DSOS}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = - \\log(0.5)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si308.png). Such a score suggests that $s\_{DSOS}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) < - \\log(0.5)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si309.png) represents closed-set clean-label sample. On the other hand, samples with $s\_{DSOS}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) > - \\log(0.5)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si310.png) show a bimodal distribution that can be fit by a Beta mixture model, with the smaller score component containing closed-set noisy-label samples, and the larger score component containing open-set samples. The DSOS optimization roughly follows [(4.63)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq65), with 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) containing the closed-set samples and 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si74.png) having the open-set samples.

A promising sample selection technique, referred to as filtering noisy instances via their eigenvectors (FINE) ([Kim et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0890)), relies on the eigen-decomposition of the gram matrix of each class **c** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si228.png), with

**U**[**c**]*Λ*[**c**]**U**[**c**]^( − 1) = *Σ*[**c**],

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si311.png)(4.73) 

where $\\Sigma\_{\\mathbf{c}} = \\sum\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\delta(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{c})f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x})f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\top}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si312.png) denotes the gram matrix (with *f*[*θ̂*] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si313.png) producing an image representation **z** ∈ 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si314.png), and *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si315.png) representing the indicator function), and **U**[**c**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si316.png), *Λ*[**c**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si317.png) denote the matrices with eigenvectors and eigenvalues. The FINE score for each sample is computed with

$\\text{FINE}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = {\\langle\\mathbf{u}\_{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(1)},f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rangle}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si318.png)(4.74) 

where $\\mathbf{u}\_{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(1)}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si319.png) represents the eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue from the class $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png). The class-wise scores are computed using a 2-component Gaussian mixture model, where the component with smallest mean denotes the clean-label component. Then, samples whose probability of belonging to the clean-label component is larger than a threshold *τ* are classified as clean. The selected samples can then be used in semi-supervised learning approaches or robust loss functions.

Sample selection based on the predictions from teacher and student models has been proposed in ([Kaiser et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0830)). This approach adopts a teacher-student architecture ([Gou et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0590)), where the teacher model is trained by minimizing a classification loss using the labels from the training set, while the student model is trained to reproduce the logits produced by the teacher for each training sample. Assuming the teacher model is denoted by *f*[*θ*^((*t*))] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si320.png) and the student model is represented by *f*[*θ*^((*s*))] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si321.png), their aggregate classification is denoted by

$p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{f\_{\\theta^{(t)}}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\times f\_{\\theta^{(s)}}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x})}{\\sum\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}f\_{\\theta^{(t)}}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\times f\_{\\theta^{(s)}}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si322.png)(4.75) 

where *f*[*θ*^((*t*))]^((**y**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si323.png) represents the probability prediction for class **y** from the teacher model (similarly for the student model *f*[*θ*^((*s*))]^((**y**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si324.png)). Then the set of pseudo-clean images are the ones in the set $\\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},p(Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x}) > \\tau\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si325.png), while the pseudo-noisy images are the ones in $\\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},p(Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x}) \\leq \\tau\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si326.png), where the threshold *τ* is estimated with the Otsu's algorithm ([Otsu, 1979](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1385)).

Another way of selecting noisy-label samples is based on the use of uncertainty measures ([Köhler et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0920)), such as variation-ratio or standard deviation of the predictions. These measures, computed from deep ensembles ([Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1005)) or Monte-Carlo dropout ([Gal et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0530)), have shown to be relatively effective, where the more uncertain samples are assumed to have incorrect labels, and new pseudo-labels are applied to them. The use of peer loss has also been considered in ([Cheng et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0290)) for the problem of sample selection, where samples that have the peer loss score in [(4.6)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq8) below a certain threshold are selected for training.

A critical point present in all methods above is how to determine the threshold *τ* for the clean-label criterion in [(4.64)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq66). A relatively common way is to set *τ* based on the pre-defined proportion *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png) of training samples to be selected as noisy at each training epoch *t*. For instance, [Han et al. (2018c)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645) pre-define a curriculum, where at the first training iterations, *R*(*t*) ≈ 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si327.png), which means that most of the training samples are classified as clean-label. This is sensible since the model has not started the overfitting process at this early training stage. As training progresses, *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png) is reduced using a pre-defined function, to prevent the model to overfit the noisy-label training samples. More specifically, Co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)) introduced the following schedule:

*R*(*t*) = 1 − *τ* × min (1, (*t*/*t*[*k*])^(*α*)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si328.png)(4.76) 

where *τ*, *α*, *t*[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si329.png) are hyper-parameters. A more principled way of designing *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png) has been proposed in ([Yao et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2025)), as the following bi-level algorithm:

$R^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{R \\in \\mathcal{F}}\\mathcal{L}\_{val}(\\theta^{\\ast},R,\\mathcal{D}\_{val})\\text{s.t.~}\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\mathcal{L}(\\theta,R,\\mathcal{D}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si330.png)(4.77) 

where 𝒟[*v**a**l*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si331.png) represents a clean-label validation set, 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) is the usual noisy-label training set, ℒ[*v**a**l*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si332.png) and ℒ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si333.png) denote validation and training loss functions, and ℱ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si334.png) is a search space for *R*. This search space represents the prior for *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png), explained above, where *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png) should be large at the beginning of the training and it should reduce as training progresses. [Yao et al. (2020a)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2025) suggested the use of *K* basis functions to build ℱ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si334.png), each one following the prior about *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png). Hence, the optimization for *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png) comprises an estimation of the basis functions weights and parameters. Results show that the *R*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si274.png) learned is more effective than the one manually defined ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)). In ([Cheng et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0290)) the threshold is automatically defined at each training epoch with

$\\tau = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}\\sum\\limits\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\ell\_{peer}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si335.png)(4.78) 

where ℓ[*p**e**e**r*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si336.png) is as defined in [(4.6)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq8).

Sample selection has been a fertile research topic in noisy-label learning. The two main points of study in sample selection are the clean-label sample selection criteria and the threshold. Many techniques have been proposed for the selection criteria, ranging from small-loss trick approaches, to graph-based methods. The research into the threshold has received comparatively less attention, where the focus is whether it should be manually defined ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)), or automatically optimized ([Yao et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2025)). Even though we do not have a standard sample selection method, this technique is ubiquitously present in noisy-label learning approaches, which suggests that this technique is an important stage in noisy-label learning methods.

### 4.3.4 Multi-rater learning

As presented in Section [3.3](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml), there have been papers ([Liu, 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1140); [Nguyen et al., 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1330)) that show that the identifiability of the learning from noisy-label problem requires a minimum number of labels per training sample. The experimental setup that relies on a certain number of labels per training sample is generally referred to as multi-rater learning ([Sudre et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1660); [Ji et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0790); [Schaekermann et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1535); [Becker et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0110); [Tanno et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1700)), and it has been usually studied from the perspective of uncertainty learning instead of noisy-label learning. Multi-rater learning tries to estimate the degree of uncertainty in the predictions of the model and the annotators and use this information to guide the learning process. Given the direct connection between multi-rater learning and noisy-label learning, we present some papers that provide links between the two problems.

In multi-rater learning, such as the one depicted in [Fig. 4.20](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0105), the training set is defined as $\\mathcal{D} = {\\{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M})\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si339.png), with each image **x**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si340.png) having multiple labels ${\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si341.png). The first methods designed to handle multi-rater learning explored two strategies, namely ([Tanno et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1700)): 1) two-stage, and 2) simultaneous. The first step in two-stage approaches ([Smyth et al., 1994](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1630); [Warfield et al., 2004](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1870); [Whitehill et al., 2009](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1910); [Welinder et al., 2010](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1900); [Rodrigues et al., 2013](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1485)) use the observed noisy labels to estimate the latent variables representing the true label and annotator skills. The second step consists of training a model using the estimated true labels. These methods are criticized for a few reasons, such as: 1) the input data is not explored when estimating the true label, 2) the trained models tend to underestimate uncertainty ([Jungo et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0825); [Jensen et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0780)), and 3) the two-stage training is unlikely to provide an optimal optimization. On the other hand, simultaneous approaches ([Raykar et al., 2009](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1455), [2010](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1460); [Branson et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0205); [Van Horn et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1785); [Khetan et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0880)) merge the two stages using expectation-maximization (EM) like algorithms and, except for ([Khetan et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0880)), they require a large number of labels per example, which constrains their application. [Kaster et al. (2011)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0860) show an experimental evaluation of previously proposed multi-rater models using approximate variational techniques for inference.

![Figure 4.20 Multi-rater learning.The multi-rater learning technique takes the annotation from M labelers for every data point, denoted by (\\mathbf{x},{\\{{\\widetilde{y}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M}) \\in \\mathcal{D}Image, to learn labeler-specific transition models, represented by {\\{\\mathbf{T}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M}Image, and the clean-label model predictor fθ(x). The learning of the label transition models is usually regularized by some smoothing function, such as the minimization of the trace of the transition matrices.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr020.jpg)

[Figure 4.20](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2065) Multi-rater learning.The multi-rater learning technique takes the annotation from *M* labelers for every data point, denoted by (**x**, {*ỹ*[*j*]}[*j* = 1]^(*M*)) ∈ 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si337.png), to learn labeler-specific transition models, represented by {**T**[*j*]}[*j* = 1]^(*M*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si338.png), and the clean-label model predictor *f*[*θ*](**x**). The learning of the label transition models is usually regularized by some smoothing function, such as the minimization of the trace of the transition matrices.

The general learning of current multi-rater models can be summarized by the formulation by [Tanno et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1700), where the multi-rater annotation probability is computed with

$p\\left( {\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M}|\\mathbf{x} \\right) = \\prod\\limits\_{j = 1}^{M}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si342.png)(4.79) 

where *p*(**y**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si343.png) is the true label distribution and $p({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si344.png) is the transition probability from the true label to the *j*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si345.png) noisy annotation. In ([Tanno et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1700)), the proposed optimization estimates the transition matrices and the model parameters, as in

$\\theta^{\\ast},{\\{\\mathbf{T}\_{j}^{\\ast}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,{\\{\\mathbf{T}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{{(\\mathbf{x},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M})} \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell\\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},\\mathbf{T}\_{j}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) + \\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{M}\\mathsf{tr}(\\mathbf{T}\_{j}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si346.png)(4.80) 

where **T**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si347.png) denotes the label transition matrix for annotator *j* ∈ {1, ..., *M*}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si348.png), and tr(**T**[*j*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si349.png) denotes the trace of matrix **T**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si347.png). This minimization of the trace of the label transition matrix in [(4.80)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq82) encourages the annotators to be maximally unreliable to induce a maximal amount of confusion which explains the noisy labels ([Tanno et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1700)). We show an example of multi-rater noisy-label learning in [Fig. 4.21](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0110).

![Figure 4.21 Classifier trained with multi-rater learning.We use the classification problem described in Fig. 4.3 to train the classifier for multi-rater learning from (4.80) for 1000 epochs. The problem is modified to have three labelers, one with noise rate 0.25, another with rate 0.15, and the other rate 0.4.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr021.jpg)

[Figure 4.21](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2165) Classifier trained with multi-rater learning.We use the classification problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020) to train the classifier for multi-rater learning from [(4.80)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq82) for 1000 epochs. The problem is modified to have three labelers, one with noise rate 0.25, another with rate 0.15, and the other rate 0.4.

The multi-rater optimization in [(4.80)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq82) does not attempt to characterize the difficulty of labeling the image. For example, images where multi-rater labels show general consensus should be considered easy cases, while images where labels disagree should be considered hard cases ([Paletz et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1390); [Schaekermann et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1535)). This fact is explored by [Yu et al. (2020a)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2065) with multiple classification branches, each one representing predictions under three different sensitivity settings (high sensitivity, high specificity, and in-between the two settings). These three branches share a common feature extractor, referred to as *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si350.png), but each branch has a separate output, with the high sensitivity branch denoted by *f*[*θ*[*s**n*]] : 𝒵 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si351.png), the high specificity branch represented by *f*[*θ*[*s**p*]] : 𝒵 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si352.png), and the in-between branch *f*[*θ*[*f**s*]] : 𝒵 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si353.png). The model is optimized with

$\\theta^{\\ast},\\theta\_{sn}^{\\ast},\\theta\_{sp}^{\\ast},\\theta\_{fs}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,\\theta\_{sn},\\theta\_{sp},\\theta\_{fs}}\\sum\\limits\_{{(\\mathbf{x},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M})} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{sp}}\\ell\\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},f\_{\\theta\_{sp}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right) + \\ell\_{con}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{sp}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),f\_{\\theta\_{sn}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),a \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{{(\\mathbf{x},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M})} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{sn}}\\ell\\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},f\_{\\theta\_{sn}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right) + \\ell\_{con}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{sp}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),f\_{\\theta\_{sn}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),a \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{{(\\mathbf{x},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M})} \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell\_{fs}\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathbf{w}}\\left\\lbrack {\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M} \\right\\rbrack,f\_{\\theta\_{fs}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),f\_{\\theta\_{sp}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),f\_{\\theta\_{sn}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si354.png)(4.81) 

where 𝒟[*s**p*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si355.png), 𝒟[*s**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si356.png) denote the high specificity dataset (with twice more positive than negative labels) and high sensitivity dataset (with twice more negative than positive labels), respectively, ℓ(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si122.png) represents the cross-entropy loss,

$\\ell\_{con}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sp},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{se},a) = \\frac{a}{2}{\\|{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sp} - {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{se}\\|}\_{2}^{2} + \\frac{1 - a}{2}\\left( \\max\\left( 0,1 - \\|{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sp} - {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{se}\\| \\right) \\right)^{2}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si357.png)(4.82) 

is the consensus loss between the sensitivity and specificity branches denoted by ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sp} = f\_{\\theta\_{sp}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si358.png) and ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sn} = f\_{\\theta\_{sn}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si359.png), respectively,

$\\ell\_{fs}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{fs},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sp},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sn}) = u \\times \\mathsf{KL}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}\\|{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{fs})$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si360.png)(4.83) 

denotes the fusion loss weighted by the uncertainty $u = 0.5\\left( 1 - \\frac{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sp}^{\\top}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sn}}{\\|{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sp}\\|\\|{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{sn}\\|} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si361.png), with $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathbf{w}}\\left\\lbrack {\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M} \\right\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si362.png) calculating the average label weighted by **w** = {**w**[*j*]}[*j* = 1]^(*M*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si363.png) that is the weight of the *j*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si345.png) rater, determined by the rating accuracy against the ground-truth label.

When discussing uncertainty, it is important to differentiate between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties ([Der Kiureghian and Ditlevsen, 2009](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0410)). The noise found in the data, such as the label noise, defines the aleatoric uncertainty, while the epistemic uncertainty is related to the noise in the estimation of the model parameters. [Hu et al. (2019a)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0730) noticed that epistemic uncertainty is hard to estimate because we cannot access the groundtruth model to measure it. However, aleatoric uncertainty can be estimated from a multi-rater label with the variance $\\mathbb{V}\_{p(\\mathcal{D})}\\lbrack\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack = \\frac{1}{M}\\sum\_{j = 1}^{M}{({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} - \\overline{\\mathbf{y}})}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si364.png), where $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\frac{1}{M}\\sum\_{j = 1}^{M}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si365.png). The method in ([Hu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0730)) extends the Probabilistic U-Net ([Kohl et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0915)) by exploring multi-rater variability to account for aleatoric uncertainty and to estimate epistemic uncertainty. To explain the approach in ([Hu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0730)) in more detail, we first need to explain the posterior predictive distribution given by *p*(*Y*|*X*, 𝒟) = ∫[*θ*]*p*(*Y*|*X*, *θ*)*p*(*θ*|𝒟)*d**θ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si366.png), where *p*(*Y*|*X*, *θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si367.png) denotes a prediction model parameterized by *θ* and *p*(*θ*|𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si368.png) represents an intractable posterior distribution that is approximated by a tractable *q*[*λ*](*θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si369.png), which is estimated with

$\\min\\limits\_{\\lambda}\\mathsf{KL}\\left( q\_{\\lambda}(\\theta)\\| p(\\theta|\\mathcal{D}) \\right) = \\max\\limits\_{\\lambda}\\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\lambda}(\\theta)}\\left\\lbrack \\log\\prod\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x},\\theta) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathsf{KL}\\left( q\_{\\lambda}(\\theta)\\| p(\\theta) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si370.png)(4.84) 

where *p*(*θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si371.png) is a prior on *θ*. The predictive uncertainty is the variance of the posterior predictive distribution, defined by the following decomposition

$\\underset{\\text{predictive\\ uncertainty}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{V}\_{p(Y|X)}\\lbrack\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack}} = \\underset{\\text{aleatoric\\ uncertainty}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\lambda}(\\theta)}\\left\\lbrack \\mathbb{V}\_{p(Y|X,\\theta)}\\left\\lbrack \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\right\\rbrack \\right\\rbrack}} + \\underset{\\text{epistemic\\ uncertainty}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{V}\_{q\_{\\lambda}(\\theta)}\\left\\lbrack \\mathbb{E}\_{p(Y|X,\\theta)}\\left\\lbrack \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\right\\rbrack \\right\\rbrack}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si372.png)(4.85) 

In [(4.85)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq87), the aleatoric uncertainty measures the average of the output variance, while the epistemic uncertainty measures fluctuations in the mean prediction. Putting all together, the model trained in ([Hu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0730)) extends the probabilistic U-net ([Kohl et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0915)) by adding a mechanism to measure epistemic uncertainty with the following loss function

$\\ell\_{vd}(\\lambda,\\mathcal{D}) = - \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\lambda}(\\theta)q\_{\\lambda}(Z|X = \\mathbf{x}\_{i},Y = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i})}\\left\\lbrack \\log p\_{\\lambda}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}|\\mathbf{x}\_{i},\\mathbf{z},\\theta) \\right\\rbrack + \\frac{\\beta}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\mathsf{KL}\\left( q\_{\\lambda}(\\mathbf{z}|\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i})\\| p\_{\\lambda}(\\mathbf{z}\\|\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) \\right) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\mathsf{KL}\\left( q\_{\\lambda}(\\theta)\\| p(\\theta)) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si373.png)(4.86) 

where **z** ∈ 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si314.png). In [(4.86)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq88), the model uncertainty is minimized when *q*[*λ*](*θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si369.png) approximates a delta peak on the maximum likelihood model parameters. The aleatoric uncertainty $\\mathbf{p}\_{m} = \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\lambda}(\\theta)}\\left\\lbrack \\mathbb{V}\_{p(Y|X,\\theta)}\\left\\lbrack \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\right\\rbrack \\right\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si374.png) is then trained to approximate the multi-grader variability $\\mathbf{p}\_{g} = \\mathbb{V}\_{p(\\mathcal{D})}\\lbrack\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si375.png) with

$\\ell\_{al} = - \\frac{\\gamma}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\left\\lbrack \\mathbf{p}\_{g}\\log\\mathbf{p}\_{m} + (1 - \\mathbf{p}\_{g})\\log(1 - \\mathbf{p}\_{m}) \\right\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si376.png)(4.87) 

A relatively different approach from the ones above is the Classifier Refinement Of croWD-sourced LABels (CROWDLAB) ([Goh et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0570)) that takes a trained classifier and estimates a consensus label (with a confidence score) per training sample, and a rating for each annotator to assess the correctness of their labels. CROWDLAB relies on a weighted ensemble of classifier predictions, where weights are estimated based on the trustworthiness of each annotator relative to the given classifier. After training a model *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si227.png) using consensus labels derived from majority voting using $\\mathcal{D} = {\\{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M})\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si339.png), they first score the consensus label quality with:

$f\_{\\theta\_{CR}}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{w \\times f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\sum\_{j = 1}^{M}w\_{j} \\times f\_{\\theta\_{j}}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})}{w + \\sum\_{j = 1}^{M}w\_{j}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si377.png)(4.88) 

where $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si378.png) denotes the consensus label, $f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si379.png) represents the trained model prediction for class $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si378.png),

$f\_{\\theta\_{j}}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\begin{cases} {P,} & {\\text{~if~}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} = \\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}} \\\\ {\\frac{1 - P}{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1},} & \\text{~otherwise} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si380.png)(4.89) 

is the annotator-specific model prediction, with $P = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\frac{1}{M}\\sum\_{j = 1}^{M}\\delta({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i,j} = {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si381.png) (*δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si315.png) is the indicator function), and the trustworthiness weights *w* and {*w*[*j*]}[*j* = 1]^(*M*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si382.png) represent the ensemble weights of the model and annotators, respectively, that are in general computed as 1 minus the estimated relative error of the trained model and annotator-specific models ([Goh et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0570)). Furthermore, CROWDLAB also ranks the annotators using the score {*a*[*j*]}[*j* = 1]^(*M*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si383.png), with *a*[*j*] ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si384.png) computed with the weighted average of the label quality score and the annotator agreement with consensus labels ([Goh et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0570)). Armed with the consensus labels, their confidence score, and the annotator ratings, it is then possible to eliminate the labels produced by low-ranked annotators and request the re-labeling of low-confidence labels.

Multi-rater learning is a fertile and relatively unexplored research topic, with applications in noisy-label learning and uncertainty estimation. The main issue with these approaches is the cost associated with the collection of multiple labels per image. Techniques that can generate new labels per image from its estimated label distribution ([Nguyen et al., 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1330)) can mitigate this labeling cost problem if they can reliably substitute human labeling. The next years should witness an increasing investigation of multi-rater learning for noisy-label learning.

### 4.3.5 Prior knowledge

Prior information can be helpful when handling noisy-label learning, particularly when the information can constrain the optimization process. An interesting prior information about noisy-label learning is studied in ([Seo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1560)) that explores the idea that by transforming the original problem containing |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si50.png) classes into another problem where subsets of these classes are merged to form |𝒞| < |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si385.png) meta-classes, we reduce the noise rate in the training set (see [Fig. 4.22](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0115)). Consider that the original noise rate is provided by

$\\eta(\\mathcal{D}) = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\delta(\\mathbf{y} \\neq \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si386.png)(4.90) 

where **y** is the hidden true label of **x**, and *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si315.png) is the indicator function. Also assume that the new set of meta classes 𝒞^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si387.png) merged a few of the classes from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) to form a new training set 𝒟^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si388.png), so the new noise rate is

$\\eta(\\mathcal{D}^{m}) = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}^{m}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{c}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}^{m}}\\delta(\\mathbf{c}^{m} \\neq {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{c}}}^{m}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si389.png)(4.91) 

where **c**[*i*]^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si390.png) and ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{c}}}\_{i}^{m}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si391.png) are the hidden true and visible noisy meta class for **x**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si340.png) in 𝒟^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si388.png). It is trivial to show that *η*(𝒟^(*m*)) < *η*(𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si392.png) ([Seo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1560)).
