For instance, let us say that two samples **x**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si340.png) and **x**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si301.png) belong to the same class (i.e., **y**[*i*] = **y**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si393.png)), but the label for **x**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si301.png) has been corrupted, which means that ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} \\neq {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si394.png). By merging ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si285.png) and ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si395.png) into the same meta class, we have ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{c}}}\_{i}^{m} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{c}}}\_{j}^{m}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si396.png), i.e., the two samples share the same clean label again. [Seo et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1560) propose the implementation of {𝒟^(*m*)}[*m* = 1]^(*M*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si397.png) meta-class sets and the training of *M* separate classifiers {*f*[*θ*^(*m*)] : 𝒳 → 𝒞^(*m*)}[*m* = 1]^(*M*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si398.png) for those training sets. Inference is performed with

$p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{\\prod\_{m = 1}^{M}f\_{\\theta^{m}}^{\\mathsf{meta}(\\mathbf{y},m)}(\\mathbf{x})}{\\sum\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\prod\_{m = 1}^{M}f\_{\\theta^{m}}^{\\mathsf{meta}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},m)}(\\mathbf{x})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si399.png)(4.92) 

where meta(**y**, *m*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si400.png) outputs the meta class from the *m*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si401.png) set of meta classes that contains the label **y**. The meta classes should be formed by merging the original classes that have common properties, which can be achieved by applying the k-means clustering algorithm. The prior information above is always true, but to properly explore this idea, one may need to have a large number of meta-class sets, with the inconvenience of needing to train one classifier per meta-class set.

![Figure 4.22 Prior knowledge with meta classes.In the exploration of prior knowledge with meta classes, classes are merged to form new meta classes (e.g., the initial four classes are merged into two sets of two meta classes), which are guaranteed to have fewer mistakes than the original problem, as seen in this example (the original 4-class problem has 12 mislabeled samples, while the top 2-meta-class problem has nine mistakes, and the bottom 2-meta-class problem has three mistakes).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr022.jpg)

[Figure 4.22](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2260) Prior knowledge with meta classes.In the exploration of prior knowledge with meta classes, classes are merged to form new meta classes (e.g., the initial four classes are merged into two sets of two meta classes), which are guaranteed to have fewer mistakes than the original problem, as seen in this example (the original 4-class problem has 12 mislabeled samples, while the top 2-meta-class problem has nine mistakes, and the bottom 2-meta-class problem has three mistakes).

A widely adopted noisy-label learning technique is the one that aims to estimate the noise transition matrix from clean-label to noisy-label learning, which will be explained in more detail in Section [4.5.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0125). The reliability of this estimation process requires clean-label samples or a large training set. An alternative based on a prior knowledge provided by humans is proposed in ([Han et al., 2018b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635)), where the idea is to constrain the optimization with a transition matrix mask that eliminates the possibility of estimating invalid class transition probabilities (e.g., images of beach cannot be confused with images of mountain), as shown in [Fig. 4.23](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0120). In general, the optimization involving a transition matrix is formulated by

$\\theta^{\\ast},\\mathbf{T} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,\\mathbf{T}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{T}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))\\text{s.t.~}\\mathbf{T} \\in {\\lbrack 0,1\\rbrack}^{|\\mathcal{Y}| \\times |\\mathcal{Y}|}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si402.png)(4.93) 

where **T** represents the noisy-label transition matrix. In principle, this can be solved by adding an explicit structure constraint *s*(**T**) = **S**[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si403.png), with *s*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si404.png) extracting **T**'s matrix structure **S**[0] ∈ {0, 1}^(|𝒴| × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si405.png). However, as pointed out in ([Han et al., 2018b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635)), such training strategy has a few issues, such as: 1) it is unclear which distance measure to use to compute the distance between the learned transition matrix **T** and the prior **S**[0]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si406.png); and 2) the complexity of training [(4.93)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq95) for large-scale problems using Lagrange multipliers. [Han et al. (2018b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635) proposed the use of variational learning to maximize the following evidence lower bound (ELBO) that approximates the log-likelihood of the noisy data, as follows

$\\log p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}) \\geq \\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{T})}\\left\\lbrack \\log\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{T})p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}) - \\log\\left( q(\\mathbf{S}\_{0})/p(\\mathbf{S}\_{0}) \\right)|\_{\\mathbf{S}\_{0} = s(\\mathbf{T})} \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si407.png)(4.94) 

where *q*(**T**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si408.png) represents the variational distribution to approximate the posterior of the noise transition matrix **T**, $q(\\mathbf{S}\_{0}) = q(\\mathbf{T})\\frac{d\\mathbf{T}}{d\\mathbf{S}\_{0}}|\_{\\mathbf{S}\_{0} = s(\\mathbf{T})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si409.png), and *p*(**S**[0])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si410.png) is the structure prior.

![Figure 4.23 Prior knowledge with label transition matrix structure prior.A prior on the possible label transitions can be provided by a prior with a binary label transition matrix, where 1 (white square) means a possible transition (e.g., label transition between dog and cat or between bird and plane), and 0 (black square) represents a prohibited transition (e.g., no label transition between dog and airplane).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr023.jpg)

[Figure 4.23](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2285) Prior knowledge with label transition matrix structure prior.A prior on the possible label transitions can be provided by a prior with a binary label transition matrix, where 1 (white square) means a possible transition (e.g., label transition between dog and cat or between bird and plane), and 0 (black square) represents a prohibited transition (e.g., no label transition between dog and airplane).

Another possible prior knowledge to explore in noisy-label learning is the fact that models with simpler hypothesis and smoother decision boundaries are less prone to overfit to the noisy-label samples, and consequently generalize better ([Luo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1180)). The low dimensionality of the deep representation subspace of training samples is a way to represent such simpler hypothesis and smoother decision boundaries ([Ma et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1200)). The dimensionality can be measured with the Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) of the underlying data subspace/submanifold ([Houle, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0725)). In practice, the LID of the deep representation **z** from a data point **x** can be estimated as follows ([Levina and Bickel, 2004](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1050); [Amsaleg et al., 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0040)):

$\\widehat{\\mathsf{LID}}(\\mathbf{z}) = - \\left( \\frac{1}{K}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{K}\\log\\frac{r\_{i}(\\mathbf{z})}{r\_{\\max}\\left( \\mathbf{z} \\right)} \\right)^{- 1}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si412.png)(4.95) 

where *r*[*i*](**z**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si413.png) represents the distance between **z** and its *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si48.png) nearest neighbor, and *r*[max](**z**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si414.png) is the maximum distance to all the K nearest neighbors from **z**. In general, noisy-label learning has a LID compression in the early training stages, followed by a LID expansion in later training stages ([Fig. 4.24](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0125) shows LID values for clean and noisy-label samples). On the contrary, when labels are clean, LID reduces continuously until the last training stages. [Ma et al. (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1200) proposed a training optimization with:

$\\theta\_{t}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell\\left( \\alpha\_{t} \\times \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} + (1 - \\alpha\_{t}) \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si415.png)(4.96) 

where *t* indexes the training epoch, and

$\\alpha\_{t} = \\exp\\left( - (t/T)\\frac{{\\widehat{\\mathsf{LID}}}\_{t}}{\\min\_{j = 0}^{t - 1}{\\widehat{\\mathsf{LID}}}\_{j}} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si416.png)(4.97) 

with ${\\widehat{\\mathsf{LID}}}\_{t} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\widehat{\\mathsf{LID}}(\\mathbf{z}\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si417.png) denotes the mean LID score at training epoch *t* ∈ {1, ..., *T*}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si418.png). Hence, this optimization is a simulated annealing algorithm that finds a balance between LID and prediction performance. In particular, at the LID compression stage (early training epochs), *α*[*t*] → 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si419.png) and training relies on the training labels. At the LID expansion stage (i.e., overfitting phase at later training epochs), *α*[*t*] → 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si420.png), favoring model prediction. [Fig. 4.25](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0130) shows a comparison between a training using the LID prior from [(4.96)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq98) and a regular training with CE loss without any regularization. Notice that the probability map from the LID training looks closer to the clean-label map, and the LID values tend to go down during training, differently from the LID values from the CE loss training.

![Figure 4.24 Prior knowledge with Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID).The LID computed with \\widehat{\\mathsf{LID}}(\\mathbf{z})Image from (4.95) is used to weight the re-labeling of training samples, as shown in (4.96), where high LID values suggest that the sample has been mislabeled, while low LID values indicate a clean label.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr024.jpg)

[Figure 4.24](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2330) Prior knowledge with Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID).The LID computed with $\\widehat{\\mathsf{LID}}(\\mathbf{z})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si411.png) from [(4.95)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq97) is used to weight the re-labeling of training samples, as shown in [(4.96)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq98), where high LID values suggest that the sample has been mislabeled, while low LID values indicate a clean label.

![Figure 4.25 Classifier trained with Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) prior knowledge.Using the classification problem described in Fig. 4.3 to train a classifier for 300 iterations using the LID prior knowledge from (4.96), where K = 50 in (4.95). We show not only the final training losses and probability maps, but also the average LID values for the training samples using the optimization in (4.96), in comparison with a training that solely relies on CE loss without any regularization.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr025.jpg)

[Figure 4.25](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2340) Classifier trained with Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) prior knowledge.Using the classification problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020) to train a classifier for 300 iterations using the LID prior knowledge from [(4.96)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq98), where *K* = 50 in [(4.95)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq97). We show not only the final training losses and probability maps, but also the average LID values for the training samples using the optimization in [(4.96)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq98), in comparison with a training that solely relies on CE loss without any regularization.

Exploring prior data knowledge is a strategy that can lead to strong results. However, discovering sensible priors to explore is a challenging task that requires good knowledge of the problem and creativity. Furthermore, some priors may be specific to particular applications and do not generalize well to all possible applications. The optimization using priors can also introduce operational challenges, such as with the optimization presented in ([Han et al., 2018b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635)).

### 4.3.6 Data augmentation

Data augmentation ([Shorten and Khoshgoftaar, 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1595); [Cubuk et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0335), [2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0340); [DeVries and Taylor, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0415); [Hendrycks et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0695)) is a method to generate new training samples from the original ones in the training set with the goal of increasing the diversity and size of the training set to regularize training and improve generalization. For images, this generation is based on applying relatively small transformations to the original training samples using several techniques, such as cropping, rotation, flipping, scaling, or image noise addition. The selection of data augmentation functions is a challenging task that can be automated ([Cubuk et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0335), [2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0340)) for specific datasets and learning tasks.

In noisy-label learning, data augmentation has been used mostly as a regularization technique ([Song et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1645)). For image-based problems, data augmentation usually relies on the traditional techniques of cropping, rotation, flipping, etc. However, [Nishi et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1350) introduced the Augmented Descent (AugDesc) technique into noisy-label learning. AugDesc relies on two sets of data augmentation strategies: a weak augmentation based on traditional techniques of cropping, rotation, flipping, etc.; and a strong augmentation based on automated data augmentation selection methods ([Cubuk et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0335), [2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0340)) (see [Fig. 4.26](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0135)). Then, AugDesc uses the weak augmentation for sample selection and re-labeling, and the strong augmentation for the back-propagation step. The optimization of AugDesc is as follows (see [Fig. 4.27](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0140)): 

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{S}}\\left\\lbrack \\mathsf{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x})) + (1 - \\mathsf{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})) \\times \\ell(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si423.png)(4.98) 

where

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{W}}\\left\\lbrack f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si424.png)(4.99) 

with 𝒜[*S*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si422.png) and 𝒜[*W*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si421.png) representing the sets of strong and weak augmentation functions *a* : 𝒳 → 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si425.png), and clean : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si426.png) being a function that classifies a training sample into clean (returns 1) or noisy (returns 0). We show an example of the optimization from [(4.98)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq100) in [Fig. 4.28](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0145). A similar idea has been explored in ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1625)), where the proposed method uses weak augmentation to train with samples selected as clean and maximizes the consistency between the model predictions of the weakly and strongly augmented training samples classified as noisy, with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\mathsf{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times \\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{W}}\\left\\lbrack \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x}))) \\right\\rbrack + \\left( 1 - \\mathsf{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right) \\times \\ell\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{S}}\\left\\lbrack f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack,\\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{W}}\\left\\lbrack f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si427.png)(4.100) 

![Figure 4.26 Data augmentation functions.Examples of strong and weak data augmentation techniques.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr026.jpg)

[Figure 4.26](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2410) Data augmentation functions.Examples of strong and weak data augmentation techniques.

![Figure 4.27 Data augmentation.The training using data augmentation is based on learning a single model with both the weak augmentations in \\mathcal{A}\_{W}Image and strong augmentations in \\mathcal{A}\_{S}Image and a consistency loss between predictions affected by both augmentations, as explained in (4.98).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr027.jpg)

[Figure 4.27](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2415) Data augmentation.The training using data augmentation is based on learning a single model with both the weak augmentations in 𝒜[*W*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si421.png) and strong augmentations in 𝒜[*S*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si422.png) and a consistency loss between predictions affected by both augmentations, as explained in [(4.98)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq100).

![Figure 4.28 Classifier trained with data augmentation.The data augmentation optimization AugDesc from (4.98), where a(x)=x + ϵ, with \\epsilon \\sim \\mathcal{N}(\\mu = 0,\\Sigma = \\mathbf{I} \\times \\sigma)Image, where σ = 0.001 for weak augmentations in \\mathcal{A}\_{W}Image, and σ = 0.01 for strong augmentations in \\mathcal{A}\_{S}Image, and \\mathsf{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\delta(\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\frac{\\tau \\times \\text{iteration}}{500})Image.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr028.jpg)

[Figure 4.28](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2425) Classifier trained with data augmentation.The data augmentation optimization AugDesc from [(4.98)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq100), where *a*(**x**)=**x** + *ϵ*, with *ϵ* ∼ 𝒩(*μ* = 0, *Σ* = **I** × *σ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si428.png), where *σ* = 0.001 for weak augmentations in 𝒜[*W*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si421.png), and *σ* = 0.01 for strong augmentations in 𝒜[*S*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si422.png), and $\\mathsf{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\delta(\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\frac{\\tau \\times \\text{iteration}}{500})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si429.png).

Another type of data augmentation explored for noisy-label learning is MixUp ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2110)) that trains on convex combinations of training samples and respective labels, such as

$(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\mathsf{MixUp}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},\\mathbf{x}\_{j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j})\\text{,\\ where}\\mathbf{x} = \\lambda\\mathbf{x}\_{i} + (1 - \\lambda)\\mathbf{x}\_{j},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\lambda{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} + (1 - \\lambda){\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si430.png)(4.101) 

and *λ* ∼ *β*(*a*, *b*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si431.png) representing a sample from a beta distribution parameterized by *a* and *b*. [Arazo et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0050) proposed the use of MixUp in noisy-label learning with the following robust per-sample loss correction approach:

$\\ell(i,j) = - \\lambda \\times \\left\\lbrack {((1 - w\_{i}) \\times {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} + w\_{i} \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}))}^{\\top}\\log(h) \\right\\rbrack - (1 - \\lambda) \\times \\left\\lbrack {((1 - w\_{j}) \\times {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} + w\_{i} \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j}))}^{\\top}\\log(h) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si432.png)(4.102) 

where *h* = *f*[*θ*](*λ* × **x**[*i*] + (1 − *λ*) × **x**[*j*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si433.png), and *w*[*i*], *w*[*j*] ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si434.png) denote the confidence in the ground-truth labels and network predictions estimated from an unsupervised noise model.

Data augmentation has become a standard training technique in noisy-label learning. Virtually all modern approaches rely on some sort of data augmentation, ranging from simple approaches, such as with the use of regular augmentations during training, to sophisticated methods, like the ones described in this section. Consequently, we expect that data augmentation will continue to be explored in future methods as an essential technique to address noisy-label learning.

Test time augmentation (TTA) is a common post-hoc (i.e., applied after the training process is finished) machine learning technique used to improve generalization and robustness of models during testing. The basic idea is run the trained model on several augmented test samples, modified by applying several data transformations, and then the final prediction is based on aggregating the results from each augmented data ([Shanmugam et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1570); [Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1625)). The data augmentations, particularly when applied to image samples, consist of: random rotations, translations, scaling, flips, and color distortions. The application of these data transformations to the test samples followed by the calculation of the predictions for each augmented version effectively produces an ensemble of predictions. In particular, given a test image **x** and a set of image transformations denoted by 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si435.png), the TTA prediction is:

${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\ast} = \\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}}\\left\\lbrack f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(a(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si436.png)(4.103) 

Although quite simple, TTA shows substantial improvements in noisy-label classification ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1625)). One can argue that this will significantly increase testing time, but since the data augmentations are mutually independent, they can in principle be applied in parallel, which means that this will not increase testing time. This is a topic that deserves further research.

### 4.3.7 Pseudo-labeling

Pseudo-labeling is a data-processing technique that is usually integrated with other methods, such as semi-supervised learning in Section [4.4.4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0105). It is derived from the bootstrapping method ([Reed et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1470)) that modifies the training label with

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\beta \\times \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} + (1 - \\beta) \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si437.png)(4.104) 

where *β* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si110.png). However, instead of indiscriminately changing the labels of all training samples, pseudo-labeling is more selective and modifies only the samples that are more likely to contain noisy labels. For instance, in ([Zhang et al., 2021c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2160); [Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1625)), pseudo-labeling consists of updating the training sample $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si60.png) with $(\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si438.png), where $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si439.png) if $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\neq \\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si440.png) and max[**y** ∈ 𝒴](*f*[*θ*]^(**y**)(**x**)) > *τ*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si441.png), where *τ*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si442.png) is the prediction confidence threshold at training epoch *t*.

Modern pseudo-labeling methods tend to sub-divide the training set even more (e.g., clean-label, closed-set label noise, and open-set label noise) and apply different strategies to each sub-set, such as shown in [Fig. 4.29](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0150). In DSOS ([Albert et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0015)), which addresses open and closed-set label noise problems, the pseudo-labeling is achieved by the function

$h(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},u\_{i},v\_{i},\\theta) = \\frac{\\exp\\left( \\frac{v\_{i} \\times {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}}{\\alpha} \\right)}{\\sum\_{c = 1}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}\\exp\\left( \\frac{v\_{i} \\times {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}(c)}{\\alpha} \\right)}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si443.png)(4.105) 

with *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si134.png), *v*[*i*] ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si444.png), *u*[*i*] ∈ {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si445.png), and

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} = (1 - u\_{i}) \\times {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} + u\_{i} \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si446.png)(4.106) 

The optimization of DSOS ([Albert et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0015)) dynamically estimates {*u*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(|𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si447.png) and {*v*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(|𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si448.png), such that for open-set samples (*v*[*i*] ≈ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si449.png)), the pseudo-label is a uniform distribution over the class labels, for closed-set label noise, the pseudo-label is the model prediction, and for clean-label samples, the pseudo-label is the original training label. JoSRC ([Yao et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2045)) proposes a similar pseudo-labeling technique as DSOS ([Albert et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0015)).

![Figure 4.29 Pseudo-labeling.Pseudo-labeling is usually used together with other techniques, such as sample selection (as shown in this diagram) and semi-supervised learning. The main idea is to first classify the training sample (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}Image into clean label, closed-set noisy label, or open-set noisy label, and then modify the training label accordingly. For example, clean-label samples should keep their original training labels \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}Image, closed-set noisy label samples should switch their labels to the model prediction, and open-set noisy label samples should replace their original labels to a uniform class distribution since they do not belong to any of the training classes.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr029.jpg)

[Figure 4.29](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2480) Pseudo-labeling.Pseudo-labeling is usually used together with other techniques, such as sample selection (as shown in this diagram) and semi-supervised learning. The main idea is to first classify the training sample $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si60.png) into clean label, closed-set noisy label, or open-set noisy label, and then modify the training label accordingly. For example, clean-label samples should keep their original training labels $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png), closed-set noisy label samples should switch their labels to the model prediction, and open-set noisy label samples should replace their original labels to a uniform class distribution since they do not belong to any of the training classes.

## 4.4 Training algorithms

This is one of the most fertile areas of research to address noisy-label learning. We begin by discussing meta-learning methods ([Ren et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1475); [Zhang et al., 2020c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2180); [Zhang and Pfister, 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2170); [Xu et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1980); [Shu et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1605); [Hoang et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0715); [Dehghani et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0380)) that automatically learn to weight and re-label training samples. Next, we present self-supervised pre-training techniques ([Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2190)), which are present in virtually all methods that produce state-of-the-art results in the main benchmarks. Then, we describe multi-model approaches that use more than one model to mitigate the confirmation bias risk ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805); [Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1225); [Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645); [Yu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2070); [Wei et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1880)), which is the risk of models learning from mistaken re-labellings and selected samples. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) is then presented ([Ding et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0440); [Nguyen et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1335); [Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055); [Zhou et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2220)), where the goal is to separate the training samples into a labeled set and an unlabeled set, and then to treat the problem as an SSL task. Next, we present probabilistic graphical model techniques that aim to provide insightful understanding about the process of generating noisy labels for training samples ([Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1025); [Xiao et al., 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1960); [Vahdat, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1765); [Yao et al., 2021a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2030); [Garg et al., 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0540); [Bae et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0090)). We conclude the section with another type of training algorithm that has not received much attention for noisy-label learning, which is active learning ([Bouguelia et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0195); [Bernhardt et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0135); [Goh and Mueller, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0565)). Training algorithm techniques have been studied intensively in the field, and the most competitive noisy-label learning methods usually employ one of the algorithms presented in this section.

### 4.4.1 Meta-learning

In noisy-label learning problems, meta-learning algorithms ([Ren et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1475); [Zhang et al., 2020c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2180); [Zhang and Pfister, 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2170); [Xu et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1980); [Shu et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1605); [Hoang et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0715); [Dehghani et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0380)) are typically defined by two important features: 1) a bi-level optimization, and 2) the presence of a meta-parameter that weights the training samples. The bi-level optimization contains two nested optimization problems. The outer (or upper) optimization maximizes the performance of the meta-learner on the training task using a validation set, while the inner (or lower) optimization maximizes the performance of the model on the training task using the training set. The usual goal of the meta-learner is to automatically weight the training samples to facilitate the optimization of the training task, which usually results in down-weighting noisy-label samples and up-weighting clean-label samples.

An early example of a meta-learning method [Dehghani et al. (2017)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0380) is shown in [Fig. 4.30](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0155). In ([Dehghani et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0380)), the model architecture has a representation learning network *g*[*ϕ*] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si450.png) that extracts features **z** ∈ 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si314.png) from data **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si451.png). It also has the target network, denoted by *f*[*θ*] : 𝒵 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si452.png), and the confidence classifier *w*[*γ*] : 𝒵 × 𝒴 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si453.png) that returns the confidence of matching the data **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si451.png) and label **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si128.png). We also have a training set with noisy labels $\\mathcal{D}\_{t} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si454.png) and a small validation set containing both noisy and clean labels, defined by $\\mathcal{D}\_{v} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si455.png), where |𝒟[*v*]| <  < |𝒟[*t*]|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si456.png). Training is achieved in two stages, where the first stage optimizes the confidence model as follows:

$\\phi^{\\ast},\\gamma^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\phi,\\gamma}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{v}}\\ell(\\mathsf{diff}(\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),w\_{\\gamma}(g\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si457.png)(4.107) 

where $\\mathsf{diff}(\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si458.png) computes the difference between true label **y** and noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png). The second training stage then optimizes the target network as follows:

$\\phi^{\\ast},\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\phi,\\gamma}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{t}}w\_{\\gamma^{\\ast}}(g\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(g\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{x}))).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si459.png)(4.108) 

The trained target network is then using to label test data. This work was followed by more sophisticated meta-learning approaches described below.

![Figure 4.30 Meta-learning.Meta-learning for dealing with noisy-label learning, as proposed in (Dehghani et al., 2017). (a) shows the optimization in (4.107) for training the feature extractor gϕ(.) and the sample confidence classifier wγ(.). (b) displays the optimization in (4.108) for training the feature extractor gϕ(.) and the classifier fθ(.), while keeping the confidence classifier frozen.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr030.jpg)

[Figure 4.30](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2675) Meta-learning.Meta-learning for dealing with noisy-label learning, as proposed in ([Dehghani et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0380)). (a) shows the optimization in [(4.107)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq109) for training the feature extractor *g*[*ϕ*](.) and the sample confidence classifier *w*[*γ*](.). (b) displays the optimization in [(4.108)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq110) for training the feature extractor *g*[*ϕ*](.) and the classifier *f*[*θ*](.), while keeping the confidence classifier frozen.

Arguably the most representative meta-learning method for noisy-label learning is the learning to re-weight (L2R) by [Ren et al. (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1475). L2R divides the original training set containing noisy labels, denoted by 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png), into mutually exclusive training and a validation sets 𝒟[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si460.png) and 𝒟[*v*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si461.png), respectively, where 𝒟[*t*]⋃𝒟[*v*] = 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si462.png) and the labels of 𝒟[*v*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si461.png) are guaranteed to be clean. L2R uses 𝒟[*v*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si461.png) to learn a meta-parameter **w** ∈ *Δ*^(|𝒟[*t*]| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si463.png) which weights the loss ℓ(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si122.png) for each training sample in 𝒟[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si460.png), similarly to the loss re-weighting technique in Section [4.2.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0030). This training sample weighting follows many utility criteria, such as informativeness, class-balanced distribution, and label cleanliness ([Ren et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1475); [Hoang et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0715)). The meta-learning optimization is defined as:

$\\mathbf{w}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{w} \\in \\Delta^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}| - 1}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\ell(\\mathbf{y}\_{j},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{w})}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j}))\\text{s.t.:~}\\theta^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{w}) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\mathbf{w}\_{i} \\times \\ell\\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si464.png)(4.109) 

where the label **y**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si465.png) from 𝒟[*v*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si461.png) is assumed to be clean. In [(4.109)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq111), the inner (lower) optimization trains the model *f*[*θ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si142.png) using a weighted loss on the training set 𝒟[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si460.png), while the outer (upper) optimization trains the meta-parameter **w** ∈ *Δ*^(|𝒟[*t*]| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si463.png) that weights the training set losses in the inner level.

The optimization in [(4.109)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq111) is performed iteratively with the inner and outer stages. The inner stage is based on a one-step-ahead model parameter estimation to produce *θ*^(\*)(**w**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si466.png) using the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on the training subset 𝒟[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si460.png), defined by:

$\\theta^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{w}) \\approx \\theta - \\eta\_{\\theta}\\nabla\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\mathbf{w}\_{i} \\times \\ell\\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si467.png)(4.110) 

where *η*[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si468.png) is the learning rate. The outer stage consists of updating the meta-parameter **w** with a one SGD step on the loss computed from the validation set 𝒟[*v*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si461.png) using the model's parameter *θ*^(\*)(*ω*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si469.png) from [(4.110)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq112), as in

$\\mathbf{w}^{\\ast} \\approx \\mathbf{w} - \\eta\_{\\mathbf{w}}\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{w}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\ell\\left( \\mathbf{y}\_{j},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}(\\omega)}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j}) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si470.png)(4.111) 

where *η*[**w**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si471.png) represents the step size to update **w**. The learned meta-parameter **w**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si472.png) is then projected to the probability simplex *Δ*^(|𝒟[*t*]| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si473.png) before it is used to train the model in [(4.109)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq111).

[Ren et al. (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1475) analyze the optimization in [(4.109)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq111) and formulate the following expression on the weighting of each training sample loss:

$\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\left. \\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\mathbf{w}\_{i}}\\ell\\left( \\mathbf{y}\_{j},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}(\\omega,\\lambda)}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j}) \\right) \\right\\rbrack \\right|\_{\\mathbf{w}\_{i} = 0}\\quad \\propto - \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\left\\lbrack \\sum\\limits\_{l = 1}^{L}({\\mathbf{z}\_{j,l - 1}^{(v)}}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z}\_{i,l - 1}^{(t)})({\\mathbf{g}\_{j,l}^{(v)}}^{\\top}\\mathbf{g}\_{i,l}^{(t)}) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si474.png)(4.112) 

where **z**[*j*, *l* − 1]^((*v*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si475.png) denotes the feature produced by model layer *l* for validation sample **x**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si301.png), **z**[*i*, *l* − 1]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si476.png) represents the *l*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si477.png)\-layer feature from the model for training sample **x**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si340.png), **g**[*j*, *l*]^((*v*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si478.png) is the *l*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si477.png)\-layer gradient for validation data **x**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si301.png), and **g**[*i*, *l*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si479.png) denotes the feature produced by model layer *l* for training data **x**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si340.png). Therefore, the loss reweighting factor **w**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si94.png) for training sample **x**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si340.png) is high if its feature and gradient are similar to at least one of the validation samples' feature and gradient; otherwise, **w**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si94.png) is low.

A similar approach to L2R above is the Meta-weight-net (MWN) ([Shu et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1605)) that introduces a sample weighting model parameterized by *ϕ* ∈ *Φ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si480.png) and represented with *w*[*ϕ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si481.png) that receives a loss value and returns a sample weight. The optimization is formulated as (see [Fig. 4.31](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0160)):

$\\phi^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\phi}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{v}}\\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta\_{\\phi}^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\text{s.t.:~}\\theta\_{\\phi}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{t}}w\_{\\phi}(\\ell\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)) \\times \\ell\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si482.png)(4.113) 

This algorithm runs in three iterative steps. Assuming the current training epoch represented by *t*, MWN first updates *θ̂*[*ϕ*](*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si483.png) with

${\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\phi}(t) \\approx \\theta(t) - \\eta\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{t}}w\_{\\phi}\\left( \\ell\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta(t)}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right)\\nabla\_{\\theta}\\ell\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)|\_{\\theta(t)},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si484.png)(4.114) 

where *η*[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si468.png) represents the learning rate, and *θ*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si485.png) denotes the model parameters at training iteration *t*. Then the parameter *ϕ* of the sample weighting model *w*[*ϕ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si481.png) is updated with: 

$\\phi(t + 1) \\approx \\phi(t) - \\eta\_{\\phi}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{v}}\\nabla\_{\\phi}\\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{{\\widehat{\\theta}}\_{\\phi}(t)}(\\mathbf{x}))|\_{\\phi(t)},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si486.png)(4.115) 

where *η*[*ϕ*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si487.png) represents the learning rate, and *ϕ*(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si488.png) is the sample weighting model's parameter at training iteration *t*. The last step consists of updating the model parameters with

$\\theta(t + 1) \\approx \\theta(t) - \\eta\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{t}}w\_{\\phi(t + 1)}\\left( \\ell\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta(t)}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right)\\nabla\_{\\theta}\\ell\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)|\_{\\theta(t)}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si489.png)(4.116) 

![Figure 4.31 Classifier trained with meta-learning.The training of classifier with the Meta-weight-net (MWN) (Shu et al., 2019) using the same problem described in Fig. 4.3. We train for 50 iterations using the optimization in (4.113). At the bottom, in the middle, we also show a histogram of confidence for the clean and noisy-label samples and a scatter plot of the weight versus loss (note that samples with large loss value have zero weight).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr031.jpg)

[Figure 4.31](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2740) Classifier trained with meta-learning.The training of classifier with the Meta-weight-net (MWN) ([Shu et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1605)) using the same problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020). We train for 50 iterations using the optimization in [(4.113)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq115). At the bottom, in the middle, we also show a histogram of confidence for the clean and noisy-label samples and a scatter plot of the weight versus loss (note that samples with large loss value have zero weight).

The L2R approach is extended by [Zhang et al. (2020c)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2180) with the introduction of a second meta-parameter *β*[*i*] ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si490.png), *i* ∈ {1, …, |𝒟[*t*]|}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si491.png) that provides a re-labeling similar to the technique presented in Section [4.2.4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0035). The re-labeling of training sample *i* is provided by

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}(\\beta\_{i}) = \\beta\_{i} \\times {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} + (1 - \\beta\_{i}) \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si492.png)(4.117) 

which is a convex combination between the original training label and label produced by the model. The optimization in [(4.109)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq111) is then reformulated as follows:

$\\mathbf{w}^{\\ast},\\beta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{w},\\beta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\ell\\left( \\mathbf{y}\_{j},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}{(\\mathbf{w},\\beta)}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j}) \\right)\\text{s.t.:~}\\theta^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{w},\\beta) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\mathbf{w}\_{i} \\times \\ell\\left( \\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\beta\_{i}),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si493.png)(4.118) 

The meta-parameter **w** is optimized as explained in [(4.111)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq113), but *β* is updated as follows:

$\\beta\_{i}^{\\ast} = \\left\\lbrack {sign}\\left( - \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\beta\_{i}}\\ell\\left( \\mathbf{y}\_{j},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{w},\\beta)}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j}) \\right) \\right\\rbrack \\right) \\right\\rbrack\_{+},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si494.png)(4.119) 

with \[.\][+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si495.png) representing the rectification operator. The loss function proposed by [Zhang et al. (2020c)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2180) is defined as:

$\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x}) = \\mathbf{w}^{\\ast} \\times \\ell\\left( \\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(\\beta\_{0}),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) + \\frac{\\ell\\left( \\mathbf{y}^{\\ast}(\\beta^{\\ast}),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)}{B}\\quad + \\rho \\times \\ell\\left( \\mathbf{y}^{\\gamma},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}^{\\gamma}) \\right) + \\kappa \\times {KL}\\left\\lbrack f\_{\\theta}\\left( \\mathbf{x} \\right)||f\_{\\theta}\\left( \\widehat{\\mathbf{x}} \\right) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si496.png)(4.120) 

where $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}(.)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si497.png) is the re-labeling defined in [(4.117)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq119), *β*[0] = 0.9![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si498.png), *B* is the batch size,

$\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast}(\\beta^{\\ast}) = \\begin{cases} \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} & {\\text{if~}\\beta^{\\ast} > 0,} \\\\ {f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})} & {\\text{otherwise},} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si499.png)

**y**^(*γ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si500.png) and **x**^(*γ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si501.png) are calculated from the mixup operator ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2110)) using the training and validation sets, *K**L*\[.||.\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si502.png) represents the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si503.png) is an augmented sample of **x**, and *ρ* and *κ* denote hyper-parameters.

All meta-learning methods above require a clean-label validation set 𝒟[*v*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si461.png), which is problematic to acquire, particularly in problems with many classes. [Zhang and Pfister (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2170) address this problem by replacing the clean-label dataset by a pseudo-clean validation set automatically built with a pusher function *u*[*θ*] : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si504.png), as in:

$\\mathcal{D}\_{v}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathcal{D}\_{v} \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{v}}u\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si505.png)(4.121) 

where $u\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta(t)}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta(t + 1)}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si506.png). The maximization in [(4.121)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq124) selects validation samples with the largest drops in losses between the models trained in steps *t* and *t* + 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si507.png), representing unstable samples that the model has started to fit, and leaves behind samples with continuous high or low losses because they are too hard or too easy to fit. [Xu et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1980) propose a way to automatically detect a clean-label validation set by exploring the small-loss hypothesis with a Gaussian mixture model (GMM), similar to the approach in [(4.24)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq26). [Hoang et al. (2022)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0715) introduce a method to automatically select a clean-label validation set that has high-utility samples according to samples that maximize the gradient in [(4.112)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq114).

Meta-learning methods provide a sound theoretical framework for the development of noisy-label learning methods since it automatically learns how to weight or re-label training samples to better optimize the target model. Nevertheless, such nice property comes with a relatively high computational cost since training takes 2 to 3 times longer compared with non meta-learning approaches, as can be seen from the 3-stage training in [(4.114)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq116), [(4.115)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq117), and [(4.116)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq118), with each stage involving one-step SGD and the training of *ϕ*(*t* + 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si508.png) containing a second-order backpropagation. Additionally, the need for a clean (and balanced) validation set is a shortcoming that has recently been addressed ([Zhang and Pfister, 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2170); [Xu et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1980); [Hoang et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0715)) with the caveat that the samples in this clean-label validation set may not actually be clean and may not be highly informative for the training process since these clean-label samples are likely to be the easy (or non-informative) samples to fit.

### 4.4.2 Self-supervised pre-training

Pre-training is a well-known technique to provide a strong initialization for a model by training it on a large amount of data using a general objective function to build effective representations of the training data ([Erhan et al., 2010](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0480)). These models can be trained using an external dataset ([Krizhevsky et al., 2012](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0955)), such as ImageNet ([Deng et al., 2009](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0400)), or they can rely on self-supervision ([Noroozi and Favaro, 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1355); [Chen et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0265); [He et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0670)). Self-supervised pre-training trains a model on a large amount of unlabeled data using a pretext task that does not require any labels. As shown in [Fig. 4.32](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0165), examples of pretext tasks are the prediction of an image transformation ([Gidaris et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0555); [Novotny et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1365)), or the contrastive learning based on the maximization of the similarity of the representations obtained from two views of the same training image and the minimization of the similarity between the representations from different training images ([Chen et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0265); [He et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0670)).

![Figure 4.32 Self-supervised pre-training.There are many ways to perform pre-training with self-supervision. For example, one way is based on predicting the transformations applied to input images, such as rotation (Gidaris et al., 2018) (a). Another example is contrastive learning (Chen et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020) (b), where feature representations are learned to pull together image embeddings from different views of the same image (e.g., one image is a rotated version of the other), while pushing apart embeddings coming from different images.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr032.jpg)

[Figure 4.32](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2870) Self-supervised pre-training.There are many ways to perform pre-training with self-supervision. For example, one way is based on predicting the transformations applied to input images, such as rotation ([Gidaris et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0555)) (a). Another example is contrastive learning ([Chen et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0265); [He et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0670)) (b), where feature representations are learned to pull together image embeddings from different views of the same image (e.g., one image is a rotated version of the other), while pushing apart embeddings coming from different images.

The use of ImageNet pre-trained models in noisy-label learning methods is quite common ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055)), but more recently, sophisticated self-supervised pre-training techniques were explored with outstanding results ([Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2190)). In contrast to divide (C2D), [Zheltonozhskii et al. (2022)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2190) define the “warm-up obstacle” as the inability of early-stopping discriminative learning processes to produce effective model initialization that can prevent the overfitting of noisy-label training samples. [Zheltonozhskii et al. (2022)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2190) also observed that ImageNet pre-training is not only impractical, given the difficulty in finding relevant large-scale training sets that can be helpful for certain applications, but it can also be detrimental in some cases. C2D consists of simply pre-training the noisy-label learning model with the contrastive learning pre-training method SimCLR ([Chen et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0265)), and then train the model with a state-of-the-art noisy-label learning method ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055); [Liu et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1120)).

Self-supervised pre-training has become a model initialization technique present in virtually all state-of-the-art approaches that we will study in Chapter [5](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml). In fact, methods that do not rely on self-supervised pre-training are unlikely to produce competitive results in the main benchmarks in the field. Nevertheless, it is unlikely that new self-supervised pre-training methods will be proposed in noisy-label learning literature. Instead, what is usually seen in noisy-label learning is the utilization of self-supervised pre-training techniques developed for general downstream tasks.

### 4.4.3 Multi-model training

The use of multiple models in noisy-label learning is a dominant technique usually designed to work together with sample selection to mitigate an issue widely known as confirmation bias. In this issue, a noisy-label sample may be classified as clean, which encourages the model to overfit such noisy-label sample, so it is again classified as clean in the next training iteration. This issue is mitigated by the training of multiple models because of the difficulty that multiple models will overfit the same noisy-label samples at the same training epoch, as shown in [Fig. 4.33](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0170).

![Figure 4.33 Multi-model training.Multi-model training relies on the training of multiple models to address the issue of confirmation bias, where mistakes made by the model are reinforced during the training of the same model. MentorNet (Jiang et al., 2017) relies on the training of a teacher model Image that weights samples based on their losses for the training of a student model Image, as explained in (4.123). Decouple (Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017) trains two models Image and Image, described in (4.122), where both models are trained with samples for which both models disagree. Co-teaching (Han et al., 2018c) and Co-teaching+ (Yu et al., 2019a) use a similar strategy, where models Image and Image are trained by swapping small-loss samples (Han et al., 2018c) as explained in (4.125), or swapping small-loss samples for which both models disagree (Yu et al., 2019a), as described in (4.126). JoCor (Wei et al., 2020) trains two models Image and Image with small-loss samples, and at the same time reduce the prediction divergence between the two models, as explained in (4.127).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr033.jpg)

[Figure 4.33](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf2930) Multi-model training.Multi-model training relies on the training of multiple models to address the issue of confirmation bias, where mistakes made by the model are reinforced during the training of the same model. MentorNet ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805)) relies on the training of a teacher model ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/fx001.jpg)that weights samples based on their losses for the training of a student model ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/fx002.jpg), as explained in [(4.123)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq126). Decouple ([Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1225)) trains two models ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/fx002.jpg)and ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/fx001.jpg), described in [(4.122)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq125), where both models are trained with samples for which both models disagree. Co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)) and Co-teaching+ ([Yu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2070)) use a similar strategy, where models ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/fx002.jpg)and ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/fx001.jpg)are trained by swapping small-loss samples ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)) as explained in [(4.125)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq128), or swapping small-loss samples for which both models disagree ([Yu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2070)), as described in [(4.126)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq129). JoCor ([Wei et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1880)) trains two models ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/fx002.jpg)and ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/fx001.jpg)with small-loss samples, and at the same time reduce the prediction divergence between the two models, as explained in [(4.127)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq130).

Decouple ([Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1225)) is a pioneer multi-model training approach for noisy-label learning, where two networks *f*[*θ*[1]] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si509.png) and *f*[*θ*[2]] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si510.png) are trained only on the training samples that they disagree, with

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{2}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\text{s.t.~}\\mathcal{S} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\neq f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si511.png)(4.122) 

The issue with decouple ([Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1225)) was that the disagreement set 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si138.png) in [(4.122)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq125) could contain many noisy-label samples that can lead to overfitting and confirmation bias.

The multi-model in ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805)) relies on a collaborative learning of two models, the MentorNet and the StudentNet, with the StudentNet optimizing a loss re-weighted function, where the sample weights are dynamically estimated by the MentorNet with a data-driven curriculum using the features from the StudentNet. The MentorNet, denoted by the model *g*[*ϕ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si512.png) parameterized by *ϕ* ∈ *Φ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si480.png), provides a data-driven curriculum learning to train the StudentNet. The MentorNet model is trained as follows:

${\\phi^{\\ast},\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\phi,\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}g\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{z}\_{i}) \\times \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) + G(g\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{z}\_{i});\\lambda\_{1},\\lambda\_{2}) + \\gamma\\ \\times |\\theta\\|}\_{2}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si513.png)(4.123) 

where *λ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si514.png), *λ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si515.png) are regularization parameters for the penalization function *G*(*w*[*i*]; *λ*[1], *λ*[2]) = 0.5*λ*[2]²*w*[*i*] − (*λ*[1] + *λ*[2])*w*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si516.png), and **z**[*i*] = *h*(**x**[*i*], **y**[*i*], *θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si517.png) is a feature comprising the loss, loss difference to the moving average, label and epoch percentage. In [(4.123)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq126), the first term denotes the curriculum-weighted loss, while the second term specifies the curriculum, defined by a sequence of samples and respective weights for training the StudentNet. The optimization of [(4.123)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq126) leads to the following closed-form solution:

$g\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{z}\_{i}) = \\begin{cases} {\\delta(\\ell\_{i} \\leq \\lambda\_{1}),} & {\\text{~if~}\\lambda\_{2} = 0} \\\\ {\\min\\left( \\max\\left( 0,1 - \\frac{\\ell\_{i} - \\lambda\_{1}}{\\lambda\_{2}} \\right),1 \\right),} & {\\text{~if~}\\lambda\_{2} \\neq 0} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si518.png)(4.124) 

where $\\ell\_{i} = \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si83.png), and *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si315.png) represents an indicator function. Hence, when *λ*[2] = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si519.png), we have a self-paced curriculum learning ([Kumar et al., 2010](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0980)), where the StudentNet is trained only with small-loss samples (i.e., samples with ℓ[*i*] ≤ *λ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si520.png) will have *g*[*ϕ*^(\*)](**z**[*i*]) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si521.png)). On the other hand, when *λ*[2] ≠ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si522.png), the StudentNet is not trained with large-loss samples where ℓ[*i*] ≥ *λ*[2] + *λ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si523.png), but it will be trained with samples weighted linearly by $1 - \\frac{\\ell\_{i} - \\lambda\_{1}}{\\lambda\_{2}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si524.png). Hence, similarly to ([Kumar et al., 2010](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0980)), *λ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si514.png) and *λ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si515.png) control the learning pace. Also, similarly to the decouple method presented before in [(4.122)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq125), if the MentorNet mistakenly weights up a noisy-label sample, confirmation bias will follow.

These issues motivated the development of co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)) that explores the small-loss hypothesis ([Arpit et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0065)) in a multi-model scenario. Motivated by co-training ([Blum and Mitchell, 1998](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0180)), co-teaching has two models that will continuously select small-loss samples to train the peer model, as follows:

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}\_{2}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S}\_{2}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{2}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}\_{1}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S}\_{1}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\text{s.t.~}\\mathcal{S}\_{1} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\tau) \\right\\},\\mathcal{S}\_{2} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\tau) \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si525.png)(4.125) 

where *τ* varies during the training. The two models in [(4.125)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq128) filter different types of label noise, which makes it difficult that both models will overfit the same noisy-label samples. Furthermore, even though one model can give noisy-label samples to the peer model, the robustness of both models to noisy-label samples from the early learning stages ([Arpit et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0065)) will mitigate the overfit to these noisy-label samples. We show an example of co-teaching in [Fig. 4.34](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0175). Nevertheless, the two models in co-teaching soon reach a consensus during training, which means that both models become too similar, leading to a self-training strategy that becomes vulnerable to confirmation bias. Such issue can be mitigated with the decouple strategy ([Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1225)), described in [(4.122)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq125), which can slow down the convergence rate of the co-teaching models. This led to the development of co-teaching+ ([Yu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2070)), which updates the models using small-loss samples with prediction disagreement between the classifiers, with:

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}\_{2}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S}\_{2}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{2}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}\_{1}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S}\_{1}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x}))\\text{s.t.~}\\mathcal{S} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\neq f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\},\\mathcal{S}\_{1} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\tau) \\right\\},\\mathcal{S}\_{2} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S},\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x})) < \\tau) \\right\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si526.png)(4.126) 

Unfortunately, the combined constraints of small-loss and prediction disagreement in co-teaching+ ([Yu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2070)) can severely reduce the size of 𝒮[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si527.png) and 𝒮[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si528.png) in [(4.126)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq129), particularly when the noise rate in 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) is too high. Such inefficient use of the training set can damage the training process, which motivated [Wei et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1880) to develop Joint Training with Co-Regularization (JoCoR). JoCor moves away from the maximization of the prediction disagreement to the maximization of the prediction agreement between the two classifiers *f*[*θ*[1]](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si529.png) and *f*[*θ*[2]](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si530.png) using a joint training loss for the two models and a regularization that replaces the sampling proposed in ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)). This joint loss is also used to select the small-loss samples, which complicates the selection of noisy-label samples since they will need to have a small loss in both models to be selected. JoCor ([Wei et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1880)) optimizes the following loss function:

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast},\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{S}}\\mathcal{L}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2})\\text{s.t.~}\\mathcal{S} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\mathcal{L}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2}) < \\tau) \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si531.png)(4.127) 

where

$\\mathcal{L}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2}) = (1 - \\lambda) \\times \\left( \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right) + \\lambda \\times \\left( \\mathsf{KL}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})\\| f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack + \\mathsf{KL}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{x})\\| f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si532.png)(4.128) 

with *λ* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si533.png) and KL\[.\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si534.png) representing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence.

![Figure 4.34 Multi-model training with co-teaching.The training of classifier with Co-teaching (Han et al., 2018c) using the same problem described in Fig. 4.3. We train for 500 iterations using the optimization in (4.125).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr034.jpg)

[Figure 4.34](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf3005) Multi-model training with co-teaching.The training of classifier with Co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)) using the same problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020). We train for 500 iterations using the optimization in [(4.125)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq128).

The use of the mean teacher model ([Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1710)) that relies on a temporal ensembling of models, combined with the soft re-labeling of training samples based on a temporal ensembling of label and predictions are the two techniques explored by the self-ensemble label filtering (SELF) method ([Nguyen et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1335)). SELF filters out noisy-label samples by maintaining a temporal ensembling of predictions with ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t + 1)} = \\alpha \\times {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t)} + (1 - \\alpha) \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si535.png), where ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(0)} = 0$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si267.png) and ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t)}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si268.png) represents the prediction ensemble at training iteration *t*. Then, training samples where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\neq \\mathsf{OneHot}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t + 1)})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si269.png) have their labels erased (i.e., they become un-labeled). Given these un-labeled and the remaining labeled training samples, SELF trains the mean-teacher model ([Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1710)), which is a semi-supervised teacher-student learning model that outputs *f*[*θ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si142.png). This model consists of the best teacher model, represented by the training epoch that provided the best accuracy in the validation set.

Multi-model training is one of the best tools developed to mitigate the confirmation bias problem, typically found in noisy-label learning methods.
