However, the need for training two separate models is generally seen as problematic given the larger run-time and memory complexity compared with other approaches based on a single model.

### 4.4.4 Semi-supervised learning

The experimental setup of semi-supervised learning (SSL) and noisy-label learning have one important commonality, which is that part of the dataset cannot be used for fully-supervised training. While in SSL, a subset of the training samples does not have labels, in noisy-label learning, a subset of the training set has wrong labels. The major difference between SSL and noisy-label learning is that the un-labeled samples in SSL are clearly marked, but we do not have clear demarcation of the training samples that carry a noisy label. Therefore, if sample selection techniques work effectively, then we can simply keep the labels of the samples classified as clean, and remove the labels from the training samples classified as noisy, and apply one of the SSL techniques. There are two challenges in noisy-label SSL methods, namely: it is inevitable that the training samples classified as clean will contain a small subset of noisy-label samples, and the samples classified as noisy may just be the clean-label informative samples that are quite important for the training process. Hence, much of the work in the application of SSL in noisy-label learning focus on addressing these two challenges.

There are three assumptions explored by the SSL approaches ([Van Engelen and Hoos, 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1780)) that are useful in noisy-label learning: 1) images with neighboring representations in the feature space have similar labels; 2) decision boundary passes through low-density areas of the feature space; and 3) representations sharing a low-dimensional manifold in the feature space also share the same label. The main techniques explored by SSL approaches are the pseudo-labeling ([Berthelot et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0140); [Sohn et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1635); [Arazo et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0055)) (such as the ones presented in Section [4.3.7](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0080)) and consistency learning ([Laine and Aila, 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0990); [Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1710); [Polyak and Juditsky, 1992](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1430)). Pseudo-labeling methods work by progressively annotating part of the un-labeled dataset, while consistency-based approaches minimize prediction discrepancies produced by the model using different input views obtained, for example, from data perturbations produced by augmentation functions. It has been noted that consistency-learning approaches tend to outperform pseudo-labeling methods, most likely because pseudo-labeling methods disregard part of the training set during optimization ([Liu et al., 2022d](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1150)). In fact, SSL approaches applied to noisy-label learning are mostly based on consistency-learning techniques, as we present below.

The first method to use SSL for noisy-label learning was the one proposed by ([Ding et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0440)), which explored consistency learning with the loss (see [Fig. 4.35](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0180)):

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}{\\| f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) - f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x})\\|}\_{2}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si540.png)(4.129) 

where $\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\delta(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))) = 1,f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) > \\tau\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si541.png) denotes the set of pseudo-clean label samples, *f*[*θ̂*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si159.png) represents the model prediction after being perturbed with dropout ([Srivastava et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1655)), and the second loss maximizes the consistency between the prediction outputs after dropout perturbation applied to the model. We show the result produced by this model in [Fig. 4.36](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0185). The approach proposed by [Kong et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0925) explored the SSL assumption about the decision boundary passing through low-density areas of the feature space, with the following loss:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{n}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}}\\mathbb{H}\_{r}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}),\\alpha),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si542.png)(4.130) 

where 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) is the set of pseudo-clean samples as defined in [(4.64)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq66), 𝒟[*n*] = 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si256.png), and ℍ[*r*](*f*[*θ*](**x**), *α*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si543.png) denotes the Renyi entropy, defined by

$\\mathbb{H}\_{r}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}),\\alpha) = \\frac{1}{1 - \\alpha}\\log\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)^{\\alpha} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si544.png)(4.131) 

with *α* > 0, *α* ≠ 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si545.png).

![Figure 4.35 Semi-supervised learning.Semi-supervised learning methods work by automatically selecting clean-label samples to form the set \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image that is used with a training loss \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))Image, while the whole training set \\mathcal{D}Image (or sometimes just the set difference \\mathcal{D}\_{n} = \\mathcal{D} \\smallsetminus \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image) is trained with another loss that does not take the training label into account, such as the loss in this figure represented by {\\| f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) - f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x})\\|}\_{2}^{2}Image, with f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(.)Image being a model perturbed with dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr035.jpg)

[Figure 4.35](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf3115) Semi-supervised learning.Semi-supervised learning methods work by automatically selecting clean-label samples to form the set 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) that is used with a training loss $\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si536.png), while the whole training set 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) (or sometimes just the set difference 𝒟[*n*] = 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si256.png)) is trained with another loss that does not take the training label into account, such as the loss in this figure represented by ∥*f*[*θ*](**x**) − *f*[*θ̂*](**x**)∥[2]²![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si537.png), with *f*[*θ̂*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si538.png) being a model perturbed with dropout ([Srivastava et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1655)).

![Figure 4.36 Semi-supervised learning.Working with the problem described in Fig. 4.3, we show the functionality of the semi-supervised learning proposed by Ding et al. (2018) with a training of 500 iterations using the optimization in (4.129), where the clean-label dataset \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image is formed by only checking if f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} > \\tauImage, with τ = 0.1.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr036.jpg)

[Figure 4.36](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf3125) Semi-supervised learning.Working with the problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020), we show the functionality of the semi-supervised learning proposed by [Ding et al. (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0440) with a training of 500 iterations using the optimization in [(4.129)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq132), where the clean-label dataset 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) is formed by only checking if $f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} > \\tau$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si539.png), with *τ* = 0.1.

As already explained in Section [4.4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0100), the use of the mean teacher model ([Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1710)) that relies on a temporal ensembling of models, combined with the soft re-labeling of training samples based on a temporal ensembling of predictions are the two techniques explored by the self-ensemble label filtering (SELF) method ([Nguyen et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1335)). SELF has the student and teacher models respectively denoted by *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 × ℝ → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si546.png) and *f*[*θ̂*] : 𝒳 × ℝ → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si547.png), where the student is optimized with

$\\theta^{(t)} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\eta)) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}{\\| f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\eta) - f\_{{\\widehat{\\theta}}^{(t - 1)}}(\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\eta})\\|}\_{2}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si548.png)(4.132) 

where *η*, *η̂* ∈ ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si549.png) denote noise variables (e.g., noise to the inputs or noise applied to the model), and *t* denotes the training epoch. The teacher is trained by ensembling its previous model with the student model from epoch *t*, as follows:

*θ̂*^((*t*)) = *α* × *θ̂*^((*t* − 1)) + (1 − *α*) × *θ*^((*t*)).

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si550.png)(4.133) 

SELF selects the samples to be inserted into 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) in [(4.132)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq135) by maintaining a temporal ensembling of predictions with ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t)} = \\alpha \\times {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t - 1)} + (1 - \\alpha) \\times f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x},0)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si551.png), where ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}^{(0)} = 0$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si552.png) and ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}^{(t)}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si553.png) represents the prediction ensemble at training epoch *t*. Then, training samples where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathsf{OneHot}({\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{(t + 1)})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si554.png) are inserted into 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png). SELF also uses a noisy-label validation set to select the highest accuracy teacher model during the training process.

The application of the data augmentation technique MixUp ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2110)), defined in [(4.101)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq103), into semi-supervised learning produced the MixMatch approach ([Berthelot et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0140)). MixMatch combines consistency learning and pseudo-labeling techniques and it was applied in noisy-label learning by the influential DivideMix method ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055)). MixMatch takes as input, a labeled and an un-labeled set. The labeled set is represented by training samples classified as clean-label and denoted by $\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\mathsf{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = 1\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si555.png), and the un-labeled set, represented by training samples classified as noisy-label and denoted by $\\mathcal{D}\_{n} = \\{(\\mathbf{x})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\mathsf{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = 0\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si556.png). Then, two sets of data augmented samples are built with

${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c} = \\left\\{ (\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}} = a(\\mathbf{x}),a \\sim \\mathcal{A},(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c} \\right\\},{\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{n} = \\left\\{ (\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}},\\mathbf{q})|\\mathbf{q} = \\mathsf{sharpen}\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}}\\left\\lbrack f\_{\\theta}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}}) \\right\\rbrack \\right),\\widehat{\\mathbf{x}} = a(\\mathbf{x}),a \\sim \\mathcal{A},\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n} \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si557.png)(4.134) 

where 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si435.png) is a set of random horizontal flips and crops augmentation functions, denoted by *a* : 𝒳 → 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si425.png), and sharpen : *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1) → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si558.png) denotes a function to sharpen the categorical distribution by adjusting the distribution's temperature. The next stage of MixMatch relies on augmenting the data from ${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si559.png) and ${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{n}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si560.png) with MixUp ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2110)) defined in [(4.101)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq103), as

$\\mathcal{D}\_{c}^{\\prime} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\mathsf{MixUp}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},\\mathbf{x}\_{j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}),(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in {\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c},(\\mathbf{x}\_{j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}) \\in \\mathcal{W} \\right\\},\\mathcal{D}\_{n}^{\\prime} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\mathsf{MixUp}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},\\mathbf{x}\_{j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}),(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in {\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{n},(\\mathbf{x}\_{j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}) \\in \\mathcal{W} \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si561.png)(4.135) 

where $\\mathcal{W} = \\mathsf{shuffle}({\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}\\bigcup{\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{n})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si562.png) is a set containing the shuffled contents of the union between the labeled and unlabeled sets from [(4.134)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq137). The last step in MixMatch consists of the following optimization using the sets built in [(4.135)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq138):

${\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}^{\\prime}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}^{\\prime}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\frac{\\lambda\_{n}}{|\\mathcal{Y}| \\times |\\mathcal{D}\_{n}^{\\prime}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}^{\\prime}}\\|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} - f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))\\|}\_{2}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si563.png)(4.136) 

where *λ*[*U*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si564.png) weights the loss from the un-labeled set.

Another type of SSL based on consistency loss for noisy-label learning is the RoCL ([Zhou et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2220)), introduced in Section [4.3.2](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0055). Essentially, the first stage of RoCL consists of a supervised learning from pseudo-clean samples, which is followed by a second stage represented by SSL on pseudo-labeled noisy samples produced by a time-ensemble of the model and data augmentations. The optimization of RoCL is defined by

$\\theta^{(t + 1)} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\left( \\frac{\\lambda}{\\tau\_{1}} \\right) \\times \\log\\left( \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\exp\\left( \\tau\_{1}\\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) \\right) \\right) + \\left( \\frac{1 - \\lambda}{\\tau\_{2}} \\right) \\times \\log\\left( \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\exp\\left( \\tau\_{2} \\times \\zeta\_{i}^{(t)} \\right) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si565.png)(4.137) 

where 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) is the dataset containing pseudo-clean samples defined in [(4.56)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq58), and *ζ*[*i*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si566.png) is the instantaneous consistency loss defined in [(4.55)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq57).

Some SSL methods developed for noisy-label learning are based on pseudo-labeling, as is the case with the modified co-teaching with self-supervision and re-labeling (mCT-S2R) ([Mandal et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1235)). The mCT-S2R approach extends co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)), presented in [(4.125)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq128), by adding pseudo-labeling and re-training stages. The pseudo-labeling approach is done by selecting one of the models, say the one parameterized by *θ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si567.png), and dividing the training set into samples with small loss 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) with the remaining samples with large loss, forming the set 𝒟[*n*] = 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si256.png). Then, taking the features, denoted by **z** ∈ 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si314.png), from an intermediate layer of *f*[*θ*[1]](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si568.png), we form the set of small-loss features $\\mathcal{Z}\_{c} = \\{(\\mathbf{z},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|\\mathbf{z}\\text{~extracted\\ from~}f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}),(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si569.png), and the set of large-loss features $\\mathcal{Z}\_{n} = \\{(\\mathbf{z},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|\\mathbf{z}\\text{~extracted\\ from~}f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}),(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si570.png). Next, we compute the class-wise prototype vectors, computed with the mean vector {*μ*[**y**]}[**y** ∈ 𝒴]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si571.png) with $\\mu\_{\\mathbf{y}} = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\_{(\\mathbf{z},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{Z}\_{c}}\\delta(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y}) \\times \\mathbf{z}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si572.png), where $N = \\sum\_{(\\mathbf{z},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{Z}\_{c}}\\delta(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si573.png), and *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si315.png) is the indicator function. The new labels for the large-loss features are computed with:

$\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathsf{OneHot}\\left( \\mathsf{softmax}\\left( \\lbrack - d\_{1},..., - d\_{|\\mathcal{Y}|}\\rbrack \\right) \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si574.png)(4.138) 

if max (softmax(\[−*d*[1],...,−*d*[|𝒴|]\])) > *κ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si575.png), where *d*[**y**] = ∥**z** − *μ*[**y**]∥[2]²![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si576.png) represents the distance to the prototype of class **y**, softmax(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si577.png) returns a categorical distribution using the softmax activation, and OneHot(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si578.png) returns the one-hot vector from this categorical distribution. The last step consists of taking 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) and the pseudo-labeled samples from 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si74.png) to fine-tune the model *f*[*θ*[1]](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si529.png). The pseudo-labeling approach above has two weaknesses: 1) it only uses a single prototype per class, which may not allow a reliable representation of the feature distribution for each class when it has multiple modes; and 2) its non-iterative nature may under-utilize the training set if part of it never gets pseudo-labeled. Both issues have been addressed by [Han et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0650), who proposed the estimation of multiple prototypes to represent each class, where the re-labeling and training follows an iterative process. Another interesting point explored in ([Han et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0650)) is that the loss function is represented by a convex combination of the loss with the original label and a loss with the pseudo-label, as in:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{pl}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{pl}}\\alpha \\times \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + (1 - \\alpha) \\times \\ell(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si579.png)(4.139) 

where *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si134.png) is close to 1 at the first training iterations and it decreases toward 0 as training progress, and $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si378.png) is the pseudo-label for the training sample stored in 𝒟[*p**l*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si580.png) that has both the original training label and the pseudo label.

Lately, the combination of pseudo-labeling and consistency learning has been explored in SSL methods for noisy label learning. The Sample Selection and Relabeling (SSR) approach ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0515)), which has a sample selection technique discussed in Section [4.3.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0060) and a data cleaning method explained in Section [4.3.2](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0055), explores a consistency loss with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{pl}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{pl}}\\ell(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\ell\_{fc}(f\_{\\theta}(a\_{1}(\\mathbf{x})),f\_{\\theta}(a\_{2}(\\mathbf{x}))),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si581.png)(4.140) 

where *a*[1], *a*[2] ∼ 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si582.png) denote data augmentation functions sampled from a set of functions 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si435.png), ℓ[*f**c*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si583.png) is a consistency loss represented by the cosine distance between two augmented views of the training data **x**, and $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si378.png) is the pseudo-label for training sample **x** obtained from the model if the confidence of the classifier in the pseudo-labeled class (i.e., $f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si379.png)) is above a certain threshold, otherwise, $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si585.png).

Semi-supervised learning is a technique that has been shown to produce outstanding results in noisy-label learning, particularly the methods based on consistency learning. The main issue with SSL-based approaches is the need to classify training samples into clean and noisy, which produces a non-negligible set of samples that are mistakenly classified as clean, but contain noisy labels, biasing the training process. It also mistakenly classifies hard clean-label samples as noisy-label ones, reducing the robustness of the classifier to those hard samples. Hence, much of the research in this area has focused on how to design the best possible classifier of clean and noisy-label samples.

### 4.4.5 Probabilistic graphical model

Probabilistic graphical models (PGM) have been used in the development of noisy-label learning methods even before deep learning started dominating the field ([Krizhevsky et al., 2012](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0955)). For example, the PGM introduced by [Lawrence and Schölkopf (2001)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1025) for noisy-label learning using a kernel Fisher discriminant (KFD), was proposed with a random variable *X* representing the data, another random variable *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si26.png) denoting the noisy label, and a latent random variable *Y* representing the clean label, as shown in [Fig. 4.37](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0190)(a). The learning using such PGM is based on

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\theta}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si586.png)(4.141) 

where *θ* parameterizes the class conditional density, and

$\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\frac{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\log\\frac{p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\frac{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\log\\frac{p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} + \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\log\\frac{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} = \\underset{\\text{ELBO}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log\\frac{p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} \\right\\rbrack}} + \\underset{\\geq 0}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\| p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si587.png)(4.142) 

In [(4.142)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq145), we have the evidence lower bound (ELBO) and the (non-negative term) Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the variational posterior $q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si588.png) and the true posterior $p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si589.png). Note that variational posterior is designed to approximate the complex true posterior. The maximization in [(4.141)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq144) relies on the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm ([Dempster et al., 1977](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0395)), where in the *t*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si224.png) iteration, the E-step consists of computing the posterior distribution of *Y* with

$p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\frac{p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{x}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si590.png)(4.143) 

followed by setting $q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si591.png) to make the KL divergence in [(4.142)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq145) equal to zero. The M-step then maximizes the ELBO in [(4.142)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq145) with respect to *θ* = {*θ*[1], *θ*[2]}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si592.png), by representing

$p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = p\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}|\\mathbf{y})p\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si593.png)(4.144) 

where *p*[*θ*[1]](**x**|**y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si594.png) is modeled with a normal distribution, and $p\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si595.png) is a label transition modeled with a transition table. We show the functionality of this approach in [Fig. 4.38](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0195).

![Figure 4.37 Probabilistic graphical model.Probabilistic graphical models (PGM) proposed in the field to address the noisy-label learning problem, where a shaded circle represents an observed variable, while the unshaded circle denotes a latent variable. In (a), the data X is generated by the clean label Y, which in turn is generated by the noisy label \\widetilde{Y}Image. (b) shows that the model uses the generated data X to produce the clean label Y and noise type N (i.e., no noise, symmetric, asymmetric), which are then explored to generate the noisy label \\widetilde{Y}Image. In (c), the undirected graphical model relies on the latent variable H that models the correlations between labels. (d) introduces a latent data representation Z that, together with the label Y, generates X that is in turn used with Y to generate \\widetilde{Y}Image. In (e) the clean label Y is generated only by data X, while the noisy label is generated by Y and X.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr037.jpg)

Figure 4.37 Probabilistic graphical model.Probabilistic graphical models (PGM) proposed in the field to address the noisy-label learning problem, where a shaded circle represents an observed variable, while the unshaded circle denotes a latent variable. In (a), the data *X* is generated by the clean label *Y*, which in turn is generated by the noisy label *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si26.png). (b) shows that the model uses the generated data *X* to produce the clean label *Y* and noise type *N* (i.e., no noise, symmetric, asymmetric), which are then explored to generate the noisy label *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si26.png). In (c), the undirected graphical model relies on the latent variable *H* that models the correlations between labels. (d) introduces a latent data representation *Z* that, together with the label *Y*, generates *X* that is in turn used with *Y* to generate *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si26.png). In (e) the clean label *Y* is generated only by data *X*, while the noisy label is generated by *Y* and *X*.

![Figure 4.38 Probabilistic graphical model.The PGM approach from (Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001) is tested on the problem described in Fig. 4.3 with a training of 1000 iterations using the optimization in (4.141) (Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001), where the covariance of the normal distribution p\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}|\\mathbf{y})Image in (4.144) is constrained to be the same across all classes. Differently from other graphs in this chapter, we show the training and testing classification accuracies (as a function of number of epochs), with respect to their noisy and clean labels, respectively.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr038.jpg)

[Figure 4.38](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf3300) Probabilistic graphical model.The PGM approach from ([Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1025)) is tested on the problem described in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020) with a training of 1000 iterations using the optimization in [(4.141)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq144) ([Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1025)), where the covariance of the normal distribution *p*[*θ*[1]](**x**|**y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si594.png) in [(4.144)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq147) is constrained to be the same across all classes. Differently from other graphs in this chapter, we show the training and testing classification accuracies (as a function of number of epochs), with respect to their noisy and clean labels, respectively.

The PGM in ([Xiao et al., 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1960)) uses two latent variables, namely the clean label *Y* and the label noise type *N*, with the graph structure displayed in [Fig. 4.37](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0190)(b). The label noise type is a ternary random variable associated with the following semantic classes: 1) **n** = \[1, 0, 0\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si596.png): label is noise free, which implies that *Y* = *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si597.png); 2) **n** = \[0, 1, 0\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si598.png): symmetric noise, where the label has random noise, so *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si26.png) can take any possible label, except *Y*; and 3) **n** = \[0, 0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si599.png): asymmetric noise, so *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si26.png) can take labels that are confusing with *Y*. Using the graph structure above, we can formulate the following decomposition:

$p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x}) = p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n})p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x})p(\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si600.png)(4.145) 

where

$p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}) = \\begin{cases} {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\mathbf{I}\\mathbf{y},} & {\\text{if~}\\mathbf{n} = \\lbrack 1,0,0\\rbrack} \\\\ {\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(\\mathbf{U} - \\mathbf{I})\\mathbf{y},} & {\\text{if~}\\mathbf{n} = \\lbrack 0,1,0\\rbrack} \\\\ {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\mathbf{C}\\mathbf{y},} & {\\text{if~}\\mathbf{n} = \\lbrack 0,0,1\\rbrack} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si601.png)(4.146) 

where **I** represents the |𝒴| × |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si25.png) identity matrix, **U** denotes the |𝒴| × |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si25.png) matrix with all elements equal to one, C is a |𝒴| × |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si25.png) sparse stochastic matrix with tr(**C**) = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si602.png), and **C**[*i**j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si603.png) represents the transition probability between classes *i* and *j*. The optimization maximizes the following log-likelihood

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si604.png)(4.147) 

where we introduce the variational posterior $q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si605.png), with

$\\begin{aligned} {\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x})} & {= \\underset{\\text{ELBO}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log\\frac{p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{z}|\\mathbf{x})}{q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} \\right\\rbrack}} + \\underset{\\geq 0}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})||p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{z}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack}}} \\\\ \\end{aligned},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si606.png)(4.148) 

using the same derivation steps as in [(4.142)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq145). This optimization is also based on the EM algorithm ([Dempster et al., 1977](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0395)), where in the E-step at the *t*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si224.png) iteration, we set the KL divergence to zero, by setting $q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si607.png), where

$p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\frac{p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x})}{p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x})} = \\frac{p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n})p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x})p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{n}|\\mathbf{x})}{\\sum\_{\\mathbf{y}^{\\prime},\\mathbf{n}^{\\prime}}p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y}^{\\prime},\\mathbf{n}^{\\prime})p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{y}^{\\prime}|\\mathbf{x})p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{n}^{\\prime}|\\mathbf{x})}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si608.png)(4.149) 

The M-step maximizes the ELBO in [(4.148)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq151) with respect to *θ* = {*θ*[1], *θ*[2], *θ*[3]}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si609.png) that is a set of parameters for the models $p\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si610.png), *p*[*θ*[2]](**y**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si611.png), and *p*[*θ*[3]](**n**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si612.png). While *p*[*θ*[2]](**y**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si611.png) and *p*[*θ*[3]](**n**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si612.png) are modeled with deep learning models, $p\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{n})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si610.png) is a label transition model trained with a separate set of data containing clean and noisy labels with $\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si613.png).

A similar PGM has been proposed by [Vahdat (2017)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1765) that relies on an undirected graphical model depicted in with the graph structure of [Fig. 4.37](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0190)(c), where *Y* represents the latent clean label random variable and *H* denotes the random binary variable in the space ℋ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si614.png) that models the correlations between labels. The model is estimated with the following optimization

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si615.png)(4.150) 

where 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) is the original training set with noisy labels and 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) is a separate training set containing noisy and clean labels. The first term in [(4.150)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq153) is decomposed as

$\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}) = \\underset{\\text{ELBO}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log\\frac{p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x})}{q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} \\right\\rbrack}} + \\underset{\\geq 0}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})||p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si616.png)(4.151) 

while the second term is decomposed as

$\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}) = \\underset{\\text{ELBO}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log\\frac{p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x})}{q(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} \\right\\rbrack}} + \\underset{\\geq 0}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})||p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si617.png)(4.152) 

where $q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si618.png) is a variational posterior that approximates the true posterior $p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si619.png), and $q(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si620.png) is another variational posterior to approximate the posterior $p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si621.png). [Vahdat (2017)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1765) mentions that these variational distributions can overfit the data, particularly at the beginning of the training, so a regularization based on auxiliary (e.g., non-image) sources of information to extract the relationship between noisy and clean labels is proposed. This auxiliary distribution is denoted by the joint probability of noisy and clean labels and hidden binary states $p\_{aux}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si622.png), which is modeled by restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM). The regularization for [(4.151)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq154) is $\\alpha \\times \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})||p\_{aux}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si623.png), where *α* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si624.png); and for [(4.152)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq155) is $\\alpha \\times \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})||p\_{aux}(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si625.png), where *α* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si624.png). Finally, the training is based on the EM algorithm ([Dempster et al., 1977](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0395)), where the E-step during the *t*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si224.png) iteration sets

$q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\propto \\left\\lbrack p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times p\_{aux}^{\\alpha}(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack^{\\frac{1}{\\alpha + 1}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si626.png)(4.153) 

and

$q(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\propto \\left\\lbrack p\_{\\theta^{(t)}}(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times p\_{aux}^{\\alpha}(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack^{\\frac{1}{\\alpha + 1}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si627.png)(4.154) 

The M-step maximizes the ELBO terms in [(4.151)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq154) and [(4.152)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq155) with respect to *θ* by fixing *q*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si628.png) and following the direction of the gradients:

$\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\theta}\\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack\\text{~,and~}\\frac{\\partial}{\\partial\\theta}\\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{h}|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si629.png)(4.155) 

where

$p\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h}|\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{1}{Z\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})}\\exp\\left( - \\mathsf{E}\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{x}) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si630.png)(4.156) 

with *θ* representing the bias terms *a*[*ϕ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si631.png), *b*[*ϕ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si632.png), **c** and the matrix **W** denoting the pairwise interactions, as follows

$\\mathsf{E}\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{x}) = - a\_{\\phi}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\top}\\mathbf{y} - b\_{\\phi}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\top}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} - \\mathbf{c}^{\\top}\\mathbf{h} - \\mathbf{y}^{\\top}\\mathbf{W}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} - \\mathbf{h}^{\\top}\\mathbf{W}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si633.png)(4.157) 

Also in [(4.156)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq159), the normalization is defined by

$Z\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y},\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y},\\mathbf{h} \\in \\mathcal{H}}\\exp\\left( - \\mathsf{E}\_{\\theta}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{h},\\mathbf{x}) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si634.png)(4.158) 

The PGMs introduced in ([Garg et al., 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0540); [Yao et al., 2021a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2030)) follow the model shown in [Fig. 4.37](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0190)(d), where *Y* is a latent clean random variable and *Z* is a latent image feature random variable. The optimization is performed by

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si635.png)(4.159) 

where

$\\log p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\underset{\\text{ELBO}}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{z},\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log\\frac{p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{z},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{q\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{z},\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})} \\right\\rbrack}} + \\underset{\\geq 0}{\\underset{︸}{\\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{z},\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\| p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{z},\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si636.png)(4.160) 

In [(4.160)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq163), we have

$p\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{z},\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = p(\\mathbf{y})p(\\mathbf{z})p\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{z})p\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si637.png)(4.161) 

where *p*(**z**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si638.png) is modeled by a multivariate normal distribution (zero mean, identity covariance), *p*(**y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si639.png) by a uniform distribution, and *p*[*θ*[1]](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si640.png) and *p*[*θ*[2]](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si641.png) are the decoders modeled by deep learning networks. Also in [(4.160)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq163), we have

$q\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{z},\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = q\_{\\phi\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x})q\_{\\phi\_{2}}(\\mathbf{z}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si642.png)(4.162) 

representing the encoders modeled by deep learning networks. The optimization in [(4.159)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq162) consists of maximizing the ELBO, as follows:

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast},\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast},\\phi\_{1}^{\\ast},\\phi\_{2}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2},\\phi\_{1},\\phi\_{2}}\\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\phi\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x})q\_{\\phi\_{2}}(\\mathbf{z}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})}\\left\\lbrack \\log p\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{z}) \\right\\rbrack + \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\phi\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x})}\\left\\lbrack \\log p\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q\_{\\phi\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x})\\| p(\\mathbf{y}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\phi\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x})}\\left\\lbrack \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q\_{\\phi\_{2}}(\\mathbf{z}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})\\| p(\\mathbf{z}) \\right\\rbrack \\right\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si643.png)(4.163) 

In practice, this optimization leverages two sets of encoders and decoders, where *q*[*ϕ*[1]](**y**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si644.png) is learned with co-teaching techniques, *q*[*ϕ*[2]](**z**|**y**, **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si645.png) is trained as an encoder of a variational auto-encoder (VAE) ([Kingma and Welling, 2013](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0910)), conditioned on the input data and label sampled as **y** ∼ *q*[*ϕ*[1]](**y**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si646.png), *p*[*θ*[1]](**x**|**y**, **z**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si647.png) is learned using a reconstruction loss with the original image, similarly to how a VAE decoder is trained, and $p\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si648.png) is trained as a classifier conditioned on the data and clean label to predict the noisy label.

Even though the Robust Generative classifier (RoG) ([Lee et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1040)) does not propose a new PGM, it transforms a discriminative model, represented by *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si227.png) and pre-trained on the noisy-label dataset, into a generative model that tends to be more robust to noisy data. Assuming that *f*[*θ*](**x**) = *h*[*θ*[2]](*g*[*θ*[1]](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si649.png), with *θ* = {*θ*[1], *θ*[2]}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si592.png), *g*[*θ*[1]] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si650.png) and *h*[*θ*[2]] : 𝒵 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si651.png), the central idea is to take the features from one of the hidden layers of the pre-trained model, say denoted by **z** = *g*[*θ*[1]](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si652.png), and learn |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si50.png) Gaussian distributions with a tied covariance Σ ([Fisher, 1936](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0520)). More specifically, each class conditional distribution is denoted by

*p*(*Z* = *g*[*θ*[1]](**x**)|*Y* = **y**) = 𝒩(*g*[*ϕ*](**x**)|*μ*[**y**], *Σ*),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si653.png)(4.164) 

with class prior *p*(*Y* = **y**) = *β*[**y**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si654.png), where 𝒩(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si655.png) is a multivariate Gaussian distribution with mean *μ*[**y**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si656.png) and covariance Σ. Then, the classifier is defined using the Bayes rule, as follows:

$p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{p(Z = g\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})|Y = \\mathbf{y})p(Y = \\mathbf{y})}{\\sum\_{\\mathbf{y}^{\\prime}\\ in\\mathcal{Y}}p(Z = g\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})|Y = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime})p(Y = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime})}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si657.png)(4.165) 

The class-conditional model parameters are learned with:

$\\mu\_{\\mathbf{y}} = \\frac{1}{\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}}}}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\widehat{\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}}}}g\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})\\beta\_{\\mathbf{y}} = \\frac{|\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}}}|}{|\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}|}\\Sigma = \\frac{1}{|\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}|}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\widehat{\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}}}}(g\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) - \\mu\_{\\mathbf{y}}){(g\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) - \\mu\_{\\mathbf{y}})}^{\\top},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si658.png)(4.166) 

where

$\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}}} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}}^{\\prime} \\subset \\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}}}\\mathsf{\\det}(\\Sigma\_{\\mathbf{y}})\\text{~s.t.~}|\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}}^{\\prime}| = K\_{\\mathbf{y}}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si659.png)(4.167) 

for all **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si128.png), where $\\mathcal{D}\_{\\mathbf{y}} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si660.png), det (.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si661.png) denotes the matrix determinant operator, *Σ*[**y**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si662.png) is the sample covariance of 𝒟[**y**]^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si663.png), *K*[**y**] ∈ (0, |𝒟[**y**]|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si664.png).

The Noisy Prediction Calibration (NPC) approach ([Bae et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0090)) is a post-processing approach that assumes the presence of a classifier trained on a noisy-label training set to train a transition model from the trained classifier prediction to a clean label, as shown in [Fig. 4.37](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0190)(e). More specifically, assume that we have a classifier training with one of the algorithms presented in this chapter (e.g., Co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)), JoCoR ([Wei et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1880)), etc.), which is denoted by $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si665.png), then the goal is to represent the clean label distribution with

$p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\mathbf{y}|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})p\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si666.png)(4.168) 

where $p\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}) = f\_{\\widehat{\\theta}}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si667.png) denotes the prediction probability for class $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si378.png). Then, the goal is to learn the transition model $p(\\mathbf{y}|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si668.png), which is referred to as NPC. Given the intractability of this model, [Bae et al. (2022)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0090) introduce the variational model $q\_{\\phi}(Y|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si669.png) and a noisy-label reconstruction model $p\_{\\theta}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}|Y,\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si670.png) that is learned with the minimization of the following KL divergence:

$KL\\lbrack q\_{\\phi}(\\mathbf{y}|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})\\| p(\\mathbf{y}|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack = \\int\_{Y}q\_{\\phi}(Y|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})\\log\\frac{q\_{\\phi}(Y|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})}{p(Y|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})}dY = \\int\_{Y}q\_{\\phi}(Y|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})\\log\\frac{q\_{\\phi}(Y|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})p(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x})}{p\_{\\theta}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}|Y,\\mathbf{x})p(Y|\\mathbf{x})}dY = \\log p(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}) - \\underset{\\text{ELBO}}{\\underset{︸}{\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\phi}(Y|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})}\\left\\lbrack \\log p\_{\\theta}(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}|Y,\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q\_{\\phi}(Y|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{x})\\| p(Y|\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack \\right)}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si671.png)(4.169) 

Given that *Y* follows a Dirichlet distribution, [Bae et al. (2022)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0090) propose the use of a reparameterization trick from ([Joo et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0820)) for maximizing the ELBO in [(4.169)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq172).

As shown above, PGMs have been widely explored in noisy-label learning, with the latest results from ([Garg et al., 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0540)) achieving state-of-the-art results in many benchmarks. However, there are many challenges involved with PGM-based approaches, such as the need for sampling variational posteriors, which tends to make the training much slower, and the learning of generative models that are generally harder to train than discriminative models.

### 4.4.6 Active learning

In active learning, we assume the availability of a small labeled training set and a large unlabeled training set. The classifier is then trained with the labeled training set, and then it is used to select the most informative samples from the unlabeled set. An informative sample is typically defined by classification uncertainty ([Settles, 2012](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1565)) (e.g., a sample that produces a high-entropy classification prediction). Informative samples can also be identified based on how much they reduce overall classification uncertainty, change the probabilistic output of the model, or change the model after training on that sample ([Settles, 2012](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1565)). The selected samples are annotated by an oracle (e.g., a human expert), and used for re-training the classifier. The steps above are iterated until the training converges, where the expectation is that the classifier achieves a performance comparable with another classifier trained with a much larger labeled training set, where samples were randomly selected to be annotated by an oracle ([Settles, 2012](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1565)).

There are two possible scenarios for active learning in noisy-label learning. In scenario one (see [Fig. 4.39](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0200)(a)), we have a small set of clean-label training sets 𝒟[*c*] = {(**x**, **y**)[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(|𝒟[*c*]|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si673.png) and a large set of unlabeled samples 𝒟[*u*] = {**x**[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(|𝒟[*u*]|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si674.png). The model is trained with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si675.png)(4.170) 

Then, informative samples from the unlabeled set are selected with

$\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{u}}u(f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si676.png)(4.171) 

where *u* : *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1) → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si677.png) represents the uncertainty function (e.g., *u*(*f*[*θ*^(\*)](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si678.png) can be represented by the entropy ℋ(*f*[*θ*^(\*)](**x**)) =  − *f*[*θ*^(\*)](**x**)^⊤log (*f*[*θ*^(\*)](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si679.png). Next, the oracle provides a potentially noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) to **x**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si680.png), where datasets are then updated with $\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\mathcal{D}\_{c}\\bigcup(\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si681.png) and 𝒟[*u*] = 𝒟[*u*] ∖ (**x**^(\*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si682.png). The whole process starts over after this step, with a re-training of the classifier.

![Figure 4.39 Active learning.There are two possible scenarios for active learning in noisy-label learning problems, where in both scenarios it is assumed that the oracle can still make mistakes and provide noisy labels. In the first scenario, we have a small clean label dataset \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image and a large unlabeled dataset \\mathcal{D}\_{u}Image, where the model is iteratively trained with an updated \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image that includes a new training sample (selected by an uncertainty function that tends to select highly informative samples) transferred from \\mathcal{D}\_{u}Image to \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image and labeled by the oracle. For the second scenario, samples from the training set \\mathcal{D}Image are selected, based on their informativeness and label noisiness, to be re-labeled by an oracle.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr039.jpg)

Figure 4.39 Active learning.There are two possible scenarios for active learning in noisy-label learning problems, where in both scenarios it is assumed that the oracle can still make mistakes and provide noisy labels. In the first scenario, we have a small clean label dataset 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) and a large unlabeled dataset 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si672.png), where the model is iteratively trained with an updated 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) that includes a new training sample (selected by an uncertainty function that tends to select highly informative samples) transferred from 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si672.png) to 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) and labeled by the oracle. For the second scenario, samples from the training set 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) are selected, based on their informativeness and label noisiness, to be re-labeled by an oracle.

In scenario two (see [Fig. 4.39](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0200)(b) and [Fig. 4.40](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0205)), the classifier *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si22.png) is trained with the usual noisy-label dataset 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) to minimize classification loss. The next step is to select an informative noisy-label training sample, with

$(\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\ast}) = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\iota(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si683.png)(4.172) 

where *ι* : 𝒴 × *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1) → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si684.png) measures the informativeness of the training sample and the noisiness of the training label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png). Next, the sample is re-labeled with a potentially noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) by an oracle and re-inserted into the training set with:

$\\mathcal{D} = \\left( \\mathcal{D} \\smallsetminus (\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\ast}) \\right)\\bigcup(\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si685.png)(4.173) 

which is then used to re-train the classifier. In scenarios one and two, it is assumed that we have a limited budget to access the oracle's labels.

![Figure 4.40 Active learning.Using the problem in Fig. 4.3, we test active learning where a noisy oracle (same IDN noise rate as the original training set) is called to relabel the sample with largest loss every 10 epochs for a total of 1000 iterations, as described by the second scenario from (4.172) and (4.173).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr040.jpg)

[Figure 4.40](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf3495) Active learning.Using the problem in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020), we test active learning where a noisy oracle (same IDN noise rate as the original training set) is called to relabel the sample with largest loss every 10 epochs for a total of 1000 iterations, as described by the second scenario from [(4.172)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq175) and [(4.173)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq176).

The method proposed by [Bouguelia et al. (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0195) assumes scenario one above with a clean training set 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) and an un-labeled training set 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si672.png). The first stage in the approach consists of selecting informative samples, where a sample is informative if the re-training of the model using that sample disagrees significantly with the original model on the labeling of other samples. Hence, in [(4.171)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq174), the uncertainty of **x** ∈ 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si686.png) is measured with

$u(f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{u}}\\delta\\left( f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime}) \\neq f\_{\\theta\_{\\mathbf{x}}^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime}) \\right) \\times w\_{\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si687.png)(4.174) 

where *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si315.png) represents the indicator function, *f*[*θ*[**x**]^(\*)](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si688.png) denotes the model from [(4.174)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq177) that is re-trained using the training set 𝒟[*c*]⋃(**x**, *f*[*θ*^(\*)](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si689.png), and

$w\_{\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime}} = \\left| \\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{\\mathbf{x}}^{\\ast}}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime}) \\right) - \\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\left( f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime}) \\right) \\right|,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si690.png)(4.175) 

with *f*[*θ*[**x**]^(\*)]^((**y**))(**x**^′)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si691.png) representing the model prediction for the sample **x**^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si692.png) with respect to class **y**. Hence, in [(4.174)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq177), the uncertainty of selecting **x** ∈ 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si686.png) is measured by not only how many instances are affected (i.e., their predicted label change), but also by how much those instances are affected. Then, the algorithm that selects the most informative un-labeled sample with

$\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{u} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{u}}u(f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}))$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si693.png)(4.176) 

where *u*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si694.png) is defined in [(4.174)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq177), and the new clean training set is $\\mathcal{D}\_{c}\\bigcup(\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si695.png), with $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) being the noisy label provided by the oracle. The model is then re-trained to produce the new parameter *θ*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si46.png) with the new clean training set, and after a few rounds of re-labeling, it detects which samples have been mislabeled by the oracle, using the measure

$m(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y}^{\\prime} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime} \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{u}}\\delta\\left( \\mathbf{y} \\neq f\_{\\theta\_{\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime} \\smallsetminus \\mathbf{x}}^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\times f\_{\\theta\_{\\mathbf{x}^{\\prime} \\smallsetminus \\mathbf{x}}^{\\ast}}^{(\\mathbf{y}^{\\prime})}(\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si696.png)(4.177) 

where *f*[*θ*[**x**^′ ∖ **x**]^(\*)](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si697.png) denotes the model re-trained using the training set (𝒟[*c*]⋃(**x**^′,*f*[*θ*^(\*)](**x**^′))) ∖ (**x**, **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si698.png). The mislabeled sample is detected with

$(\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast},\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast}) = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}m(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si699.png)(4.178) 

which is then removed from 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png) or re-labeled by the oracle.

The scenario two explained above is assumed in ([Bernhardt et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0135)), which selects noisy-label samples from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) for re-annotation. However, the proposed method selects and allows multiple labels for samples based on estimated label correctness and labeling difficulty. Assuming a budget *B* ∈ ℕ[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si700.png), the goal of the method is the following

$\\max\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\delta(\\mathsf{OneHot}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) = \\mathbf{y}\_{i})\\text{s.t.}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}{\\|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\|}\_{1} \\leq B,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si701.png)(4.179) 

where **y**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si702.png) denotes the clean label for the *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si48.png) sample, ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} \\in \\mathbb{N}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si703.png) is defined differently from previous approaches that usually assume ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si285.png) to be a one-hot vector, and consequently ${\\|{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}\\|}\_{1}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si704.png) represents the number of labels for the *i*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si48.png) sample in 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png). The training employed in ([Bernhardt et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0135)) first ranks the training samples according to predicted label correctness and annotation difficulty, with respect to the following measure:

$m(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = - \\mathbb{E}\_{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}/{\\|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\|}\_{1}}\\left\\lbrack \\log f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack - \\left( - \\mathbb{E}\_{f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})}\\left\\lbrack \\log f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si705.png)(4.180) 

where the first term is the cross-entropy loss (larger values are associated with samples with noisy labels), and the second term is the negative classification entropy (larger values are associated with unambiguous samples). The training sample to be re-labeled is selected with

$(\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\ast}) = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}m(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si706.png)(4.181) 

This selected sample is re-labeled by requesting new labels from the oracle with

${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\ast}\\leftarrow{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\ast} + \\mathsf{Oracle}(\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si707.png)(4.182) 

where Oracle : 𝒳 → 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si708.png) draws a sample from the true categorical distribution of the data **x**, until a majority is formed in ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\ast}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si709.png) (i.e., one of the classes is selected more often than all others). The training set with the newly re-labeled sample is then used to re-train the model.

The method described in ActiveLab ([Goh and Mueller, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0565)) merges the two scenarios above, leveraging a dataset 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) containing noisy-label samples, together with a dataset 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si672.png) that has un-labeled samples. Note that each sample in 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) can contain multiple labels. The active learning algorithm proposed by ActiveLab assesses when the re-labeling of a sample in 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) will be more effective than the labeling of a sample 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si672.png). Such decision depends on the following acquisition score:

$\\text{If~}\\mathbf{x}\\text{~in~}\\mathcal{D}:\\ s(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{w\_{M} \\times f\_{\\theta}^{(\\overline{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\frac{w\_{A}}{|\\mathcal{Y}|} + \\sum\_{j = 1}^{\\mathcal{A}\_{\\mathbf{x}}}w\_{j}p\_{j}(\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x})}{w\_{M} + w\_{A} + \\sum\_{j = 1}^{\\mathcal{A}\_{\\mathbf{x}}}w\_{j}}\\text{If~}\\mathbf{x}\\text{~in~}\\mathcal{D}\_{u}:\\ s(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{w\_{M} \\times \\left( \\max\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) + \\frac{w\_{A}}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}}{w\_{M} + w\_{A}}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si710.png)(4.183) 

where $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si711.png) is the consensus label from CrowdLab ([Goh et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0570)) for the sample obtained using its multiple annotations, the classifier *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si22.png) is trained using the consensus label $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si711.png), *w*[*M*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si712.png) is the model weight ([Goh et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0570)), $w\_{A} = \\frac{1}{A}\\sum\_{j = 1}^{A}w\_{j}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si713.png) represents the average annotator weight computed from the individual annotator weights {*w*[*j*]}[*j* = 1]^(*A*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si714.png) ([Goh et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0570)), 𝒜[**x**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si715.png) denotes the set of annotations for image **x**, and $p\_{j}(\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si716.png) is the probability of the consensus label $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si711.png) from the annotator *j*. From [(4.183)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq186), the samples in 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) that have the lowest scores are the ones that have fewer annotations, where annotators disagree with the consensus label, or where the classifier predicts the consensus label to be unlikely. Also from [(4.183)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq186), the samples in 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si672.png) that have the lowest scores are the ones that the classifier is least confident. In general, ActiveLab prefers to re-label a sample from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) than to label a sample from 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si672.png), except when annotations disagree, classifier has low confidence in its prediction, or the classifier is confident in a prediction that disagrees with the annotations. The *B* samples that have the lowest scores *s*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si717.png) are selected, with each one receiving one additional label, and the sets 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) and 𝒟[*u*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si672.png) being updated with the new labels.

Active learning is a relatively unexplored area in noisy-label learning. One possible reason is the difficulty in setting up an experiment with real-world datasets involving an oracle to re-label samples. Another reason is the lack of a well-defined experimental setup that is widely available for other researchers. Nevertheless, active learning studies many important aspects of noisy-label learning, such as the need to explicitly identify samples that are hard to fit (i.e. ambiguous) and samples that have noisy labels. Another interesting aspect of active learning is the discussion of the utility of re-labeling a new sample versus the utility of labeling a new un-labeled sample.

## 4.5 Model architecture

In this section, we present methods that effectively change the model architecture by adding new modules to the network. We focus on two approaches, namely: label transition methods and graph-based models. Label transition models add a module (e.g., a network or a matrix) to learn the transition from clean to noisy labels. On the other hand, graph-based models rely on graph neural networks (GNN) that generalize convolutional networks to a non-Euclidean space to allow a more reliable selection of noisy-label training samples using a graph built from the training set. Label transition is likely to be the most studied topic in noisy-label learning, for reasons that are explained below, so we believe that the understanding of this technique is critical for the progress of the field.

### 4.5.1 Label transition methods

In Section [4.2.4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0035), we have presented loss correction approaches, where the method by [Patrini et al. (2017)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1400) leverages a label transition matrix **T** and its estimate $\\widehat{\\mathbf{T}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si116.png), defined in [(4.36)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq38), to formulate a loss function that takes into account the transition from the latent clean label to the observed noisy label.
