In other words, it builds a risk-consistent estimator via loss correction ([Han et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0640)). A risk-consistent method has a statistically consistent estimator of the clean risk, which means that by increasing the size of the noisy-label training set, the empirical risk computed from the noisy-label samples and the modified loss function converges to the expected risk computed from the clean-label samples and original loss function ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1950)).

In this section, we provide an alternative strategy to the loss correction approach by ([Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1400)) for the use of label transition methods to build a classifier-consistent estimation via hypothesis correction ([Han et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0640); [Xia et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1950)). Similarly to the risk-consistent argument above, a classifier-consistent approach provides theoretical guarantees that the model learned from the noisy-label data is consistent to the optimal model, where by increasing the noisy-label training set, the learned model will converge to the optimal classifier learned from clean-label samples ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1950)). Due to this theoretical guarantee, this strategy consists of one of the most studied noisy-label learning techniques.

Let us start with the discussion present in ([Song et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1645); [Han et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0640)). The optimization considered by label transition methods is (see [Fig. 4.41](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0210)):

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast},\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}} - \\log p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si719.png)(4.184) 

where

$p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{1}) \\times p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{2}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si720.png)(4.185) 

with *θ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si567.png), *θ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si721.png) denoting the parameters for the label transition model (first term) and the clean-label classifier (second term), respectively. The label transition model $p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{1})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si718.png) can be defined by two types of model, namely: a stochastic matrix, or a regression module usually represented by a deep neural network. Such label transition model depends on the clean label **y** and the input data **x** when handling instance-dependent noise, but, when dealing with instance-independent noise (a.k.a. asymmetric noise or class-dependent noise), the model only depends on **y**, with $p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\theta\_{1}) = p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{1})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si722.png).

![Figure 4.41 Label transition methods.In label transition models, we usually learn two models, i.e., the clean label classifier denoted by p(y|x,θ2) and the label transition model p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{1})Image.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr041.jpg)

[Figure 4.41](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf3620) Label transition methods.In label transition models, we usually learn two models, i.e., the clean label classifier denoted by *p*(**y**|**x**,*θ*[2]) and the label transition model $p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{1})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si718.png).

After presenting these two label transition models, it is important to ask why the field did not focus only on the instance-dependent noise model since it is likely to be more effective given that it has more information to produce the label transition. The main issue with such an instance-dependent noise model is that it is in general ill-posed ([Han et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0640)) given that we normally have an under-constrained learning problem with only a single noisy label per training sample ([Menon et al., 2016](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1260); [Cheng et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0295)). This issue is discussed by [Scott (2015)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1540), who introduced a discussion for the identifiability of this instance-dependent noise model. That work ([Scott, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1540)) influenced the development of many solutions focused on the estimation of the instance-independent model $p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\theta\_{1})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si723.png) by leveraging irreducibility ([Scott, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1540)), anchor points ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1950); [Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130); [Yao et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2035)), masking ([Han et al., 2018b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635)), separability ([Cheng et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0295)), rankability ([Northcutt et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1360)), clusterability ([Zhu et al., 2021c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2240)), among other strategies ([Zhang et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2150); [Li et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1075)).

An early proposal of a risk-consistent estimator explored the learning of a transition matrix for binary classifiers using cross validation with noisy-label data ([Natarajan et al., 2013](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1315)). However, such approach was not extensible to multi-class problems because of the exponential increase in computational complexity with the number of classes. Furthermore, risk-consistent estimators tend to estimate the inverse of the transition matrix that may not be invertible, which can cause performance degradation ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1950); [Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1400)).

[Scott (2015)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1540) explored the theory of mixture proposition estimation (MPE) to address noisy-label learning under the irreducibility assumption for binary classification problems (i.e., with labels { − 1,  + 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si724.png)). More specifically, MPE is related to the estimation of *κ* in the following relation:

*F* = *κ* × *H* + (1 − *κ*) × *J*,

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si725.png)(4.186) 

by observing *F* and *H*, where *F*, *J*, and *H* are distributions defined in a Hilbert space ([Liu, 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1140)). The mixture proportion *κ* is identifiable if *J* is irreducible with respect to *H*, i.e., *J* cannot be written as *J* = *γ* × *H* + (1 − *γ*) × *F*^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si726.png), with *γ* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si206.png) and *F*^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si727.png) being another distribution. In a binary classification problem, the noisy-label learning problem can be formulated as an MPE ([Yao et al., 2020c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2040)) by defining the clean-label positive and clean-label negative class conditional distributions with *p*[+] = *p*(*X*|*Y* =  + 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si728.png) and *p*[−](*X*|*Y* =  − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si729.png), respectively. The noisy-label positive and negative class conditional distributions are defined by *p̃*[+] = *p*(*X*|*Ỹ* =  + 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si730.png) and *p̃*[−](*X*|*Ỹ* =  − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si731.png), respectively. Noisy-label learning involves the estimation of *λ*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si732.png) and *λ*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si733.png) with the following two equations ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)):

*p̃*[−] = *λ*[−] × *p*[+] + (1 − *λ*[−]) × *p*[−], *p̃*[+] = *λ*[+] × *p*[−] + (1 − *λ*[+]) × *p*[+],

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si734.png)(4.187) 

where *λ*[−] = *p*(*Y* =  + 1|*Ỹ* =  − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si735.png) and *λ*[+] = *p*(*Y* =  − 1|*Ỹ* =  + 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si736.png) denote the mixture proportions representing the inverse label flipping rates. Given that *λ*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si733.png), *λ*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si732.png), *p*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si737.png), and *p*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si738.png) are unknown, the estimation of *λ*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si733.png) and *λ*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si732.png) is done with the following substitution:

*p̃*[−] = *λ̃*[−] × *p̃*[+] + (1 − *λ̃*[−]) × *p*[−], *p̃*[+] = *λ̃*[+] × *p̃*[−] + (1 − *λ̃*[+]) × *p*[+],

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si739.png)(4.188) 

with ${\\widetilde{\\lambda}}\_{-} = \\frac{\\lambda\_{-}}{(1 - \\lambda\_{+})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si740.png) and ${\\widetilde{\\lambda}}\_{+} = \\frac{\\lambda\_{+}}{(1 - \\lambda\_{-})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si741.png) being the mixture proportions. Given that we have samples from *p̃*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si742.png) and *p̃*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si743.png), we can estimate *λ̃*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si744.png) and *λ̃*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si745.png) with MPE given that, from [(4.188)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq191), *p̃*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si742.png) and *p̃*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si743.png) correspond to *F* and *H* in [(4.186)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq189), *p*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si738.png) and *p*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si737.png) denote unobserved *J*s, and *λ̃*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si744.png) and *λ̃*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si745.png) represent the mixture proportion *κ*. Hence, noisy-label binary classification learning can be written as two MPE problems for the distributions *p̃*[−]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si743.png) and *p̃*[+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si742.png). The only remaining point is then to estimate *e*[−] = *p*(*Ỹ* =  + 1|*Y* =  − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si746.png) and *e*[+] = *p*(*Ỹ* =  − 1|*Y* =  + 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si747.png) so we can recover the label transition model. This is achieved by the equivalence theorem in ([Liu, 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1140)), which says that estimating {*λ*[−], *λ*[−]}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si748.png) is equivalent with identifying {*e*[−], *e*[−]}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si749.png).

This work inspired other developments in the field, such as leveraging the anchor point condition ([Yao et al., 2020c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2040)), which can be seen as a stronger requirement of the irreducibility. In particular, [Yao et al. (2020c)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2040) showed that *κ* in [(4.186)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq189) is identifiable if there exists a subset of the Hilbert space, denoted by *S*, where *H*(*S*) > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si750.png) and $\\frac{J(S)}{H(S)} = 0$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si751.png), where *H*(*S*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si752.png) and *J*(*S*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si753.png) represent the probability of the subset *S* from the distributions *J* and *H*. This subset *S* forms the anchor set that can be used to identify the label transition models. In fact, many of the early instance-independent noise approaches leverage anchor points. Anchor points are defined as samples **x**[**y**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si754.png) assumed to be a representative, or a prototype, for a particular class **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si128.png), because they have *p*(*Y* = **y**|**x**[**y**]) ≈ 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si755.png). Methods that rely on anchor points ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1950); [Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130); [Yao et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2035)) need to extract such anchor points from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) by classifying them as an anchor point of clean class **y** if *p*(*Y* = **y**|**x**[**y**]) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si756.png). Using this anchor point assumption, the transition model can be easily obtained with

$p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y}^{\\prime} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime},\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}})p(Y = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime}|\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}}) = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}})p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}}) = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si757.png)(4.189) 

assuming we have reliable estimates for $p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si758.png). In practice, finding the anchor point **x**[**y**]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si754.png) for which *p*(*Y* = **y**|**x**[**y**]) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si756.png) will require manual or external assistance, which tends to be undesirable in the context of noisy-label learning. Therefore, it is common for methods to also propose a way to automatically select class-wise anchor points with **x**[**y**]^(\*) = arg max[**x** ∈ 𝒳]*p*(*Ỹ* = **y**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si759.png) ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)) in order to estimate the transition model with [(4.189)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq192). Hence, anchor points are assumed to be present in a dataset, independently if they are manually provided ([Yu et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2080)) or estimated ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130); [Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1400)).

However, what happens when anchor points are not available? This is a question explored by [Xia et al. (2019)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1950), who proposed a revised label transition model learning called Reweight T-Revision. This approach is initialized with the learning of a noisy-label learning model

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si760.png)(4.190) 

which approximates the noisy-label classifier denoted by *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si761.png). Next, the pseudo anchor points for class **y** are detected with

$\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{X}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{x} \\in \\mathcal{X}}f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si762.png)(4.191) 

Then, we can initialize the transition matrix using [(4.189)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq192), which produces $\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x}\_{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si763.png) that is regarded as a prior transition model. Next, the model is fine-tuned by the minimization of the following empirical risk with respect to *θ* and *Δ***T**![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si764.png):

$r(\\theta,\\Delta\\mathbf{T}) = \\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) \\sim p(X,Y)}\\left\\lbrack \\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack = \\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{p(Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})}{p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack \\approx \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\frac{p(Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})}{p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x})}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\frac{f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})}{\\left( \\mathbf{T} + \\Delta\\mathbf{T} \\right)^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}))$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si765.png)(4.192) 

where *f*[*θ*]^((**y**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si766.png) represents the clean label predictor *p*(*Y* = **y**|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si767.png) in this second stage, and **T** + *Δ***T**![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si768.png) represents the stochastic label transition matrix with **T** being the prior transition model defined above in [(4.191)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq194).

The learning methods above require the challenging estimation of the noisy-label class posterior to approximate the transition matrix. This issue has been addressed with dual-*T* estimator ([Yao et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2035)) with the following factorization of the label transition matrix:

$\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y}^{\\prime} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y^{\\prime} = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime},Y = \\mathbf{y})p(Y^{\\prime} = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime}|Y = \\mathbf{y}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si769.png)(4.193) 

where *Y*^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si770.png) is the intermediate class random variable. Note that the decomposition in [(4.193)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq196) represents a divide-and-conquer approach that leverages the intermediate class to avoid the learning of the noisy class posterior for the estimation of the label transition matrix. This intermediate class enables the factorization of the original label transition matrix into the product of two easy-to-estimate transition matrices, namely: the transition matrix from clean and intermediate labels to noisy labels, and the transition matrix from clean to intermediate labels. The training involves the learning of noisy-label class posterior with [(4.190)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq193), and the definition of the intermediate class posterior with *p*(*Y*^′ = **y**|*X* = **x**) = *f*[*θ*^(\*)]^((**y**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si771.png). Then, anchor points are detected with [(4.191)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq194), which are then used to estimate the transition matrix **T**[**y**, **y**^′] = *p*(*Y*^′ = **y**|*Y* = **y**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si772.png) with the model *p*(*Y*^′ = **y**|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si773.png) using the strategy in [(4.189)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq192). The estimation $p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y^{\\prime} = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime},Y = \\mathbf{y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si774.png) is as follows: We can then estimate intermediate class label with arg max[**y**]*p*(*Y*^′ = **y**|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si775.png) for training sample **x**, allowing the approximation of the transition matrix $p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y^{\\prime} = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si776.png) (assumed to be equal to $p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y^{\\prime} = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime},Y = \\mathbf{y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si774.png)) via counting, as follows:

$p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y^{\\prime} = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime}) = \\frac{\\sum\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\delta\\left( \\left( \\arg\\max\_{\\mathbf{y}}p(Y^{\\prime} = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}\_{i}) = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime} \\right)\\text{~AND~}\\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\right) \\right)}{\\sum\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\delta\\left( \\left( \\arg\\max\_{\\mathbf{y}}p(Y^{\\prime} = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}\_{i}) = \\mathbf{y}^{\\prime} \\right) \\right)},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si777.png)(4.194) 

where *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si315.png) is an indicator function.

As noted in ([Zhu et al., 2021c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2240)), methods based on anchor points have many disadvantages. First, when the number of classes is high and the number of training samples is small, it is hard to fit the noise distributions. Second, the accuracy of the estimations depends on the number of anchor points that are available and can be identified. Third, it is challenging to extend anchor point-based methods to more complicated label noise problems. As a result, many methods that do not depend on anchor points have been proposed, as described below.

When considering label transition matrices, it is worth noting that some label transitions are impossible to realize (e.g., the transition probability between labels car and cat should be approximately 0). However, when estimating such matrices with the approaches above, the computational resources spent for the estimation of the transition probability between such invalid pairs of labels are the same as the resources for estimating the transition probability between dog and cat, which is substantially more common. This motivates the method called Masking ([Han et al., 2018b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635)) that consists of a human-assisted learning method to mask invalid label transitions, such that it focuses on the probability estimation of valid label transitions. The incorporation of this prior label transition matrix structure is performed via a generative model that given data **x**, it first generates a label **y** ∼ *p*(*Y*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si778.png), then a label transition matrix **T** ∼ *p*(**T**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si779.png) and its mask **T**[*o*] ∼ *p*(**T**[*o*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si780.png), where *p*(**T**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si781.png) is an implicit distribution modeled by neural networks, $p(\\mathbf{T}\_{o}) = p(\\mathbf{T})\\frac{d\\mathbf{T}}{d\\mathbf{T}\_{o}}|\_{\\mathbf{T}\_{o} = f(\\mathbf{T})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si782.png), with *f*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si783.png) being the mapping function from **T** to **T**[*o*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si784.png), and it finally generates the noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\sim p(\\widetilde{Y}|Y = \\mathbf{y},T = \\mathbf{T})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si785.png). [Han et al. (2018b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635) introduced the evidence lower bound (ELBO) to estimate the log-likelihood of the noisy data, as follows:

$\\log p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}) \\geq \\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{T})}\\left\\lbrack \\log\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{T})p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}) - \\log\\left( q(\\mathbf{T}\_{o})/p(\\mathbf{T}\_{o}) \\right)|\_{\\mathbf{T}\_{o} = f(\\mathbf{T})} \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si786.png)(4.195) 

where *q*(**T**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si408.png) is the variational posterior distribution that approximates the true posterior of the label transition matrix *p*(**t**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si787.png), and $q(\\mathbf{T}\_{o}) = q(\\mathbf{T})\\frac{d\\mathbf{T}}{d\\mathbf{T}\_{o}}|\_{\\mathbf{T}\_{o} = f(\\mathbf{T})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si788.png) denotes the variational distribution of the structure **T**[*o*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si784.png). In [(4.195)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq198), the first term inside the expectation represents the usual log likelihood from data **x** to noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png), while the second term penalizes inconsistencies between the learned distribution *q*(**T**[*o*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si789.png) and the manually provided prior *p*(**T**[*o*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si790.png). The training algorithm explored in [(4.195)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq198) leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) ([Goodfellow et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0580)) with three modules, using a given label transition structure **T**[*o*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si784.png) (e.g., block diagonal matrix). The generator module is responsible for generating the label transition matrix **T** using *q*(**T**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si408.png). The discriminator module implements the second part inside the expectation of [(4.195)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq198), while the reconstructor module is responsible for the first term inside the expectation. The main issue faced by this approach is the notoriously difficult training of the GAN model.

By assuming the rankability of training samples, the confident learning (CL) method ([Northcutt et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1360)), presented in Section [4.3.2](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0055), introduces a robust estimation for the instance-independent label transition matrix, by exploring a 3-step strategy, namely: 1) pruning noisy-label samples to avoid overfitting, 2) counting with probabilistic thresholds to estimate label noise, and 3) ranking samples for training. The main difference from the methods presented above is that instead of estimating $p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si791.png) and *p*(**y**|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si343.png) separately, CL directly estimates $p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si792.png) to eliminate samples where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\neq \\mathbf{y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si793.png). The method by [Cheng et al. (2020b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0295) assumes separability, whereby the training relies on distilled samples, selected based on the probability that their labels are identical with the annotated labels, to enable the model to converge to the Bayes optimal classifier. Hence, this model explores the pruning of inseparable training samples to avoid overfitting. Even though the approaches above do not depend on anchor points, the identification of confident samples ([Northcutt et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1360)) or inseparable samples ([Cheng et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0295)) is as challenge as the identification of anchor points.

The assumption of feature clusterability has been explored in ([Zhu et al., 2021c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2240)) to estimate the label transition matrix. Clusterability is defined as a property where the *K* nearest neighbors of a training sample and the sample itself have the same clean label. Let us assume clusterability to explain how to estimate *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si794.png) and *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si795.png) in a binary classification problem, where

*   •  *e*[1] = **T**[1, 2] = *p*(*Ỹ* = 2|*Y* = 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si796.png);
*   •  *e*[2] = **T**[2, 1] = *p*(*Ỹ* = 1|*Y* = 2)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si797.png);
*   •  **p**[1] = *p*(*Y* = 1|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si798.png).

The noisy labels for a training sample and its 2-nearest neighbors are denoted by *Ỹ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si799.png) and *Ỹ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si800.png), *Ỹ*[3]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si801.png), respectively. The 2-NN clusterability assumes that *Y*[1] = *Y*[2] = *Y*[3]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si802.png). Following from [(4.185)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq188), we have $p(\\widetilde{Y} = j|X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{2}p(\\widetilde{Y} = j|Y = i)p(Y = i|X = \\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si803.png). Hence, we have two first order consensus equations:

*p*(*Ỹ*[1] = 1|*X* = **x**) = *p*[1](1 − *e*[1]) + (1 − *p*[1])(*e*[2])*p*(*Ỹ*[1] = 2|*X* = **x**) = *p*[1](*e*[1]) + (1 − *p*[1])(1 − *e*[2])

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si804.png)(4.196) 

The second order consensus equations are: 

$p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{1} = j\_{1},{\\widetilde{Y}}\_{2} = j\_{2}|X = \\mathbf{x}) = = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{2}p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{1} = j\_{1},{\\widetilde{Y}}\_{2} = j\_{2}|Y\_{1} = i,Y\_{2} = i) \\times p(Y\_{1} = i|X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{2}p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{1} = j\_{1}|Y\_{1} = i) \\times p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{2} = j\_{2}|Y\_{2} = i) \\times p(Y\_{1} = i|X = \\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si805.png)(4.197) 

given the 2-NN clusterability holds and the conditional independency between *Ỹ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si799.png) and *Ỹ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si800.png) given their clean labels. This leads to the four second-order equations for different combinations of *Ỹ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si799.png), *Ỹ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si800.png):

*p*(*Ỹ*[1] = 1, *Ỹ*[2] = 1|*X* = **x**) = *p*[1](1 − *e*[1])² + (1 − *p*[1])(*e*[2])²*p*(*Ỹ*[1] = 1, *Ỹ*[2] = 2|*X* = **x**) = *p*[1](1 − *e*[1])*e*[1] + (1 − *p*[1])(*e*[2])(1 − *e*[1])

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si806.png)(4.198) 

The eight third order consensus equations are similarly defined, e.g.,

*p*(*Ỹ*[1] = 1, *Ỹ*[2] = 1, *Ỹ*[3] = 1) = *p*[1](1 − *e*[1])³ + (1 − *p*[1])(*e*[2])³

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si807.png)(4.199) 

Such first-, second-, or third-order consensus above can be estimated with *D̃*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si808.png), which are used to estimate a unique solution for the label transition matrix **T** and the clean label classifier **p**. It is worth noting that the approach was extended from the binary to multi-class classification problems in ([Zhu et al., 2021c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2240)).

Note that the noisy-label posterior $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{p}} = p(\\widetilde{Y}|X)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si809.png) is computed from the product of the label transition matrix $\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si113.png) and clean-label posterior **p** = *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si810.png), with $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{p}} = \\mathbf{T}^{\\top}\\mathbf{p}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si811.png). However, the computation of **p** from $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{p}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si812.png) and **T** is not always unique, so **p** and **T** may not be identifiable from $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{p}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si812.png), which means that multiple equivalent **p** and **T** can produce exactly the same $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{p}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si812.png). Such problem requires the introduction of additional assumptions, such as the assumption that anchor points exist in the training set, but the method does not need to identify them ([Zhang et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2150)). In particular, [Zhang et al. (2021b)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2150) introduce a regularization of the clean label predictions based on the observation that the “cleanest” clean class-posterior has the highest pairwise total variation, as follows:

$\\theta^{\\ast},\\mathbf{T}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,\\mathbf{T} \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\mathcal{L}(\\theta,\\mathbf{T}) - \\lambda \\times \\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{1} \\sim p(X)}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathbf{x}\_{2} \\sim p(X)}\\left\\lbrack 0.5{\\| f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{1}) - f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{2})\\|}\_{1} \\right\\rbrack$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si813.png)(4.200) 

where 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png) is the space of stochastic matrices, *λ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si155.png),

ℒ(*θ*, **T**) = 𝔼[**x** ∼ *p*(*X*)]\[KL\[*p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)∥**T**^⊤*f*[*θ*](**x**)\]\],

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si814.png)(4.201) 

and the second term denotes the pairwise total variation, with the expectation operators being computed with Monte Carlo approximation. Note that the optimization in [(4.200)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq203) can estimate both *θ* and **T** using, for example, stochastic gradient descent, where **T** needs to be adjusted with column-wise softmax, so it represents a stochastic matrix. A similar strategy has been explored in ([Li et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1075)) with a simultaneous minimization of the cross entropy loss between the noisy label and model prediction, and the volume of the simplex formed by the columns of the transition matrix. Assuming that the clean-label posterior probabilities are sufficiently scattered, this strategy estimates an identifiable transition matrix and a statistically consistent classifier. More specifically, the optimization in ([Li et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1075)) is defined as:

$\\theta^{\\ast},\\mathbf{T}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,\\mathbf{T} \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\mathsf{vol}(\\mathbf{T}) + \\lambda \\times \\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\sim p(X,\\widetilde{Y})}\\left\\lbrack \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{T}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si815.png)(4.202) 

where 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png) is the space of stochastic matrices, *λ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si155.png),

vol(**T**) = log det (**T**),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si816.png)(4.203) 

with the expectation operator being computed with Monte Carlo approximation.

A potential issue with label transition methods is that it is hard to extend them to open-set noisy-label learning problems, since images that belong to a class outside the set of training labels will not have a reliable *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si794.png) because the open-set class is not in 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si170.png). Similarly, the learned label transition model will be of little use to images affected by symmetric label noise. These two issues can be addressed by introducing a label quality random variable S ([Yao et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2020)), which is a quality variable embedded in D-dimensional Gaussian space to represent the annotation quality of *Ỹ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si26.png). The log likelihood of this model has the following evidence lower bound:

$\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\log p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{x}) \\geq \\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log p(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{s}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\| p(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\| p(\\mathbf{s}) \\right\\rbrack \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si817.png)(4.204) 

where $q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si588.png) and $q(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si818.png) represent variational distributions that approximate the true distributions of *Y* and *S*. [Yao et al. (2018)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2020) also introduce a learning regularization for the variational distributions of *Y* and *S* based on the maximization of their mutual information, as follows:

$\\max\\mathsf{I}(Y,S|X,\\widetilde{Y}) \\approx \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\left( \\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log q(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack + \\mathbb{E}\_{q(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log q(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si819.png)(4.205) 

where I(.|.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si820.png) denotes the mutual information operator. The optimization relies on both [(4.204)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq207) and [(4.205)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq208) to produce:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2},\\theta\_{3},\\theta\_{4}}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\left( - \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log p\_{\\theta\_{3}}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{s}) \\right\\rbrack + \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\| p\_{\\theta\_{4}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\rbrack + \\mathsf{KL}\\left\\lbrack q\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\| p(\\mathbf{s}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log q\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{y}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack - \\mathbb{E}\_{q\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\\left\\lbrack \\log q\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\mathbf{s}|\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\right\\rbrack \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si821.png)(4.206) 

which trains a model parameterized by *θ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si567.png), *θ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si721.png), *θ*[3]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si822.png), *θ*[4]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si823.png).

The method proposed by [Sukhbaatar et al. (2014)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1665) introduces a noise layer, consisting of a label transition matrix represented by **T**, on top of the prediction layer of a deep neural network (see [Fig. 4.42](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0215)). The optimization of such network is defined by

$\\theta^{\\ast},\\mathbf{T}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,\\mathbf{T} \\in \\mathcal{T}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{T}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\lambda \\times \\mathsf{tr}(\\mathbf{T}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si824.png)(4.207) 

where tr(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si825.png) denotes the trace operator, and 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png) is the space of stochastic matrices. Such an optimization is sensible because under strong assumptions the minimization of the trace of **T** enables the learning of the true label transition matrix ([Sukhbaatar et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1665)). The optimization in [(4.207)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq210) starts by setting *λ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si826.png) and **T** = **I**[|𝒴| × |𝒴|]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si827.png), allowing the early learning phase to fit the clean-label samples with the model *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si22.png). Then, *λ* is slowly increased such that the fitting of the noisy-label samples is done with the help of changes in **T**.

![Figure 4.42 Label transition model.Using the problem in Fig. 4.3, we test the label transition model from (Sukhbaatar et al., 2014) using the optimization in (4.207) with λ = 0.01.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr042.jpg)

[Figure 4.42](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf3970) Label transition model.Using the problem in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020), we test the label transition model from ([Sukhbaatar et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1665)) using the optimization in [(4.207)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq210) with *λ* = 0.01.

One of the first instance-dependent label transition estimation approaches was proposed by [Goldberger and Ben-Reuven (2017)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0575) with the introduction of a nonlinear label noise adaptation layer on top of the clean label prediction layer, similarly to ([Sukhbaatar et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1665)) explained above. Assuming that the network backbone is defined by *f*[*θ*[1]] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si828.png), the clean-label prediction is achieved with

$p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x},\\theta) = \\frac{\\exp(\\mathbf{u}\_{\\mathbf{y}}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z} + b\_{\\mathbf{y}})}{\\sum\_{\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\exp(\\mathbf{u}\_{\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z} + b\_{\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si829.png)(4.208) 

where **z** = *f*[*θ*[1]](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si830.png), **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si128.png), and $\\theta = \\{\\theta\_{1},{\\{\\mathbf{u}\_{\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}},b\_{\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}}\\}}\_{\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si831.png). The output layer to predict the noisy label is conditioned on the clean label and the data feature, as follows:

$p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x},\\phi) = \\frac{\\exp(\\mathbf{v}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z} + c\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}})}{\\sum\_{\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\exp(\\mathbf{v}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z} + c\_{\\mathbf{y},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si832.png)(4.209) 

where $\\phi = {\\{\\mathbf{v}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}},c\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\\}}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si833.png), and **z** = *f*[*θ*[1]](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si830.png), allowing the formulation of the c-model as follows:

$p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x},\\theta,\\phi) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x},\\phi) \\times p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x},\\theta).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si834.png)(4.210) 

Note that this can be simplified for the formulation of the s-model's instance-independent label transition model with

$p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},\\phi) = \\frac{\\exp(c\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}})}{\\sum\_{\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\exp(c\_{\\mathbf{y},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si835.png)(4.211) 

where $\\phi = {\\{ c\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\\}}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si836.png), and

$p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x},\\theta,\\phi) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},\\phi) \\times p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x},\\theta).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si837.png)(4.212) 

Training is based on the following optimization:

$\\theta^{\\ast},\\phi^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\theta,\\phi}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\log\\left( \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x},\\phi) \\times p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x},\\theta) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si838.png)(4.213) 

The algorithm consists of first training the model *p*(*Y* = **y**|*X* = **x**, *θ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si839.png) using 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png) without the output layer to predict the noisy label, disregarding the fact that the training labels are noisy. Next, the label predictions from this model are treated as clean, allowing the initialization of the bias parameters in the output layer to predict the noisy label, as follows:

$c\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = \\log\\left( \\frac{\\sum\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\delta({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}\_{i},\\theta)}{\\sum\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x}\_{i},\\theta)} \\right)\\mathbf{v}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = 0\\text{~for\\ all~}\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si840.png)(4.214) 

where *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si315.png) is the indicator function. The training of the c-model in [(4.213)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq216) is challenged by the lack of a regularization to mitigate the identifiability issue. This problem motivated the development of instance-dependent label transition methods that make strong assumptions about the problem.

One example of a label transition method that makes a strong assumption about the problem is the one by [Xia et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1945), who assume that the label noise of a training image depends only on its image parts. Specifically, assume that the training samples are denoted by **x**[*i*] ∈ ℝ^(*D*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si841.png) for *i* ∈ {1, ..., |𝒟|}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si842.png), the part-based representations are learned with non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) with:

$\\mathbf{W}^{\\ast},{\\{\\mathbf{h}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{W},{\\{\\mathbf{h}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}{\\|\\mathbf{x}\_{i} - \\mathbf{W}\\mathbf{h}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})\\|}\_{2}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si843.png)(4.215) 

where **W** ∈ ℝ^(*D* × *R*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si844.png) is the matrix of image parts (each of the *R* columns of **W** represents an image part), and **h**(**x**[*i*]) ∈ ℝ[+]^(*R*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si845.png) (s.t. ∥**h**(**x**[*i*])∥[1] = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si846.png)) denotes the combination coefficients to reconstruct **x**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si340.png). Assuming that we can estimate the part-dependent transition matrices, denoted by **P**^((*j*)) ∈ \[0, 1\]^(|𝒴| × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si847.png), for each learned image part **W**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si848.png), for *j* ∈ {1, ..., *R*}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si849.png) as defined in [(4.215)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq218), the instance-dependent label transition matrix for sample **x**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si340.png) is defined by

$\\mathbf{T}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{R}\\mathbf{h}^{(j)}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) \\times \\mathbf{P}^{(j)},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si850.png)(4.216) 

where **h**^((*j*))(**x**[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si851.png) represents the *j*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si345.png) component of **h**(**x**[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si852.png), learned from [(4.215)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq218). The part-dependent label transition matrices can be learned using anchor points, so assuming that **x**^((**y**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si853.png) is an anchor point for the class **y** (i.e., *p*(*Y* = **y**|*X* = **x**^((**y**))) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si854.png)), we have

$p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x}^{(\\mathbf{y})}) = \\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{c} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{c},X = \\mathbf{x}^{(\\mathbf{y})})p(Y = \\mathbf{c}|X = \\mathbf{x}^{(\\mathbf{y})}) = \\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}(\\mathbf{x}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si855.png)(4.217) 

Given that we have *R* part-dependent transition matrices, we will need at least *R* anchor points per class to be able to robustly estimate {**P**^((*j*))}[*j* = 1]^(*R*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si856.png), as follows:

${\\{\\mathbf{P}^{(j) \\ast}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{R} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{{\\{\\mathbf{P}^{(j)}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{R}}\\sum\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\sum\\limits\_{l = 1}^{K}{\\|\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},:}(\\mathbf{x}\_{l}^{(\\mathbf{y})}) - \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{R}\\mathbf{h}^{(j)}(\\mathbf{x}\_{l}^{(\\mathbf{y})}) \\times \\mathbf{P}\_{\\mathbf{y},:}^{(j)}\\|}\_{2}^{2}\\text{s.t.~}{\\|\\mathbf{P}\_{\\mathbf{y},:}^{(j)}\\|}\_{1} = 1,\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y},j \\in \\{ 1,...,R\\},K \\geq R,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si857.png)(4.218) 

where **T**[**y**, :](**x**[*l*]^((**y**)))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si858.png) and **P**[**y**, :]^((*j*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si859.png) denote the row of these two matrices related to class **y**. The training algorithm starts with a pre-training of the model to learn the image features, then, the optimization in [(4.215)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq218) is run to estimate the matrix of image parts **W**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si860.png) and the reconstruction coefficients for the training samples {**h**^(\*)(**x**[*i*])}[*i* = 1]^(|𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si861.png). Next, the part-dependent transition matrices are learned with [(4.218)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq221). The last step consists of estimating the instance-dependent transition matrix with [(4.216)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq219). After learning the instance-based transition matrix, the training focuses on learning the clean label classifier *f*[*θ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si142.png) that is used for testing.

In instance-dependent label transition methods, most columns of the transition matrix do not have much influence on the class posterior estimation. Also, as shown in Sections [4.3.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0060) and [4.2.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#s0030), some training samples are more reliable than others. These facts are explored in ([Zhang and Sugiyama, 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2155)) with an instance-confidence embedding to model instance-dependent noise that relies on a variational approximation that avoids the estimation of a noise transition matrix. In particular, each training sample is associated with a confidence parameter denoted by *w* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si862.png) that is computed from the function *g*[*ϕ*] : 𝒳 → \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si863.png), where *w* = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si864.png) means that the training sample is ambiguous or mislabeled. In detail, this paper ([Zhang and Sugiyama, 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2155)) uses a variational approximation to the true noisy-label posterior distribution *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si761.png), which is defined by *q*[*θ*, *ϕ*](*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si865.png), with the variational lower bound of the expected log-likelihood, defined by

$\\theta^{\\ast},\\phi^{\\ast} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\theta,\\phi}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\log q\_{\\theta,\\phi}(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|X = \\mathbf{x}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si866.png)(4.219) 

In [(4.219)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq222), the variational noisy-label posterior function is defined by:

*q*[*θ*, *ϕ*](*Ỹ*|*X*) = *h*(*f*[*θ*](**x**), *g*[*ϕ*](**x**)),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si867.png)(4.220) 

where *h* : *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1) → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si868.png) is a transformation function that returns a categorical distribution with the following properties: it is potentially non-linear and it is an argmax-preserving function. In practice, when the confidence from *g*[*ϕ*] : 𝒳 → \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si863.png) is approximately one, then *h*(**p**, 1) = **p**![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si869.png), but when the confidence is approximately zero, then $h(\\mathbf{p},0) = \\mathbf{u} = \\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{Y}|},...,\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{Y}|} \\right\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si870.png) (i.e., it is a uniform probability vector of size |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si50.png)). Possible examples for the function *h*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si871.png) are:

$h(\\mathbf{p},w) = w \\times \\mathbf{p} + (1 - w) \\times \\mathbf{u},h(\\mathbf{p},w) = \\frac{\\mathbf{p}^{w}}{\\left( \\left( 1\_{|\\mathcal{Y}|} \\right)^{\\top}\\mathbf{p}^{w} \\right)},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si872.png)(4.221) 

where 1[|𝒴|]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si873.png) is a column vector with |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si50.png) ones. The function *g*[*ϕ*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si512.png) in [(4.220)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq223) is defined as an instance embedding, with a single trainable parameter for each training sample. The idea of exploring confidence for training samples has also been explored in ([Berthon et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0145)), but following a different strategy, where it is assumed that confidence scores are available for the training samples. For example, this can be computed from the multiple annotations present in multi-rater annotator problems. A confidence score in this case is defined as:

$r = p(Y = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},X = \\mathbf{x}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si874.png)(4.222) 

This allows the training set to be defined by $\\mathcal{S} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},r)}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{S}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si875.png). The transition matrix is estimated first with respect to its diagonal terms:

$\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{y}}(\\mathbf{x}) = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\mathbf{y}|Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x}) = p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|\\widetilde{Y} = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x})\\frac{p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}{p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x})} = r \\times \\beta\_{\\mathbf{y}}(\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si876.png)(4.223) 

where $\\beta\_{\\mathbf{y}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}{p(Y = \\mathbf{y}|X = \\mathbf{x})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si877.png). The non-diagonal terms of the transition matrix are estimated with:

$\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x}) = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widetilde{Y} \\neq \\mathbf{y}|Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x}) = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\widetilde{Y} \\neq \\mathbf{y},Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x}) \\times p(\\widetilde{Y} \\neq \\mathbf{y}|Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x}) = \\alpha\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\times (1 - \\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{y}}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si878.png)(4.224) 

where $\\alpha\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|\\widetilde{Y} \\neq \\mathbf{y},Y = \\mathbf{y},X = \\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si879.png) denotes the probability that a sample **x** with clean label **y** has a noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) given that *Ỹ* ≠ **y**![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si880.png). The training for the clean-label classifier first initializes *β*[**y**](**x**) = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si881.png) for all training samples, and follows the steps: 1) train noisy-label classifier *h*[*ϕ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si882.png) to approximate *p*(*Ỹ*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si761.png) using all samples from 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si138.png); 2) estimate the diagonal of the transition matrix with [(4.223)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq226) for each **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si128.png) and train the clean label classifier *f*[*θ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si22.png) to approximate *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si795.png) for one epoch; 3) update $\\beta\_{\\mathbf{y}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\frac{h\_{\\phi}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x})}{f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si883.png) (where *h*[*ϕ*]^((**y**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si884.png) represents the prediction probability of class **y**, and similarly for *f*[*θ*]^((**y**))(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si766.png)). The estimation of $\\alpha\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si885.png) in [(4.224)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq227) is performed with the off diagonal terms of the transition matrix using an instance-independent label transition model, which implies that $\\alpha\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}(\\mathbf{x}) = \\alpha\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si886.png). Taking the expectation with respect to *p*(*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si887.png) on both sides of [(4.224)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq227), we have:

$\\alpha\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}} = \\frac{\\mathbb{E}\_{p(X)}\\lbrack\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack}{1 - \\mathbb{E}\_{p(X)}\\lbrack\\mathbf{T}\_{\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{y}}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si888.png)(4.225) 

which is computed with Monte-Carlo estimation using the anchor points present in 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si138.png).

Instead of learning the transition matrix between clean and noisy labels, [Yang et al. (2021)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2005) propose the learning of the Bayes-label transition matrix between Bayes optimal labels and noisy labels. Assuming that the Bayes label is represented by *Y*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si889.png), a key observation from this paper is that while the clean label posterior is defined by a soft categorical distribution, where *P*(*Y*|*X*) ∈ *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si890.png), the Bayes optimal labels are obtained by maximizing the clean label posterior with *Y*^(\*)|*X* = arg max[*Y*]*P*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si891.png), forming a one-hot vector. Then, ([Yang et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2005)) directly estimates the transition matrix $T\_{\\mathbf{y},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{x}) = p(\\widetilde{Y} = \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}|Y^{\\ast} = \\mathbf{y}^{\\ast},X = \\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si892.png) that relates the Bayes optimal distribution and noisy distribution. A critical point of this method is how to find Bayes optimal labels for training, which rely on noisy dataset distillation from ([Cheng et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0295)) to collect a set of distilled examples $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si893.png) from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si20.png), where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si21.png) is the noisy label, and **y**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si894.png) is the inferred Bayes optimal label. These distilled samples are noisy-label samples $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si60.png) that satisfy ${\\widetilde{\\eta}}\_{\\mathbf{y}}(\\mathbf{x}) > \\frac{1 + \\rho\_{max}}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si895.png), which are assigned to the inferred Bayes optimal label, i.e., **y**^(\*) = **y**![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si896.png), where *η̃*[**y**](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si897.png) is the noisy class posterior of **x** for **y** and the *ρ*[*m**a**x*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si898.png) is the upper bound to the noise rate. The selection of distilled samples will form the distilled set $\\mathcal{S} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{S}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si899.png). The Bayes label transition model is then trained with the following optimization:

$\\phi^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\phi}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast}) \\in \\mathcal{S}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},T\_{\\phi}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\top}\\mathbf{y}^{\\ast}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si900.png)(4.226) 

where *T*[*ϕ*] : 𝒳 → 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si901.png), with 𝒯![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si139.png) denoting the space of |𝒴| × |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si25.png) stochastic matrices. The last training stage comprises the optimization of the clean-label classifier *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si227.png) with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},T\_{\\phi}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\top}f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si902.png)(4.227) 

Instance-dependent or instance-independent label transition methods are one of the most studied techniques in noisy-label learning. This technique can provide some theoretical guarantees, such as classification consistency, where the learned model will converge to the optimal classifier learned from clean-label samples with an increase in the size of the noisy-label training set ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1950)). However, the identifiability problem, particularly for instance-dependent methods, is still an open research problem being actively studied ([Liu, 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1140)). Also, the assumptions made (e.g., separability ([Cheng et al., 2020b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0295)), rankability ([Northcutt et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1360)), clusterability ([Zhu et al., 2021c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2240))) to avoid the use of anchor points still need further investigation. Nevertheless, the methods presented in this section are critical for the understanding of noisy-label learning.

### 4.5.2 Graph-based models

Graph neural networks (GNN) are generalizations of convolutional networks to a non-Euclidean space ([Bronstein et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0215)) that have been widely studied in machine learning ([Hamilton et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0620)). The extension of GNN to noisy-label learning is not straightforward because of the presence of noise corrupting the edges and nodes of the graph, which can cause a performance deterioration. Hence, much of the work using GNNs is focused on how to make it robust to corrupted labels.

One of the first papers exploring GNNs for noisy-label learning is ([Iscen et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0770)), which proposes a few-shot learning method that is trained with small clean-label training set, denoted by 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si72.png), and a large noisy-label training set 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si74.png), where the GNN is a binary classifier that discriminates training samples as clean-label or noisy-label, as shown in [Fig. 4.43](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0220). The union of the two sets forms 𝒟 = 𝒟[*c*]⋃𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si905.png). Assuming we have a feature extractor *z*[*ϕ*] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si906.png) that produces training sample embeddings **z** ∈ 𝒵 ⊂ ℝ^(*Z*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si907.png), the GNN first needs to compute an adjacency matrix **A** ∈ ℝ^(|𝒟| × |𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si908.png), where **A**[*i*, *j*] = \[**z**[*i*]^⊤**z**[*j*]\][+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si909.png) if **z**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si910.png) and **z**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si911.png) are reciprocal nearest neighbors (otherwise **A**[*i*, *j*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si912.png)), with **z** = *z*[*ϕ*](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si913.png), and \[.\][+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si495.png) being the ReLU operator ([Nair and Hinton, 2010](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1305)). This matrix is then modified to have non-zero diagonals as follows: $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}} = \\mathbf{D}^{- 1}(\\mathbf{A} + \\mathbf{I})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si914.png), where **D** = diag((**A** + **I**)1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si915.png) represents the degree of matrix **A** + **I**![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si916.png) and **1** is a vector of ones. The class-wise graph convolutional network (GCN) is defined by

$g\_{\\omega}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}},\\mathbf{Z}) = \\sigma(\\mathbf{\\Omega}\_{2}^{\\top}{\\lbrack\\mathbf{\\Omega}\_{1}^{\\top}\\mathbf{Z}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}\\rbrack}\_{+}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si917.png)(4.228) 

where **Z** = \[**z**[1], ..., **z**[|𝒟|]\] ∈ ℝ^(*Z* × |𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si918.png), *ω* = {**Ω**[1] ∈ ℝ^(*Z* × *M*), **Ω**[2] ∈ ℝ^(*M* × 1)}![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si919.png), \[.\][+]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si495.png) is the ReLU operator ([Nair and Hinton, 2010](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1305)), and *σ*(*a*) = (1 − exp ( − *a*))^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si920.png) is the sigmoid function, with *a* ∈ ℝ![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si921.png). The output of $g\_{\\omega}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}},\\mathbf{Z})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si922.png) in [(4.228)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq231) is a vector of size |𝒟|![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si81.png) indicating the relevance of each sample **x** (i.e., when the output for sample **x** is approximately 1, then the sample is relevant, otherwise, it is not relevant). The learning of *ω* is based on a binary classification of training samples into 1 (clean label) or 0 (noisy label), with 

$\\omega^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\omega} - \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\log(g\_{\\omega}^{(\\mathbf{x})}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}},\\mathbf{Z})) - \\frac{\\lambda}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{n}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}}(\\log(1 - g\_{\\omega}^{(\\mathbf{x})}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}},\\mathbf{Z}))),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si923.png)(4.229) 

where $g\_{\\omega}^{(\\mathbf{x})}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}},\\mathbf{Z})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si924.png) represents the relevance prediction for sample **x**. The learning of the classifier is then based on a sample weighting technique, as follows:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{1^{\\top}\\mathbf{w}}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\mathbf{w}\_{\\mathbf{x}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si925.png)(4.230) 

where $\\mathbf{w} = g\_{\\omega}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}},\\mathbf{Z})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si926.png), and $\\mathbf{w}\_{\\mathbf{x}} = g\_{\\omega}^{(\\mathbf{x})}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}},\\mathbf{Z})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si927.png) is the relevance of sample **x**. We show the experiment with the GCN model trained with [(4.229)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq232) and [(4.230)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq233) in [Fig. 4.44](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0225).

![Figure 4.43 Graph-based models.The graph-based model in (Iscen et al., 2020) explores an adjacency graph, denoted by \\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}Image, which contains a graphical representation of the training samples, where samples that are closer in the feature space \\mathcal{Z}Image have large pairwise adjacency value, and samples far from each other have low adjacency value. After estimating \\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}Image, we train a graph convolutional network (GCN), denoted by g\_{\\omega}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}})Image to learn how to differentiate clean and noisy samples, as in (4.229). The last step is then to optimize the classifier fθ(x) with a classification loss weighted by the training sample relevance, as in (4.229).](images/B9780443154416000137/gr043.jpg)

[Figure 4.43](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf4135) Graph-based models.The graph-based model in ([Iscen et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0770)) explores an adjacency graph, denoted by $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si903.png), which contains a graphical representation of the training samples, where samples that are closer in the feature space 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si293.png) have large pairwise adjacency value, and samples far from each other have low adjacency value. After estimating $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si903.png), we train a graph convolutional network (GCN), denoted by $g\_{\\omega}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si904.png) to learn how to differentiate clean and noisy samples, as in [(4.229)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq232). The last step is then to optimize the classifier *f*[*θ*(**x**)] with a classification loss weighted by the training sample relevance, as in [(4.229)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq232).

![Figure 4.44 Graph-based methods.Using the problem in Fig. 4.3, we test the graph-based method proposed in (Iscen et al., 2020) using the sample weighting optimization from (4.229), which lasts 100 epochs with λ = 1, and the model training in (4.230) that takes 500 epochs.](images/B9780443154416000137/gr044.jpg)

[Figure 4.44](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#cf4165) Graph-based methods.Using the problem in [Fig. 4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0020), we test the graph-based method proposed in ([Iscen et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0770)) using the sample weighting optimization from [(4.229)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq232), which lasts 100 epochs with *λ* = 1, and the model training in [(4.230)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq233) that takes 500 epochs.

A general method to handle graph corruption is presented in ([Wang et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1820)), where the paper assumes that the input graph, represented by the adjacency matrix **A** ∈ {0, 1}^(|𝒟| × |𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si928.png), has redundant edges. Such assumption and the formulation proposed in ([Wang et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1820)) can be potentially used in noisy-label learning. More specifically, the proposed approach consists of a GCN that has the following encoder

$\\mathbf{Z} = f(\\Omega\_{2}^{\\top}f(\\Omega\_{1}^{\\top}\\mathbf{X}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}})\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si929.png)(4.231) 

where **Z** ∈ ℝ^(*Z* × |𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si930.png) is the matrix containing the input data embeddings, **X** ∈ ℝ^(*X* × |𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si931.png) represents the original training sample matrix, *f*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si783.png) denotes a non-linear activation function, $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si903.png) is defined above in [(4.228)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq231), *Ω*[1] ∈ ℝ^(*X* × *M*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si932.png), and *Ω*[2] ∈ ℝ^(*M* × *Z*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si933.png). The GCN decoder is defined by

${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}}^{\\prime} = \\sigma(\\mathbf{Z}^{\\top}\\mathbf{Z})$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si934.png)(4.232) 

that produces the reconstructed input matrix $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si903.png). The training is then achieved by minimizing the reconstruction error with a binary cross entropy loss between **A** and $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si903.png). To increase the robustness of this optimization, [Wang et al. (2020)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1820) introduce a cross-graph approach that uses a co-teaching strategy with the optimization in [(4.232)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq235).

The use of graphs to address noisy-label learning with open-set noise (i.e., training samples that do not belong to any of the training classes) has been considered in ([Wu et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1935)). The proposed noisy graph leaning (NGC) leverages a nearest neighbor graph built with training sample embeddings to remove open-set samples and to correct the instance-dependent label noise. More specifically, NGC starts by building a K nearest neighbor (KNN), where training samples are denoted by graph nodes and edges represent sample similarities, with

$\\mathbf{A}\_{i,j} = \\begin{cases} {{\\lbrack\\mathbf{z}\_{i}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z}\_{j}\\rbrack}\_{+},} & {\\text{if~}i \\neq j\\text{~and~}\\mathbf{z}\_{i} \\in \\mathcal{N}\_{K}(\\mathbf{z}\_{j})} \\\\ {0,} & \\text{otherwise} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si935.png)(4.233) 

where *z*[*ϕ*] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si906.png) produces training sample embeddings **z** ∈ 𝒵 ⊂ ℝ^(*Z*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si907.png), and 𝒩[*k*](**z**[*j*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si936.png) represents the set of *K* nearest neighbors of **z**[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si911.png). Then, the labels are propagated in the graph by first defining the one-hot label matrix $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{Y}} = \\lbrack{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1},...,{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\rbrack \\in {\\{ 0,1\\}}^{|\\mathcal{Y}| \\times |\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si937.png). Then, we compute the degree of each node in the adjacency matrix **A** from [(4.233)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq236) with *d*[*i*] = ∑[*j*]**A**[*i*, *j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si938.png) for the estimation of the pseudo labels $\\widehat{\\mathbf{Y}} = \\lbrack{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{1},...,{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\rbrack \\in {\\lbrack 0,1\\rbrack}^{|\\mathcal{Y}| \\times |\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si939.png), with

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{Y}}}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{Y}}}\\frac{\\alpha}{2}\\sum\\limits\_{i,j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\mathbf{A}\_{i,j}\\left\\| \\frac{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}}{\\sqrt{d\_{i}}} - \\frac{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}}{\\sqrt{d\_{j}}} \\right\\|^{2} + (1 - \\alpha){\\|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{Y}} - \\widehat{\\mathbf{Y}}\\|}\_{F}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si940.png)(4.234) 

where *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si134.png) and ∥.∥[*F*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si941.png) represents the Frobenius norm. Samples are then removed from the graph using predictive confidence and geometric data structure, with

$\\mathbf{w}\_{i} = \\begin{cases} {\\delta(i \\in \\mathcal{S}),} & {\\text{if~}{\\widehat{Y}}\_{i,{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}} > \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}} \\\\ {\\delta(\\max\_{k}{\\widehat{\\mathbf{Y}}}\_{i,k} > \\eta) \\times \\delta(i \\in \\mathcal{S}),} & \\text{otherwise} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si942.png)(4.235)
