where 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si138.png) is the largest connected component of the class with the largest prediction probability in ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000137/si943.png) from [(4.234)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq237). Note that in [(4.235)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq238), samples are removed when: 1) graph nodes in the largest connected component of class **y** have a different label produced by [(4.234)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#deq237); and 2) uncertain prediction of one of the in-distribution labels, with maximum probability less than *η*. The method also includes a contrastive learning of the training sample embeddings, taking into account the graph connections. Then the training is based on minimizing the cross-entropy loss using the weighted and re-label training samples and the contrastive learning loss mentioned above.

The use of graphs to address noisy-label learning problems has received relatively little attention, compared with other techniques presented in this chapter. An interesting advantage is that it is an elegant technique that can perform sample selection and re-label simultaneously. Nevertheless, there are some challenges involved in the approaches presented in this section, such as: how to construct the adjacency matrix, how to train the feature extractor for building the adjacency matrix, and how to integrate the GNN training with the classifier training.

## 4.6 Conclusions

In this chapter, we presented the core techniques developed for addressing noisy-label learning, as presented in the hierarchy from [Fig. 4.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#f0010). Even though noisy-label learning explores a wide range of ideas and strategies, they all aim to solve the problem of overfitting noisy-label samples during the optimization of classifiers and regressors.

The ideas proposed are divided into four topics: loss function, data processing, training algorithm, and model architecture. Loss function methods work by modifying the usual classification and regression losses with losses or regularization functions that show robustness to noisy labels ([Zhang and Sabuncu, 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2175); [Liu et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1120)), losses that weight training samples ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)), losses that correct the model prediction or the training label ([Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1400); [Reed et al., 2014](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1470)), losses that enable the adaptation of model trained with noisy labels to a domain where labels are clean ([Konstantinov and Lampert, 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0930)). Data processing techniques aim to modify training data or labels to make the model more robust to noisy labels. For instance, adversarial training ([Alayrac et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0010); [Fatras et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0490); [Zhu et al., 2021b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2230)), removal of noisy-label data from the training set ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805); [Shen and Sanghavi, 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1585); [Chen et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0260); [Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645)), separation of clean and noisy-label data to be trained using different strategies ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055)), use of multiple labels per training sample ([Tanno et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1700)), prior data knowledge exploration ([Seo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1560); [Han et al., 2018b](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0635); [Luo et al., 2019](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1180)), and data augmentation ([Nishi et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1350)) represent effective data processing techniques to handle noisy-label learning. Training algorithms consist of modifying the optimization of models, which are exemplified by meta-learning ([Ren et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1475); [Dehghani et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0380)), self-supervised pre-training ([Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2190)), training with multiple models ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805); [Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1225); [Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645); [Yu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2070); [Wei et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1880)), semi-supervised learning ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055); [Ding et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0440)), probabilistic graphical model ([Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1025); [Xiao et al., 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1960); [Vahdat, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1765); [Yao et al., 2021a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2030); [Garg et al., 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0540); [Bae et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0090)), and active learning ([Bouguelia et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0195); [Bernhardt et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0135); [Goh and Mueller, 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0565)). Model architecture techniques modify the model's network structure to enable to inclusion of new modules, such as a label transition method ([Scott, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1540); [Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)) or a graph neural network ([Iscen et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0770)).

As we shall see in the next chapter, top-performing approaches usually rely on multiple techniques, such as sample selection, self-supervised pre-training, multiple models, data augmentation, and semi-supervised learning ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055)). In fact, it is hard to obtain state-of-the-art results in any of the noisy-label learning benchmarks without exploring multiple techniques. Current papers tend to start from a top-performing method and change just one of the modules to improve results at least in a subset of the benchmarks. Nevertheless, it is important to recognize that some techniques are currently dominating the solutions, including: separation of clean and noisy-label data to be trained using different strategies ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055)), data augmentation ([Nishi et al., 2021](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1350)), self-supervised pre-training ([Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2190)), training with multiple models ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0805); [Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1225); [Han et al., 2018c](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0645); [Yu et al., 2019a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2070); [Wei et al., 2020](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1880)), semi-supervised learning ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1055); [Ding et al., 2018](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0440)), probabilistic graphical model ([Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1025); [Xiao et al., 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1960); [Vahdat, 2017](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1765); [Yao et al., 2021a](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br2030); [Garg et al., 2023](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0540); [Bae et al., 2022](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br0090)), and label transition method ([Scott, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1540); [Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml#br1130)). Next, we present the currently best methods for the main noisy-label learning benchmarks, and we will refer back to this chapter and explain only the main differences, with respect to what has already been presented.

# Chapter 5: Benchmarks, methods, results, and code

## Abstract

In this chapter we present the main noisy-label learning benchmarks and state-of-the-art methods being studied in the field. These benchmarks form a subset of the challenges presented in Chapter [2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), and they are used to compare the performance of methods with the goal of understanding which techniques are more effective to solve particular noisy-label learning problems. We also show the top-performing methods per benchmark, where we aim to list all techniques (from Chapter [4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml)) that each method explores. We conclude the chapter by summarizing the most explored techniques by the top-performing methods.

### Keywords

Noisy-label learning techniques; Noisy-label learning benchmark; Noisy-label learning state-of-the-art

## 5.1 Introduction

In this chapter, we present the most accurate methods in the field for various benchmarks representing the many types of noisy-label problems introduced in Chapter [2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml). We summarize each method by explaining it with respect to the techniques introduced in Chapter [4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml). We also aim to provide a summary of the most successful techniques being explored by the field to mitigate the noisy-label learning problem in Section [5.10](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#s0055). This chapter is up-to-date with the methods published until July 2023, but new methods will be proposed almost on a monthly basis, so it is important for the reader to understand that by the time this book is published, the methods contained in this chapter are likely to no longer represent to most accurate for at least some of the benchmarks. In Chapter [6](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml), we provide some ideas on how to find the next generation of state-of-the-art approaches.

## 5.2 Closed set label noise problems

Let us start with the **CIFAR-10** ([Krizhevsky et al., 2014](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0950)) and **CIFAR-100** (Kryzhevsky et al., [2014](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0950)) datasets that have been heavily explored for the assessment of noisy-label learning methods. Using these two datasets, the **closed-set symmetric label noise problems** ([Tanaka et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1695); [Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1400)) relied on noise rate *η* ∈ {20%, 50%, 80%, 90%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si1.png) and the **closed-set asymmetric label noise problems** ([Tanaka et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1695); [Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1400)) relied on noise rate *η* = 40%![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si2.png), as explained in Section [2.7.1.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml). The results shown in [Table 5.1](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0010) and [Table 5.2](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0015) are obtained using the same PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) model for all approaches, which allows a reasonably fair comparison between the proposals.

![Figure 5.1 DivideMix (Li et al., 2020a).Diagram of the main steps of DivideMix (Li et al., 2020a), consisting of two models Image and Image, small-loss based sample selection that divides training set \\mathcal{D}Image into clean \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image and noisy \\mathcal{D}\_{n}Image sets, data augmentation (forming augmented sets {\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}Image and noisy {\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{n}Image), semi-supervised learning with MixMatch (Berthelot et al., 2019), and regularized loss function with a robust loss for the noisy set.](images/B9780443154416000149/gr001.jpg)

[Figure 5.1](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf1245) DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)).Diagram of the main steps of DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)), consisting of two models ![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/fx003.jpg)and ![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/fx004.jpg), small-loss based sample selection that divides training set 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png) into clean 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si3.png) and noisy 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si4.png) sets, data augmentation (forming augmented sets ${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si6.png) and noisy ${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{n}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si7.png)), semi-supervised learning with MixMatch ([Berthelot et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0140)), and regularized loss function with a robust loss for the noisy set.

DivideMix has been extended in multiple ways, such as with a self-supervised pre-training method (C2D) ([Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2190))^([^(42)](#fn42))

Considering the results in [Table 5.1](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0010) and [Table 5.2](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0015), the top-performing methods (July/2023) to handle CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 symmetric and asymmetric label noise are the self-supervised adversarial noisy masking (SANM) ([Tu et al., 2023b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1760)), decoupled meta label purifier (DMLP) ([Tu et al., 2023a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1755)), OT-Filter ([Feng et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0510)), and sample selection and relabeling (SSR) ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0515)). We now provide more details about some of these methods below.

SANM ([Tu et al., 2023b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1760)),^([^(43)](#fn43))

DMLP ([Tu et al., 2023a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1755))^([^(44)](#fn44))

${\\{{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{{\\{\\mathbf{y}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\ell\\left( \\mathbf{y}\_{j},f\_{\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast}{({\\{\\mathbf{y}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|})}}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j}) \\right) \\right)\\text{s.t.:~}\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast}\\left( {\\{\\mathbf{y}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|} \\right) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{2}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\ell\\left( {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si15.png)(5.1) 

The meta-learning training proposed in DMLP is combined with DivideMix to produce the reported results in this chapter.

SSR ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0515))^([^(45)](#fn45))

$\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\begin{cases} {\\mathsf{OneHot}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{2}}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right),} & {\\text{if~}\\max\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{2}}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right) > \\tau} \\\\ {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},} & \\text{otherwise} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si16.png)(5.2) 

where the original training set $\\mathcal{D} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si17.png) is replaced by $\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si18.png). The second stage of sample selection relies on a K-nearest neighbor classifier, denoted by *k*[*N*] : 𝒵 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si19.png), to select clean samples to be inserted into ${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si6.png) if $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathsf{OneHot}(k\_{N}(f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si20.png). The third stage trains the classifier with ${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si6.png) and $\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si21.png) as follows:

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast},\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2}}\\frac{1}{|{\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in {\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}}\\ell\\left( \\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right) + \\frac{1}{|\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\\ell\_{cl}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{1}}\\left( a\_{1}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right),f\_{\\theta\_{1}}\\left( a\_{2}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si22.png)(5.3) 

where ℓ(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si23.png) is the cross-entropy loss, ℓ[*c**l*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si24.png) is a consistency loss that penalizes low cosine similarity of the representations extracted from the augmented versions *a*[1](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si25.png) and *a*[2](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si26.png) of the image **x**, with *a*[1](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si27.png) and *a*[2](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si28.png) denoting two augmentation functions.

The **instance-dependent noise (IDN) benchmarks** ([Xia et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1945)) on **CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100**, shown in [Table 5.3](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0020), are based on noise rates *η* ∈ {20%, 30%, 40%, 45%, 50%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si31.png), as explained in Section [2.7.1.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml). To allow for a fair comparison, we concentrate on approaches that use the model PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)), but we include two exceptions, namely CC ([Zhao et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2185)) and DISC ([Li et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1085)), to enable a more complete presentation of modern approaches. A natural technique to explore in IDN problems is the method based on the estimation of a label transition model, as depicted in [Fig. 4.41](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml). Typical examples of these approaches are the T-Revision ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1950)),^([^(46)](#fn46))

Methods that explore multiple models (see [Fig. 4.33](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml)), such as MentorNet ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0805)),^([^(47)](#fn47))

The most accurate methods proposed in the field are based on sample selection and semi-supervised learning ([Zhao et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2185)), sample selection correction and loss regularization ([Li et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1085)), and probabilistic graphical model with semi-supervised learning ([Garg et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0540)). The centrality and consistency (CC) method ([Zhao et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2185)),^([^(48)](#fn48))

$\\mathbf{z}\_{\\mathbf{y}} = \\frac{\\sum\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{z}} \\in \\mathcal{Z}\_{\\mathbf{y}}}\\widehat{\\mathbf{z}}}{{\\|\\sum\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{z}} \\in \\mathcal{Z}\_{\\mathbf{y}}}\\widehat{\\mathbf{z}}\\|}\_{2}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si38.png)(5.4) 

where $\\mathcal{Z}\_{\\mathbf{y}} = \\left\\{ \\widehat{\\mathbf{z}} \\middle| (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\mathbf{z} = f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}),\\widehat{\\mathbf{z}} = \\frac{\\mathbf{z}}{{\\|\\mathbf{z}\\|}\_{2}},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y} \\right\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si39.png), and **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si236.png). Then, the initial sample selection is produced using a score computed from the cosine similarity between each feature and its class center, with $s = {\\widehat{\\mathbf{z}}}^{\\top}\\mathbf{z}\_{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si41.png), for each $\\widehat{\\mathbf{z}} \\in \\mathcal{Z}\_{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si42.png) and **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si236.png). This sample selection is achieved using the two-component Gaussian mixture model (GMM) strategy, similarly to the approach presented in [(4.24)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml), where the GMM component with the larger mean is denoted as the clean component. The clean samples are the ones with clean probabilities larger than a threshold *τ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si43.png), which form the set 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si3.png), with the noise set denoted by 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si4.png). The second stage consists of training the two classifiers with a cross-entropy classification loss and a regularization defined by

$\\mathcal{L}\_{con} = - \\lambda\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}d\\left( \\mathbf{p}^{(a)}(\\mathbf{x}),\\mathbf{p}^{(b)}(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si44.png)(5.5) 

that minimizes the consistency between the two classifiers defined by

$d\\left( \\mathbf{p}^{(a)}(\\mathbf{x}),\\mathbf{p}^{(b)}(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\right) = w\_{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\\left\\| d\\left( \\mathbf{p}^{(a)}(\\mathbf{x}) - \\mathbf{p}^{(b)}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right\\|\_{1},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si45.png)(5.6) 

with **p**^((*a*)) = *f*[*θ*[2]^((*a*))](*f*[*θ*[1]](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si46.png), **p**^((*b*)) = *f*[*θ*[2]^((*b*))](*f*[*θ*[1]](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si47.png), and $w\_{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si48.png) being a class weight to handle class imbalances. The last step to form the final clean and noisy sets consists of training a two-component GMM using the classification consistency score [(5.6)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq6). The GMM component with the smaller mean is denoted as the clean component, and the clean samples are the ones with clean probabilities smaller than a threshold *τ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si49.png), which form the set ${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{c}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si6.png), with the noise set denoted by ${\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}\_{n}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si7.png). These two sets are then used to train a DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)) semi-supervised learning classifier.

![Figure 5.4 CC (Zhao et al., 2022).Diagram of the two-stage sample selection proposed by the centrality and consistency (CC) approach (Zhao et al., 2022), where the first step consists of a clustering step using the features extracted by the model f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})Image, with clean samples being selected based on how close they are to the class centers, and the second step detects clean samples given the classification consistency between the two classifiers f\_{\\theta\_{2}^{(a)}}(.)Image and f\_{\\theta\_{2}^{(b)}}(.)Image. The clean and noisy samples from this second step are then given to the semi-supervised learning approach based on DivideMix (Li et al., 2020a).](images/B9780443154416000149/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 5.4](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf1560) CC ([Zhao et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2185)).Diagram of the two-stage sample selection proposed by the centrality and consistency (CC) approach ([Zhao et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2185)), where the first step consists of a clustering step using the features extracted by the model *f*[*θ*[1]](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si32.png), with clean samples being selected based on how close they are to the class centers, and the second step detects clean samples given the classification consistency between the two classifiers *f*[*θ*[2]^((*a*))](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si33.png) and *f*[*θ*[2]^((*b*))](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si34.png). The clean and noisy samples from this second step are then given to the semi-supervised learning approach based on DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)).

The Dynamic Instance-specific Selection and Correction method (DISC) ([Li et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1085)),^([^(49)](#fn49))

$\\tau\_{w}(t) = \\lambda \\times \\tau\_{w}(t - 1) + (1 - \\lambda) \\times \\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\left( f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(a\_{w}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si55.png)(5.7) 

where *t* is the training epoch, *f*[*θ*]^((**y**))(*a*[*w*](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si56.png) denotes the prediction for class **y** ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si236.png), and *τ*[*w*](0) = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si57.png). The threshold for the strongly augmented images is defined similarly as in [(5.7)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq7), with *τ*[*s*](*t*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si58.png) using *f*[*θ*]^((**y**))(*a*[*s*](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si59.png). The dynamic threshold for label correction is defined slightly differently, with

$\\tau^{\\prime}(t) = \\max\\left( \\frac{\\tau\_{w}(t) + \\tau\_{s}(t)}{2} + \\sigma,0.99 \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si60.png)(5.8) 

where *σ* is a positive offset value. The clean subset of the training set 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png) is defined with the training samples that the model is confident in the prediction of the training label for the weak and strong augmentations, as in

$\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\left( f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(a\_{w}(\\mathbf{x})) > \\tau\_{w}(t)\\text{~AND~}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(a\_{s}(\\mathbf{x})) > \\tau\_{s}(t) \\right) \\right\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si61.png)(5.9) 

On the other hand, the hard subset is formed with the samples that the model is confident for at least one of the augmentations, with

$\\mathcal{D}\_{h} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in (\\mathcal{D} \\smallsetminus \\mathcal{D}\_{c}),\\left( f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(a\_{w}(\\mathbf{x})) > \\tau\_{w}(t)\\text{~OR~}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(a\_{s}(\\mathbf{x})) > \\tau\_{s}(t) \\right) \\right\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si62.png)(5.10) 

The purified, or commonly known in the literature as label-corrected, subset is formed with

$\\mathcal{D}\_{p} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\left( \\mathcal{D} \\smallsetminus \\left( \\mathcal{D}\_{c}\\bigcup\\mathcal{D}\_{h} \\right) \\right),\\left( \\frac{f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(a\_{w}(\\mathbf{x})) + f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(a\_{s}(\\mathbf{x}))}{2} > \\tau^{\\prime}(t) \\right),\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\arg\\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\left( \\frac{f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(a\_{w}(\\mathbf{x})) + f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(a\_{s}(\\mathbf{x}))}{2} \\right) \\right\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si63.png)(5.11) 

To avoid the confirmation bias issue in the training with 𝒟[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si64.png), DISC proposes the use of a mix set, defined by

$\\mathcal{D}\_{m} = \\left\\{ (\\overline{\\mathbf{x}},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}})|\\overline{\\mathbf{x}} = \\gamma \\times \\mathbf{x} + (1 - \\gamma) \\times \\mathbf{x}\_{j},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\gamma \\times \\mathbf{y} + (1 - \\gamma) \\times \\mathbf{y}\_{j},(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}),(\\mathbf{x}\_{j},\\mathbf{y}\_{j}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}\\bigcup\\mathcal{D}\_{h}\\bigcup\\mathcal{D}\_{p} \\right\\}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si65.png)(5.12) 

with *j* being a random index to an element in the set formed by 𝒟[*c*]⋃𝒟[*h*]⋃𝒟[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si66.png) and *γ* ∼ Beta(*α*, *α*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si67.png). Training is conducted with a separate loss function per subset, as in

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta} + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\ell\_{CE}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a\_{w}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right) + \\ell\_{CE}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a\_{s}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{h}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{h}}\\ell\_{MAE + CE}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a\_{w}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right) + \\ell\_{MAE + CE}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a\_{s}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{m}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\overline{\\mathbf{x}},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{m}}\\ell\_{BCE}\\left( \\overline{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a\_{w}(\\overline{\\mathbf{x}})) \\right) + \\ell\_{BCE}\\left( \\overline{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a\_{s}(\\overline{\\mathbf{x}})) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si68.png)(5.13) 

where ℓ[*C**E*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si69.png) and ℓ[*B**C**E*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si70.png) represent the CE and BCE losses defined in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), and ℓ[*M**A**E* + *C**E*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si71.png), defined in [(4.3)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml), is the noise-robust loss that combines CE and MAE losses ([Zhang and Sabuncu, 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2175)).

![Figure 5.5 DISC (Li et al., 2023).Diagram of the main steps of DISC (Li et al., 2020a), which comprises a sample selection that uses two augmented versions of the input image and an image-wise dynamic threshold to classify training samples into clean, hard, and purified subsets, where the samples in the purified subset are re-labeled. Training uses different loss functions for samples belonging to different subsets, where samples from the purified set are mixed up with samples from other sets to improve robustness to confirmation bias.](images/B9780443154416000149/gr005.jpg)

Figure 5.5 DISC ([Li et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1085)).Diagram of the main steps of DISC ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)), which comprises a sample selection that uses two augmented versions of the input image and an image-wise dynamic threshold to classify training samples into clean, hard, and purified subsets, where the samples in the purified subset are re-labeled. Training uses different loss functions for samples belonging to different subsets, where samples from the purified set are mixed up with samples from other sets to improve robustness to confirmation bias.

Probabilistic graphical models have been heavily explored for IDN problems, with the CausalNL ([Yao et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2030))^([^(50)](#fn50))

![Figure 5.6 PGM (Yao et al., 2021a; Garg et al., 2023).Diagram of the PGM approaches (Yao et al., 2021a; Garg et al., 2023) that are based on a classifier, denoted by q\_{\\phi\_{1}}(Y|\\mathbf{x})Image and trained with co-teaching (Han et al., 2018c) (as in the PGM in (Yao et al., 2021a)), or DivideMix (Li et al., 2020a) (as in (Garg et al., 2023)). This classifier allows for the sampling of (pseudo) “clean” labels \\mathbf{y}\_{1},\\mathbf{y}\_{2} \\in \\mathcal{Y}Image, which are used by the encoder q\_{\\phi\_{2}}(Z|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})Image to produce low-dimensional image representations \\mathbf{z}\_{1},\\mathbf{z}\_{2} \\in \\mathcal{Z}Image. Next, the input image is reconstructed given the low-dimensional representations and (pseudo)“clean” labels with p\_{\\theta\_{1}}(X|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{z})Image, to produce images \\mathbf{x}\_{1},\\mathbf{x}\_{2} \\in \\mathcal{X}Image. Then, a noisy-label classifier, conditioned on the (pseudo) “clean” labels and reconstructed images, denoted by p\_{\\theta\_{2}}(\\widetilde{Y}|\\mathbf{y},\\mathbf{x})Image, is trained to produce the training noisy labels.](images/B9780443154416000149/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 5.6](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf1635) PGM ([Yao et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2030); [Garg et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0540)).Diagram of the PGM approaches ([Yao et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2030); [Garg et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0540)) that are based on a classifier, denoted by *q*[*ϕ*[1]](*Y*|**x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si72.png) and trained with co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0645)) (as in the PGM in ([Yao et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2030))), or DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)) (as in ([Garg et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0540))). This classifier allows for the sampling of (pseudo) “clean” labels **y**[1], **y**[2] ∈ 𝒴![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si73.png), which are used by the encoder *q*[*ϕ*[2]](*Z*|**y**, **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si74.png) to produce low-dimensional image representations **z**[1], **z**[2] ∈ 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si75.png). Next, the input image is reconstructed given the low-dimensional representations and (pseudo)“clean” labels with *p*[*θ*[1]](*X*|**y**, **z**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si76.png), to produce images **x**[1], **x**[2] ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si77.png). Then, a noisy-label classifier, conditioned on the (pseudo) “clean” labels and reconstructed images, denoted by *p*[*θ*[2]](*Ỹ*|**y**, **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si78.png), is trained to produce the training noisy labels.

**The Polynomial Margin Diminishing (PMD) Noise benchmark** ([Zhang et al., 2021c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2160)) on **CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100** ([Krizhevsky and Hinton, 2009](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0945)) is shown in [Table 5.4](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0025). Recall from Chapter [2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml) that PMD is an instance-dependent noise, where noisy labels appear at a higher rate for the samples located near the decision boundaries, compared with samples far from the boundaries. This benchmark has not been widely used by researchers in the field, but it is a reasonably challenging problem that deserves more attention by the community. The backbone model used in this benchmark is the PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) in ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)) and PreActResNet-34 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) in PLC and Cross-Entropy ([Zhang et al., 2021c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2160)). An important point about this benchmark is the noise rate of 70% on both CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. For CIFAR-10, this 70% noise rate may effectively swap the labels of a particular class, as observed by [Smart and Carneiro (2023)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625). This occurs because with such 70% IDN noise rate, some classes have ‘flipped’ to another class, as observed between classes ‘cats’ and ‘dogs’ or classes ‘trucks’ and ‘airplanes’. On the other hand, such phenomenon is not observed in CIFAR-100 because the 70% noisy samples are more evenly distributed among many neighbors, so the class label cannot swap with a particular class.

[Table 5.4](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf1650)

**Test accuracy (%) on the instance-dependent noise Polynomial Margin Diminishing (PMD) benchmark on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (**[Zhang et al., 2021c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2160)**).** Cross-entropy and PLC results are from ([Zhang et al., 2021c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2160)), and BootLN(M)(+TTA) are from ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)). The backbone model used in this benchmark is the PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) in ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)) and PreActResNet-34 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) in PLC and Cross-Entropy ([Zhang et al., 2021c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2160)).

| --- |

The top methods for the PMD noise benchmark are the Progressive Label Correction (PLC) ([Zhang et al., 2021c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2160))^([^(51)](#fn51))

BootLN ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)), depicted in [Fig. 5.7](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#f0040), is a three-stage approach to train the modified (M) classification model *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si88.png) that takes as input not only an image **x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si89.png), but also the given noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si90.png) to predict the clean label distribution ([Gu et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0605); [Inoue et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0760); [Veit et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1805)). Such modified model aims to learn patterns associated with the transition between noisy to clean labels. BootLN also considers the training of a normal (N) classifier defined by *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si50.png), which does not take the noisy label as input. In the first training stage, referred to as bootstrapping, the model is pre-trained with self-supervision ([Chen et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0265)) and trained with early stopping with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{S}}\\left\\lbrack \\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x}),0\_{|\\mathcal{Y}|})) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si91.png)(5.14) 

where ℓ[*C**E*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si69.png) is the cross-entropy loss, *a*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si92.png) represents a data augmentation sampled from a set of strong data augmentations 𝒜[*S*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si93.png), and 0[|𝒴|]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si94.png) is a vector of |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si95.png) zeros. The initial pseudo clean labels are produced with

$\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{W}}\\left\\lbrack f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(a(\\mathbf{x}),0\_{|\\mathcal{Y}|}) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si96.png)(5.15) 

where *a*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si92.png) denotes an augmentation function sampled from the set of weak augmentation functions 𝒜[*W*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si97.png). The method then relies on sample selection and pseudo-labeling of clean samples, which forms the following clean and noisy sets:

$\\mathcal{D}\_{c} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathsf{OneHot}(\\overline{\\mathbf{y}})\\text{,\\ where~}\\max\\limits\_{c \\in \\{ 1,...,|\\mathcal{Y}|\\}}\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}(c) > \\tau\\}\\mathcal{D}\_{n} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\max\\limits\_{c \\in \\{ 1,...,|\\mathcal{Y}|\\}}\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}(c) \\leq \\tau\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si98.png)(5.16) 

The second stage involves a semi-supervised learning (SSL) ([Sohn et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1635)) that uses the clean and noisy sets defined in [(5.16)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq16) to pseudo-label the samples in 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si4.png). The SSL uses the following optimization:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta} + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}}\\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{W}}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}))\\rbrack + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{n}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}}\\delta(\\max\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} > \\tau)\\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{S}}\\lbrack\\ell(\\mathsf{OneHot}(\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}),f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}))\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si99.png)(5.17) 

where *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si100.png) represents an indicator function, $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{W}}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x}),\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si101.png), and OneHot(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si102.png) returns the one-hot vector from the categorical distribution $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si86.png). This SSL stage enables the pseudo-labeling of the whole training set with:

$\\overline{\\mathcal{D}} = \\left\\{ (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathsf{OneHot}(\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}))|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}\_{W}}\\left\\lbrack f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}}(a(\\mathbf{x}),0\_{|\\mathcal{Y}|}) \\right\\rbrack \\right\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si103.png)(5.18) 

The third stage simply trains the modified (M) or normal (N) model with strong and mixup ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2110)) augmentations using the training set $\\overline{\\mathcal{D}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si87.png) from [(5.18)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq18). An interesting point about the testing procedure of BoostLN is that the authors ran the method with and without test-time augmentation, where results with test-time augmentation (TTA) tend to be surprisingly better. This suggests that there is potential in the use of TTA, which is a technique relatively unexplored by the field. Also, the modified model (M) that takes image and noisy-label in the input showed better results than the normal (N) model that only takes the input image, indicating that BoostLN can uncover some relationship between the given noisy label and produced clean label. One important point is the cases with 70% noise rate in CIFAR-10, where BoostLN shows rather poor results. The reason for this poor results is related to the issue explained above, where this 70% noise rate can effectively swap the labels between two classes in CIFAR-10.

![Figure 5.7 BootLN (Smart and Carneiro, 2023).Diagram of BootLN (Smart and Carneiro, 2023) which takes as input the image x (after being processed by a feature extractor) and noisy label \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}Image to output a clean label \\overline{\\mathbf{y}}Image. Training is divided into 3 stages: 1) bootstrapping: self-supervised pre-training of the feature extractor + training with early stopping + sample selection and pseudo-labeling of clean samples; 2) semi-supervised learning with pseudo-clean set \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image assumed to be labeled and noisy set \\mathcal{D}\_{n}Image assumed to be un-labeled, followed by a pseudo-labeling of the whole training set to form \\overline{\\mathcal{D}}Image; and 3) training of the classifier with \\overline{\\mathcal{D}}Image.](images/B9780443154416000149/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 5.7](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf1710) BootLN ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)).Diagram of BootLN ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)) which takes as input the image **x** (after being processed by a feature extractor) and noisy label $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si85.png) to output a clean label $\\overline{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si86.png). Training is divided into 3 stages: 1) bootstrapping: self-supervised pre-training of the feature extractor + training with early stopping + sample selection and pseudo-labeling of clean samples; 2) semi-supervised learning with pseudo-clean set 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si3.png) assumed to be labeled and noisy set 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si4.png) assumed to be un-labeled, followed by a pseudo-labeling of the whole training set to form $\\overline{\\mathcal{D}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si87.png); and 3) training of the classifier with $\\overline{\\mathcal{D}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si87.png).

The results of **the instance-dependent noise RoG benchmarks** introduced by [Lee et al. (2019)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1040) on **CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100** ([Krizhevsky and Hinton, 2009](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0945)) are shown in [Table 5.5](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0030). In RoG, noisy labels are provided by trained models VGG-13 (that produces a noise rate of 34% on CIFAR-10 and 37% on CIFAR-100) ([Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1610)), DenseNet-100 (that produces a noise rate of 32% on CIFAR-10 and 34% on CIFAR-100) ([Huang et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0745)), and ResNet-34 (that produces a noise rate of 38% on CIFAR-10 and 37% on CIFAR-100) ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)). The backbone model used in this benchmark is the PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) in ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625); [Cordeiro et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0320)) and ResNet-44 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) in D2L+RoG and CE+RoG ([Lee et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1040)). In this benchmark, the top performing method is BoostLN ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)) explained above, but using the normal (N) model instead of the modified (M) model. Again, the use of TTA is noticeably advantageous. The other approaches listed in [Table 5.5](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0030) are the Robust Generative classifier (RoG) ([Lee et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1040))^([^(52)](#fn52))

Table 5.5

**Instance-dependent noise RoG benchmark on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (**[Lee et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1040)**).** D2L+RoG and CE+RoG results are from ([Lee et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1040)), PropMix result is from ([Cordeiro et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0320)), and BootLN(N)(+TTA) results are from ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)). The backbone model used in this benchmark is the PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) in ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625); [Cordeiro et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0320)) and ResNet-44 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) in D2L+RoG and CE+RoG ([Lee et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1040)).

A real-world instance-dependent noise introduced in the training images of CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 ([Krizhevsky et al., 2014](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0950)) formed the **CIFAR-10N, CIFAR-100N benchmarks** ([Wei et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1885)), with results shown in [Table 5.6](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0035). These two benchmarks have gained well-deserved attention since this is a well-designed noisy-label learning benchmark. One method that works particularly well is the ELR+ ([Liu et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1120)) that consists of DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)) trained with a robust early-learning regularization loss function. Another competitive approach in this benchmark is the COnfidence REgularized Sample Sieve (CORES) method ([Cheng et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0290)),^([^(53)](#fn53))

$\\ell\_{peer}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si104.png)(5.19) 

where the training samples $(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si105.png) and $(\\mathbf{x}\_{j},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si106.png) are randomly sampled from 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png) with replacement. CORES ([Cheng et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0290)) defines two independent and uniform random variables *X*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si107.png) and *Ỹ*[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si108.png) where $p(X\_{i} = \\mathbf{x}\_{i}|\\mathcal{D}) = p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{j} = {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}|\\mathcal{D}) = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si109.png) for all *i*, *j* ∈ {1, ..., |𝒟|}![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si110.png). The peer loss has the following equivalent form ([Cheng et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0290)):

$\\ell\_{peer}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\mathbb{E}\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}) \\sim p(X\_{i},{\\widetilde{Y}}\_{j}|\\mathcal{D})}\\left\\lbrack \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) \\right\\rbrack = \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}p(X\_{i} = \\mathbf{x}\_{i}|\\mathcal{D})\\mathbb{E}\_{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} \\sim p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{j}|\\mathcal{D})}\\left\\lbrack \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i})) \\right\\rbrack = \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\mathbb{E}\_{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} \\sim p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{j}|\\mathcal{D})}\\left\\lbrack \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si111.png)(5.20) 

where *p*(*Ỹ*[*j*]|𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si112.png) represents the distribution of *Y*[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si113.png) given dataset 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png). Instead of training directly with the loss function in [(5.20)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq20), [Cheng et al. (2020a)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0290) propose a sample selection approach to improve training convergence using the second term of this loss function. The selection is achieved with:

$w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = \\delta\\left( \\left( \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\mathbb{E}\_{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} \\sim p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{j}|\\mathcal{D})}\\left\\lbrack \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack \\right) < \\tau \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si114.png)(5.21) 

where $\\tau = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{Y}|}\\sum\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}\\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\mathbb{E}\_{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} \\sim p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{j}|\\mathcal{D})}\\left\\lbrack \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si115.png), where the optimization is performed with:

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}w(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\times \\left( \\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) - \\mathbb{E}\_{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} \\sim p({\\widetilde{Y}}\_{j}|\\mathcal{D})}\\left\\lbrack \\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right\\rbrack \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si116.png)(5.22)

**Test accuracy (%) on the CIFAR-10N and CIFAR-100N instance-dependent noise benchmarks (**[Wei et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1885)**)**. Results are collected from the cited papers in each row. The backbone model used in this benchmark is the PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) for all methods, except for the methods marked with ^†, which have been trained with a ResNet-34.

Sparse Over-Parameterization (SOP) ([Liu et al., 2022c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1125))^([^(54)](#fn54))

$\\theta^{\\ast},{\\{\\mathbf{u}\_{i}^{\\ast},\\mathbf{v}\_{i}^{\\ast}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,{\\{\\mathbf{u}\_{i},\\mathbf{v}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}}\\ell({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) + \\mathbf{s}\_{i})\\text{s.t.~}\\mathbf{s}\_{i} = \\mathbf{u}\_{i} \\odot \\mathbf{u}\_{i} \\odot {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} - \\mathbf{v}\_{i} \\odot \\mathbf{v}\_{i} \\odot (1 - {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i})\\mathbf{u}\_{i} \\in {\\lbrack - 1,1\\rbrack}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|},\\ \\mathbf{v}\_{i} \\in {\\lbrack - 1,1\\rbrack}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|},\\ i \\in \\{ 1,...,|\\mathcal{D}|\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si121.png)(5.23) 

where ⊙ is the element-wise vector product. The SOP+ in [Table 5.6](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0035) adds a consistency regularizer that minimizes the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-divergence between the predictions from the augmented images and the predictions of the images generated with Unsupervised Data Augmentation (UDA). The SOP+ also minimizes the KL divergence between the probability distribution of class labels and the mean prediction of the training set.

ProMix\* ([Wang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1830)),^([^(55)](#fn55))

$\\left( \\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}f\_{\\theta}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}) > \\tau \\right)\\text{~AND~}\\left( \\max\\limits\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}f\_{\\overline{\\theta}}^{(\\mathbf{y})}(\\mathbf{x}) > \\tau \\right)\\text{~AND~}\\left( \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\mathsf{OneHot}(f\_{\\overline{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si130.png)(5.24) 

Then the samples that meet this condition are re-labeled as (**x**, OneHot(*f*[*θ*](**x**)))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si131.png), which are added to 𝒟[*c*]^′![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si132.png). The training of the two models is based on the optimization that minimizes a classification loss (CE loss), consistency loss (using a strong image augmentation), and a MixUp loss ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2110)), as follows:

$\\theta^{\\ast},{\\overline{\\theta}}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,\\overline{\\theta}}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}\\bigcup\\mathcal{D}\_{c}^{\\prime}}\\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\overline{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\beta \\times \\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a\_{S}(\\mathbf{x}))) + \\beta \\times \\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\overline{\\theta}}(a\_{S}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\beta \\times \\ell\_{CE}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{m},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}^{m})) + \\beta \\times \\ell\_{CE}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{m},f\_{\\overline{\\theta}}(\\mathbf{x}^{m})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si133.png)(5.25) 

where *a*[*S*] ∼ 𝒜[*S*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si134.png) represents a strong augmentation function, **x**^(*m*) = *σ* × *a*[*W*](**x**) + (1 − *σ*) × *a*[*W*](**x**[*j*])![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si135.png), and $\\mathbf{y}^{m} = \\sigma \\times \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} + (1 - \\sigma) \\times {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si136.png), are samples obtained via MixUp ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2110)), with *σ* ∼ Beta(*ξ*, *ξ*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si137.png), for *ξ* = 4![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si138.png), and *a*[*W*] ∼ 𝒜[*W*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si139.png) represents a weak augmentation function.

![Figure 5.8 ProMix (Wang et al., 2022).ProMix (Wang et al., 2022) relies on two models, three separate sample selection approaches, and one pseudo-labeling mechanism to train a model by combining a classification loss with two robust losses, one based on consistency training using a strong image augmentation and another loss based on MixUp (Zhang et al., 2018).](images/B9780443154416000149/gr008.jpg)

[Figure 5.8](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf1970) ProMix ([Wang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1830)).ProMix ([Wang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1830)) relies on two models, three separate sample selection approaches, and one pseudo-labeling mechanism to train a model by combining a classification loss with two robust losses, one based on consistency training using a strong image augmentation and another loss based on MixUp ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2110)).

Similarly to the IDN applied in CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 in [Table 5.3](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0020), the same IDN proposed by [Xia et al. (2020)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1945) is applied to the **Fashion-MNIST IDN benchmark** ([Xiao et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1955)) in [Table 5.7](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0040), and to the **SVHN IDN benchmark** ([Netzer et al., 2011](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1325)) in [Table 5.8](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0045). The backbone model for the F-MNIST benchmark is ResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)), and for the SVHN benchmark, ResNet-34 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)). The main results in these two datasets have been produced by the multi-model approach MentorNet ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0805)), and label transition methods Reweight ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1130)), T-Revision ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1950)), PTD-R-V ([Xia et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1945)), and kMEIDTM ([Cheng et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0285)). All these approaches have already been presented above under other benchmarks. The state-of-the-art in these datasets is the Bayes-label Transition Matrix (BLTM) ([Yang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2010)).^([^(56)](#fn56))

BLTM ([Yang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2010)), shown in [Fig. 5.9](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#f0050), aims to model an instance-dependent label transition matrix from Bayes optimal labels to noisy labels and learn the classifier to predict the Bayes optimal labels. While the clean label posterior is a categorical distribution denoted by *p*(*Y*|*X*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si144.png) (defined as in Chapter [2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml)) that is used for sampling clean labels, the Bayes optimal labels are defined as one-hot vectors that maximize the clean label posteriors with (*Y*^(\*)|*X* = **x**) = arg max[**y** ∈ 𝒴]*p*(*Y* = **y**|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si145.png). The proposed modeling of the instance-dependent label transition matrix for sample **x** from Bayes optimal labels to noisy labels is defined by **T**^(\*)(*X* = **x**) = *p*(*Ỹ*|*Y*^(\*), *X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si146.png), which can then be used to estimate the Bayes optimal labels with *p*(*Y*^(\*)|*X* = **x**) = (**T**^(\*)(*X* = **x**)^⊤)^( − 1)*p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si147.png), where *p*(*Ỹ*|*X* = **x**)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si148.png) can be estimated from the noisy-label training set 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png). The fact that the Bayes optimal label posteriors are represented by one-hot vectors has two advantages ([Yang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2010)): 1) it is possible to find a set of samples with theoretically guaranteed Bayes optimal labels in a noisy-label dataset; and 2) the solution space to find the Bayes-label transition matrix is smaller than the solution space for the clean-label transition matrix. BLTM first collects a set of distilled examples $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si149.png) to form the distilled training set $\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si21.png), where $f\_{\\eta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x}) > \\frac{1 + \\rho\_{max}}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si150.png), with $f\_{\\eta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si151.png) being the noisy label posterior probability distribution of **x** for the one-hot label $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{Y}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si152.png) (obtained from a model trained with the noisy-label dataset 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png)), *ρ*[*m**a**x*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si153.png) representing the noise rate upper bound, $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si85.png) denoting the noisy label, and $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si29.png) the theoretically guaranteed Bayes optimal label ([Cheng et al., 2020b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0295)). Next, BLTM estimates a Bayes label transition network **T**[*θ*[1]] : 𝒳 → ℝ^(|𝒴| × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si142.png) using the following optimization:

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1}}\\frac{1}{|\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\log\\left( {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\mathbf{T}\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si155.png)(5.26) 

Then, we train the classifier *f*[*θ*[2]] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si143.png) to predict the Bayes optimal labels with

$\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{2}}\\frac{1}{|\\widehat{\\mathcal{D}}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}^{\\top}\\log\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{2}}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\top}\\mathbf{T}\_{\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si156.png)(5.27) 

In Tables [5.7](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0040) and [5.8](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0045) the BLTM-V applies the transition matrix revision technique ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1950)) to boost performance.

![Figure 5.9 BLTM (Yang et al., 2022).BLTM (Yang et al., 2022) is a 4-stage training approach to estimate the instance-dependent label transition matrix from Bayes optimal labels to noisy labels and learn the classifier to predict the Bayes optimal labels. The first stage trains the classifier f\_{\\eta}:\\mathcal{X}\\rightarrow\\Delta^{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1}Image from the noisy-label dataset \\mathcal{D}Image. The second stage distills the dataset \\mathcal{D}Image by selecting samples where \\max\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}f\_{\\eta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})} > \\frac{1 + \\rho\_{max}}{2}Image, where ρmax denotes a noise rate upper-bound. The third stage trains the Bayes label transition network \\mathbf{T}\_{\\theta\_{1}}:\\mathcal{X}\\rightarrow\\mathbb{R}^{|\\mathcal{Y}| \\times |\\mathcal{Y}|}Image with (5.26), and the fourth stage trains the Bayes optimal posterior classifier f\_{\\theta\_{2}}:\\mathcal{X}\\rightarrow\\Delta^{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1}Image with (5.27).](images/B9780443154416000149/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 5.9](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf2070) BLTM ([Yang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2010)).BLTM ([Yang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2010)) is a 4-stage training approach to estimate the instance-dependent label transition matrix from Bayes optimal labels to noisy labels and learn the classifier to predict the Bayes optimal labels. The first stage trains the classifier *f*[*η*] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si140.png) from the noisy-label dataset 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png). The second stage distills the dataset 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png) by selecting samples where $\\max\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}f\_{\\eta}^{(\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}})} > \\frac{1 + \\rho\_{max}}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si141.png), where *ρ*[*max*] denotes a noise rate upper-bound. The third stage trains the Bayes label transition network **T**[*θ*[1]] : 𝒳 → ℝ^(|𝒴| × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si142.png) with [(5.26)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq26), and the fourth stage trains the Bayes optimal posterior classifier *f*[*θ*[2]] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si143.png) with [(5.27)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq27).

As detailed in Section [2.7.1.1](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), another **IDN benchmark** was proposed by [Jiang et al. (2020)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0800) using the **Mini-ImageNet** ([Vinyals et al., 2016](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1815)) and **Stanford Cars** ([Krause et al., 2013](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0935)) datasets. Even though ([Jiang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0800)) proposes four benchmarks, the field has concentrated on only two of them, the Red Mini-ImageNet and the Red Stanford Cars, so we present results for these two benchmarks in Tables [5.9](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0050) and [5.10](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0055), where the base models are the PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) and Inception-ResNetV2 ([Szegedy et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1675)).

Methods marked with “-SS” have been pre-trained with self-supervised consistency learning ([Caron et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0245)). Most approaches that produce competitive results in these benchmarks have been presented before, such as MixUp ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2110)), DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)), FaMUS ([Xu et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1980)), self-supervised pre-trained PropMix (PropMix-SS) ([Cordeiro et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0320)), and self-supervised pre-trained InstanceGM (InstanceGM-SS) ([Garg et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0540)).

The two methods that are new in Tables [5.9](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0050) and [5.10](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0055) are the MentorMix ([Jiang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0800)) and the Dynamic Softening of Out-of-distribution Samples (DSOS) ([Albert et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0015)). MentorMix ([Jiang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0800))^([^(57)](#fn57))

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\ell\\left( h(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},u\_{i},v\_{i},\\theta),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}) \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si157.png)(5.28) 

where *u*[*i*] ∈ {0, 1}![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si158.png) corresponds to the probability given $s\_{DSOS}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si159.png) in [(4.72)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml) for the left-most Beta mixture component being superior to 0.5 (i.e., *u*[*i*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si160.png) indicates a clean sample); *v*[*i*] ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si161.png) represents the posterior probability of the right-most Beta mixture component (i.e., *v*[*i*] ≈ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si162.png) indicates an open-set noisy-label sample), and

$h(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i},u\_{i},v\_{i},\\theta) = \\frac{\\exp\\left( \\frac{v\_{i} \\times {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}}{\\alpha} \\right)}{\\sum\_{c = 1}^{|\\mathcal{Y}|}\\exp\\left( \\frac{v\_{i} \\times {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}(c)}{\\alpha} \\right)}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si163.png)(5.29) 

with *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si164.png), and

${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} = (1 - u\_{i}) \\times {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i} + u\_{i} \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si165.png)(5.30) 

The optimization in [(5.28)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq28) involves the dynamic evaluation of {*u*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(|𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si166.png) and {*v*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(|𝒟|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si167.png) at every epoch, and the gist of the training is to force the model to produce a uniform prediction for open-set samples (*v*[*i*] ≈ 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si162.png)), to predict its own output for closed-set noisy labels (*v*[*i*] ≈ 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si168.png), *u*[*i*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si169.png)), and to predict the training label for clean samples (*u*[*i*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si160.png)). The final proposed training for DSOS includes MixUp data augmentation and an entropy-based regularization.

The **Animal-10N benchmark** ([Song et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1640)) shown in [Table 5.11](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0060) is a small, but challenging dataset that has been explored by many researchers to assess the robustness of noisy-label learning methods to IDN noise. The main approaches tested in this benchmark are DISC ([Li et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1085)), SSR+ ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0515)), BootLN(M) ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)), SANM(SSR) ([Tu et al., 2023b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1760)), and BootLN(M) + *TTA* ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)). All these methods have been explained before and rely on the backbone model VGG-19 ([Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1610)), where the top approaches SANM(SSR) and BootLN(M)+TTA show almost the same result. Both approaches combine many techniques, such as adversarial training, semi-supervised learning, sample selection, pseudo-labeling, and self-supervised pre-training.

All methods use the VGG-19 ([Simonyan and Zisserman, 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1610)) backbone model.
