Co-learning ([Tan et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1690))^([^(59)](#fn59))

$\\theta\_{1}^{\\ast},\\theta\_{2}^{\\ast},\\theta\_{3}^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2},\\theta\_{3}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell\_{sup}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right) + \\ell\_{int}\\left( \\mathbf{x},\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{3} \\right) + \\ell\_{str}\\left( \\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2},\\theta\_{3} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si172.png)(5.31) 

where the supervised loss ℓ[*s**u**p*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si173.png) is defined with MixUp ([Zhang et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2110)) augmentation, as follows

$\\ell\_{sup}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) = \\lambda \\times \\ell\_{CE}\\left( \\overline{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(a\_{1}(\\mathbf{x}))) \\right) + (1 - \\lambda) \\times \\ell\_{CE}\\left( \\overline{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(a\_{2}(\\mathbf{x}\_{m}))) \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si174.png)(5.32) 

with *a*[1], *a*[2] ∼ 𝒜[*W*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si175.png) represent two weak augmentation functions, *m* ∈ {1, ..., |𝒟|}![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si176.png) representing a randomly chosen training sample, and

$\\overline{\\mathbf{x}} = \\lambda \\times \\mathbf{x} + (1 - \\lambda) \\times \\mathbf{x}\_{m},\\overline{\\mathbf{y}} = \\lambda \\times \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} + (1 - \\lambda) \\times {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{m},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si177.png)(5.33) 

with *λ* ∼ Beta(*α*, *α*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si178.png). Also in [(5.31)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq31), the intrinsic similarity loss ℓ[*i**n**t*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si179.png) enforces training samples to have intrinsic similarity through strong data augmentations with

ℓ[*i**n**t*](**x**,*θ*[1],*θ*[3]) = ℓ[*I**n**f**o**N**C**E*](*f*[*θ*[3]](*f*[*θ*[1]](*a*[1](**x**))),*f*[*θ*[3]](*f*[*θ*[1]](*a*[2](**x**)))) + ℓ[*I**n**f**o**N**C**E*](*f*[*θ*[3]](*f*[*θ*[1]](*a*[2](**x**))),*f*[*θ*[3]](*f*[*θ*[1]](*a*[1](**x**)))),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si180.png)(5.34) 

where *a*[1], *a*[2] ∼ 𝒜[*S*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si181.png) denote two strong augmentation functions, and

$\\ell\_{InfoNCE}\\left( \\mathbf{v}\_{1},\\mathbf{v}\_{2} \\right) = - \\log\\frac{\\exp(\\mathsf{d}(\\mathbf{v}\_{1},\\mathbf{v}\_{2})/\\tau)}{\\sum\_{i,j = 1;i \\neq j}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\exp(\\mathsf{d}(\\mathbf{v}\_{1}^{(i)},\\mathbf{v}\_{2}^{(j)})/\\tau)}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si182.png)(5.35) 

with $\\mathsf{d}(\\mathbf{v}\_{1},\\mathbf{v}\_{2}) = \\frac{\\mathbf{v}\_{1}^{\\top}\\mathbf{v}\_{2}}{\\|\\mathbf{v}\_{1}\\|\\|\\mathbf{v}\_{2}\\|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si183.png), *τ* is a temperature parameter, **v**[1]^((*i*)) = *f*[*θ*[3]](*f*[*θ*[1]](*a*[1](**x**[*i*])))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si184.png), and **v**[2]^((*j*)) = *f*[*θ*[3]](*f*[*θ*[1]](*a*[2](**x**[*j*])))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si185.png) (here, *a*[1], *a*[2] ∼ 𝒜[*S*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si181.png)). The last term in [(5.31)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq31) is the structural similarity loss ℓ[*s**t**r*](.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si186.png) that enforces the similarity between pairs of samples with respect to the predictions from the classifier and projection heads, as follows:

$\\ell\_{str}\\left( \\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\theta\_{1},\\theta\_{2},\\theta\_{3} \\right) = \\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\mathsf{p}({\\|\\mathbf{v} - \\mathbf{v}\_{j}\\|}\_{2})\\log\\frac{\\mathsf{p}({\\|\\mathbf{v} - \\mathbf{v}\_{j}\\|}\_{2})}{\\mathsf{p}({\\|\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} - {\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\|}\_{2})},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si187.png)(5.36) 

where $\\mathsf{p}(d) = \\exp\\left( \\frac{0.5 \\times d^{2}}{{(0.5)}^{2}} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si188.png), **v** = *f*[*θ*[3]](*f*[*θ*[1]](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si189.png), **v**[*j*] = *f*[*θ*[3]](*f*[*θ*[1]](**x**[*j*]))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si190.png), $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} = f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si191.png), and ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j} = f\_{\\theta\_{2}}(f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}\_{j}))$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si192.png).

![Figure 5.10 Co-learning (Tan et al., 2021).Co-learning (Tan et al., 2021) is a multi-model approach that shares the encoder and has a classifier and projection heads, where training consists of minimizing the classification loss ℓsup(.) (with MixUp augmentation), the intrinsic similarity loss ℓint(.) that enforces image features to be robust to strong data augmentations in \\mathcal{A}\_{S}Image, and the structural similarity loss ℓstr(.) that enforces similarity between pairs of images with respect to classifier and projection outputs.](images/B9780443154416000149/gr010.jpg)

[Figure 5.10](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf2270) Co-learning ([Tan et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1690)).Co-learning ([Tan et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1690)) is a multi-model approach that shares the encoder and has a classifier and projection heads, where training consists of minimizing the classification loss *ℓ*[*sup*](.) (with MixUp augmentation), the intrinsic similarity loss *ℓ*[*int*](.) that enforces image features to be robust to strong data augmentations in 𝒜[*S*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si93.png), and the structural similarity loss *ℓ*[*str*](.) that enforces similarity between pairs of images with respect to classifier and projection outputs.

The other top-performing method in [Table 5.12](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0065) is DISC ([Li et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1085)), which is a feature selection and loss regularization already presented above and depicted in [Fig. 5.5](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#f0030).

The **Clothing1M benchmark** ([Xiao et al., 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1960)) in [Table 5.13](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0070) is one of the most explored benchmarks to compare noisy-label learning methods. All methods in this table use the ResNet-50 ([He et al., 2016a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0680)) backbone model. The results from the top-performing methods e.g., C2D ([Zheltonozhskii et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2190)), AugDesc ([Nishi et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1350)), PGDF ([Chen et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0270)), and SANM(DivideMix) ([Tu et al., 2023b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1760)) are all between 74% and 75%, with DMLP(DivideMix) ([Tu et al., 2023a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1755)) reaching 78% because it relies on a clean validation set.

All methods use the ResNet-50 ([He et al., 2016a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0680)) backbone model. The **WebVision benchmark** ([Li et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1070)) in [Table 5.14](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0075) is another heavily explored benchmark of noisy-label learning methods. The backbone model for WebVision is the Inception-ResnetV2 model ([Szegedy et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1675)). Top-performing methods, such as ELR+ ([Liu et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1120)), PropMix ([Cordeiro et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0320)), NGC ([Wu et al., 2021b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1935)), FaMuS ([Xu et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1980)), DISC ([Li et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1085)), BootLN(M) ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)), SSR+ ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0515)), and BootLN(M) + *TTA* ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)), have all been already explained in this book. Similarly to what is being observed in Clothing1M from [Table 5.13](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0070), the WebVision results in [Table 5.14](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0075) seem to be quite close to each other, with the exception of BootLN(M) + *TTA* ([Smart and Carneiro, 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1625)), which has been obtained with test-time augmentation (TTA). The use of TTA suggests an interesting note, which is the potential performance gain that other methods can achieve with TTA, which is a point that needs further study.

## 5.3 Open set label noise problems

Open-set label noise is, together with IDN, a real-world type of label noise that can be present in training datasets, given that images not belonging to any of the training classes may be mistakenly present in the training set. For this reason, the field has introduced benchmarks to compare methods designed to address this type of label noise. [Table 5.15](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0080) shows one of these benchmarks which combines **closed-set symmetric label noise in CIFAR-10 and open-set label noise using samples from CIFAR-100** ([Sachdeva et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1505)). Also, [Table 5.16](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0085) shows the results of a benchmark that combines **symmetric closed set noise in CIFAR-10 and open-set noise from ImageNet32** ([Sachdeva et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1505)). The backbone model used in these experiments is the PreActResNet-18 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)). The results in Tables [5.15](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0080) and [5.16](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0085) suggest that EvidentialMix (EDM) ([Sachdeva et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1505)) (presented in [(4.5)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml)) and SSR+ ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0515)) (presented in [Fig. 5.3](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#f0020)) show the best results. Interestingly, even though SSR+ and DivideMix are general label noise methods, they show competitive or better results than EDM that has been implemented to specifically address the combined open-set and closed-set label noise problem. This suggests that the differences between open-set and closed-set label noise may not be as large as initially anticipated.

The second best method is the Joint Sample Selection and Model Regularization based on Consistency (JoSRC) ([Yao et al., 2021b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2045)),^([^(60)](#fn60))

$p\_{clean}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) = 1 - \\mathsf{JS}(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})\\|\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}), = 1 - 0.5 \\times \\mathsf{KL}{\\left( f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right\\|\\left. \\frac{f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}{2} \\right)} - 0.5 \\times \\mathsf{KL}{\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} \\right\\|\\left. \\frac{f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) + \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}{2} \\right)}$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si197.png)(5.37) 

where JS(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si198.png) and KL(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si199.png) are the Jensen-Shannon (JS) and KL divergence operators. Hence, samples classified as clean form the dataset 𝒟[*c**l**e**a**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si194.png), while the remaining samples form the 𝒟[*n**o**i**s**y*] = 𝒟 ∖ 𝒟[*c**l**e**a**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si200.png) Then, a sample in 𝒟[*n**o**i**s**y*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si201.png) is classified as open-set label noise if *p*[*o**p**e**n*](**x**) > *τ*[*o**p**e**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si202.png), where

*p*[*o**p**e**n*](**x**) = min (1, ∥*f*[*θ*](*a*[1](**x**)) − *f*[*θ*](*a*[2](**x**)∥[1])),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si203.png)(5.38) 

where *a*[1], *a*[2] ∈ 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si204.png) denote two different augmentation functions sampled from 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si205.png). Samples classified as open set are inserted into 𝒟[*o**p**e**n*] ⊂ 𝒟[*n**o**i**s**y*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si206.png), while the remaining samples form 𝒟[*c**l**o**s**e**d*] ⊂ 𝒟[*n**o**i**s**y*] ∖ 𝒟[*o**p**e**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si207.png). All samples are then pseudo-labeled, where samples in 𝒟[*c**l**e**a**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si194.png) have their training labels modified to contain a small uniform distribution spread over all classes. Samples in 𝒟[*c**l**o**s**e**d*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si195.png) are re-labeled with the mean-teacher's prediction $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = f\_{\\theta\_{mt}}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si208.png), where *θ*[*m**t*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si209.png) represents the mean-teacher model parameters that are updated from the model parameters during all training steps, using an exponential moving average (EMA) ([Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1710)), as in

*θ*[*m**t*] = *λ* × *θ*[*m**t*] + (1 − *λ*) × *θ*.

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si210.png)(5.39) 

Samples in 𝒟[*o**p**e**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si196.png) are re-labeled by assigning $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si85.png) to a uniform distribution. The training of JoSRC uses the following optimization

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in {(\\mathcal{D}\_{clean}\\bigcup\\mathcal{D}\_{closed}\\bigcup\\mathcal{D}\_{open})}}\\mathbb{E}\_{a \\sim \\mathcal{A}}\\lbrack\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x})))\\rbrack + \\rho \\times \\left( \\mathsf{KL}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})\\| f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x}))\\rbrack + \\mathsf{KL}\\lbrack f\_{\\theta}(a(\\mathbf{x}))\\| f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})\\rbrack \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si211.png)(5.40) 

where $\\rho = \\delta\\left( (\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\left( \\mathcal{D}\_{clean}\\bigcup\\mathcal{D}\_{closed} \\right) \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si212.png) is an indicator function, and *a* ∼ 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si213.png) is an augmentation function.

![Figure 5.11 JoSCR (Yao et al., 2021b).JoSCR (Yao et al., 2021b) is a multi-model approach that first selects samples to in the clean-label set \\mathcal{D}\_{clean}Image, closed-set \\mathcal{D}\_{closed}Image, and open-set \\mathcal{D}\_{open}Image. Then, a mean teacher (Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017) pseudo-labels samples belonging to \\mathcal{D}\_{closed}Image or \\mathcal{D}\_{open}Image. Samples from the clean set and pseudo-labeled samples from the closed and open sets are then used to train the model with the robust loss function (5.40).](images/B9780443154416000149/gr011.jpg)

[Figure 5.11](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf2495) JoSCR ([Yao et al., 2021b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2045)).JoSCR ([Yao et al., 2021b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2045)) is a multi-model approach that first selects samples to in the clean-label set 𝒟[*c**l**e**a**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si194.png), closed-set 𝒟[*c**l**o**s**e**d*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si195.png), and open-set 𝒟[*o**p**e**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si196.png). Then, a mean teacher ([Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1710)) pseudo-labels samples belonging to 𝒟[*c**l**o**s**e**d*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si195.png) or 𝒟[*o**p**e**n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si196.png). Samples from the clean set and pseudo-labeled samples from the closed and open sets are then used to train the model with the robust loss function [(5.40)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq40).

Differently from Tables [5.15](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0080) and [5.16](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0085), results in [Table 5.17](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0090) suggest that DSOS and JoSRC, which have been designed to deal specifically with the combined closed-set and open-set label noise, are the best approaches tp deal with this specific problem. This apparent contradiction with the conclusion from the previous combined CIFAR-10 and open-set label noise benchmarks indicates that more study needs to be conducted until we are able to reach a more coherent analysis of the results.

## 5.4 Imbalanced noisy-label problems

All benchmarks presented so far assume a balanced distribution of samples per class in the training set, which facilitates the selection of noisy-label samples because samples that are hard to fit can either be located close to the classification boundary, or have a noisy label. However, when the training set contains an imbalanced distribution of samples per class, then samples belonging to minority classes (i.e., classes that have a relatively small number of training samples, compared to other classes in the training set) also tend to be hard to fit because of the dominance of majority classes in the minimization of a classification loss function. Hence, imbalanced noisy-label problems tend to be more challenging than the problems presented so far in this chapter. The combination of **symmetric label noise and imbalanced class distribution** has been proposed by three papers, referred to as FSR/RoLT/INOLML ([Zhang and Pfister, 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2170); [Wei et al., 2021b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1890); [Hoang et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0715)), with results shown in Tables [5.18](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0095) and [5.19](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0100). The backbone model used in this experiment is the Resnet-32 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)). The baseline methods for this problem are CRUST ([Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1295))^([^(61)](#fn61))

The best methods in both benchmarks (FSR ([Zhang and Pfister, 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2170))^([^(62)](#fn62))

$\\mathbf{c}\_{\\mathbf{y}} = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}^{(\\mathbf{y})}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}^{(\\mathbf{y})}}f\_{\\theta\_{1}}(\\mathbf{x}),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si214.png)(5.41) 

where $\\mathcal{D}^{(\\mathbf{y})} = \\{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})|(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}} = \\mathbf{y}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si215.png), and *f*[*θ*[1]] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si10.png) is a feature extractor. The sample selection is performed in a class-wise manner using the distance of each sample to its respective class prototype, computed with *d*(**x**, **c**[**y**]) = ∥*f*[*θ*[1]](**x**) − **c**[**y**]∥[2]²![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si216.png) for $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}^{(\\mathbf{y})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si217.png). Then, for each class, a GMM with two components is fit to ${\\{ d(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{c}\_{\\mathbf{y}})\\}}\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}^{(\\mathbf{y})}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si218.png), where the component with the smallest mean represents the clean-label samples for class **y**, where clean samples are selected with *p*[*c**l**e**a**n*](**x**) > *τ*![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si219.png) to be inserted into 𝒟[*c*]^((**y**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si220.png), with the noisy set denoted by 𝒟[*n*]^((**y**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si221.png). The next step consists of pseudo-labeling the samples $(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}^{(\\mathbf{y})}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si222.png) with:

$\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}(c) = \\begin{cases} {\\sum\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{G}}\\mathsf{prior}(\\text{clean\\ label}) \\times \\mathbf{e}\_{c}^{\\top}\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}},} & {\\text{~if~}\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{G}} \\\\ {\\frac{1 - \\sum\_{\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{G}}\\mathsf{prior}(\\text{clean\\ label})}{|\\mathcal{Y}| - |\\mathcal{G}|},} & \\text{~otherwise} \\\\ \\end{cases},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si223.png)(5.42) 

where $\\mathcal{G} = \\{\\mathbf{y}\_{erm},\\mathbf{y}\_{ncm},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si224.png) (with **y**[*e**r**m*] = arg max[**y** ∈ 𝒴]*f*[*θ*[2]]^((**y**))(*f*[*θ*[1]](**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si225.png), **y**[*n**c**m*] = arg min[**y** ∈ 𝒴]∥**c**[**y**] − *f*[*θ*[1]](**x**)∥[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si226.png)), **e**[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si227.png) represents a one-hot |𝒴|![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si95.png)\-dimensional vector with the value of one in the *c*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si228.png) position, and prior(clean label)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si229.png) is the probability that the label $\\widehat{\\mathbf{y}} \\in \\mathcal{G}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si230.png) agrees with the clean label. The parameters *θ*[1]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si231.png), *θ*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si232.png) are then learned by minimizing the cross entropy loss using the original labels from the clean-label sets {𝒟[*c*]^((**y**))}[**y** ∈ 𝒴]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si233.png) and the pseudo-labels of the noisy-label sets {𝒟[*n*]^((**y**))}[**y** ∈ 𝒴]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si234.png). The extension RoLT-DRW is implemented by applying the Deferred Re-Weighting (DRW) ([Cao et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0240)) to improve the performance on minority classes.

![Figure 5.12 RoLT (Wei et al., 2021b).RoLT (Wei et al., 2021b) consists of class-wise sample selection and pseudo-labeling method designed to handle imbalanced noisy-label learning problems. Sample selection is performed by first estimating class prototypes {\\{\\mathbf{c}\_{\\mathbf{y}}\\}}\_{\\mathbf{y} \\in \\mathcal{Y}}Image with (5.41). ## 5.5 Noisy multi-label learning

For multi-label learning, we first present results using two chest X-ray benchmarks ([Liu et al., 2022a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1110)) that used **noisy multi-label training sets (Chest X-ray14 (NIH) (**[Wang et al., 2017b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1850)**) and CheXpert (CXP) (**[Irvin et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0765)**)) and clean-label testing sets (OpenI (OPI) (**[Demner-Fushman et al., 2016](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0390)**) and PadChest (PDC) (**[Bustos et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0220)**))**. The results from these benchmarks are presented in Tables [5.20](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0105) and [5.21](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0110) and all methods relied on the DenseNet121 ([Huang et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0745)) backbone model. The noisy multi-label learning problem has only recently been addressed more directly with the release of these two benchmarks, but the only approach that has been designed to address this challenge is NVUM ([Liu et al., 2022a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1110)), which delivers the best result in both benchmarks. The approaches presented in ([Rajpurkar et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1445)),^([^(63)](#fn63))

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x}\_{i},{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{i}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\sigma(f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}))) + \\ell\_{reg}(\\mathbf{t}\_{i},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}\_{i}))$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si239.png)(5.43) 

where ℓ(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si23.png) is the BCE loss defined in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), *σ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si240.png) denotes the sigmoid activation function, and

ℓ[*r**e**g*](**t**[*i*], *f*[*θ*](**x**[*i*])) = log (1 − *σ*(**t**[*i*]^⊤(*σ*(*f*[*θ*](**x**[*i*])))),

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si241.png)(5.44) 

with

**t**[*i*]^((*t*)) = *λ* × **t**[*i*]^((*t* − 1)) + (1 − *λ*) × (*f*[*θ*](**x**[*i*]) − *π*)

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si242.png)(5.45) 

representing a memory bank of logits that keeps the noisy-label early classification predictions produced by the model, which also takes into account the class prior distribution $\\pi = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si243.png) to mitigate the imbalanced learning problem that is generally present in noisy multi-label benchmarks.

Another **benchmark that uses the Chest X-ray14 (NIH)** ([Wang et al., 2017b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1850)) noisy multi-label training set has been proposed in ([Xue et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1990)), which provides a **clean test set for two labels, namely Pneumothorax and Mass/Nodule**. In this benchmark, with results shown in [Table 5.22](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0115), we can see results of many baseline noisy-label learning methods, such as a training with binary cross entropy (BCE), F-correction ([Patrini et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1400)), MentorNet ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0805)), Decoupling ([Malach and Shalev-Shwartz, 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1225)), Co-teaching ([Han et al., 2018c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0645)), and ELR ([Liu et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1120)). All of these methods have been explained before and rely on the backbone model DenseNet121 ([Huang et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0745)). The top-performing methods are NVUM ([Liu et al., 2022a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1110)), described above, and the Global and Local Representation Guided Co-training (GloCal) method ([Xue et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1990)). GloCal, shown in [Fig. 5.13](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#f0070), is a method that combines co-training with student-teacher training, exploring a self-supervised loss with global and local regularization. More specifically, GloCal co-trains two student-teacher models, denoted by *f*[*θ*[(*s*)]^((*A*))] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si244.png), *f*[*θ*[(*t*)]^((*A*))] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si245.png), *f*[*θ*[(*s*)]^((*B*))] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si246.png), and *f*[*θ*[(*t*)]^((*B*))] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si247.png), where students are trained with a set of loss functions, described below, and teachers are trained with exponential moving average (EMA), e.g., *θ*[(*t*)]^((*A*)) = *λ* × *θ*[(*t*)]^((*A*)^′) + (1 − *λ*) × *θ*[(*s*)]^((*A*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si248.png) (note that *θ*[(*t*)]^((*A*)^′)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si249.png) is the parameter of teacher A from the previous training iteration, and we have the same EMA update for teacher B). After computing the losses of the training samples by models A and B, the first step consists of selecting samples (using the small loss hypothesis based on fitting a two-component Gaussian mixture model ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055))) to form the clean and noisy subsets for each model, denoted by 𝒟[*c*]^((*A*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si250.png) and 𝒟[*n*]^((*A*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si251.png) for model A and 𝒟[*c*]^((*B*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si252.png) and 𝒟[*n*]^((*B*))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si253.png) for model B. Then, similarly to DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)), the clean and noisy subsets produced by A are used to train B, and vice-versa. Next, samples from the clean subsets are trained with cross-entropy loss, while samples from the noisy subset are trained with a global and local losses, and all samples are used to minimize a teacher-student consistency loss. Assuming that the model is represented by a feature extractor *f*[*θ̂*] : 𝒳 → 𝒵![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si254.png) and a classifier $f\_{\\overline{\\theta}}:\\mathcal{Z}\\rightarrow\\Delta^{|\\mathcal{Y}| - 1}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si255.png) (where $\\theta = \\{\\widehat{\\theta},\\overline{\\theta}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si256.png)), the global loss computes the relationship between features extracted from training samples to form the |𝒟| × |𝒟|![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si257.png) matrix

$\\mathbf{M}(i,j) = \\frac{\\mathbf{f}\_{i}^{\\top}\\mathbf{f}\_{j}}{{\\|\\mathbf{f}\_{i}\\|}\_{2}{\\|\\mathbf{f}\_{j}\\|}\_{2}},$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si258.png)(5.46) 

which allows the minimization of the following loss

$\\ell\_{glo}(\\mathcal{D}) = \\frac{1}{2}\\left( \\mathsf{KL}\\lbrack\\mathbf{M}\_{(t)}||\\lbrack\\mathbf{M}\_{(s)}\\rbrack + \\mathsf{KL}\\lbrack\\mathbf{M}\_{(s)}||\\lbrack\\mathbf{M}\_{(t)}\\rbrack \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si259.png)(5.47) 

where KL\[.\]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si260.png) represents the KL divergence. This global loss aligns the inter-sample relationship of samples between the teacher and student models. The local loss minimizes the contrastive loss of augmented images, as defined in [(5.35)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq35). The training also depends on the minimization of a consistency loss between the teacher and student models, defined by ℓ[*c**o**n*](**x**) = ∥*f*[*θ*[(*s*)]^((*A*))](**x**) − *f*[*θ*[(*t*)]^((*A*))](**x**)∥[2]²![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si261.png). Hence, the student model A from GloCal is trained with 

$\\theta\_{(s)}^{(A) \\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{(s)}^{(A)}}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{c}^{(B)}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{c}^{(B)}}\\ell\_{CE}\\left( \\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta\_{(s)}^{(A)}}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) + \\lambda \\times \\left( \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{n}^{(B)}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{n}^{(B)}}\\ell\_{InfoNCE}\\left( f\_{\\theta\_{(s)}^{(A)}}(a\_{1}(\\mathbf{x})),f\_{\\theta\_{(s)}^{(A)}}(a\_{2}(\\mathbf{x})) \\right)\\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ \\ + \\ell\_{glo}(\\mathcal{D}\_{c}^{(B)}) + \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell\_{con}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si262.png)(5.48) 

where *a*[1], *a*[2] ∼ 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si263.png) denote augmentation functions, and *θ*[(*s*)]^((*B*)\*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si264.png) is similarly estimated using the clean and noisy samples from model A.

[Figure 5.13](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf2735) GloCal ([Xue et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1990)).GloCal ([Xue et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1990)) is an approach to co-train two student-teacher models, where the selected clean and noisy samples from one model are used to train the other model. Such training involves an optimization described in [(5.48)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq48) to minimize a classification loss with the clean set, a consistency loss between the teacher and student, and a local and global regularization losses. This optimization trains the student model, while the teacher model is trained with an exponential moving average using the student parameters.

The **synthetic benchmarks using symmetric noise rates in** {0%, 5%, 10%![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si265.png)**,** 20%, 40%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si266.png) **on ISIC 2017 and PatchCamelyon**, introduced by [Xue et al. (2022)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1990), are shown in Tables [5.23](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0120) and [5.24](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0125). The results in these two tables show relatively similar results as the one in [Table 5.22](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0115), with GloCal [Xue et al. (2022)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1990) showing the best performance, compared to other baseline methods. [Xue et al. (2022)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1990) also introduced the **Inter-observer Variability benchmark based on the Gleason 2019** dataset ([Nir et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1345)), shown in [Table 5.25](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0130). In this benchmark, six pathologists with high inter-observer variation annotated the images, where the clean label is obtained from the application of the Simultaneous Truth and Performance Level Estimation (STAPLE) algorithm ([Warfield et al., 2004](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1870)), while the noisy label is represented by the label provided by one of the pathologists. Similar to the benchmarks above, compared to the baseline methods, GloCal ([Xue et al., 2022](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1990)) displays the top performance. All results from these benchmarks are computed with the ResNet-34 ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0685)) backbone model.

![Figure 5.14 HSA-NRL (Zhu et al., 2021a).HSA-NRL (Zhu et al., 2021a) is a two-stage approach that, in the first stage, explores sample selection to divide the training set \\mathcal{D}Image into clean \\mathcal{D}\_{c}Image, hard \\mathcal{D}\_{h}Image, and noisy \\mathcal{D}\_{n}Image. Then, samples in \\mathcal{D}\_{h}Image and \\mathcal{D}\_{n}Image are pseudo-labeled, and another round of sample selection is performed to form the almost-clean dataset \\mathcal{D}\_{o}Image. The second stage of HSA-NRL consists of a co-training approach, similar to the ones presented in Section 4.4.3.](images/B9780443154416000149/gr014.jpg)

[Figure 5.14](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf2830) HSA-NRL ([Zhu et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2225)).HSA-NRL ([Zhu et al., 2021a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2225)) is a two-stage approach that, in the first stage, explores sample selection to divide the training set 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si5.png) into clean 𝒟[*c*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si3.png), hard 𝒟[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si282.png), and noisy 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si4.png). Then, samples in 𝒟[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si282.png) and 𝒟[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si4.png) are pseudo-labeled, and another round of sample selection is performed to form the almost-clean dataset 𝒟[*o*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si285.png). The second stage of HSA-NRL consists of a co-training approach, similar to the ones presented in Section [4.4.3](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml).

There are other approaches that show competitive results in Tables [5.26](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0135), [5.27](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0140), and [5.28](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0145). For instance, DivideMix ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1055)) (explained above) presents competitive results in all benchmarks, but not quite as good as HSA-NRL. OUSM ([Xue et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1985)) is another competitive approach that relies on the small-loss hypothesis to select clean samples, followed by loss re-weighting to address imbalanced learning The INCV approach ([Chen et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0260))^([^(65)](#fn65))

## 5.6 Noisy-label segmentation problems

The **symmetric and asymmetric instance segmentation noise benchmarks** presented in [Table 5.29](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0150) show a consistent ranking of recently proposed approaches ([Yang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2000)). All methods in this benchmark rely on Mask R-CNN ([He et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0675)) as the instance segmentation model and the ResNet-50-FPN ([He et al., 2016a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0680); [Lin et al., 2017a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1090)) as the backbone model. The top-performing approach is the Learning with Noisy Class Labels for Instance Segmentation (LNCIS) ([Yang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2000))^([^(66)](#fn66))

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})).$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si296.png)(5.49) 

The warmed-up model is used to select training samples into NS, PSN, PON, and OS. Then, for the next *E*[2]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si297.png) epochs, LNCIS trains the model with

$\\theta^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\delta((\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\text{~is\\ NS}) \\times \\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\delta((\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\text{~is\\ PSN}) \\times \\ell\_{CE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) + \\delta((\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})\\text{~is\\ OS}) \\times \\ell\_{RCE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si298.png)(5.50) 

where *δ*(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si100.png) is the indicator function, and $\\ell\_{RCE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = - f\_{\\theta}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\top}\\log(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si299.png) (with log 0![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si300.png) clipped to −4) denotes the reverse cross-entropy (RCE) loss ([Wang et al., 2019c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1865)) that is empirically demonstrated to be more robust to noisy labels, but converges slower than the CE loss. The optimization in [(5.50)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#deq50) aims to achieve a good trade-off between fast convergence and noise robustness by using the CE loss with samples that are more likely to be correct and the RCE loss with samples less likely to be correct.

Table 5.29

**mAP (%) for the closed set symmetric and asymmetric segmentation noise benchmark (**[Yang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2000)**) on the Pascal VOC dataset.** Results are from ([Yang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2000)), where all methods rely on Mask R-CNN ([He et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0675)) as the instance segmentation model and the ResNet-50-FPN ([He et al., 2016a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0680); [Lin et al., 2017a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1090)) as the backbone model.

![Figure 5.15 LNCIS (Yang et al., 2020).LNCIS (Yang et al., 2020) combines sample selection with a robust loss function. The sample selection step takes a warmed-up model to classify samples first into positive and negative samples (NS), with the positive samples being further sub-divided into pseudo negative samples (PNS), potential noisy samples (PON), and other samples (OS). The next training stage trains the model with a robust loss function that discards samples in the PON set and uses the cross-entropy (CE) loss for NS and PSN samples and the (label noise robust) reverse cross-entropy (RCE) loss for OS samples).](images/B9780443154416000149/gr015.jpg)

[Figure 5.15](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf2895) LNCIS ([Yang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2000)).LNCIS ([Yang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2000)) combines sample selection with a robust loss function. The sample selection step takes a warmed-up model to classify samples first into positive and negative samples (NS), with the positive samples being further sub-divided into pseudo negative samples (PNS), potential noisy samples (PON), and other samples (OS). The next training stage trains the model with a robust loss function that discards samples in the PON set and uses the cross-entropy (CE) loss for NS and PSN samples and the (label noise robust) reverse cross-entropy (RCE) loss for OS samples).

[Table 5.29](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0150) also shows several baseline results that are competitive with the proposed LNCIS ([Yang et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2000)). A robust loss method, called LSR ([Pereyra et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1410)), which is based on adding an entropy minimization regularization, is applied to this instance segmentation noise benchmark with a surprisingly accurate result. As described above, Joint ([Tanaka et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1695)) is a pseudo-labeling approach to jointly optimize labels and model parameters, which shows competitive results, except for symmetric noise larger than 40%. Generalized cross entropy (GCE) ([Zhang and Sabuncu, 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2175)) explores a robust loss function, which is defined as ℓ[*M**A**E* + *C**E*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si301.png) in [(4.3)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml), which combines CE and MAE losses and produces competitive results, except for symmetric noise larger than 40%. Symmetric Cross Entropy (SCE) ([Wang et al., 2019c](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1865))^([^(67)](#fn67))

## 5.7 Noisy-label detection problems

[Shen et al. (2020)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1575) introduce several **noisy-label detection benchmarks on Pascal VOC 2007, Pascal VOC 2012 (**[Everingham et al., 2010](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0485)**), and COCO (**[Lin et al., 2014](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1100)**)** with the goal of testing object detectors that are trained with noisy image-level labels. The results on these benchmarks are presented in Tables [5.30](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0155), [5.31](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0160), and [5.32](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0165). [Table 5.30](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0155) shows detection results on PASCAL VOC 2007, with clean-label training sets (PASCAL VOC 2007) and noisy-label training sets (all others). Tables [5.31](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0160) and [5.32](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0165) show similar benchmarks with PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO datasets. The base detection model adopted for these benchmarks is the Weakly Supervised Deep Detection Network (WSDDN) ([Bilen and Vedaldi, 2016](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0160)). WSSDN consists of a feature extractor that branches out into classification and detection streams that produce two normalized score matrices **X**[*c*], **X**[*d*] ∈ ℝ^(*N*[*b*] × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si302.png), where *N*[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si303.png) is the number of region proposals. The Hadamard product of the normalized matrices from the two streams outputs the detection score matrix **X**[*s*] ∈ ℝ^(*N*[*b*] × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si304.png) that is used to compute the image-level classification scores with $\\mathbf{y}\_{s}(k) = \\sum\_{r = 1}^{N\_{b}}\\mathbf{X}\_{s}(r,k)$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si305.png), where **X**[*s*](*r*, *k*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si306.png) is the score of the *r*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si307.png) proposal and the *k*^(*t**h*)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si308.png) category in **X**[*s*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si309.png). The training from WSDDN is performed by minimizing the binary cross entropy (BCE) $\\ell\_{BCE}(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},\\mathbf{y}\_{s})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si310.png), defined in [(2.13)](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml).

[Shen et al. (2020)](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1575) propose fWebSOD^([^(68)](#fn68))

![Figure 5.16 fWebSOD (Shen et al., 2020).fWebSOD (Shen et al., 2020) modifies the WSDDN (Bilen and Vedaldi, 2016) object detection architecture to include two detection heads: the weak detection head and the residual detection head. A robust loss function is proposed to select (via the estimation of λ by the spatially-sensitive entropy) which head to use for the training. Essentially, if the training sample is likely to be clean, λ ≈ 0 will suppress the residual detection head and train the weak detection head. However, when the sample is likely to be noisy, then λ ≈ 1, which trains the residual head to “fix” the prediction of the weak detection head to fit the noisy-label from the training set. Additionally, the bagging-mixup data augmentation is used to combine training images that are annotated with the same foreground label. This increases the likelihood that the augmented image contains at least one instance of the foreground class.](images/B9780443154416000149/gr016.jpg)

[Figure 5.16](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf3000) fWebSOD ([Shen et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1575)).fWebSOD ([Shen et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1575)) modifies the WSDDN ([Bilen and Vedaldi, 2016](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0160)) object detection architecture to include two detection heads: the weak detection head and the residual detection head. A robust loss function is proposed to select (via the estimation of *λ* by the spatially-sensitive entropy) which head to use for the training. Essentially, if the training sample is likely to be clean, *λ* ≈ 0 will suppress the residual detection head and train the weak detection head. However, when the sample is likely to be noisy, then *λ* ≈ 1, which trains the residual head to “fix” the prediction of the weak detection head to fit the noisy-label from the training set. Additionally, the bagging-mixup data augmentation is used to combine training images that are annotated with the same foreground label. This increases the likelihood that the augmented image contains at least one instance of the foreground class.

Most of results in Tables [5.30](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0155), [5.31](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0160), and [5.32](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0165) show the competitive performance of the method described above ([Shen et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1575)). As baseline methods, these tables show FasterRCNN ([Ren et al., 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1480)), WS-JDS ([Shen et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1580)), which are common visual object detection methods. The main competitor of fWebSOD is the method by ([Tao et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1705)), which consists of a multi-instance multi-label domain adaption learning framework that transfers knowledge from data collected from the web.

## 5.8 Noisy-label medical image segmentation problems

The noisy-label benchmark shown in [Table 5.33](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0170) ([Zhang et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2120)) forms the **IDN ISBI2015 MS lesion segmentation** ([Jesson and Arbel, 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0785)), **IDN BraTS** ([Menze et al., 2014](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1265)), and the **IDN LIDC-IDRI** ([Armato et al., 2011](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0060)). These benchmarks contain images, each annotated by multiple labelers with different biases and competence levels, where methods are tested for the joint learning of the reliability of labelers and clean segmentation labels. The method Disentangle ([Zhang et al., 2020a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2120))^([^(69)](#fn69))

$\\theta^{\\ast},\\phi^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta,\\phi}\\sum\\limits\_{{(\\mathbf{x},{\\{{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{j}\\}}\_{j = 1}^{M})} \\in \\mathcal{D}}\\sum\\limits\_{r = 1}^{|\\mathcal{S}\_{i}|}\\ell\\left( {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}}\_{r},\\mathbf{T}\_{\\phi}(r,\\mathbf{x}) \\times f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x}) \\right) + \\lambda \\times \\left( \\mathsf{tr}\\left( \\mathbf{T}\_{\\phi}(r,\\mathbf{x}) \\right) \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si321.png)(5.51) 

where **T**[*ϕ*] : ℕ × 𝒳 → \[0, 1\]^(*W* × *H* × |𝒴| × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si322.png) represents a model that predicts the pixel-wise label transition matrix for user *r* ∈ {1, ..., |𝒮[*i*]|}![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si323.png) and image **x**, *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → \[0, 1\]^(*W* × *H* × |𝒴|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si324.png) denotes the model that predicts the clean label segmentation for image **x**, tr(**T**[*ϕ*](*r*,**x**))![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si325.png) denotes the trace of the pixel-wise label transition matrix predicted for each user, and ℓ(.)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si23.png) is the pixel-wise cross-entropy loss function.

## 5.9 Non-image noisy-label problems

The benchmark **IDN NEWS** ([Xia et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1945)) in [Table 5.34](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0175) uses the dataset NEWS ([Lang, 1995](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1015)) with the same type of instance-dependent noise (IDN) presented in Tables [5.3](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0020), [5.7](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0040), and [5.8](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0045). Backbone model consists of a network with three convolutional layers and one fully connected layer. Similarly to the results in Tables [5.7](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0040) and [5.8](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0045), PTD-R-V ([Xia et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1945)) is a competitive approach for IDN NEWS, with methods T-revision ([Xia et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1950)), Re-weight ([Liu and Tao, 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1130)), and MentorNet ([Jiang et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0805)) also being competitive.

[Table 5.34](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf3125)

**Test accuracy (%) for the instance-dependent noise benchmark on text data (**[Xia et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1945)**) using the NEWS dataset (**[Lang, 1995](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1015)**).** Results are from ([Xia et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1945)), and backbone model consists of a network with three convolutional layers and one fully connected layer.

The benchmark in [Table 5.35](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0180) tests the robustness of text classification methods to **symmetric and asymmetric noisy-label (**[Zheng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2195)**) with respect to the datasets AG News (**[Zhang et al., 2015](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2140)**), Amazon reviews (**[Xie et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1970)**), Yelp reviews (**[Yang et al., 2016](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2015)**), and Yahoo answers (**[Conneau et al., 2016](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0315)**)**. For all these datasets, a subset of the training image is guaranteed to be clean (400 for AG News, 500 for Amazon reviews, 500 for Yelp reviews, and 1000 for Yahoo answers), while the rest of the dataset is affected by symmetric and asymmetric label noise with *η* ∈ {0%, 10%, 20%, ..., 80%, 90%, 100%}![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si326.png). All approaches in this experiment rely on a pre-trained BERT-base model. The top-performing approach in [Table 5.35](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0180) is the Meta Label Correction (MLC) ([Zheng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2195)), which is a meta-learning approach that defines the meta parameters as the parameters of the label correction network (LCN) *g*[*α*] : 𝒳 × 𝒴 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si327.png). The optimization of MLC is as follows:

$\\alpha^{\\ast} = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\alpha}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{v}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{y}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{v}}\\ell(\\mathbf{y},f\_{\\theta^{\\ast}(\\alpha)}(\\mathbf{x}))\\text{s.t.~}\\theta^{\\ast}(\\alpha) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\theta}\\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}\\sum\\limits\_{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}) \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{t}}\\ell(g\_{\\alpha}(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}),f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})),$

![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si328.png)(5.52) 

where *f*[*θ*] : 𝒳 → *Δ*^(|𝒴| − 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si50.png) represents the classifier, 𝒟[*v*] = {(**x**, **y**)[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(|𝒟[*v*]|)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si329.png) is the clean validation set, $\\mathcal{D}\_{t} = {\\{{(\\mathbf{x},\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}\_{i}\\}}\_{i = 1}^{|\\mathcal{D}\_{t}|}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si330.png) is the noisy training set (with |𝒟[*t*]| > |𝒟[*v*]|![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si331.png)). [Table 5.35](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0180) shows that MLC ([Zheng et al., 2020](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2200)) is more accurate than gold loss correction (GLC) ([Hendrycks et al., 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0690)), defined in [(4.36)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml) as a loss correction approach that relies on a label transition matrix built with anchor points from the clean validation set 𝒟[*v*]![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si9.png), and MWN ([Shu et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1605)), defined in [(4.113)](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml) as a meta-learning approach where the meta parameter is represented by the parameters in the sample weighting function.

[Table 5.39](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0200) is a **benchmark to assess models trained with the distantly labeled Docred dataset** ([Yao et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2050)), where the training set contains 50.9% of label noise ([Deng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0405)) and has an imbalance distribution of samples per class. All methods in this experiment use the BiLSTM backbone ([Yao et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2050)). Results on the clean-label sets Test and Dev show that the most robust method in [Table 5.39](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0200) is the DisRel method ([Yao et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2050)), which minimizes a robust loss function that mitigates the negative impacts of the noisy label and class imbalance problems. DisRel minimizes a loss function defined by $\\ell(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}},f\_{\\theta}(\\mathbf{x})) = \\sum\_{n = 0}^{M}\\mathbf{a}\_{n} \\times f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}{(\\mathbf{x})}^{\\frac{n}{M}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si340.png), where *M* ≥ 3![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si341.png), **a** ∈ ℝ^(*M* + 1)![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si342.png), and $f\_{\\theta}^{(\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}})}(\\mathbf{x})$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si343.png) represents the output related to class $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{y}}$![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/si85.png). Competing approaches in this benchmark also rely on loss functions designed to handle imbalanced learning problems, such as the Range loss ([Zhang et al., 2017b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2135)), focal loss (FL) ([Lin et al., 2017b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1095)), class-balanced loss (CBL) ([Cui et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0345)) Other approaches rely on label noise robust losses, such as the bounded mean square error (BMSE) ([Ghosh et al., 2017](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0550)) (see Section [4.2.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml)), and generalized cross entropy (GCE) ([Zhang and Sabuncu, 2018](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2175)) (see Section [4.2.1](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml)).

All methods use the BiLSTM backbone ([Yao et al., 2019](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br2050)). ## 5.10 Conclusion

To conclude this chapter, we summarize the main techniques used by the top-performing methods for each benchmark presented in this chapter. [Table 5.42](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0215) shows the techniques, presented in Chapter [4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml), explored by the top methods introduced in this chapter. In [Fig. 5.17](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#f0090), we show the word cloud built using the list of techniques from [Table 5.42](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0215) weighted by how many times they are used by the top-performing methods.

Table 5.42

Noisy-label learning techniques, from Chapter [4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml), explored by top-performing methods in the benchmarks of Chapter 5.

 
| ![Image](images/B9780443154416000149/fx044.jpg) |
| --- |

![Figure 5.17 Word cloud of the main noisy-label learning techniques from Chapter 4.Word cloud generated from https://www.wordclouds.com using the list of techniques from Table 5.42 weighted by how many times they are used by the top-performing methods of Chapter 5.](images/B9780443154416000149/gr017.jpg)

[Figure 5.17](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#cf3355) Word cloud of the main noisy-label learning techniques from Chapter [4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml).Word cloud generated from [https://www.wordclouds.com](https://www.wordclouds.com) using the list of techniques from [Table 5.42](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0215) weighted by how many times they are used by the top-performing methods of Chapter 5.

It is clear that sample selection, pseudo-labeling, robust loss, and data augmentation are the main techniques explored to handle noisy-label learning problems by the top-performing approaches. For imbalanced noisy-label learning problems, meta-learning appears to provide a good mitigation solution mostly because of the use of a balanced (pseudo-)clean validation set. It is interesting to see that even though label transition methods have theoretical guarantees of consistent performance, they do not show particularly competitive results, except in benchmarks that do not have many results available for comparison, such as the ones in Tables [5.7](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0040) and [5.8](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0045). It is clear that the current state-of-the-art approaches (in July 2023) explore a combination of many techniques. For example, SANM ([Tu et al., 2023b](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1760)), DMLP ([Tu et al., 2023a](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br1755)), SSR+ ([Feng et al., 2021](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0515)), and InstanceGM ([Garg et al., 2023](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#br0540)) explore most of the techniques listed in [Table 5.42](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml#t0215).

A particularly concerning problem involved in the benchmarks presented in this chapter is the fact that each benchmark relies on the use of a specific backbone model, which needs to be fixed to enable a fair comparison between methods. However, new models are being proposed at a fast rate, and it is important to verify if these new models can improve the state-of-the-art results. This point is currently not well-studied in the field.

# Chapter 6: Conclusions and final considerations

## Abstract

This chapter concludes the book with a summary of what has been presented in the previous five chapters. We then discuss how the book has addressed the challenges listed in Chapter [1](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml). A discussion about future developments in noisy-label learning is then presented with suggestions about on-line resources.

### Keywords

Noisy-label learning on-line resources

## 6.1 Conclusions

We conclude the book with a summary of what has been presented. The study of noisy-label learning algorithms and models is motivated by the widespread availability of poorly curated large-scale datasets that contain a substantial amount of label noise, and also of datasets that contain samples with intrinsically noisy labels. Unfortunately, the regular training of machine learning models, and deep learning models in particular, will eventually overfit the noise present in the training set labels, causing poor generalization to clean-label testing sets. Hence, the development of noisy-label learning algorithms and models aims to mitigate this overfitting issue.

Chapter [1](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml) introduces the different types of label noise and their impacts on the learning of machine learning models. In general, label noise can be divided into closed-set (i.e., all training images belong to the set of training labels) or open-set (i.e., some training images belong to classes outside of the set of training labels). Furthermore, open-set and closed-set label noise can be subdivided into symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise, where symmetric refers to a random flipping from the clean label to any of the other available labels, asymmetric follows a specific label transition pattern that defines the probability of pairwise flipping, and instance-dependent follows a data-specific label transition pattern. These label noise types were defined in Chapter [2](#Chp002_15-71_B9780443154416000113.xhtml), which also listed the main datasets and benchmarks used to assess noisy-label learning approaches.

Chapter [3](#Chp003_73-91_B9780443154416000125.xhtml) introduces theoretical aspects of noisy-label learning. First, we explained how the bias-variance decomposition divides the training error into bias, variance, and irreducible noise components, and how each component is affected in terms of symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise. Second, we defined the necessary and sufficient conditions for the identifiability of the transition matrix for noisy-label learning problems. A particularly interesting identifiability condition is the need for multiple labels per training sample, which is a problem referred to as the multi-rater learning ([Guan et al., 2018](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0610); [Jensen et al., 2019](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0780); [Jungo et al., 2018](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0825); [Baumgartner et al., 2019](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0105); [Sudre et al., 2019](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1660); [Yu et al., 2020a](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br2065)). Third, we overviewed the application of Valiant's probably approximately correct (PAC) model of learning in noisy-label learning. Even though PAC learning already showed important aspects of noisy-label learning, it is still too constrained to unrealistically simple classification models and problems.

The main techniques explored in practice to mitigate the noisy-label learning problem were presented in Chapter [4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml). We first introduced an example of a noisy-label learning and showed how a deep learning classifier overfits to the label noise. This example was used throughout the chapter to show the functionality of each presented technique. We also proposed a new hierarchical structure to organize the available techniques in the field and briefly explained each technique. Then, in Chapter [5](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml), we introduced the state-of-the-art methods for the main benchmarks being considered in the field. We concluded this chapter by listing the main methods and the techniques that they explore.

This book proposes solutions to all challenges listed at the end of Chapter [1](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml). To recap, the challenges are: 1) how to define label noise models, 2) how to define the experimental setup to test the robustness of methods with respect to label noise, 3) theoretical understanding of label noise, 4) practical understanding of label noise, and 5) how to estimate rate and type of label noise in a dataset. Chapter [1](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml) introduces the definition of label noise generation based on a label transition process ([Pérez et al., 2007](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1415); [Lawrence and Schölkopf, 2001](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1025)), or on a label distribution ([Thiel, 2008](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1715); [Domingos, 2000](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0450)). Even though we believe that both definitions are likely to be equivalent, this requires further study by our research community. Chapter [1](#Chp001_1-14_B9780443154416000101.xhtml) also presents many noisy-label learning benchmarks that are actively being used to assess methods. As shown in Chapter [5](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml), no method is the best for all benchmarks, and the main challenge for the community is to understand the association between techniques and the particular problems represented by the benchmarks. For instance, if we are dealing with a symmetric closed-set label noise problem, which techniques would be more appropriate. Also, the theoretical understanding of label noise, particularly based on the application of PAC learning methods, needs to consider the complex models and learning problems that the field is studying in practice. Finally, estimating the rate and type of label noise is a relevant problem because many of the methods presented in Chapter [5](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml) require the setting of hyper-parameters depending on the rate and type of noise ([Li et al., 2020a](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1055)). An alternative solution to this problem is the design of methods that are robust to all types and rates of label noise.

## 6.2 Final considerations and future work

We conclude the book with some considerations about future developments in the field. It is important to reiterate that this book was written in July 2023, and as with any topic in machine learning, by the time it gets published, it will already be outdated. Therefore, let us explain how the reader can find more about future publications and benchmarks. Regarding publications, the top computer vision and machine learning conferences (CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, NeurIPS, ICLR, AAAI, WACV, BMVC, ACCV) are the main source of new methods. Journals (TPAMI, TIP, PR, JMLR, TMLR) are also good sources of new methods, but the published papers tend to be more outdated than the conference papers. The PapersWithCode site^([^(72)](#fn72))

Regarding the future of noisy-label learning, apart from the points already raised in the last paragraph of Section [6.1](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#s0010), we list below some potentially interesting topics that need to be considered by researchers. As already mentioned in the last paragraph of Section [5.10](#Chp005_193-252_B9780443154416000149.xhtml), one point that needs further investigation is the issue with the relatively old models used to evaluate noisy-label learning methods. The models that are generally used in the benchmarks are ResNet ([He et al., 2016b](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0685)), DenseNet ([Huang et al., 2017](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0745)), and Inception ([Szegedy et al., 2017](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1675)). These models no longer represent the state of the art in computer vision and machine learning, and need to be replaced by more modern models ([Dosovitskiy et al., 2020](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0455)), but the community has acted slowly to accept such new models given that this would make comparisons unfair with current approaches based on the old models.

Another interesting point about noisy-label learning is that it is related to other problems being studied by relatively different research communities. For instance, multi-rater learning ([Sudre et al., 2019](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1660); [Ji et al., 2021](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0790); [Schaekermann et al., 2019](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1535); [Becker et al., 2019](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0110); [Tanno et al., 2019](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1700)) (Section [4.3.4](#Chp004_93-191_B9780443154416000137.xhtml)) optimizes a model using multiple labels per data point and aims to estimate the model's and annotators' uncertainty. Such set-up is quite relevant for noisy-label learning given that the identifiability of the learning from noisy labels requires a minimum number of labels per training sample ([Liu, 2022](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1140); [Nguyen et al., 2023](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1330)). Another related research topic is that of uncertainty ([Mena et al., 2021](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1250)) that aims to investigate the ambiguities present in the predictions of deep learning models. In principle, uncertainty is a powerful tool to be used in sample selection and pseudo-labeling, but that is a technique that has not received enough attention. Also, multi-rater learning combined with uncertainty learning could also be used to solve noisy-label learning problems involving multiple labelers. Another interesting research topic that can be potentially useful in noisy label learning is anomaly detection ([Pang et al., 2021](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1395)) which aims to train a model to detect out-of-distribution samples that can be regarded as open-set noisy-label samples. In particular, there is a line of research in anomaly detection that designs training algorithms that can handle contaminated training data ([Qiu et al., 2022](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1440)), which is exactly the same problem as the open-set noisy-label learning problem. Finally, as noted by [Liu and Tao (2015)](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1130), noisy-label learning problem is fundamentally a domain adaptation problem given that the distribution of the data in the training set, with its noisy label samples, is different from the distribution of the testing set data. Hence, the whole point of noisy label learning is to take or discover the clean-label subset in the training set, and adapt the distribution of the noisy-label subset to that of the clean-label subset.

Interesting problems that deserve further investigation by researchers in the area is the impact of the combination of noisy-label problems (e.g., closed-set and open-set symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise) on noisy-label learning models and algorithms. So far, there have been some attempts with the combination of open and closed-set label noise ([Sachdeva et al., 2021](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1505)) and closed-set label noise with imbalanced learning ([Zhang and Pfister, 2021](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br2170); [Wei et al., 2021b](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br1890); [Hoang et al., 2022](#Chp006_253-256_B9780443154416000150.xhtml#br0715)). Another important problem that has not received enough attention is the formulation of the label transition problem for multi-label problems, where the transition matrix can serve the dual purpose of modeling pairwise label noise flipping and pairwise label correlation.

Noisy-label learning has the potential to be one of the most important problems in machine learning given that the vast majority of datasets that will become available for machine learning practitioners and researchers are likely to contain relatively large amounts of noisy labels. In fact, when these datasets become available, researchers and practitioners usually assume that they contain only clean labels, but that assumption is in most cases unwarranted, which means that the dataset needs to be investigated to see how much label noise it contains. Alternatively, these datasets can be assumed to contain noisy labels, forcing researchers and practitioners to explore noisy-label learning algorithms. With the knowledge acquired from this book, we expect that the reader is better equipped to deal with the noisy-label learning problems that will be become widespread in machine learning.
